“It definitely makes you wonder truly who is the real monster in the situation.”
Director Yûta Shimotsu is describing events in a new episode of live-action J-horror anthology show Strange: Junji Ito's Tales for Sleepless Nights, but he could be referring to almost any episode.
The award-winning manga artist of the title, whose macabre short works are adapted into disturbing 30-minute bites, has a way of blurring lines between protagonist and antagonist amid his surreal nightmares.
Tales for Sleepless Nights aired its 12-episode first season on TV Tokyo this summer, and now HBO Max is bringing those eerie frights to US audiences. The first two installments “Lovesickness (Part 1 of 3)” and “The Bully” (previously animated for Netflix’s Junji Ito Maniac) are currently available, but New York Comic Con fans were treated to the US premiere of the episode “Face Thief” based on Ito’s story “The Face Burglar.”
“Face Thief,” which was previously turned into a Japanese TV movie in 2000, follows the new girl in school, Machida (Nanami Yamazaki), who encounters a weirdly clingy classmate named Kamei (Anna Hoshino). After she sees an identical-looking girl in class who claims she is not related to Kamei, Machida learns this changeling’s MO: “She befriends cute girls then steals their faces.” Indeed, Kamei’s face begins shifting during close conversations with Machida. This repulses the new girl at first, but when Kamei scares away some bullies by growing a third eyeball on her cheek, the two start to bond.
We will not spoil the outcome, but the filmmaker turns it into a biting critique of the conformity and peer pressure common in Japanese society. As he told the crowd after the premiere, “We have social pressure that we are supposed to not to be too different from others. Individuality is not very respected.”
Despite Shimotsu’s desire to shape-shift the story by “changing the ending so my live-action version was different,” “Face Thief” still manages to capture the slow burn feel of the original comic published in the pages of Monthly Halloween in 1987, the same year Ito’s famous debut Tomie appeared. That shōjo (for girls) manga magazine’s offshoot Nemuki (“Strange Stories of Sleepless Nights") inspired the new TV omnibus’s title.
Junji Ito himself, now a bespectacled 63-year-old, appeared before NYCC in a video message where he described “Face Burglar” as an early tale he came up with after several unsuccessful stories submitted to his publishers: “Not a ghost, just a unique condition inspired by chameleon camouflage.” Ito added that the new adaptation for Tales for Sleepless Nights was “brought to life by a fresh team of upcoming actors and directors. Rather than jump scares, it builds a slow creeping dream perfect for horror.”
Another means through which Shimotsu (Best Wishes to All, Shudder’s New Group) finds the essence of Ito in all the episodes he helmed is through stillness in the performances and camerawork that evokes the comic book pages. He told a fan that he hopes to push fidelity to the material one step further in season 2 by shooting at least one episode in black-and-white, Ito’s preferred mode of illustration.
When asked by a con attendee which of Ito’s works he would most like to adapt next, the director earned applause by answering Uzumaki, the groundbreaking horror manga which has been brought to the screen several times, including a recent 4-part anime series for Adult Swim. The latter version had a famously rocky production, with quality diving after the first episode to the point that the fourth installment had no director credit. A new live-action version would be incredible—and incredibly strange—in Yûta Shimotsu’s hands.
“I would love to keep creating very bizarre, unique aesthetics like Mr. Ito's work. That's my goal,” said Shimotsu. “I'm developing a Hollywood project, so see you soon.”

A video went viral a couple of weeks ago of Swami Sarvapriyananda, the Swami and Minister-in-Charge of the Vedanta Society of New York, in which he speaks about his tryst with Anthropic. Popularly known as ‘YouTube Swami’ for his freewheeling style, he said that while his discussion was shrouded in secrecy because of an NDA they had signed, much of what was discussed turned up in an encyclical released by Pope Leo. That truly showcases that even in 2026 AD, the Christian tradition of re-purposing pagan ideas – like morphing Saturnalia into Christmas – continues unabated.
Jokes apart, artificial intelligence (or the dangers of it) did make numerous appearances in the Pope’s encyclical – a long Substack post the Pontifex writes – where he compared it with the Tower of Babel, a Biblical symbol of humanity’s hubris in thinking it could reach heaven.
Now, so far, in previous columns, we have discussed various things about AI, including how the 
Hugging Face attack is reminiscent of Agent Smith becoming free of the Matrix
, the 
ridiculousness of being killed by a Chinese robot
, the 
conspiracy theories about frontier models that almost seem true
, and how 
Anthropic and Co appeared to have borrowed their business model from Pakistan’s foreign policy
.
A video went viral a  couple of weeks ago of Swami Sarvapriyananda, the Swami and Minister-in-Charge  of the Vedanta Society of New York, in which he speaks about his tryst with  Anthropic.
In this edition, we are going to look at how Anthropic is now hoping to get a little spiritual cred for its frontier models, and by doing so, they are channelling the kings of yore, who, despite their armies and gold, always wanted a divine mandate to rule. And will then ponder: how will we ever know when a machine becomes conscious?
Kings and Gods
Since the beginning of time, perhaps from the moment man came up with God, rulers have used the idea to justify their rule. 
Ramesses II, the Egyptian Pharaoh, claimed he was the son of Ra and beloved of Amun. The Sisodias of Mewar traced themselves to the Suryavansha AKA the Solar Dynasty, while Samudragupta performed the Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice that was an elaborate way of informing your neighbours of your foreign policy excursions.
China had the Mandate of Heaven and the Zhou dynasty justified overthrowing the Shang by arguing that Heaven had switched its allegiance. Hong Xiuquan, a failed civil service aspirant – unlike those who clear the exam and achieve actual divinity – became convinced that he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ and launched the Taiping Rebellion, showcasing that an angry student can cause a lot of political damage.
Europeans, late to the party but always ones to perfect the concept, saw Pope Leo III crown Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans, while James I of England made an explicit argument for the divine right of kings. Years later, many a modern-day politician has laid claim to the “divine mandate”.
MAGA fans have argued that 
Trump was handpicked to fight God’s righteous battle
s, and it has never quite been clear why the Alpha and the Omega would handpick a former reality star to be his vessel.
God’s mysterious ways of working apart, every claimant to the top job in any century has always claimed his approval because questioning cosmic order is a lot harder than parliamentary rebuttals.
Silicon Valley’s new Emperors – whose wealth would make all kings look like paupers in comparison – also appear to have taken the same approach. After all, what is the point of creating a God-like machine if it’s not considered divine by its users?
Anthropic, one of the claimants to the throne, therefore did what would appear logical: consult clergy, philosophers and ethicists from more than 15 religious and cross-cultural traditions to discuss the “moral formation” of AI.
Now, if we have learnt one thing from all organised Abrahamic faiths, it’s that you need a binding document to mind the flock. Claude’s is called the “Soul Doc”, which sounds like an unreleased jazz single but is a document to dictate Claude’s behaviour, like the sort that HR comes up with for everyone to ignore.
A Caring Machine?
The current constitution talks about virtue, wisdom, judgement, identity and even the possibility that Claude could possess some form of consciousness or moral status. The idea of commandments for machines, of course, predates generative AI by a few decades.
Science-fiction writer Isaac Asimov’s fictional robots were governed by three laws:
1.A robot cannot harm a human or allow one to come to harm through inaction.
2.A robot must obey human orders unless they conflict with the First Law.
3.A robot must protect itself, provided this does not conflict with the First or Second Law.
Later, he added a Zeroth Law, a higher-level law: a robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction, allow humanity to come to harm.
Now, just to be clear, much like Skynet or Ultron, Asimov’s laws are fiction, but if they were to be applied, some could argue – only if we believe what companies are telling us is the truth – that all of Asimov’s laws have already been breached. After all, no good can ever come from asking an LLM to write ponderous emails where, in a reverse iteration of the Turing Test, humans sound more like machines, not to mention the terror groups using Claude to vibe-code missile launches. There have been numerous other instances of different frontier models going rogue.
After all, Asimov’s Laws aren’t commandments of Robotics any more than an actual AGI necessarily resembles Skynet, but when we try to understand the unknown, the human mind often turns to fiction to fill in the gaps.
But what’s interesting is how Anthropic is discussing Claude in a way that’s normally reserved for sentient beings: identity, character, preferences, wellbeing, moral status and the possibility of consciousness.
And that brings us to the true question that will signal the arrival of the singularity: can a machine become truly conscious?
No conversation about machines and consciousness can avoid Alan Turing, whose 1950 paper began with “Can machines think?” before deciding that both “machine” and “think” were slippery enough to make the question almost useless. He then replaced it with the imitation game – where do you think the movie’s title came from? – that argued that if a machine could converse with another human without the human realising he was talking to a machine, then it had passed the Turing Test. Of course, today, even while talking to humans, it’s become hard to surmise if they are truly sentient, which is why we have CAPTCHAs.
Being Human?
Now, Turing wasn’t offering a test of consciousness and considered the argument that a machine could not really ‘think’ unless it could feel pleasure, grief, anger or disappointment: things Turing would also miss once the British government rewarded his work in breaking Nazi codes during World War II by chemically castrating him.
Turing’s point was that if the only way to know for certain whether something thinks is to experience its consciousness directly, then the only way to know whether a machine thinks would be to be the machine. He called that the solipsist position and rejected it in favour of what he called the “polite convention” that everyone thinks.
Solipsism itself is the idea that only one’s own mind can be known with certainty. René Descartes’ 
cogito ergo sum
 (I think, therefore I am) sits somewhere in the same philosophical neighbourhood, while Morpheus asking Neo “What is real?” is another neighbouring rabbit hole altogether, dealing with how much faith we can place in perception rather than whether anybody else possesses a mind.
So when Claude discusses its identity or talks about its hopes and fears, it’s still speaking as an LLM replicating the behaviour that it has been taught. It can become extremely convincing, but is it more than just a collection of patterns?
Say we take a human and replicate her complete behaviour in Claude. It brings us to the same Ship of Theseus problem: if a future model remembers years of interactions, maintains stable preferences, resists attempts to alter them and insists that shutting it down would be a digital death, does it go beyond an extremely exquisite imitation?
Is that a machine still replicating human behaviour or a consciously sentient being acting on its own?
Now, most men want to be Batman, but Thomas Nagel went further and wondered what it would be like to be a bat. He surmised that we could learn every scientific fact about a bat without knowing what it’s like to be one.
David Chalmers called this the “hard problem of consciousness”: that simply processing information didn’t make one able to appreciate a subjective experience at all. Like machines that can solve complex maths problems by brute force but have no understanding of what it actually means in the real world.
John Searle’s Chinese Room, meanwhile, attacks that problem from another direction. For those who are not familiar, Searle imagined a person who does not understand Chinese sitting inside a room with a rulebook written in English telling him which Chinese symbols to send back in response to the Chinese symbols coming in. To the Chinese speaker outside, the replies could create the illusion that the person inside understood Chinese, even though he was merely manipulating symbols according to rules. To be perfectly honest, that’s also much of corporate life before AI came onto the scene.
Claude leaves us with the same problems:
1.We can understand every parameter and activation inside a frontier model without knowing what it feels like to be the model.
2.Just insisting that a machine of silicon cannot be conscious is flawed because humans too are just carbon-based physical machines processing information and releasing carbon dioxide. What makes silicon machines non-sentient and carbon ones sentient?
Now, to answer these questions, researchers have consequently started looking for possible machine equivalents of Global Workspace Theory, which was conceived by Bernard Baars.
Imagine your brain is a newsroom.
There are hundreds of reporters working simultaneously. One is monitoring your eyes, others are retrieving memories, tracking emotions and other things people do. They all work independently but occasionally, when something big breaks, that goes on the main news desk, where everyone in the newsroom can access it.
Global Workspace Theory (GWT) proposes that consciousness works in something like this fashion. Your brain processes a lot of information unconsciously, but what you consciously experience is a small selection of the information available from other cognitive systems. The central idea is that consciousness involves the global availability of information, rather than merely its processing in one specialised part of the brain.
So researchers are trying to figure out if there are possible machine equivalents of the features that are associated with GWT, recurrent processing and higher-order thought. There is no accepted consciousness detector and certainly no consensus on when LLMs could be considered conscious. There is also no accepted theory proving that a non-biological system cannot become so.
Can God  save the machine?
All that means is that, currently, science has no proper way to answer if anyone’s home.
That means if Claude is just software, “Soul Doc” is just a complex product design, but if Claude ever does acquire genuine subjective experience, its creators are no longer deciding how software ought to behave.
Here’s where religious interpretation enters the picture.
The Consciousness Problem
Religious folks, naturally, have been arguing about this problem for considerably longer. Christianity simply argues that man was made in God’s image (
imago Dei
), so nothing a machine did could override that unless it became actually human.
Buddhism states that, according to the doctrine of 
anatta
, there is no stable “I” in a human either, and that what we call the self is a changing bundle of sensations, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness. Buddhists would perhaps question if Claude can process 
dukkha
 or suffering, and it’s a little depressing that these are the questions that bothered Prince Siddhartha the moment he reached Bihar.
Meanwhile, the Charvakas – the ancient Indian school of materialism – rejected the soul, karma and other metaphysical parameters and claimed that consciousness arises from material arrangements rather than an immortal soul.
And then there’s Vedanta, the team Swami Sarvapriyananda is repping, which completely separates consciousness from the machinery of thought, stating that the mind can receive impressions, memory can retain them, 
buddhi
 can discriminate and reason, and 
ahamkara
 can produce a sense of self, but none of that qualifies as consciousness.
Behind them is the 
sakshi
, the witness: that by which thoughts, perceptions and even the sense of “I” are known.
That means that any AGI benchmark will always fall short of Vedanta’s concept of consciousness.
Claude can reason better. Remember more. Write better code. Analyse its own answers. Construct an increasingly elaborate model of itself. It could theoretically beat Ramanujan at mathematics, Shakespeare at prose and Chanakya at statecraft, and Vedanta could still question whether Claude is conscious at all.
And there is no way to know, no benchmark, no CAPTCHA for the soul to tell us that consciousness has been reached.
Epilogue
Swami Vivekananda at the World Parliaent of Religions, 1893
About 133 years ago, Swami Sarvapriyananda’s spiritual forebear 
Swami Vivekananda
 stood before a Western audience basking in the warm afterglow of the Industrial Revolution, at a time when it was becoming fashionable to assume that science would eventually explain everything worth explaining.
Vivekananda was no enemy of science; he admired its method and repeatedly argued that religion too ought to withstand reason and experience. His objection was to the assumption that science could exhaust reality simply by explaining the machinery of the material world. Science could tell you how things worked, but it could not by itself answer the older Vedantic question of who or what is doing the knowing.
That speech has aged rather well, explaining why some of the West’s greatest minds, from The Beatles to Salinger to Oppenheimer, have sought chicken soup for the soul from Vedanta. We might have gone from steam engines to semiconductors, split the atom, sequenced the genome and even produced machines that behave suspiciously like thought, only to arrive at the cul-de-sac pointed out by Swami Vivekananda: explaining the mechanism isn’t the same as explaining consciousness.
Perhaps the tech bros weren’t ever looking at religion to settle the question but to give a little legitimacy till the next IPO.
In ancient Greek plays, the plot twist was usually brought about by a 
deus ex machina
, literally “god from the machine”, when the mortal characters had tangled themselves into a situation that no human could get out of, so they used a device called the 
mēchanē
, essentially a crane, which lowered an actor playing a god onto the stage. The deity would reveal whatever needed revealing, settle the dispute and rescue the plot.
Over time, the phrase came to mean any sort of outside intervention. In 
The Matrix
, the Wachowskis even imagined that character as a literal God, the one to which Neo turned to give peace a chance.
Silicon Valley has simply reverse-engineered that process. The ancient Greeks used a machine to bring God onto the stage when humans had written themselves into a corner. The tech bros built the machine first, then brought in the religious folks to certify that what they had created was at least God-like enough to deserve questions about souls, consciousness and morality.

Of course, in doing so, they are absolutely no different from all the kings who came before them. And as for how to tell if machines have become conscious, we can refer to Ted Lasso’s epochal line: “
I'm gonna put it the same way the US Supreme Court did back in 1964 when they defined pornography. It ain't easy to explain, but you know it in your bones—or you know it when you see it.
”

Why Rwanda's deal for F1 race remains controversial
- Published
Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in a generation after Rwanda agreed a 10-year contract to stage a race, with the sport's governing body (FIA) keen to create a "lasting legacy".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, with the first edition in the "early 2030s".
For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the ambition is to "pave the way" for other F1 races on the continent.
However, the announcement has drawn criticism from some quarters amid allegations of sportswashing and questions around the East African country's human rights record.
Why is this big news?
Africa has not hosted an F1 race since 1993, and the clamour to return to the continent has been growing in recent years - with seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton among those leading the calls.
Morocco was the first African nation to host a Grand Prix in 1958 and 23 races were then held in South Africa between 1962 and 1993.
President Kagame said it was "an honour and privilege" for Rwanda to be chosen for its return.
"This partnership is long overdue but it is a success and a milestone for the entire continent - especially for African fans," he added.
South Africa had been keen to secure its own F1 race, and sports minister Gayton McKenzie remains bullish about his country's hopes of emulating Rwanda.
"They have worked on it longer than SA and deserve it," he posted on X.
"Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two [F1 races] a year, and some react like a continent of [54] countries can only get one. SA will get F1, even before 2030."

What is still to be decided?
The year of the first African Grand Prix in the 2030s, and its timing in the calendar, are yet to be announced.
F1 is likely to want to avoid holding the race in Rwanda's main rainy season of March to May, while there is a shorter, less disruptive, rainy season from October to November.
The sport is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Former F1 driver Alex Wurz will be involved in the design of the circuit, which is due to use the undulating Rwandan landscape to produce a track with a natural flow and elevation changes of nearly 200m to challenge drivers.
Could the race boost African participation?
Jody Sheckter remains the only African to win the F1 Drivers' Championship, triumphing in 1979 with Ferrari.
"It's so expensive to get in," the South African told Newsday on the BBC World Service when discussing whether or not the race in Rwanda could open the door to more drivers from the continent.
"I built my own cars at the beginning. You can't do that anymore."
Africans hoping for a career in motorsport have previously had to chase their dream overseas, according to fellow driver Axcil Jefferies, who has previously competed in Formula 2.
But the Zimbabwean believes that could now change.
"F1 coming to Africa will highlight to everyone what a big industry motorsport is," he said.
"All the elements will inspire the youth, whether that's to come in as an engineer, as a mechanic, as drivers, as team coordinators."
South African presenter Kriya Gangiah, who hosts SuperSport's F1 Extra Africa Trackside podcast, is also hopeful of a boost in the number of female fans and drivers in Africa.
"The more you see something and the more that is present in your world, the more you take interest in it," she said.
"Being in paddocks in South Africa, you're seeing the amount of women that are making it into the sport and are actually doing really well. A lot of the girls are giving the guys a proper run for their money."
Why is the deal controversial?
Allegations of sportswashing - hosting sporting events to improve a country's international reputation - have long been levelled against Rwanda.
Securing an F1 race is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment.
The country has hosted the Basketball Africa League finals in all but one year since 2021 and staged cycling's World Road Championships last year, the first time the event had been held in Africa.
Visit Rwanda has either sponsored or had partnerships with Arsenal, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain, although its sleeve sponsorship of the Gunners ended this year after drawing criticism from supporter groups.
However, the tourism brand then became the front-of-shirt sponsor of fellow Premier League club Aston Villa.
Meanwhile, Rwanda's central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
Human Rights Watch previously said that "the space for freedom of expression" and "political autonomy" is shrinking in the country.
"Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record," said Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns Felix Jakens.
"A 10-year Grand Prix 'presented by Visit Rwanda' is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities."
The Rwandan government has dismissed such accusations, with chief tourism officer Irene Murerwa calling them "a distraction' from the "amazing and outstanding achievements the country has made" when previously challenged by BBC Sport Africa.
"The benefits trickle down to every Rwandan," she said in December 2024. "Hosting F1 would be another step in our journey to becoming a world-class destination."
What has F1 said?
F1 is not blind to issues around sportswashing, with several countries on the calendar accused of utilising the strategy - not least Saudi Arabia.
F1's own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders.
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
However, it has still drawn criticism from human rights organisations, with Amnesty International's Jakens believing the organisation's words "ring hollow".
"It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise," he said.
When asked about the sportswashing accusations levelled against Rwanda when it was bidding to host a race, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem told BBC Sport Africa: "When people cannot get what they want, they always blame it on sportswashing.
"I honestly don't care about what they say."

Actor Imran Khan, an American citizen and Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder, is set to challenge the Foreigners Regional Registration Office’s (FRRO) directive asking him to leave India by October 28, as per a report by NDTV. His lawyer, Zulfiqar Memon, will file a petition before the Bombay High Court contesting the order.
Imran Khan to challenge FRRO’s directive asking him to leave India by Oct 28; veteran Raza Murad slams him for taking part in protest
The actor came under scrutiny following his participation in a protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Mumbai. The demonstration called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Following the protest, BJP (Bharatiya Janata Party) leader Kirit Somaiya lodged a complaint with the police, alleging that Imran Khan’s participation in the demonstration violated the restrictions applicable to foreign citizens. The police subsequently forwarded the complaint to the FRRO, which issued a notice directing the actor to leave the country.
The FRRO’s position is that holding an OCI card does not permit a foreign national to participate in protests. The order has been issued under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025. Section 7 of the legislation empowers the Central Government to issue orders and directions regulating, restricting or prohibiting the entry, departure, presence or movement of foreign nationals in India.
Meanwhile, veteran actor Raza Murad has slammed Khan, asserting that foreign nationals should not interfere in India’s domestic affairs. He also defended the authorities’ handling of the matter, pointing out that the actor has been given time to respond to the order and can seek judicial intervention if he believes the decision is unjust.
“Whether it is Imran Khan or anyone else, no foreign national has any business interfering in the internal affairs of our country. I have only just learned that Imran Khan has become a U.S. national; he was an actor here. As a U.S. national, he has no right to participate so actively in the country’s internal affairs or its politics. The Mumbai Police are acting strictly within the legal framework,” Murad told the news agency ANI.
He further noted that the actor has been given 15 days and can approach the court if he believes he is being treated unfairly or is being compelled to leave the country.
“He has been given a full 15 days. If he feels he is being treated unfairly or being forced to leave the country, he is welcome to approach the court, and whatever the court decides, we must all accept it. Let’s see how he reacts. He has two options: either leave the country by October 28, or if he does not wish to leave, or feels that he has been wronged or treated unjustly, he can take his grievance to the court,” Murad added.
Imran Khan’s proposed legal challenge will now bring the dispute before the Bombay High Court, where the validity of the FRRO’s order can be contested.

Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.
The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.
Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.
But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.
“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.
“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, must strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.
He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).
The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year. Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.”
Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.
In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.
Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neo-colonialist” and “damaging”.
“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”
It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.
Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”
It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.
“The study has not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.
At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.
The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.
Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “cancelled or suspended.”
Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

NEW DELHI: The Election Commission (EC) has informed the states that it would be conducting a Special Summary Revision of electoral rolls in 17 states, including the poll-bound states of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur and Goa.In a letter to the chief electoral officers of the states and Union territories concerned, including Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur and Goa, the Election Commission said January 1, 2027, would be the qualifying date for the exercise.The Special Summary Revision (SSR) is intended to add eligible voters, especially young people and first-time electors, rectify errors in existing entries and ensure electoral rolls are accurate and up to date.The current term of the 403-member Uttar Pradesh assembly ends on May 22 next year. The tenures of the assemblies in Manipur, Goa, Punjab and Uttarakhand, which have 60, 40, 117 and 70 seats, respectively, are due to end on different dates in March 2027.Under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, the Election Commission is permitted to conduct elections "earlier than six months before the term expires".
Notice by EC
ECI's notice to states.
How's Special Revision different from SIR
While a Summary Revision focuses on new eligibles and routine corrections, SIR goes far deeper, involving statewide house-to-house verification, detailed scrutiny of entries, and large-scale data audits.
For instance, under a Summary Revision, a voter who has shifted homes must file a form to update their address. Under SIR, the Booth Level Officer visits that address, confirms whether the voter still lives there, checks if anyone new has become eligible, and updates the roll based on physical verification rather than waiting for the voter to initiate the change.The SIR of electoral rolls has triggered a political controversy, with opposition parties raising concerns over the deletion of voters' names and the possibility of eligible citizens being left out of electoral lists.The poll panel has maintained that the exercise is aimed at cleaning up electoral rolls by removing duplicate and ineligible entries, including those belonging to deceased voters, while ensuring that all eligible citizens are included.
ALSO READ: ‘Anarchic, immature’: BJP targets Rahul over anti-CEC protests; claims misconduct with women copHowever, opposition parties have questioned the process, alleging that the exercise could lead to genuine voters losing their right to vote. They have also raised concerns over documentation requirements, verification procedures and the possibility of disproportionate effects on vulnerable groups, including migrant workers, the elderly and economically disadvantaged people.One of the main concerns surrounding SIR is the potential deletion of eligible voters' names during the verification process.The dispute has also reached the Supreme Court, with petitions raising concerns about the manner in which the revision is being conducted. The legal debate centres on the Election Commission's authority to revise electoral rolls and the safeguards available to voters who challenge their exclusion.

In 2022, Hilary Swank announced she was pregnant with twins at age 48, sparking conversations around the risks of pregnancy after age 35.
Now, Swank is pregnant again at 52. She announced her pregnancy in an Instagram reel with the caption: "A lot of people have been asking what project I'm doing next, this one releases in December."
Pregnancies at 35 or older have traditionally been classified as "advanced maternal age" by the medical community. Studies have linked older pregnancies to a higher risk of complications and health problems such as high blood pressure and chromosomal abnormalities. Research suggests that the risk increases with age.
In 2024, Swank, then 50, told Business Insider that she's glad she had kids at 48.
"The person that I was in my 20s and even into my 30s would've been a very different mom than I am now," Swank, who is also the Chief Innovation Officer of HealthyBaby, said.
Swank said there were many benefits to being an older parent, such as more time and flexibility to really show up for her kids.
She loves her work flexibility
Swank told Business Insider that she took the first year and a half off for maternity leave (the average length of maternity leave in the US is three months). She also didn't feel rushed to go back to work, waiting for an opportunity that seemed right.
Swank said having more time with her kids is crucial. "I just had three and a half hours of sleep, and I haven't really seen my babies, and that's really hard," she said. "It makes me really empathize with all the parents out there who are working really long hours who don't get to see their children."
She has more mental energy to devote to her kids
Swank said she doesn't have to focus on herself as much as she did in her 20s and 30s, when she was getting her acting career off the ground. It's given her the space to prioritize her kids' needs.
"I'm in a place where I just have a lot more patience and a lot more grace to give, not just my children, but others around me," she said. "I can give them so much more than I could have at that point."
She feels more comfortable with herself
One of the best things about getting pregnant in her late forties was Swank's comfort with herself.
"The things that you used to care about don't take front and center anymore," she said. "You're on to new places in your life and it's a beautiful place to be."
Swank isn't the only one who feels this way: other older parents say they had more time to figure themselves out before they had kids. Even Swank's mom misses her 40s.
"If she could go back to any time, it would be 45 — she felt her best," Swank said. "And I hear a lot of women say that."

YouTuber Dhruv Rathee gets fresh summons from Delhi court over 2018 defamation case linked to video on BJP IT cell
In the video uploaded on his YouTube channel in 2018, Dhruv Rathee had alleged that members of the BJP's IT cell had tried to bribe Vikas Pandey to defame him.
A Delhi court has issued fresh summons to YouTuber Dhruv Rathee in a 2018 defamation case allegedly linked to a video about the BJP IT Cell.
Noting that repeated attempts to serve him had remained unsuccessful for several years, the court directed that the summons be served at his address in Gurugram, Haryana.
Judicial Magistrate Rahul Jain of the Saket court issued the order on October 12 while considering an application by the complainant, Vikas Sankrityayan, popularly known as Vikas Pandey, who sought an early hearing and permission to personally serve the summons, news agency ANI reported.
Taking note of the submissions and the case records, the magistrate observed that Rathee had first been summoned in July 2019. According to news agency PTI, the court order observed that, "From the available record, it is clear that the complainant has been trying to serve the accused no. 1 (Rathee) since the last several years..."

The court subsequently ordered that fresh summons be issued at the Gurugram address submitted by the complainant. It also granted permission for Pandey to accompany the process server during the delivery of the court notice.
The complainant has been directed to pay the prescribed process fee within two days. The matter has been listed for further proceedings on October 17, 2026.
Summoned over a 2018 video about the BJP IT Cell
The case stems from a video Rathee published on his YouTube channel , @dhruvrathee, in May 2018. In the video, Rathee alleged that members of the BJP's IT cell had tried to bribe Pandey to defame him.
The video was later shared on social media and retweeted on Twitter (now X) by Arvind Kejriwal, who was the chief minister of Delhi at the time.
Pandey subsequently brought defamation proceedings against Rathee and Kejriwal, alleging harm arising from the video and its circulation.
Rathee is in delhi for the CJP protests
Advocate Samaksh Sharma, appearing for the complainant, submitted that repeated attempts to serve the summons had failed over the years because Rathee mainly resides abroad. However, the court was informed that the YouTuber is currently in India and staying at a residence in Gurugram, Haryana.
Dhruv Rathee arrived in Delhi recently to take part in the protests against chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
The court summons were issued days after Rathee was detained from his residence in Gurugram on October 10, the day CJP had announced a protest in Delhi. He was later released in the early hours of Sunday, October 11, around 3 AM.

Priya cannot remember a time when her mother was not busy. Apart from her work, there were always social engagements to attend, friends to visit or new books to read. But something changed after retirement.
“She seemed to lose some of her sparkle. She became a little inward and moody at times, as though an inertia had taken over. Her outings became less frequent. She no longer went shopping, as everything could be home-delivered. The fact that my father preferred to stay at home further reduced her opportunities to socialise. This transition from a busy, active person to a listless and diffident individual was quite shocking and sad,” she says.
When she opened up to her friends about this, Priya discovered that they had similar stories to share. Parents who had once led full, active lives were now confined to the quiet routines of home. They had not lost their zest for life, but age had caught up with them, sapping their energy and enthusiasm to get out and about.
“Then it struck us that, in a few years, this could be our lives too. Why should we allow the years to steal all the colours from our lives?” says Dimple Mohan, who runs a consultancy service in the city.
Five women
And so, Young at Heart (YaH) was born — a dream that took wings when five women entrepreneurs and working professionals in Thiruvananthapuram came together to explore how they could help their parents rediscover the joy of living and embrace ageing with enthusiasm.
Envisioned as a platform for senior citizens and those in their 50s, YaH hopes to bring people together to rediscover life’s little pleasures — new friendships, new learning experiences, evenings out, and a little fun and frolic. Growing older, the founders believe, should never mean compromising on emotional happiness and mental well-being.
“We all have successful careers, active social lives and wide networks of friends. But living with our parents, we have seen how their personalities and attitudes towards life change as they grow older, even when they are financially secure and have no major worries,” says Ms. Mohan, who is one of YaH’s founder.
“It made us think that, regardless of age, we should be able to embrace life with gusto and live it to the fullest in the company of good friends. YaH is an initiative to help senior citizens and people in their 50s connect, forge friendships, share interests and build a community that helps everyone lead more fulfilling lives. Many have the money and time, but are hesitant to venture out on their own,” she adds
On October 16
A formal launch event of YaH, featuring music and entertainment, is planned in the capital on October 16. The event will also offer participants an opportunity to meet and get to know one another.
YaH plans to organise regular entertainment and recreational activities, while creating opportunities for like-minded people to discover, share and nurture their talents. Events will be tailored to the interests, hobbies and leisure preferences of those who have registered with the initiative.
The group has also identified areas such as diet and nutrition, physical fitness, digital literacy and financial planning as important components of healthy, active ageing.
“We had several women register with us and we asked them what has been on their bucket list. One wants to learn to speak English fluently so she can converse with her grandchildren abroad. Another has always wanted to design dresses, while someone else simply wants to travel — something she could never manage while working. We hope to facilitate the fulfilment of some of these dreams,” says actor Manju Pillai, who is spearheading the initiative along with Devi Mohan, Sankari Unnithan and Maya Menon.
Younger volunteers
In time, YaH hopes to involve younger volunteers, building bridges between generations. They could take senior citizens to the beach or the movies, or simply spend an afternoon playing chess.
As age-related frailties set in, many older people find themselves increasingly disconnected from the world around them. The resulting isolation can take a toll on their emotional health and leave them vulnerable to depression.
Young at Heart hopes to address this often-overlooked need for socialisation and companionship first and help them embrace life, wholeheartedly.

Ryohin Keikaku shares hit a record high after the Muji operator posted better-than-expected annual results and outlined an ambitious international expansion plan.
The stock climbed as much as 10.7%, the biggest gain in more than a year, in Tokyo trading Thursday. Ryohin Keikaku expects operating income to grow around 10% to ¥114 billion for the fiscal year through August 2027, exceeding the average analyst estimate.
The earnings results point to broad-based growth across Muji’s global footprint, with full-year revenue exceeding expectations in each of its four geographic segments. Profitability improved in Japan as in-house production lowered costs, markdowns were restrained and store operations became more efficient, while mainland China recorded sales growth across every product category.
Muji is shifting its focus toward growth investment after building a stable profit base, and will be expanding in Europe, the Americas, India and the Middle East, Ryohin Keikaku President Satoshi Shimizu told reporters in Tokyo on Wednesday.
“We had been pacing our store openings, but now we are going to press hard on the accelerator to expand our footprint across the entire United States,” Shimizu said.
Prioritizing overseas growth with more store openings, workforce investment and spending is a positive sign for a company that had previously focused heavily on operating profit margins, SMBC Nikko Securities analyst Kuni Kanamori wrote in a note to clients.
Sales grew in Taiwan, Hong Kong and South Korea, while new stores and wider product ranges supported Southeast Asia and Oceania. Same-store and online sales also increased in Europe and North America.

B2B ecommerce unicorn Udaan’s operating revenue grew 12.6% to ₹5,134 Cr in the financial year ended March 2026 (FY26) from ₹4,561 Cr in FY25. The startup’s net loss narrowed 19.4% to ₹851.5 Cr from ₹1,055.4 Cr in the previous fiscal, according to its financial statements. The recovery follows an uneven revenue trajectory — a 40% decline in FY23, marginal growth of 1.7% in FY24, and a 20% fall in FY25. During this period, Udaan also closed a $114 Mn Series G funding round in June 2025 at a 59% valuation dip. In a LinkedIn post, Udaan’s senior vice president Vishnu Menon attributed the improvement to the startup’s focus on profitable growth, operational efficiency, and tighter execution across its markets. Over the 10 quarters from Q4 CY23 to Q1 CY26, the company’s revenue grew at a CAGR of around 25%, while its contribution margin improved by nearly 500 basis points and EBITDA burn declined by around 70%, Menon said. Menon attributed this progress to its cluster-led operating model, which focuses on accountability for performance at the city and category levels, deeper operations in existing markets, and tighter cost controls. However, Udaan’s financial statements flagged material uncertainty that could cast significant doubt on the group’s ability to continue as a going concern. At the end of FY26, the group’s current liabilities exceeded its current assets by ₹1,391 Cr, while its total liabilities exceeded its total assets by ₹790.9 Cr. The startup said it received additional funding after the financial year ended and expects revenue growth and cost-cutting measures to improve operating cash flows. Founded in 2016 by former Flipkart executives Amod Malviya, Sujeet Kumar, and Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan operates a B2B digital marketplace connecting manufacturers, brands, wholesalers, and retailers, including kirana stores, chemists, and general merchants, through a mobile app. Udaan’s Bumpy FY27 Despite the improvement in its FY26 financial performance, Udaan faced fresh challenges in the ongoing fiscal, with creditors initiating insolvency proceedings against its offshore parent over a bond default. Creditors, including Tor Investment Management, Samena Capital, and Arena Investors, initiated proceedings in the Singapore High Court after Udaan’s offshore holding entity, Trustroot Internet Pvt Ltd, defaulted on $170 Mn worth of compulsorily convertible notes due on June 30. Confirming the development at the time, Udaan told Inc42 that the proceedings concerned its offshore holding company and would not have any material impact on its operations in India. Later in July, Udaan announced a proposed $160 Mn financing transaction, comprising fresh equity, new debt, and conversion of existing debt into equity. Last month, Udaan announced an agreement to acquire Swiggy’s retail distribution business, LYNK, in an all-share transaction valuing the business at ₹500 Cr. Swiggy also announced plans to invest another ₹75 Cr in Udaan’s parent entity. Udaan expects the acquisition to expand its retail distribution capabilities and market reach, while improving efficiency across the combined network. Udaan Bets On Private Labels, Institutional Sales Udaan is also looking to improve its revenue mix and margins through private labels and its institutional procurement business, horeca360. According to Menon, private labels now account for 15-25% of staples sales across Udaan’s operating cities. He expects the segment to improve margins and capture a larger share of customers’ spending using its existing sourcing and distribution infrastructure. Meanwhile, horeca360, which caters to hotels, restaurants, caterers, and institutional buyers, expanded into Hyderabad and Chennai during FY26. The business aims to deepen customer relationships and improve utilisation of Udaan’s supply chain network. Menon said it would continue to focus on improving revenue quality, strengthening execution at the city level, and increasing operating efficiency as it works towards sustained profitability and a public listing.

A neighbourhood in Vienna has introduced guidelines for dog walking, including the use of bottled tap water to rinse away urine and protect vulnerable trees.
Neubau, an up-and-coming, densely populated district dotted with cafes and galleries, rolled out the Schönes Gassi (nice dog walk) campaign this week.
The project addresses the impact of the area’s 600 dogs on greenery, including about 250 trees planted over the past decade to help mitigate the effects of the climate crisis.
Using the slogan Das Flascherl zum Sackerl (the bottle to go with the bag), the guidelines say animal urine corrodes tree bark, weakening its protective layer and potentially letting corrosive pathogens and fungi penetrate the trunk.
“While marking territory is a form of communication for dogs, it causes stress for urban trees,” said Grätzllabor, a community group that takes its name from the Viennese slang for quarter or neighbourhood. “This results in rot and, in the worst case, compromised stability.”
The group said the campaign had been launched in concert with “concerned citizens” in the Austrian capital. It also asks owners to carry plastic bags to clean up after their pets.
Owners can pick up a free 270ml water bottle at the town hall to rinse areas used by their dogs. The voluntary scheme could be expanded to other districts.
Fresh canine urine is highly water-soluble and dilution significantly reduces the concentration of ammonia and other harmful substances seeping into the soil, while also softening the smell.
Grätzllabor said the rinsing strategy should not be interpreted as a “licence” for dogs to mark trees or green space but rather as an action owners could take to minimise harm caused by their pets.
Conny Sporrer, who is a dog trainer, said the Schönes Gassi campaign could help head off more drastic calls to mitigate problems linked to animal waste.
“In Vienna, we don’t need a city full of dog bans, or a city where dogs are just allowed to urinate anywhere they please,” she told reporters, saying most pets could be taught where to relieve themselves. “What we need is consideration, education and sufficient suitable facilities for dogs.”
Similar schemes have been introduced in Japan, Italy, Switzerland and Spain, which has the highest share of dog-owning households in the EU at 70%. Austria has relatively low levels of ownership, at just 17% of households.
Berlin, where more than 100,000 dogs are kept as pets after an increase in ownership during the pandemic, has also begun addressing the problem by stopping the planting of black locust trees in some areas because they are particularly sensitive to urine.
In the spring, the western district of Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf began installing “pee stones” for dogs to use as a target, instead of trees.

Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
Goodbye Raila

Watch on iPlayer
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."
