A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

In summer and fall 2026, numerous posts claimed U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr said, "Infertility is genetic. If your parents can't have kids, neither can you."
For example, a meme of Kennedy featuring the purported quote spread widely on Facebook on Oct. 2.
Snopes readers have also reached out to us to verify the authenticity of the alleged remark.
(Facebook user "Truth and Accountability Project")
Though Kennedy has spread incorrect health information many times over the years, there is no evidence he said the above quote. Variations of this quote are on X and in humor books dating back years before he was sworn in as health secretary in 2025. As such, the remark is incorrectly attributed to Kennedy.
Entering variations of the quote in Google, Bing (archived) and DuckDuckGo uncovered no authentic video or reportage indicating that Kennedy ever made such a statement.
Earlier online examples of the quote are not attributed to him at all. One of the earliest variations of the quote on X, from Aug. 14, 2022, reads: "Infertility is genetic, if your parents couldn't have kids you also won't." Other X accounts, including one labeled as a parody account, shared the same quote days later.
Another variant of the quote appears in the 2002 book, "Science Askew: A Lighthearted Look at the Scientific World," by Donald E. Simanek. An even earlier version appears in the 1997 book of humor, "Living, Laughing, and Loving Life," by Dan Miller and Jeanne Zornes. Snopes contacted Zornes to learn if the quote originates from this book. We will update this article if we learn more.
While he didn't originate the quote in question, Kennedy has long been concerned with infertility issues. In May 2026, at a White House event, he raised the alarm on male infertility, saying:
The fertility crisis for women began in 2007; for men in 1970. Men had twice the sperm count as our teenagers do today. This is an existential crisis for our country. We had a series of presidents who were trying to discourage childbirth and motherhood in this country. We now have a president who is trying to encourage it.
In 2025, Kennedy said on Fox News: "We have fertility rates that are just spiraling. A teenager today, an American teenager, has less testosterone than a 68-year-old man. Sperm counts are down 50%." Experts debunked this particular claim, according to an NBC News report.
An analysis by The 19th, a nonprofit newsroom focused on gender and politics, found that while evidence shows sperm counts are lower than decades ago, it is not clear that factor influences the declining birth rate in the United States.
For further reading, Snopes has looked into numerous quotes rightly or wrongly attributed to Kennedy.

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week launched an agency-wide effort to study and document any health problems reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services said on Thursday.
The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group before taking office, to reshape federal immunization policy. The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and monitored for safety after approval.
The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 compensable injuries across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded roughly $5 billion across about 12,300 injury and death claims.
The new moves, which appear to be part of Kennedy’s decades-long efforts to sow skepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter US childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunisation rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the US since last year. The effort centers on a National Institutes of Health clinic
opened on Monday to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement. Other measures include a proposal by the Centers for
Medicare & Medicaid Services to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS; a CDC effort to update VAERS; and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.
Kennedy has said U.S. children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which has been echoed by President Donald Trump. Kennedy has long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no evidence of harm.
In his first year heading HHS, he fired all 17 independent expert members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.
In January, the CDC announced a revamped childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.
A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts of the proposed changes, finding that Kennedy and HHS had violated federal law in reshaping the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunisation Practices. The injunction has prevented ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunisations often needed for insurance coverage.

Fourteen boxes are piled in front of my desk, stacked around me like a cardboard fort. Inside one is a Form Studio 1, the new, affordable, consumer-focused 3D printer Formlabs just announced.
David Lakatos, chief product officer at the 3D printer manufacturer, assured me that the Form Studio 1 has a very economical size. “It doesn't take a lot of space,” Lakatos said. “If you have a desk, then I think you should be good to go.” I have a desk. It’s covered in boxes sent by his company.
Formlabs is one of the biggest 3D printer producers, with nearly 200,000 printers in service. The company’s customers are primarily professional businesses, like assembly shops or dentists, able to shell out $2,500 or more for a printer. (Its last affordable printer was $2,300.)
But the Form Studio 1 is Formlabs’ first consumer-oriented device. It prints with SLA (stereolithography) resins—a common 3D printing material that hardens into solid plastic when exposed to ultraviolet light—and can use Formlabs-branded products or third-party resins. It costs $699 and is now on sale; individual resin bottles start at $29.
The Studio 1 takes up roughly the same space as a minifridge. You’ll also likely need a wash unit, sold separately for $199 with a similar footprint (it removes uncured liquid resin from the surface of models). Then you’ll need room for all the tools and resin cartridges. Getting all that stuff can pile up. Or at least it did when Formlabs sent more than a dozen boxes to the WIRED office for testing. Your pileage may vary.
The front touchscreen lets you troubleshoot and ready prints. When the printer starts, it’s relatively quiet and odor-free. 3D printing with resin can be stinky, but Formlabs-branded resins are UL GreenGuard–certified, the same standard used to ensure baby products aren’t harmful from skin contact or off-gassing. Lakatos says the idea is that the Studio 1 can be used anywhere without the room being overwhelmed by resin stank.
“We know that some people are going to put it in their bedrooms,” Lakatos says. “I don't sleep with my printers, but you could if you really wanted to.”
After going through the stack of boxes, I set up the Form Studio 1 and the Form Studio Wash+Cure. They’re stylish, with translucent orange cases that conjure old-school iMac aesthetics. The printing process itself is supposedly quick. Lakatos says you can print a casing for a Raspberry Pi setup in around eight minutes.
I’ve only printed a couple of things so far, but have had a good experience with the orders. (Full review coming soon.) I printed a clear cover for the toolbox that comes with the Studio 1. It took about 17 minutes and came out clean and intact. The process was relatively quiet. The resin smell was there, but really only when lifting the hood after the process was done. I’m excited to use it more and see what kind of very detailed unholy abominations I can make.
The SLA printing enables very detailed constructions. In Formlabs’ internal testing, the company says it has had a roughly 2 percent failure rate for its prints. If that holds in the real world, it’ll be a big jump over competitors. That’s if you use its own resins, though.
“You can use any material,” Lakatos says. “If you want to use the toxic resin on Amazon, you can do it. We don't recommend it, but you can do it.”
Formlabs also has an app called Form Mobile that can control prints or send designs to the Form Studio 1. The overall printer experience feels surprisingly straightforward.
“It’s great if you want to mess around with some stuff,” Lakatos says. “For serious, beautiful things and projects that really require better material properties, beautiful resolution, stuff like that—it's hard to compete with it.”

An assistant professor at Assam University in Silchar was booked for allegedly molesting a woman researcher during a conference held in Bengaluru, police said.
The woman researcher lodged a complaint at the Assam University police outpost on October 11, alleging sexual harassment, Cachar senior superintendent of police (SSP) Partha Pratim Das said. “We received a complaint and we are probing it,” Das said.
He added that the matter involves a central university and that, under the Vishaka guidelines, the university’s internal investigation report is important before the police intervene.
Registrar of Assam University, Silchar (AUS), Pradosh Kiran Nath, said that the woman researcher lodged a complaint alleging molestation around October 7, and the matter was referred to the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC).
“We held a meeting, and the ICC has been asked to complete the investigation as soon as possible and submit its report,” he said, adding that the university has a strict policy on sexual harassment.
The woman researcher told HT on Thursday that the incident occurred during an international academic conference held in Bengaluru in September and that she was subsequently threatened by the assistant professor several times.
“On the night of September 26, after an academic discussion, the supervisor insisted on accompanying me to my allotted room. We were alone at the lift when he made an inappropriate personal proposition and asked me to engage in physical intimacy. When I refused, he said that it could have adverse consequences for my academic progress,” she said.
She said that she later contacted her fiance and sought help from two female faculty members from other universities. “The two faculty members extended their support and stayed with me that night,” she added.
She alleged that the assistant professor from the department of performing arts later began creating obstacles in her academic progress and that she was denied information about two Research Advisory Committee (RAC) meetings.
“He threatened to create difficulties for me and said he would not let me complete my PhD. He also said that my research work would not progress unless I complied with his instructions,” she said.
HT reached out to the assistant professor accused of molestation, but his official contact number remained switched off until the report was filed.
Registrar Nath said that the assistant professor attended an online meeting last week and that the ICC was examining his attendance after the complaint was lodged.
Assam University has witnessed similar incidents in the past as well, and the registrar said that strict action had been taken against the accused in those cases.

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

European Union antitrust regulators accepted concessions from Sanofi to settle an investigation into an allegedly “misleading” campaign that disparaged the only rival flu vaccine recommended for vulnerable patients at risk for developing the illness. In doing so, the company avoided being fined.
The European Commission had suggested that Sanofi portrayed the Fluad vaccine marketed by CSL Seqirus as inferior to its own Efluelda vaccine in a communication campaign that primarily targeted health care professionals in Germany and France. Sanofi holds a dominant position in both countries, according to the EC.
To resolve the probe, Sanofi committed to a corrective communication campaign rectifying its “possible disparaging behavior” and to refrain from such behavior in the future, according to Teresa Riberta, the European Commission executive vice president for Clean, Just and Competitive Transition. The agreement is legally binding.

Starlink restrictions would hamper Ukraine's war effort. But the country can adapt, experts say
SpaceX interrupted functioning of military-grade terminals, Ukrainian officials say
Shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, then-Ukrainian vice-prime minister Mykhailo Fedorov went on what was then known as Twitter to publicly plead with Elon Musk to activate his company SpaceX's Starlink satellites for use in the country.
Soon after, Musk posted, "Starlink service is now active in Ukraine. More terminals en route."
Since then, Starlink and the military-grade version known as Starshield have been integral to Ukraine's war effort against Russia. Indeed, in February, Musk appeared to acquiesce to a request from Fedorov, who most recently served as Ukraine's defence minister, to block Russia's access to Starlink.
But earlier this week, according to Ukrainian officials, its military lost some access to the system.
By Thursday, Starshield's satellite internet functionality had been restored, Reuters reported, citing a source in Ukraine's defence ministry.
It's still not clear why the restrictions would have been imposed. In a post on X on Wednesday, Musk said Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government and that any limits would have been ordered by the U.S military and ultimately the president.
He added that use of Starlink "is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
So far, there has been no response from the U.S. government. But the restrictions come as U.S. President Donald Trump has criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for attacking Russian refineries, which he blames for the high cost of oil.
Here's a look at how the Ukrainian military has used Starlink, and what impact these restrictions could have on its capabilities.
How does Ukraine's military use Starlink?
Starlink is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites with roughly 13 million subscribers. Its low Earth orbit satellites around the planet deliver faster connections than traditional counterparts.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has since restricted Starlink for certain military uses, instead developing Starshield, a more secure network, for government and military purposes.
Ukraine has used the technology for both offensive and defensive operations, with the military using thousands of terminals connected to the system, according to the New York Times.
A September 2022 photo shows an antenna of the Starlink satellite-based broadband system donated by Elon Musk, in Izyum, Ukraine. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images)
The network is used for long-range drone missions, interceptor air defence systems and front-line logistics, according to a recent social media post from Serhii Beskrestnov, defence tech adviser to Zelenskyy.
He said the system has been key for Ukraine’s aerial defence and helped intercept the drones that Moscow has unleashed on cities in the country in recent months.
"It's just an incredibly capable communication system that has proven very valuable to the Ukrainians," said Thomas Withington, a military sciences associate fellow with the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, in an interview with CBC News.
He said the military has tended to use it primarily for tactical and operational communications. For example, if a deployed unit near the front line needs to communicate back with commanders hundreds of kilometres away, "Starlink provides an excellent way of doing that," Withington said.

He added that Starlink is also beneficial in that its system is very difficult to jam or use electronic warfare against.
Renard Sexton, an associate political science professor at Emory University and managing director of the Empirical Studies of Conflict, said that Starlink was crucial to the Ukrainians' ability to push back against Russia's initial invasion in 2022.
Sexton added that his research has found that in certain moments when Starlink was less accessible, the Ukrainian offence suffered much more than its defence.
What restrictions were imposed?
Earlier this week, SpaceX started to interrupt the functioning of its military-grade terminals when they are moving at high speed, Ukrainian officials said.
According to Beskrestnov, the Zelenskyy adviser, that included imposing a speed limit on Starlink terminals mounted on drones.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on Wednesday that a decision to restrict access to Starlink would have been made by the U.S government and military. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)
The limit disrupted operations, including making the slower-flying attack drones easier targets for Russian defences, he said.
The speed cutoff also hampered Ukraine's ability to conduct strikes on Russian targets inside Ukraine, Reuters reported.
How could the restrictions impact Ukraine's military effort?
There could be quite a significant impact on the Ukrainian army's operational level communications and its use of drones, said Withington.
"Depriving that capability through a stalling deprivation is quite serious," he said.
But the Ukrainians are incredibly innovative, Sexton said, and a restriction that might have hurt them two years ago likely hurts them a lot less now due to their ability to adapt.
"They're less likely to be relying fully on that as their only option for a given scenario," he said. "So I think there's more redundancy."
Withington agreed, saying that while the restriction is a serious inconvenience, the Ukrainians, together with their European allies, would be able to engineer workaround solutions that reduce its severity.
"It can't be done ... tomorrow, but it probably could be done in a matter of months, if not shorter."
That could include using existing capacity in both government- and private-sector-provided satellite communications in Europe, as well as looking at other systems, he said.

However, Sexton said while the Ukrainians could adapt to a short-term Starlink restriction, he cautioned that a prolonged or complete inability to access it "would be a big issue for them."
"There's no question. They don't have any way to replace it in the short run."
Sexton said he wouldn't go so far to say that it would turn the tide of the war, as at this point the conflict seems to have calcified, with both sides having difficulties making significant progress.
But he said that a long restriction could mean that any prospect of a future counteroffensive, or any prospect of holding out forever, would certainly become more difficult for Ukraine.

A cluster of Shigella infections linked to a temple festival has put health authorities in Thrissur on alert, with 10 cases reported in the district in the first nine days of October. Seven of the cases, including that of a seven-month-old child, were reported from Tholur among people who had attended a festival at a temple there.
The suspected source of the infection has been traced to a well at the temple, from which water was drawn for rituals. The well has since been chlorinated, District Medical Officer M. Sujatha said.
“The seven Shigella cases reported from Tholur were among people who attended a festival at a temple in Tholur. The source of infection has been identified as the temple well from which water was taken for rituals. The well has been chlorinated,” Dr. Sujatha said.
Health teams are closely monitoring the situation, while hospitals have been instructed to respond immediately if any further cases are detected. Awareness campaigns have also been conducted in the area, with people advised to seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms, she said.
All those who tested positive for Shigella have sought treatment, and most have recovered. The remaining patients are also recovering, according to the DMO.
The other three Shigella cases reported during the nine-day period were from Wadakkanchery, Arimbur and Adat.
The Shigella cluster comes amid a wider surge in fever cases in the district. As many as 4,914 people sought treatment for fever between October 1 and 9. During the period, 39 dengue cases and four cases of leptospirosis were also confirmed.
Dengue cases have been reported from several parts of the district, including Kodakara, Mattathur, Meloor, Thrissur Corporation, Avinissery, Chalakudy municipality, Kaiparamba, Kodassery, Pananchery, Puthukkad, Adat, Alur, Puthur, Mullurkara, Pariyaram, Tholur, Orumanayur, Thalikulam and Choondal.
Leptospirosis cases were reported from Pananchery, Pazhayannur, Porkulam and Kuzhur.
Dengue cases
The DMO said a significant number of dengue cases had been detected in migrant labour camps and among their contacts. “Most of the dengue cases have been reported from migrant labour camps and their contacts. We are keeping a close watch on them and monitoring the situation,” she said.
Health authorities have stepped up surveillance and preventive measures across the district. The DMO urged people with fever to take adequate rest, drink sufficient water and consume nutritious food, while vulnerable people, particularly those with compromised immunity, should take extra precautions and seek medical care when necessary.
With Shigella cases emerging in connection with a common gathering and dengue continuing to surface across multiple locations, health officials are keeping a close watch on possible further transmission and urging the public to maintain strict hygiene and food and water safety.

India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August.
But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention.
Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said.
A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage.
"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said.
Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment.
But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes?
India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control.
But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat.
Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods.
Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important.
A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period.
Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online.
Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau.
The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily.
And the dangers extend beyond flooding.
A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms.
While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau.
The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress.
The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations.
Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas.
In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet.
Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project.
But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort.
"One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute.
"What happened after that no one knows," he added.
Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet.
But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022.
China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said.
Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes.
"These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group.
But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved.
One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value.
"What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank.
Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders.
The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow.
"There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD.
He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks.
Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay.
"Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says.
Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain.
For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat.

Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music
If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
Writer Yiyun Li does not talk about "grief" or the "grieving process." To her, those words make it sound that at some point you emerge from grief. Instead, Li prefers to use the word "abyss," which, she says, is where she expects to be for the remainder of her life.
Li's teenage sons both died by suicide six years apart, Vincent in 2017 at age 16, and James in 2024 at age 19. Her Pulitzer Prize-winning 2025 memoir, Things in Nature Merely Grow, chronicled the loss of her sons and her effort to go on.
"James' death taught me to suffer better," she says. "To say, 'I can do it, and I can live with my pain and sorrow without ever wanting to stop feeling.'"
Li's new novel, Music Against the Night, is set in the late 1700s and early 1800s and centers on two prodigies who are brought together by music, and drawn apart because of their aspirations. The novel focuses on music, which sits outside of words.
"I think I've had the feeling both times after my children's death that words often fall short, and falling short doesn't mean not succeeding, falling short doesn't mean failing," she says. "But when I start a new project, I would like a subject [where] words naturally fall short. So music is that choice."
Li grew up in China and served a year in the Chinese military before coming to the U.S. to study immunology. She eventually left her Ph.D. program to become a writer. Li is now a professor in the creative writing program at Princeton University.
Interview highlights
On the decision to set Music Against the Night in a different time period
I was in the middle of the novel when James died. This is a novel far from my usual interests or concerns, and the reason I think I went back to history is I would like to live again through history, through historical figures, through my characters living in the late 18th and early 19th century. ... I'm making the past into a new now for myself and possibly for my readers.
On how playing piano connects to her grief
I began my piano lessons at the end of 2023, purely to get to know how to play the piano. And James died in February 2024, so two months into my piano lessons he died, and it occurred to me that piano or music is a good way for me to count time — because music is about time. It's about counting the measure, counting the rhythm. And also music is about ... be[ing] engaged with something else. You can sit in your sadness all day long, do nothing, or crying. Or, like me, I could just sit there and just play the same drill again, and again, as a way to know I was, in a way, staying in touch with the world. ...
I'm not a concert pianist, but somehow I find it liberating and healthy to do something that you absolutely love but cannot do well. Every time I go to my piano lesson, I'm so intimidated. I'm sweating because I just can't do it. I can hear other people do it, I cannot do it myself. But I think that's, again, acknowledging the limit of my capacity.
On raising two gifted children
Both my children could be called prodigies, but James, my younger son, especially was extraordinarily odd and brilliant. ... We were greatly baffled. I remember he was 5 or 6, he said, "Mommy, you will never see the world. I see it full of dots and squiggly lines." And that again was a strange perception of the world [that] we adults did not have access to. …
What is the responsibility or the difficulty of bringing up a child [who is] very brilliant? … Some people would say, well, you really have to train him to be the next Einstein, but we did not want him to be the next Einstein, we want him to be a normal, happy boy living in an ordinary life.
On her son Vincent
He was a brilliant painter and we still have all his paintings around the house. He was an oboist and when he wanted to learn the oboe, the oboe teacher said he was a bit young, because he was 8 when he want to learn oboe, but he was certain. ... [He had] started on the piano and he could articulate that piano was not his instrument. He wanted to play the oboe. But mostly, he wrote beautiful poetry. He was a great poet. And he was a greater reader. I wouldn't call him an outlier, as James was, but he was brilliant and fun and interesting.
On struggling with suicidal ideation
Sometimes I think people have all sort of thoughts about or against people who have chosen suicide, and people who've chosen or attempted suicide are often called selfish. But my experience is oftentimes people [are] in great pain, whether it's great mental pain or great physical pain. And sometimes people in deep depression cannot tell the difference between mental pain and physical pain, because everything together is a great kind of suffering. I think it's not that people who experience that kind of suicidal urge, it's not that they want to die or they want [to] use this to hurt other people.
On becoming a writer
I was born with innate curiosity and also sensitivity to things that did not quite make sense. So I grew up in China. And for instance, when I was little, all the adults would say, since you're a child, you have no right to decide who you want to be or what you want to do. And my mother even had a saying, something along the [lines] that an adult decides and the child follows. I was quite young, you know, 4 or 5. I just couldn't make sense of all of these teachings because I thought I was as capable of thinking as the adults, and why did I have to follow them? So I think that sort of sensitivity to things that are very, very nonsensical, I think maybe that's one thing that made me into a writer.

అక్టోబర్ 10న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద భారీ నిరసన చేపట్టనున్నట్లు కాక్రొచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ప్రకటించింది. ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర ఓటర్ల జాబితా సవరణ (SIR) ప్రక్రియను వెంటనే నిలిపివేయాలని, 2025 జూన్ 25 నుంచి ఓటర్ల జాబితా నుంచి తొలగించిన పేర్లన్నింటినీ తిరిగి చేర్చాలని కూడా CJP డిమాండ్ చేస్తోంది. లెఫ్ట్ వింగ్ విద్యార్థి సంఘాలు కూడా ఈ నిరసనలో పెద్ద సంఖ్యలో పాల్గొంటామని ప్రకటన విడుదల చేశాయి. జంతర్ మంతర్లోకి ప్రవేశించేందుకు ప్రయత్నించిన సీజేపీ (CJP) నేతలను పోలీసులు అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, సోషల్ మీడియాలో ఒక వీడియోను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) షేర్ చేస్తూ, 2026 అక్టోబర్ 10న ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన నిరసనలను ఇది చూపిస్తోందని ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు. దీని వెనుక ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఈ వీడియో 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలో ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ జరిగిన నిరసనలను చూపిస్తుంది.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలో జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ జరిగిన నిరసనలకు సంబంధించింది కాదు. ఈ వీడియోను ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో చిత్రీకరించారు. అయితే, ఈ వీడియోను ఖచ్చితంగా ఎప్పుడు, ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారో తెలియదు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదన తప్పుదారి పట్టిస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, ఒక ఫుట్ ఓవర్బ్రిడ్జిపై “Diyandi Festival” అనే పదాలతో ఉన్న హోర్డింగ్ కనిపించింది. దీని గురించి వెతికితే, ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో ప్రతి సంవత్సరం సెప్టెంబర్లో దియాండి పండుగను జరుపుకుంటారని తెలిసింది. నగర సంరక్షకుడైన సెయింట్ మైఖేల్ ఆర్చ్ఏంజెల్ గౌరవార్థం నిర్వహించే ఈ పండుగ సెప్టెంబర్ 29న ముగుస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోలో “Shann Gadget” అనే పేరుతో ఉన్న బోర్డులను కూడా గమనించాం. గూగుల్ మ్యాప్స్లో వెతకగా, ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో రోక్సాస్ అవెన్యూలో, గైసానో సిటీ సూపర్మాల్కు ఎదురుగా ఈ దుకాణం ఉన్నట్లు తెలిసింది.
గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూలో పరిశీలించగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపించే ప్రదేశానికి, స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ చిత్రాల్లోని ప్రదేశానికి మధ్య పలు పోలికలు కనిపించాయి. దీంతో ఈ వీడియోను ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలోనే చిత్రీకరించినట్లు నిర్ధారించాం.
అయితే, ఈ వీడియోను ఖచ్చితంగా ఎప్పుడు చిత్రీకరించారు, ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారు అనే విషయాలను మేము గుర్తించలేకపోయాం. అందుబాటులో ఉన్న ఆధారాల ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియోను ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో చిత్రీకరించారు. దీనికి ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన నిరసనలకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు.
చివరిగా, ఫిలిప్పీన్స్కు చెందిన ఒక సంబంధం లేని వీడియోను, ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనల వీడియోగా తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు

Speciality chemical manufacturing startup Scimplify has raised $25 Mn (around ₹238 Cr) in a fresh funding round led by Hitachi Ventures, the venture capital arm of Japan's Hitachi Group. The round also saw participation from existing backers such as Accel, Bertelsmann India Investments, 3one4 Capital and Omnivore. New investors including Teknor Apex, Henkel and an undisclosed Japanese chemical company also joined the round. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its research, processing and manufacturing capabilities across rare earth and critical metals purification. The funds will also go towards scaling its semiconductor chemicals and battery chemicals businesses. A chunk of the capital will also be used to strengthen SciNode, Scimplify’s agentic AI platform that connects research, process development, control and physical manufacturing. Founded in 2023 by Sachin Santhosh, Salil Srivastava, Dheeraj Dhingra and Hersh Manek, Scimplify is a B2B platform that specialises in end-to-end sourcing and manufacturing of speciality chemicals. It also offers contract research and commercial chemical manufacturing for agro-chemicals, active pharmaceutical ingredients and fragrances. The startup currently operates R&D facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, with its SciNode software platform supporting its manufacturing operations. Its network comprises more than 500 manufacturing partners and thousands of scientists and technical partners. Prior to this, Scimplify had secured $40 Mn in its Series B funding round, co-led by Accel and Bertelsmann Investments, in March last year. “In the 18 months since our initial investment, Scimplify has grown from serving 600+ customers across 16 countries to building a global platform with 1,000+ customers across 40+ countries,” Accel partner Rachit Parekh said. Scimplify's customers include Henkel, Coromandel, Dr Reddy's, Coherent, Holcim, BASF, Sanyo, Marubeni, among others. The startup claims to operate across five countries and serves more than 1,000 customers across over 40 countries. Going forward, Scimplify plans to expand its presence in the US, initially focusing on sectors where domestic processing capabilities remain limited. These will include rare earth and critical metals purification and processing as well as high-purity semiconductor and battery chemicals. Scimplify's latest fundraise comes as India looks to strengthen its position in the global chemicals value chain. Earlier this week, Bengaluru-based speciality chemicals startup NuSynth Technologies raised ₹36.5 Cr in a seed round co-led by Avaana Capital and Shastra VC. Scimplify operates in the broader Indian deeptech sector, which continues to draw investor attention on the back of regulatory push, subsidies, innovative local solutions, a thriving talent pool and growing local demand. Overall, Indian deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals in Q3 2026, a 176% increase from $105 Mn across 29 deals in the year-ago period. The sector outpaced the broader Indian startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn.

During my 10+ years of clinical experience in various States and with numerous patient populations, I have seen that dental anxiety is a constant challenge. I have seen this phenomenon in children clutching their parents’ hands before their first cleaning and in accomplished professionals quietly cancelling appointment after appointment in the hope that the problem will somehow resolve itself.
It doesn’t.
In my experience, the longer you leave a fear unchecked, the greater the clinical and human cost becomes. Dental anxiety is not a moral failing. This is a well-documented psychological response—and one with important, measurable public health consequences.
How severe is it?
Roughly a third of people have significant dental anxiety, and roughly a tenth have a clinical phobia. That’s not a little footnote. That means a lot of the population is actively avoiding or delaying care that could prevent serious disease. The downstream consequences of this avoidance are visible daily in my clinical work: infections tolerated for months, decay advanced far beyond what early intervention would have required, and patients presenting with pain that could have been prevented years ago.
Knowing where it starts
Dental anxiety typically has a definite source. A painful or poorly done procedure in childhood can be a source of dental anxiety. A provider who was in a hurry or didn’t tell the patient what was happening. The specific sensory environment of a dental office—the sounds, the smells, and the physical vulnerability of lying back with your mouth open—can leave powerful imprints, especially in young patients. That memory is not just wiped out; it impacts behaviour for decades. For some, it’s not just one event but an accumulation. Years of avoidance layered on top of embarrassment about how their teeth look now, and a fear of judgment prevents them from asking for help. This cycle of shame avoidance is one of the hardest patterns I see clinically. When these patients do come in, they need much more intervention than if they had come in sooner, and this becomes an instance of the very fear that kept them away.
The health price of avoidance
Research literature teaches us, that oral health is not an island. Untreated dental disease is a chronic inflammatory load on the body. It has been linked to cardiovascular risk, dysregulated blood sugar, and impaired immune function. When a patient avoids dental care for years, it is not just their smile that is at risk; they are carrying a preventable health load that will rise elsewhere in time.
In addition to the system effects, the impact on quality of life is immediate and real. A toothache interferes with sleep. It impacts nutrition, concentration, and the ability to speak with confidence. These are not trivial consequences; they affect how people show up in their professional and personal lives every day.
What works in practice
The most significant change I’ve made in my practice is making communication a priority before any procedure begins. When patients feel informed and in control, it greatly reduces their dental anxiety. A stop signal—a raised hand that stops everything instantly—can alter the psychological dynamic in the room. It shifts the patient from passive recipient to active participant, and that shift matters enormously. I also allow extra time for anxious patients. The problem is not that procedures take longer, but that rushing them increases anxiety. I explain everything before it happens, check in frequently, and never minimise what a patient is feeling. These should not be luxury accommodations; they should be routine parts of effective care.
For patients with more severe anxiety, pharmacological support is appropriate. Nitrous oxide is safe, effective, and rapidly reversible. There are also oral sedation choices if needed. These are clinical tools, not last resorts, and patients should feel comfortable asking about them.
A message to patients
If fear has kept you from the dentist, remember you are not alone, and you are not too far gone to be helped. What I ask of patients in this situation is one small step—not a treatment plan, not a procedure, simply a conversation. Come in and tell us about your nervousness. A good provider is a good listener and will start there. There is no need to be afraid of the dental chair. With the right approach, it can be a place where you take difficult things and make them manageable—and where the relief on the other side is worth it.
(Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula is a U.S.-licensed dentist with international training who focuses on preventive and evidence-based oral healthcare and contributes to advancing community and public health dentistry. sowji.gunukula@gmail.com)

A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they’re estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth’s environment, most proteins don’t last nearly that long. That’s because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment.
Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases.
Cutting proteins
The basic peptide bond isn’t especially interesting-looking—it’s what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)
Peptide bonds are formed by the removal of a water molecule from parts of an amino group and an acidic group.

Breaking these bonds apart simply reverses the process by breaking apart the peptide bond and a water molecule, and linking their parts. Because both components are chemically stable, the reaction requires an enzyme to occur with any frequency. Without an enzyme, a typical peptide bond would be stable for hundreds of years in water.
Life has evolved a handful of enzyme mechanisms that manage this catalysis. The research at issue here relied on two different ones. One is a zinc protease, where the positive charge of the zinc atom coordinates the peptide bond that’s being broken, key parts of the protease, and a water molecule. The protease partially pulls a proton off the water molecule, activating it to attack and break up the peptide bond.
The second protease the researchers use is called a cysteine protease. In this case, a cysteine (one of the amino acids) in the enzyme is activated to attack the peptide bond, creating a temporary intermediate where part of the protein being cut is chemically linked to the enzyme. A water molecule eventually breaks this intermediate apart, releasing the second part of the cut protein.
Both of these mechanisms require a handful of specific amino acids from the protease to be located in close proximity within the catalytic center of the protease. Other amino acids in the protease help ensure these key catalytic amino acids are brought together in the right place with the right orientation. The rest of the protease may also enforce a degree of specificity on what proteins get cut. Some proteases, like the ones active in our digestive system, can make cuts next to any amino acid. Others are slightly more selective, preferring to cut near positively or negatively charged amino acids. And a few are very highly specific, such as the protease that activates insulin, which only cuts near a very specific series of amino acids.
Designer enzymes
The people behind the new work, primarily from Nobel-winner David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, viewed designing a protease as a challenge. For one, the stability of the peptide bonds means that reactions wouldn’t take place without an effective catalyst. And to get that catalyst requires an extremely precise arrangement of specific amino acids. So it wasn’t obvious that the AI protein design tools the lab developed were up to the task.
Both projects took a similar approach. Just like evolution, they started with an existing protease. One was a zinc protease used in a crayfish’s digestive system. The other was a cysteine protease from yeast. In both cases, the protein structure was known, as were the key amino acids that catalyze cleaving other proteins. The design process started with these amino acids.
The design process started with software called RFdiffusion2, which creates a backbone for the enzyme (the backbone consists of the protein’s repeated peptide bonds). The researchers gave RFdiffusion2 a number of constraints. To start, any backbone it designed had to bring together the key catalytic amino acids needed for a functional protease. They also gave it a target amino acid sequence where the protease would eventually cut. The backbone had to accommodate that target sequence in close proximity to the catalytic center.
With a backbone laid out, the process next moved to ProteinMPNN, a tool that works along the backbone, populating it with specific amino acids. (That tool featured in Google’s efforts to watermark AI-designed proteins.) ProteinMPNN selects each amino acid based on a series of constraints. For starters, the amino acid must be compatible with the backbone folding up into its planned structure. Next, in critical areas, each amino acid chosen needs to be compatible with the formation of the enzyme’s catalytic site. And finally, in nearby areas, it has to be compatible with latching on to the intended target.
The researchers repeated this process dozens of times for both the cysteine and zinc proteases. For the cysteine protease, they made 12 different backbones and populated them with 69 different sets of amino acids. For the zinc project, they tried 135 different protein designs. They used AlphaFold3 to predict the structures of many of these designs and found nothing in the databases that looked much like them, confirming their tools weren’t simply stealing previously identified structures.
Do they work?
The researchers started by making a single, long protein that contained the protease, the sequence it was designed to target, and a fluorescent protein. They then tested to see if the fluorescent protein was cut loose. In the case of the cysteine protease, they got 13 designs that worked, a success rate of 19 percent, although all of them were considerably less active than the yeast enzyme that was used as a model.
The zinc project was a bit more complicated. They tested many designs that didn’t include the water molecule that normally takes part in that reaction. These had a relatively low success rate, with only 14 out of 89 showing weak catalytic activity. When they modeled the ones that didn’t work, they found that the designs often let a water molecule block the site where reactions should take place.
So, they also tried designs where they placed a water molecule in the right location as an additional design constraint. These had a much higher success rate, with 35 out of 38 showing some catalytic activity. Again, however, their activity was considerably lower than the enzyme that was used as the starting point for the designs. (They did get one design with a better level of activity, but it wasn’t specific about where it cut other proteins.)
To find out whether this activity could be improved, the researchers identified amino acids that were in close proximity to the active site of the protease, but not actively involved with the catalysis. And they swapped in every alternative amino acid that wasn’t predicted to disrupt the structure of the design. They found some versions that were considerably more active; the best version they identified accelerated the cleavage of the peptide bond by a factor of 109 while remaining highly specific for the intended target protein sequence.
Similar things happened with the zinc-based protease. Their v2 version of their protease, which incorporated some of the random mutations, was 30 times more active than the original design it was based on. It also accelerated peptide-bond cleavage by a factor of 1010.
As a final demonstration of this approach’s promise, the researchers designed zinc proteases that could target proteins associated with neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer’s and frontotemporal dementia. Attempting to modify their existing design to target a new sequence didn’t work well, so they started the process over from the start and managed to find something that could cut the intended target in cells. For the researchers, this suggests that we might ultimately be able to influence the course of some genetic diseases by targeting the malformed proteins that cause them.
What do the results tell us?
The potential therapeutic use of this is complicated. Proteins are often difficult to deliver to the site where they’re needed, and can often trigger an immune response. Things get even more challenging if the protease target is inside a cell rather than on the exterior. That would likely require the target cells to make the protease, which would involve delivering the gene encoding it to the cells where it’s needed. So, there are considerable hurdles that would need to be cleared before we could potentially start developing therapies using this technology.
The researchers also highlight how the work shows some limitations of the tools. As used, they successfully designed proteins that matched all the physical constraints they were given: They folded up into structures that brought the amino acids needed to catalyze a reaction into roughly the right location, and latched on to specific target amino acid sequences.
But we don’t, at the moment, have the ability to tell these tools we want any specific catalytic activity. So many designs lacked some of the subtle details that make evolved enzymes such great catalysts. In other words, the tools are great at structure, but they’re not necessarily great at activity. And, while structure is essential for function, it isn’t everything. As the researchers saw, introducing random mutation could still make subtle structural tweaks that produced enzymes that were considerably more active.
Of course, this protein design software is only a few years old, and both developers and users might have ideas for incorporating constraints beyond physical location.

The resources minister, Madeleine King, is facing calls to correct her claim in a major speech that all greenhouse gas emissions from developing a massive fossil fuel basin in the Northern Territory will be offset to limit their impact on the climate.
Speaking at the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday, King defended her support for the development of the Beetaloo gas basin south of Darwin after being asked if she was comfortable with the impact that the emissions from the gas would have on Australians.
King was photographed laughing alongside the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, as they celebrated the first gas being pumped from the basin last month. The minister told the press club the basin was a “very important resource” for the NT and to help supply gas to Australia’s east coast and export markets.
She said it was being developed after a “landmark scientific study” in 2018 into whether fracking should be allowed in the territory. Known as the Pepper inquiry, that government-commissioned investigation made 135 recommendations, including that the NT and Australian governments should aim to ensure that any onshore shale gas developments did not increase the country’s total emissions.
In practice, that would require any climate pollution from gas developments – from extraction, processing, transport and the fuel’s use – to be fully offset through the purchase of carbon credits.
King told the press club that the NT government “took up and implemented” the inquiry’s recommendations. “My understanding from those recommendations is that the emissions are accounted for and offset, but I would have to check that,” she said.
The NT government does not require emissions from Beetaloo basin to be offset. The Guardian revealed that the previous Labor territory government dropped the requirement after the gas industry objected. The Country Liberal party government maintained that position when elected in 2024.
Some emissions from gas developments in the NT will need to be offset under a federal climate policy, the safeguard mechanism, that is applied to operations that emit more than 100,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. But that applies only to pollution directly from the facility, not the full lifecycle emissions as recommended by the Pepper inquiry.
King told the press club the safeguard mechanism would be applied to Beetaloo basin developments if emissions were above the threshold. “That is how we manage dealing with emissions in this country,” she said.
But research by Tim Baxter, of the consultancy Naru Research, found about 95% of emissions expected from four gas projects in the Beetaloo basin this decade would not have to be offset.
Baxter said King either “isn’t across her brief or she’s being intentionally misleading”.
“The Pepper inquiry was clear. For the territory to begin to manage the risks of fracking and unconventional gas in the NT all emissions occurring in Australia must be fully offset,” he said.
“The safeguard mechanism does not deliver this … If NT fracking is detonated, it could single-handedly undo all efforts to cut Australia’s climate emissions.”
Kirsty Howey, a former head of Environment Centre NT, now leading the Wilderness Society, said governments had broken a promise to fully act on the recommendations of the Pepper inquiry. “It’s one of the greatest failures of climate policy in history,” she said.
The acting chief head of Environment Centre NT, Bree Ahrens, called on the minister to “correct the public record”. She said an estimate by the energy company Santos suggested if the Beetaloo basin was fully developed and its gas burned it could lead to emissions 60 times what Australia releases into the atmosphere each year.
“Frackers are being given a free pass on climate emissions, and it’s the territory that will pay the price,” she said.
A spokesperson for King said successive NT governments had “accepted and implemented all 135 recommendations of the Pepper review”. They said the safeguard mechanism required all shale gas facilities, including Beetaloo basin gas extraction facilities, to have net zero emissions if they emitted more than 100,000 tonnes of CO2 a year.

Four workers killed in explosion at chemical manufacturing unit in Gujarat’s Gandhinagar
Four workers killed in an explosion at chemical manufacturing unit in Chhatral GIDC in Gujarat’s Gandhinagar district, Gandhinagar SP Ravi Teja Vasamsetty said.
Four workers were killed in an explosion at a chemical manufacturing unit in Chhatral GIDC in Gujarat’s Gandhinagar district on Thursday afternoon, Gandhinagar SP Ravi Teja Vasamsetty said.
The incident occurred at Kovika Dyes and Intermediates in Phase 4 of the industrial estate when workers were fitting a pipe to a pressure vessel containing chemicals, according to police officials.
Kovika Dyes is a Gujarat-based manufacturer and exporter of synthetic organic chemicals, acid dyes, direct dyes and dye intermediates.
The deceased workers were identified as Vinodkumar Singh (42), Teda Dehari (18) and Sikandar Lakhan Dehari (40), all residents of Jharkhand, and Laxman Meena from Udaipur.
According to preliminary findings, the workers were fitting a pipe to a hot pressure vessel containing chemicals when one of the connecting pipes exploded, causing the casualties, officers said.
The explosion was so powerful that the four workers near the vessel were seriously injured and died on the spot, an officer said.
Although the exact cause of the explosion is not yet known, initial investigations indicate that it may have been caused by excessive pressure build-up inside the vessel.
Police are investigating the cause of the explosion, including whether it resulted from a mechanical failure, a chemical reaction during pipe fitting or a failure to follow safety procedures. Forensic officers are examining the site to establish the sequence of events and determine whether safety norms were followed.

New Delhi: India's Department of Pharmaceuticals has invited applications for the second round of its Promotion of Research and Innovation in Pharma & MedTech (PRIP) scheme, offering startups and micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) up to ₹50 crore each for new drug discovery, the government said on Thursday. The PRIP scheme has a total financial outlay of ₹5,000 crore, which includes ₹700 crore to establish Centers of Excellence (CoEs) at seven National Institutes of Pharmaceutical Education & Research (NIPERs), and ₹4,200 crore to accelerate investments in the R&D ecosystem within the sector. The initiative will operate until the financial year 2029–30. Highlighting the purpose of this second round of funding, the government said, “The second call offers a fresh opportunity for eligible industry, startups and MSMEs to undertake high-potential research and innovation in the pharmaceutical and MedTech sectors.” “The second call covers three priority areas: new medicines—including new chemical entities (NCEs), new biological entities (NBEs) and phytopharmaceutical drugs; complex generics and biosimilars; and novel medical devices," the government said in a statement. The first call under PRIP, announced on 30 September 2026, approved approximately ₹1,600 crore in financial assistance for 41 innovation projects. This grant is expected to draw ₹3,020 crore in private co-funding, mobilizing an estimated ₹4,620 crore in total R&D investment across pharma and MedTech. The newly-added Discovery Track in the second round was created to address funding shortfalls that small firms encounter during the transition from basic laboratory research to advanced experimental stages. Highlighting the distinct focus of this new window, the government said, “While the early stage track provides support for a wider range of early-stage PRIP projects, the new discovery track is specifically structured to provide larger and sustained support for indigenous NCE and NBE drug-discovery programmes, while bringing institutional capital into the development pathway.” According to the department, this track supports early-stage drug creation involving chemical and biological entities, assisting their progress up to advanced prototype and animal testing stages. To receive this grant, applicant companies must secure a minimum of 25% of their total project expenditure from bona fide institutional investors. Alongside the Discovery Track, the department has structured the second call into two other funding tiers determined by the technical maturity of each project. The early stage track is open to startups and smaller enterprises working on early laboratory research across all three priority sectors. This track offers financial aid of up to ₹5 crore per project to help technologies reach the prototype stage. For projects with an approved cost of up to ₹1 crore, the government provides the entire amount without requiring financial contributions from the applicant. If the project budget exceeds ₹1 crore, the applicant must contribute half of the amount that sits above that limit. The later stage track is accessible to larger industry players, startups, and smaller enterprises that already possess working prototypes or early experimental data. This track offers support of up to ₹100 crore per project to help candidates progress through formal testing stages. The department caps funding under this tier at 35% of the approved total project cost, leaving the applicant responsible for funding the remaining 65%. The department stated that applicants must ensure that the developmental goals and targets of their proposals can be achieved within the scheme's lifespan, which concludes in 2029–30. Projects that require a longer overall development cycle remain eligible to apply, but funding will cover only the milestones scheduled for completion before the end of the term. The department set 10 November 2026 as the final submission date for all applications under the second call. A dedicated committee will review and evaluate incoming submissions on a regular schedule based on verified evidence of project readiness, development timelines, and compliance with the co-funding criteria outlined in the official guidelines. Kipchoge, 41, breaks course record at Melbourne Marathon
- Published
Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge says "his body is still peaking" after winning the Melbourne Marathon in a course record time at the age of 41.
The Kenyan crossed the line in two hours nine minutes 10 seconds for his 17th career win over the distance and first since the Berlin Marathon in 2023.
"I believe that my body is still peaking - still able to compete with the next generation," Kipchoge said.
"The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs."
The course was partly raced along the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).
"On the course, it was really wonderful, I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering, and shouting my name," added Kipchoge, who slowed down inside the MCG to wave to the fans.
"It was actually different - running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground.
"It makes me proud to run with the younger generation and inspire the running community in Melbourne."
Australian Thomas do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35, with compatriot Reece Edwards third.
New Zealand's Camille French won the women's race in 2:28:25, followed by Australian Sinead Diver and Nichola Sheridan of Ireland.
The Melbourne Marathon was the third leg on Kipchoge's world tour, on which he hopes to complete a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years.
Each marathon will raise funds for the Eliud Kipchoge Foundation, which focuses on education, environmental sustainability and health.
Kipchoge is considered one of the greatest long-distance runners of all time, winning two Olympic marathon golds, plus a silver and bronze over 5000m.
His honours also include a world title, 12 World Marathon Major victories and two official world records.
In 2019 he became the first person to break the two-hour marathon barrier under special conditions in Vienna, clocking an unofficial time of one hour 59 minutes 40 seconds.
