Even as the Centre informed the Supreme Court on Monday (October 12, 2026) that it had decided to cap trade margins at 30% for non-scheduled cancer drugs, the court questioned why the benefit of such price regulation should be confined to cancer drugs and not extended to other essential medicines and medical products.
The development comes after a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta expressed concern over stark disparities between the price to retailer (PTR) and the maximum retail price (MRP) of certain medicines, particularly cancer drugs, with mark-ups in some instances soaring to 1,000%. The Bench had flagged that such exorbitant mark-ups constituted “broad daylight dacoity” and placed an enormous financial burden on patients.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, informed the Bench that the proposed 30% trade-margin cap would cover both patented and non-patented cancer medicines, with an expert committee headed by the Director General of Health Services tasked with identifying the drugs to be brought within its ambit. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) will examine the committee’s recommendations before issuing a price notification to implement the cap.
The Bench, however, said that while the intervention was commendable, it was inadequate, and questioned why other medicines and medical devices could not also be brought within the 16% retailer margin prescribed under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013.
“This is just the tip of the iceberg... this has come around only because of the unduly hard observations we made during earlier hearings. What about other drugs,” the Bench asked.
The top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha seeking stricter enforcement of price controls under the DPCO to curb disproportionate margins across the pharmaceutical supply chain.
Justice Mehta drew attention to steep markups on medical devices and consumables, pointing out that an India-made cardiac stent costing around ₹5,000 was being sold by hospitals for more than ₹25,000. He cited the example of a saline drip line carrying an MRP of ₹11 being sold for ₹270.
“We understand that there are transportation costs, raw material costs, R&D costs and other ancillary costs, but all these are included in the MRP. What is the logic behind allowing them to sell at 400 times the actual cost? How can you allow this? What is the benefit for the patients?” the Bench observed.
‘Balance in pricing’
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, also appearing for the Centre, cautioned against a uniform cap across medicines, arguing that low-value products often required higher margins to remain commercially viable for retailers. Excessive regulation, she said, could discourage retailers from stocking such medicines and affect their availability, particularly in rural areas.
Ms. Bhati stressed the need to preserve some room for market forces rather than subject the entire pharmaceutical sector to price controls.
“Higher margins in such cases are important for ensuring the availability of such medicines to consumers… Our concern is that there has to be a balance in pricing. There has to be some level of market play available for drugs. We do not want to control the entire ecosystem of drugs. The policy was framed with the outlook that there should be intervention only when necessary,” she submitted.
The Bench, however, was not persuaded, observing that ensuring the availability of price-controlled medicines was the government’s responsibility.
“If the DPCO -approved medicines do not reach customers, then it is the duty of the government to ensure it reaches [sic] the patient. The actual dispute is over which medicines should be on the DPCO-controlled list and which should not,” Justice Mehta observed.
Accordingly, the Bench gave the Centre until October 27 to work out the modalities for capping medicine prices, when the matter will be heard next.
Centre’s affidavit
The Centre, in its 551-page affidavit, said the proposed trade-margin rationalisation (TMR) was expected to reduce the MRP of anti-cancer drugs by 20% to 70%, translating into estimated annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore. It said the measure would reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure and improve the affordability and accessibility of cancer medicines, while retaining a 30% trade margin for the distribution chain.
The Centre cited a similar intervention by the NPPA in 2019, when a 30% trade-margin cap was imposed at the first point of sale on 42 select non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines. The margin was based on an industry-practice assumption of 10% for distributors and 20% for retailers.
The measure, it said, led to a substantial reduction in the MRP of 526 brands and annual savings of around ₹984 crore for patients, based on information furnished by pharmaceutical companies. The Centre said the 2019 exercise provided a policy and operational precedent for extending trade-margin rationalisation to a wider range of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines.
Detailing the existing price-control mechanism, the Centre said the ceiling price of medicines listed in Schedule I of the DPCO is determined by taking the simple average of the price to retailer of brands and generic versions with a market share of at least 1%, and adding a 16% margin.
“The ceiling price so fixed becomes the MRP, i.e., the price above which the drug cannot be sold in the market. However, the manufacturer is at liberty to give an appropriate margin to the wholesaler and the retailer within the ceiling price,” it said, adding that ceiling prices had so far been fixed for 935 formulations.
For non-scheduled formulations, manufacturers are free to determine the initial launch price, subject to the NPPA’s regulation of subsequent price increases. The Centre said competition in the pharmaceutical market generally acted as a restraint against arbitrary pricing.

If you have young kids or if you know somebody who does, then you know about YouTube’s AI slop problem.
Videos targeted at children on the platform are often filled with bizarre and hyperstimulating content that’s AI generated. Not all of it is age-appropriate. These videos autoplay on endless, algorithmically curated streams punctuated by ads.
Maka, a new streaming app for kids aged 0 to 6, is positioning itself as an antidote to that concern. The platform has zero ads, doesn’t allow autoplay or endless scrolling, and its algorithms intentionally do not maximize watch time.
The company’s cofounder and chief product officer Tanyella Leta tells WIRED the platform is purposely abandoning the mechanisms that “turn children’s media into an engagement machine.”
Maka’s CEO and cofounder Isabel Sheinman adds that a lot of the streamers were built to serve adults, not children. “Kids were really the afterthought,” she says. Sheinman wants to set a much higher bar for what quality looks like in children’s media, which she says has been warped by harmful incentives. “Maka was built with child development science and children's behavior first and foremost.”
Launching today, Maka’s programming slate is a mix of licensed content from global studios and independent creators. It features 25 shows in its curated catalog, including Franklin, The Wiggles, Pocoyo, Vida the Vet and Sesame Street. The platform runs on a subscription service, with a $15 monthly plan and a $107 annual plan.
It was during the Covid pandemic that Sheinman and Leta became obsessed with thinking about how to redesign kids' media. The solution? Every episode streamed on Maka is evaluated by child development experts through Imprint, a framework created with researchers at the Yale Child Study Center. The evaluation process, which examines everything from scene cuts to how fast-paced content is, maps adolescent development across seven core domains. It looks for things like emotional regulation, kindness, how child-caregiver relationships are modeled in a story, and how a story might support critical thinking or language development.
AI-generated content has only added a new wrinkle to kids’ entertainment: videos are incoherent, have no plot, or contain outright misinformation, but are packaged to look like learning. Some of it, as WIRED has previously reported, is disturbingly sexualized, featuring gore and other fetishes.
Michael Robb, director of research at the media literacy nonprofit Common Sense Media, says that on a platform like YouTube, slop videos that have the veneer of education sit side by side with carefully designed educational shows. Robb says YouTube and other kids’ streaming platforms have not done enough to distinguish educational content from slop, which has only made filtering content harder for parents. “Platforms have taken steps to reduce kids’ exposure to age-inappropriate content, and that matters. But ‘not inappropriate’ is a very low bar. There’s a big gulf between that and media created intentionally with kids in mind.”
A 2020 study by Common Sense Media on YouTube videos watched by young kids found 75 percent had “weak or no educational value.” Kids also frequently ended up watching ads and content intended for older audiences.
According to its policy for YouTube Kids, which lets parents approve specific content themselves, YouTube excludes videos that are “deceptive, sensational, or clickbait,” but acknowledges that not every video has been manually reviewed. YouTube also makes clear that automated filtering cannot guarantee every video will be appropriate. “There’s a chance that your child will find content that you don't want them to watch,” the company notes in its support docs.
Earlier this year, in an effort to encourage better digital literacy among kids, the American Academy of Pediatrics updated its guidance beyond screen time recommendations, urging children to avoid “AI-generated content,” “AI chatbots,” “short-form videos,” and “highly sensationalized content or clickbait.” The guide prioritized quality content and coviewing with parents rather than passive watching.
Tiffany Munzer, a developmental-behavioral pediatrician and digital media researcher at the University of Michigan, was the lead author on AAP’s “Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents” policy statement, and tells WIRED in an email that the proliferation of low-quality content has led kids to “miss out on important, slower learning opportunities that promote critical thinking, generate new ideas, and practice stretching their attention spans.”
In April, child advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter, signed by more than 200 organizations and individual experts, asking YouTube to address the spread of AI videos on its platforms, saying AI slop “harms children’s development by distorting their sense of reality, overwhelming their learning processes and hijacking their attention.”
A YouTube spokesperson tells WIRED that on YouTube Kids, which is meant for kids 12 and under, AI content is limited to a small set of high-quality channels, and parents have the option to block channels entirely. The platform has stricter standards for content made for younger viewers, the company says.
For Maka’s business model to succeed, its shows will need to entertain and educate kids while also establishing confidence in parents. “The value that parents want is relief, knowing that what their child is seeing has been vetted by child development experts and everything on Maka they can trust is good for their kid,” Sheiman says.
Yalda Uhls, a former film executive at Sony and MGM who is now a researcher at UCLA focusing on how media affects the social learning of young children, worries that as AI revolutionizes kids’ streaming content, people who study child development are being left out of the process. “When I was a studio executive, every story meant for children passed through layers of accountable adults,” she says. “But today, algorithms, anonymous creators, and AI tools shape what kids see, and people who study child development are rarely in the room.”
“The gatekeepers have been replaced by a metric, minutes watched,” Uhls says. “Nobody in that chain is required to ask what a child is actually learning.”
One of Maka’s core features is a timer that parents set at the start of every viewing session to help the child wind down off the screen. As the show concludes, a character Maka developed named Scoot appears on the screen to get the child ready to detach from their device. Features like that are the difference between capturing a child’s attention versus earning it, Sheinman says. “So it becomes less of a moment of tension in a family and a moment that the child is prepared for.”
The founders ultimately want Maka to help change the perception of kids' relationship to screens.
“We’re seeing a really big challenge around the judgment of parents,” says Leta, explaining that one problem with screen time is the demonization of parents who rely on it. “We have all judged parents who bring out the screen on the train or at a restaurant. Let's be real, most parents will reach for the screen at some point. We don't think that they should be judged for that choice.”
Whether any of this will work is unclear. One question at the core of Maka’s mission is whether it can build a successful streaming company without adopting the same incentives that created the problems it is trying to solve.
Robb from Common Sense Media calls competing with YouTube a Herculean task. “YouTube is free and already on the devices within their homes. Moving them away can be tricky,” he says. The real test for Maka, Robb says, “will be whether it can grow with kids and stay sustainable without being pulled back toward the engagement metrics that drive the rest of the industry.”
Leta, one of Maka’s cofounders, admits that it’s easy to be cynical when it comes to children and screens. “But TV also gave us Sesame Street. It gave us Fred Rogers who believed that the space between the child and the screen was sacred ground.”
“One of the dads in our beta told us that with other platforms, when his kid is watching, it feels like ‘a race to the bottom of my kid’s brainstem,’” Leta says. “It doesn't have to be like that.”

Schools and libraries from around the US pleaded with the Federal Communications Commission to drop the idea of ending E-Rate, a $2 billion-a-year program that connects students and library visitors to the Internet.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has criticized school districts for having “experimented with a massive increase in screen time for students,” and said E-Rate expanded too far beyond its original purpose of “supporting basic Internet access to schools and libraries for educational purposes.” In June, Carr led a 2-1 vote to issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) seeking public comment on whether E-Rate should be “limited or sunset to reflect today’s extensive connectivity rates.”
Carr’s proposal could result in E-Rate cutting the discounts that schools and libraries receive for telecom services and equipment, and imposing more restrictions on how E-Rate money can be used. The FCC seeking comment on whether to sunset the program also raises the possibility that Carr might choose to axe E-Rate entirely.
The National Association of Elementary School Principals told the FCC that it “strongly supports the continued operation of the E-Rate program and urges the Commission to reject proposals that would eliminate, substantially restrict, or impose new conditions on this essential source of connectivity assistance for schools and libraries.”
The Carr FCC already scaled E-Rate back last year by ending funding for schools and libraries to lend out Wi-Fi hotspots and for Wi-Fi service on school buses.
FCC authority to kill program in dispute
The FCC docket received comments this week opposing the proposal from state and national associations, and from many individual schools and libraries. The American Library Association told the FCC that E-Rate is working as Congress intended it to when it passed the 1996 telecommunications law that resulted in E-Rate’s creation.
“Importantly, the FCC does not have the authority to terminate the E-Rate program. The E-Rate program is mandated by Congress, and the FCC is responsible for administering it,” the national library group said.
If Carr goes through with eliminating E-Rate, he may argue that its original mission has been completed and that the FCC therefore has authority to end it.
“In establishing the program in 1996, Congress was addressing a specific problem: limited access to advanced telecommunications and Internet services in schools and libraries,” Carr’s proposal said. “Given the substantial expansion of broadband access in schools and libraries over the last three decades, we seek comment on whether and to what extent the E-Rate program has fulfilled that mission and whether continued funding is consistent with Congress’s original objective.”
There are other questions about FCC authority raised by the proceeding. For example, the American Library Association said “the FCC lacks the authority and expertise to regulate screen time or determine educational outcomes.”
The group’s filing pointed out that under US law, determinations about what content is inappropriate for children “shall be made by the school board, local educational agency, library, or other authority responsible for making the determination.” The law says the US government may not establish criteria for making those decisions or review the decisions made by local schools and libraries.
Texas and New York library groups agree
The Texas Library Association told the FCC that E-Rate should be giving more money to libraries to help them raise broadband speeds to modern standards. The group also said public libraries in the state have implemented appropriate supervision and filtering for the Internet services they offer library users.
“Only 35 percent of Texas public libraries currently receive E-Rate discounts, compared with 65 percent of public libraries nationwide, and only 55 percent meet the Commission’s own recommended broadband speed benchmarks,” the group said. “A gap this size, in the nation’s second-most populous state, is evidence of unmet need working through real obstacles—not evidence that the need has passed.”
The New York Library Association told the FCC that “E-Rate is essential for reliable broadband speeds and for regular network maintenance, safety, and security. The library can’t operate without the Internet. If the FCC terminates or limits E-Rate funding, many of New York’s libraries will be forced to reduce programs and services in order to continue providing Internet access.”
The American Indian Higher Education Consortium told the FCC that it should relax E-Rate’s eligibility restrictions and provide more funding for schools. It said that supporting Tribal colleges and universities is “one of the most cost-efficient ways the federal government can endeavor to uphold its treaty and trust obligations to Tribal Nations and Tribal citizens, while simultaneously benefiting the nation as a whole.”
A filing by the Alabama Association of School Boards urged the FCC to “preserve and strengthen the E-Rate program and to reject any proposal that would eliminate, sunset, substantially reduce, or unnecessarily restrict E-Rate support for schools and libraries.” The group said concerns about excessive screen use “should not be addressed by reducing the broadband infrastructure that students and teachers need for legitimate educational purposes.”
Principal tells FCC his school needs E-Rate
The FCC received specific examples of how E-Rate helps local communities. “We estimate our annual Internet cost at approximately $3,120 and our annual E-Rate support at approximately $1,560,” Paul Lapka, the principal of Rock Valley Christian School in Iowa, told the US agency. “E-Rate support allows us to maintain reliable, high-speed Internet and network equipment. If support were reduced, we would face higher local costs, delayed network upgrades, and pressure to redirect funds from other school priorities.”
Were the FCC to end E-Rate, schools and libraries would no longer be able to purchase new equipment and broadband service, which would upset broadband providers.
“The widespread availability of broadband connectivity and service in schools and libraries is an important E-Rate achievement, not a reason to withdraw support for the connectivity on which those institutions continue to rely,” the FCC was told by America’s Communications Association, a cable industry lobby group. “Schools and libraries must continue to pay for broadband service, maintain and replace internal network equipment, and upgrade capacity as their needs evolve.”
The Schools, Health & Libraries Broadband Coalition (SHLB) called it “disheartening and surprising that the Commission in the current proceeding asks questions that run directly counter to the goals of universal service and Congress’s directives. While most of the country and world are racing ahead to prepare for the future facing our nation’s citizens and students, the Commission is asking whether it should shelve or significantly reduce the E-Rate program, which is the financial pillar supporting most schools’ and libraries’ digital connections.”
FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against Carr’s proposal in June, saying that E-Rate helps give children in low-income neighborhoods and rural communities “the same shot at a digital education as anyone else.” She criticized the FCC’s inquiry into screen time, saying that “policing children’s behavior in schools goes far beyond our stated mandate. The FCC is not the nation’s parent. It is not the nation’s teacher. And it is not the nation’s school board.”
E-Rate typically distributes over $2 billion a year. It has a funding cap of $5.2 billion, but actual payouts are based on demand and the application approval rate. E-Rate and other Universal Service Fund (USF) programs are paid for by fees imposed on phone companies, which usually pass the cost on to consumers on their monthly bills.
The deadline for the first round of comments passed yesterday, and reply comments may be submitted until November 12. After the comment period, Carr can present his final plan to either change or eliminate E-Rate. Given that Republicans have a 2-1 majority on the FCC, whatever Carr proposes is likely to be approved. But FCC decisions are often challenged in court on the grounds that the agency exceeded its authority.

Essential items to stock in your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Is your household ready if you get hit with a stomach bug tomorrow? Sniffles on Saturday? The flu in a month or two?
Life Kit
How to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season
In the United States, cold and flu season occurs in the fall and winter, starting in October and stretching all the way through May, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The combination of dropping temperatures and drier climates makes us more susceptible to common respiratory viruses like the common cold, the flu, RSV or COVID-19, and "back-to-back illnesses," says pediatrician Mona Amin.
Get ready now by creating a cold and flu prep kit. "Have things readily available so that you're not scrambling or depending on someone else to run to the drugstore for you when you become sick," says pharmacist Alisha Reed. That includes fever and pain relievers, hydration supplements and monitoring tools to help manage symptoms.
Many viruses and fevers can be managed at home, says Amin. And the common cold and the flu are viral infections, so they can't be treated by prescription antibiotics anyway.
Below, you'll find a list of items for the whole family, recommended by Amin and Reed. Put the products in one designated place, like a shelf in your medicine cabinet or a handy "sick day" box.
You'll also want to take preventative measures like disinfecting frequently touched surfaces, getting vaccinated and washing your hands. But remember, says Reed, no prevention strategy is foolproof.
What to include in your cold and flu prep kit
Over-the-counter medications
When you're dealing with cough, congestion, sore throat, fever, fatigue or other common cold and flu symptoms, you may be tempted to reach for a medication that hits multiple symptoms.
But those meds often include extra unnecessary ingredients that can sometimes put you at risk of accidentally overmedicating yourself, says Reed. Instead, opt for medications that target individual symptoms.
These items all come with a price tag, of course. So if you don't have something like a flexible spending account to help cover costs, consider purchasing your personal sick day must-haves to start, then building from there as you're able.
Reed and Amin suggest these medications:
Pain relievers. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen can help relieve pain and discomfort from headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation, says Reed.
- For kids: Don't use children's ibuprofen for children under 6 months old; naproxen is only approved for children 12 years and older.
Fever reducer. Medications like acetaminophen and ibuprofen can safely reduce body temperature, though acetaminophen is usually the better choice for fevers.
- For kids: Look for a children's version for 12 years and under. Be sure to follow this dosing chart when using children's acetaminophen.
- For pregnant people: Acetaminophen is the recommended OTC pain reliever for pregnant people, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
Antihistamine. Yes, the same thing you take for spring allergies! Colds and allergies have similar symptoms like sneezing, runny noses and watery eyes, which is why they can both be treated by a histamine-blocking medication that can help dry up your sinuses.
- For kids: Some OTC allergy medicines are approved for children as young as 6 months, but not all — and some have more side effects than others, says Amin. Check in with your care provider first if you have questions.
Decongestant. Pseudoephedrine pills or nasal spray can relieve a stuffy nose or sinus pressure by restricting blood vessels and opening airways in your nasal passages.
- For kids: Pills are not recommended for kids under 4 and medicated sprays are not recommended for kids under 6.
Cough suppressant for a dry cough. Dextromethorphan — often referred to as "DM" on the cough syrup box — can temporarily suppress the signal in the brain that triggers your cough reflex, says Reed.
- For kids: Not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Cough expectorant for a congested cough. Guaifenesin may help relieve chest congestion by thinning mucus in your airways, says Reed. But before you buy, try just staying hydrated first. "Water is a natural expectorant," she says.
- For kids: Cough medicine is not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Read the label on the box or bottle of OTC products carefully to make sure that what you're taking isn't expired and will treat the ailment it's intended for. And always stick to the recommended dosage and usage to avoid unnecessary risks or side effects, says Reed.
Honey
Honey is a great sick day remedy for all ages, but is especially helpful for small children not yet old enough for cough medicine, says Amin. "Honey is an anti-inflammatory that also helps with coating the throat, which can help with that cough trigger that children will have."
Note: honey isn't safe for children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.
Thermometer
This is a basic, must-have tool to check your temperature on those days you suspect you or your little one are running a fever, says Amin.
Rectal thermometers are preferred for children 3 and under; oral and digital infrared thermometers are both fine choices for anyone older than that. (But oral thermometers are usually more accurate.)
Nasal saline treatment
The dryness of winter can dehydrate your nasal passages and make it easier for viruses to attach and replicate in your nose and throat.
One easy solution is to irrigate your nose with a saline spray or rinse, says Amin. This can be both preventative by helping to keep the mucous membranes in your nose moist, as well as symptom-relieving by loosening thick mucus if you have a cold.
Research even suggests that using saline drops at the first sign of a cold can reduce symptoms in small children by up to two days.
Other comfort items
Chest rub. Vapor rubs containing combinations of camphor, eucalyptus and menthol oils may provide some relief for nighttime cough and cold symptoms when applied to the chest and neck.
Use with caution, says Amin. Though a lot of families use this homeopathic remedy, there's not a lot of research supporting its effectiveness, and it can be harmful if used improperly. Vicks VapoRub, for example, should be applied only to the chest and throat and never heated up. And be sure to check age restrictions before using any products on children — baby and child chest rubs will be formulated with gentler ingredients.
Disposable vomit bags. These are useful to have, easy to store and a great replacement for sitting by the toilet if the stomach flu should hit your house this year, says Amin.
Humidifier. A humidifier adds moisture to the air, which can help loosen mucus stuck in your sinuses. Reed suggests using a cool-mist humidifier when sick, which can help ease stuffiness during a cold.
Pedialyte, apple juice, water, Gatorade. Diarrhea or vomiting, common symptoms of the flu or COVID-19, can sometimes lead to dehydration. Make sure to have a few favorite drinks handy that can help replace those lost liquids for you or your little one, Amin says.
When to call your doctor
As long as your symptoms are improving — and responding to treatment — many viruses can be dealt with from the comfort of your home.
However, if you're seeing these concerning symptoms, reach out to your doctor.
- A fever in infants younger than 3 months; above 102 F for children; 103 F for adults; or any high fevers that last longer than 1-2 days and/or don't respond to fever-reducing medicine.
- Shortness of breath or erratic breathing
- Extreme thirst, inability to drink liquids, trouble urinating or producing tears, dark urine, severe or persistent vomiting
- Confusion, disorientation, extreme irritability or weakness
These aren't the only signs to look for, so when in doubt, reach out, says Reed. "Don't be afraid to call your doctor or talk to a pharmacist about what's going on. It doesn't hurt to double check," she says.

Afcon move to every four years under review by Caf
- Published
The Africa Cup of Nations could continue to be held every two years, with discussions under way to reverse its proposed switch to a four-year cycle.
Speaking on Friday at a Confederation of African Football (Caf) strategy conference in Cape Verde, president Patrice Motsepe said: "We've discussed it over the last few days.
"We are looking at everything, including having the Afcon coming back every two years. We are very clear, the matter is being reviewed."
The tournament has taken place every two years since 1968, bar a one-year gap between the 2012 and 2013 editions.
However, in December 2025 CAF announced it would shift to being staged every four years after the 2027 Afcon in East Africa and a 2028 edition.
That planned alteration to the schedule had received widespread criticism across the continent.
National associations had raised concerns about the visibility of their teams, the commercial implications and where Africa's biggest competition would sit in the international football calendar.

Adobe rebuilt Photoshop and Premiere for NVIDIA's RTX Spark platform

RTX Spark is NVIDIA's new system-on-chip (SoC) that's meant to give Windows laptops and small desktops the capability to run AI tasks locally on device. Unlike NVIDIA's DGX Spark, which mainly targets companies and AI developers, RTX Spark is more accessible to creatives and novice developers.
"Our apps like Photoshop, Premiere and Substance are trusted by the world's most talented storytellers, from photographers and designers creating iconic campaigns, to filmmakers and editors bringing award-winning film and television to life, to artists creating characters and visual effects that bring those stories to the screen," Subramaniam said. "For this audience, performance across creative workflows is critical to allow them to stay focused on their story and craft."
Subramaniam said the optimized apps are two times faster when it comes to AI tasks and editing across workflows. The redesigned Photoshop will be more responsive and faster at rendering complex workflows on computers with RTX Spark. Users will be able to see the changes they make in real time, such as when they're applying effects like Light Leaks (example in the image above) or removing elements from images with the Remove tool.
Meanwhile, Premiere users will be able to enjoy "real, tangible speed gains" when it comes to rendering, applying effects, AI-powered editing and color-grading for audio and video. Finally, the optimized Substance 3D Painter "speeds up the heaviest steps around texturing," as well as many other tasks, such as opening and saving large projects and exporting textures.

Frederick G. Banting and John J.R. Macleod were awarded the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of insulin, a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels. Their work helped establish insulin as a treatment for diabetes, a disease that, in its severe forms, had often been fatal before insulin therapy became available.
The prize was shared equally. Banting and Macleod were recognised “for the discovery of insulin”. The award acknowledged research conducted at the University of Toronto in the early 1920s, when investigators developed pancreatic extracts that could lower blood sugar in diabetic animals and subsequently demonstrated their therapeutic potential in humans. Charles Best, who worked with Banting, and biochemist James Collip, who helped purify insulin for clinical use, also made important contributions to this work.
Research on pancreas and blood sugar
Diabetes had been linked to the pancreas decades before insulin was isolated. In 1889, researchers Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering demonstrated that removing the pancreas from dogs produced diabetes. Subsequent research established the importance of the islets of Langerhans, clusters of cells within the pancreas, in regulating blood sugar.
The challenge was to identify and extract the substance responsible for this effect. Several researchers attempted to prepare pancreatic extracts, but obtaining a preparation that could be used safely and consistently in patients remained difficult.
Frederick G. Banting was a Canadian physician and surgeon whose interest in diabetes led him to investigate the role of the pancreas in regulating blood glucose. After serving in the First World War, he returned to Canada and worked in medical practice before pursuing research.
John J.R. Macleod was a Scottish-born physician and physiologist who had built his career around teaching and research in physiology, including carbohydrate metabolism. By 1920, he was a professor of physiology at the University of Toronto.
Banting approached Macleod in 1921 with a proposal to isolate a substance from the pancreas that could regulate blood glucose. Macleod provided laboratory facilities, scientific guidance and access to experimental animals. Banting began the work with Charles Best, a medical student who assisted with the experiments. Their collaboration brought together Banting’s research hypothesis and Macleod’s experience in physiology, setting the stage for the experiments that led to the development of insulin as a treatment for diabetes.
The researchers tied off the pancreatic ducts of dogs, allowing the enzyme-producing tissue to degenerate while attempting to preserve the islets. They prepared extracts from the pancreas and tested them in dogs whose pancreases had been removed. The extracts lowered blood sugar and improved the animals’ clinical condition.
These experiments provided evidence that an extract from the pancreas could help compensate for the loss of its normal blood sugar-regulating function. However, the early preparations were not suitable for prolonged use in humans because they contained impurities that caused adverse reactions.
Purifying insulin for treatment
In 1922, biochemist James Collip joined the research team to improve the purity of the pancreatic extract. His work helped produce a preparation suitable for clinical testing.
In January 1922, insulin was administered to Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old boy with severe diabetes, at Toronto General Hospital. The first injection produced limited results, and an abscess developed at the injection site. After the preparation was further purified, a second course of treatment produced a marked improvement in his condition, with a substantial reduction in blood glucose and urinary glucose.
Thompson’s response demonstrated that insulin could be used to treat diabetes in humans. The development of more reliable preparations and the expansion of production subsequently allowed treatment to reach more patients.
Insulin did not cure diabetes, but it changed the outlook for people living with the disease. Before its introduction, severe diabetes was often managed through restrictive diets that could prolong life only for a limited period. Insulin enabled patients to use glucose more effectively and helped prevent the severe metabolic disturbances associated with insulin deficiency.
The role of Best and Collip
The Nobel decision remains a significant part of the history of insulin research. Although Banting and Macleod received the prize, the work involved a larger research team.
Banting was unhappy that Best had not been included among the laureates. He shared half of his prize money with Best. Macleod, in turn, shared half of his prize money with Collip, recognising his contribution to the purification of insulin.
Later historical assessments of the discovery acknowledged the importance of contributions made by researchers who were not included in the award.
Laboratory discovery,modern diabetes care
The introduction of insulin marked a turning point in the treatment of diabetes. It allowed many people living with severe insulin deficiency to survive and helped establish hormone replacement as a major approach to treating endocrine disorders.
Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy or stored for later use. When the body produces insufficient insulin, or cannot use it effectively, blood glucose levels can rise.
Insulin remains essential for people with type 1 diabetes, in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce the hormone. It is also used by some people with type 2 diabetes when other treatments do not adequately control blood glucose.
The treatment has evolved considerably since the first pancreatic extracts were administered. Modern insulin preparations are manufactured under controlled conditions, with different formulations developed to vary how quickly they begin working and how long their effects last.
The Nobel recognition
Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for 1923. Banting delivered his Nobel lecture, titled ‘Diabetes and Insulin’, on September 15, 1925, while Macleod’s lecture, ‘The Physiology of Insulin and Its Source in the Animal Body’, followed on May 26, 1925.
The discovery also has a lasting connection to World Diabetes Day, observed on November 14, the birthday of Banting, who was born in 1891. More than a century later, insulin remains a cornerstone of diabetes treatment, changing a condition that was once often fatal into one that can be managed with sustained treatment.

Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
- Published
Eight of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a tanker ablaze off Romania's coast, naval authorities say.
The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire on Thursday morning. Romanian President Nicușor Dan later confirmed it was struck by drones.
The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. A swarm of Russian drones was detected overnight not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island.
Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port were hit during the sea crossing. It did not name the vessels.
On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing.
Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy.
A search and rescue operation for the eight missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed.
The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel.
The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area.
The tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT).
Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader was hit by two drones.
The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked.
This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened.
The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state."
Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region.
The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area.
Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports.
On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".
Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine.
Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.
Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports.
Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.
Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

A rumor that legendary comedian and satirist George Carlin once performed a comedy bit that involved jokes about televised public executions circulated online in October.
Carlin, who died in 2008, was known for his scathing political takedowns and clever wordplay.
People on social media shared a clip that appears to be from one of Carlin's standup comedy TV specials, in which the comic allegedly waxed poetic about using public executions to help balance the United States' budget.
The clip circulated as the Pentagon announced its plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was sentenced to death in 2013 for killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 during a shooting at the Army's Fort Hood post in Texas.
Some users suggested Carlin "predicted" the Pentagon's move with his comedy bit from decades earlier.
The video was authentic and clipped from Carlin's 1996 HBO special, "George Carlin: Back in Town," recorded at The Beacon Theater in New York City on March 30 of that year. The special is available to stream for free on Tubi and was also released as an album on Sept. 17, 1996.
The clip in question is part of a segment titled "Capital Punishment," which begins around the 14:30 mark in the full special. The clip was also available to viewon Carlin's official website.
During the special, Carlin joked about performing crucifixions during "Monday Night Football" in a satirical bit about executing white collar criminals facilitating the laundering of drug money.
The joke leads into the moment shown in the viral clip, beginning around the 15:15 mark. Carlin said (emphasis ours):
I don't care about capital punishment one way or another, because I know it doesn't do anything. It doesn't do anything except maybe satisfy a Biblical need for revenge. You know, if you read the Bible, you see that it's full of retribution and revenge. So really, capital punishment is kind of a religious ritual. It's a purification rite. It's a modern sacrament. And as long as that's true, I say, let's liven it up a little!
I honestly believe that if you make the death penalty a little more entertaining, and learn to market it correctly, you just might be able to raise enough money to balance the stupid f***ing budget!
And don't forget, the polls show the American people want capital punishment and they want a balanced budget. And I think even in a fake democracy people ought to get what they want once in a while. Just to feed this illusion that they're really in charge.
Let's use capital punishment the same way we use sports and television in this country, to distract people and take their minds off how bad they're being f***ed by the upper 1 percent. Now, unfortunately, "Monday Night Football" doesn't last long enough. What we really need is year-round capital punishment on TV every night with sponsors! Gotta have sponsors. I'm sure as long as we're killing people, Marlboro cigarettes and Dow Chemical will be proud to participate.
To say Carlin "predicted" the Pentagon's planned livestream of an execution was a stretch, but it's accurate to say he joked about televised capital punishment 30 years earlier.
The special also featured Carlin's takes on other hot-button issues that continue to be part of the national discourse in 2026, including abortion and the prison system.
"Back in Town" was Carlin's ninth HBO comedy special, of which he would do 14 before his death in 2008.

A Maryland community is demanding answers after nearly 11,000 fish died in a local stream, with residents blaming a nearby dairy farm for polluting the water.
The Maryland Department of the Environment traced the mass fish kill, which affected 25 species, to manure runoff from Kilby Farm on Firetower Road in Colora, Cecil County, CBS Baltimore reports.
Now, state officials are asking a judge to hold the farm’s owner and operator, Hartland Holdings LLC, in contempt for allegedly violating a court order to stop polluting the waterway.
“Unfortunately, he's not following the rules, and the stream, and importantly, the community is paying the price,” Adam Ortiz, deputy secretary of MDE, told the outlet.
MDE says the farm’s owners took over the property in 2017 and significantly increased the cattle herd by 2021. The agency alleges the resulting waste was not properly managed, allowing manure to contaminate Basin Run.
The state has already taken the farm to court in a state lawsuit over alleged repeated manure and pollution discharges into Basin Run, with Maryland also asking a judge to hold the dairy in civil contempt for allegedly violating a 2025 settlement.
“These violations are unacceptable. We are taking this issue very seriously and have already obtained a preliminary injunction from the court barring this facility from discharging pollution into the waterway. We are now asking the judge to hold the operator in contempt of that ruling,” MDE told CBS Baltimore in a statement.
“The count is 0-2. You got to get it right this time. Otherwise, more punitive actions can take place,” Ortiz said.
Continued pollution could threaten other waterways, including the Susquehanna River and the Chesapeake Bay, officials warn.
The farm’s owners reportedly declined to comment to CBS Baltimore, which said it had also contacted their attorneys and was awaiting a response.
Longtime residents say the fish deaths reflect years of worsening pollution in Basin Run.
John Woodrow, who has lived beside the waterway for 70 years, told CBS Baltimore that conditions began deteriorating about five years ago.
“Everybody knows why it's happening. Everybody knows, but greed makes it keep on going,” he said.
“Next thing you know, you start seeing increased weeds on the side of the stream, less fish, more algae growing on the rocks, water less clear,” he added.
Nearby resident Ashley Bowley told the outlet that protecting the waterway should matter even to people who do not live along its banks.
“It hurt to see that happen. You shouldn't have to live near Basin Run or be drinking the well water to care about this,” she said.
The case is scheduled for a settlement conference in Cecil County Circuit Court in April 2027.
The Independent has contacted the MDE and Cecil County for comment. A contact for Kilby Farm or Hartland Holdings LLC could not be reached.

Chapman was a former child actor. On Oct. 10, he entered the tiger's enclosure and sustained fatal injuries from the attack. His family criticized Trump for posting the authentic footage of Chapman, who, they said, suffered from mental illness. A family statement reads:
The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened. The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this.
The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did.

Prolific first-person shooter level designer Richard “Levelord” Gray died Monday at the age of 68, based on reports shared on social media by Apogee Entertainment yesterday. He had “dealt with cancer on and off for a while now,” according to former colleague Joe Siegler.
After studying computer engineering in the ’80s and tinkering on some early games in COBOL, Gray broke into the industry at the age of 35 in 1994 with the launch of GrayDoom, a set of four maps for the then-new Doom that were widely shared on CompuServe and beyond. The work attracted the attention of Q Studios’ Nick Newhard, who contracted Gray to work on level design for the late ’90s cult classic Blood.
Gray was subsequently hired by 3D Realms, where he said he was given free rein in designing “half the levels” for Duke Nukem 3D. There, he was also responsible for the famous, signed “You’re Not Supposed to Be Here” easter egg, which players could find only by using cheats to explore outside of the usual confines of the map.
Gray said in a 2016 interview that he assumed the prevalence of cheats in Duke Nukem 3D would mean that “of course, most all of you would be flying around, seeing what you could break, find easter eggs the easy way …bingo! I gave you an easter egg that you had to cheat to find.”
Remembering Richard “Levelord” Gray.
In this interview, Richard reflects on the creative freedom he and Allen Blum had while designing the iconic levels of Duke Nukem 3D.
— Apogee Entertainment (@apogeeent.com) October 14, 2026 at 8:18 AM
In the years following, his level design work appeared in games ranging from SiN to Quake: The Offering to Half-Life: Opposing Force and Counter-Strike: Condition Zero. “The most important duty you have as a level designer is to bring the player ‘into’ your level,” he said in a 1999 interview for the book Game Design: Secrets of the Sages. ”It’s not until after this submersion that issues like action, game play, and even the Fun Factor enter the game. The more of your level to which the player can attach himself via familiarity, the stronger the player’s sense of ‘being there’ will be.”

Student protesters attack government buildings in Tirana
- Published
Thousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.
The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects.
Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.
Albania's Deputy Prime Minister Albana Koçiu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".
Riot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them.
One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania".
"The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said.
Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen".
Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things".
Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters.
"Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.
Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said.
Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters.
"The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported.
This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.

Tanmay Baloda continued from where he left off in the first innings, adding four more wickets to his match tally to make it a 10-for. His spell of 4/26 put India Under-19 in an advantageous position against Australia Under-19 at the end of day two of the second multi-day Test here at the Narendra Modi Stadium on Tuesday.
Baloda was once again accurate, bowling at the stumps, and claimed Hayden Barbulovic, Matthew Lough and Neel Patel in quick succession.
Eli Brain was the only batter who looked comfortable at the crease while the rest struggled at the other end, with the pitch showing signs of variable bounce. He hit a few crisp drives through the covers for his 39 off 35 balls before Baloda had him caught at first slip.
Australia U-19 was 86 for four at the end of day’s play, trailing the hosts by 55 runs. India U-19 was earlier bowled out for 315, taking a 141-run first-innings lead.
Despite India’s dominance, the day still belonged to leg-spinner Spencer Green, who finished with figures of 7/110 - the second-best by an Australian U-19 bowler in Youth Tests.
Green had already picked up a wicket coming into the day and was Australia’s go-to weapon from the morning. But Kushagra Ojha (29) and Yashbardhan Chauhan (52) batted with great focus to begin the proceedings.
Chauhan was particularly solid in his strokeplay and hit three boundaries off pacer Thomas Vaseo, including a textbook cover drive for four to bring up his fifty.
The 18-year-old leg-spinner continued to target the edge of the bat, and he finally had Ojha caught at first slip. In the next over, Green cleaned up Chauhan with a quicker one, uprooting his middle stump.
With only the odd ball turning, Aryan Yadav and Manal Chauhan seemed comfortable right from the outset. Yadav cut Green for a first-ball four while the majestic ground echoed when Manal middled the ball.
However, just after Lunch, Manal top-edged his sweep off Green straight to short fine leg. In the next over, Vaseo rushed Yadav and cleaned him up. The leg-spinner completed his five-wicket haul by dismissing Mohit Ulva and then trapping Ayaan Akram in front off his next ball.
Just when Australia seemed to be taking control of the proceedings, Abhiprai Biswas counter-attacked. He slog-swept his first ball for a six off Green and drove well on the on-side against the pacers. Even with the leg side packed, Biswas found comfort in taking the aerial route over the fielders. He brought up his fifty off just 36 balls.
However, in an attempt to take the aggressive route again, the left-hander missed the one that crashed into his stumps, giving Green his seventh scalp.
India added 42 runs to its lead through the last-wicket partnership between Priyanshu Singh and Baloda, whose stroke-filled 28 off 37 balls was cut short by Jacob Pietz. However, Baloda continued to have fun in the field, putting India in a commanding spot heading into the third day.

Almost nine years ago, a tanned, relatively well-rested-looking CEO named Elon Musk announced that his electric car company would make a new sports car, the Tesla Roadster 2. It would be “the fastest sports car ever made, period,” Musk said on stage in 2017. “The point of doing this is to give a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars.” Lights flashed, and the red prototype did a few speedy laps behind him.
Times have changed. Musk is the leading donor to a political party that last year nixed buying incentives for electric vehicles and last month adjusted fuel-economy standards to make it easier for automakers to skip making EVs altogether. Musk has said he’s not even in the business of making cars anymore, instructing investors to think of Tesla as a robotics and autonomy company. On Thursday night, Tesla will host what it has billed as its last unveiling event for a human-driven vehicle. Six years after it was supposed to roll into driveways, the Roadster 2 is finally here. Tesla is slated to start deliveries next year.
“EVs exist today in a massively different environment than when the Roadster was introduced,” says Ed Kim, president of AutoPacific, an automotive research firm. When Tesla announced the car back in 2017, electrics were “toys for early adopters,” he says. By 2020, other automakers saw Tesla’s sky-high valuations and lawmakers’ plans to transition vehicles to batteries and made big electric promises, investing heavily in the shift. China began to dominate EV-making. Now, after the Trump administration reversed the US’s course on the powertrain, EV sales are shrinking, not growing.
Still, lots more options are available now. In 2017, research firm Cox Automotive says, US customers had 15 EVs to choose from; today, that number has jumped to nearly 90. Potential EV buyers are more likely to be normies, and so their needs are more practical. “People are looking for range, performance, charging ability, resale value,” says Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of Industry Insights at Cox.
What success looks like for the Roadster, then, is a bit complicated. It’s a hypercar targeted squarely at, well, non-normies—people who like to show off and go very, very fast. Some of them want that signature gasoline-engine power and roar. That’s why some luxury automakers have taken pains to reproduce the sound of a V-8 without one present. And it’s why others—Porsche and Ferrari among them—have said they’ll keep developing gas engines. Lamborghini said earlier this year it would shelve electrics altogether. Even Bugatti’s CEO, who founded his own electric hypercar company, said he expects loud ICE cars to become a status symbol among the wealthiest car buyers.
“EVs in this space really have to wow the shopper with a lot more than practical things,” says Kim. “Great range, really quiet, charging at home—none of that matters.” In 2017, Tesla said the car would start at $200,000; reservation holders put down $50,000 deposits.
In 2017, Musk promised a then-record-breaking sub-2-second 0-to-60 acceleration time. Now that a handful of other production cars have broken that barrier, Tesla will have to meet a high bar. One option: Musk has suggested several times over the years that the new Roadster will fly, and reports suggest that the automaker will get help from Musk’s rocket company SpaceX. (In 2018, SpaceX used its Falcon Heavy rocket to launch the first Roadster into space.)
Going that fast “is not terribly comfortable," says Shea Burns, a partner in the automotive and industrial practice at AlixPartners. “The laws of physics are catching up with them, outside of the rocket piece.” It would be an interesting way for an EV-maker to exit human driving.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Actor Seth Green—yes, that one—has seen Godzilla Minus Zero and says it’s awesome.
While introducing the New York Comic Con panel for the 39th film in the Godzilla franchise, Green stressed that the filmmakers behind the movie “have created kaiju that feel physically real and, trust me, emotionally terrifying.”
While a lot of that terror came from the work of Oscar-winning visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima, some it came from the shrieking of Godzilla and his three-headed nemesis, King Ghidorah. Those roars were the work of sound designer Natsuko Inoue and her team, who created the monsters’ outsize vocalizations by rolling speakers to the top of an outdoor dam—much to the horror of people nearby.
“There were people having a picnic, maybe people just taking a stroll,” Hisafumi Takeuchi, who also worked on sound for the film, said during the panel. “The person walking their dog, though—they had the worst time, because the dog was freaking out and barking back at us.”
Since the creatures are imaginary, getting their screams to sound realistic is essential to making them seem believable—and genuinely scary—onscreen. At first, Inoue wasn’t sure if the idea of recording at the dam would work. Those fears were quickly put to rest.
“The first time we sent that roar out on the speakers, I could see the relief and confidence in everyone's eyes,” Inoue said. “By using speakers and projecting it into the real world, capturing the reverb, the echo, the reflection of the sound back with the mic, it manifests it in our world.”
For other kaiju sound effects, Inoue’s team took an analog foley approach. To simulate Ghidorah’s dragon-like wings, for example, they flapped a rubber fisherman’s suit and mixed that noise with the sounds of an accordion-like air duct.
Getting two of Toho’s most famous monsters right was a huge undertaking, especially after the success of Zero’s predecessor, Godzilla Minus One, which brought home $114 million worldwide at the box office. Following that 2023 film’s harrowing mix of post–World War II malaise and bracing kaiju destruction will be tough, but a new trailer shown during the film’s panel at NYCC promised a sequel full of aerial dogfights and a punch-’em-up for the ages between Godzilla and Ghidorah.
Like the previous film, Godzilla Minus Zero is directed by Takashi Yamazaki and features visual effects from Tatsuji Nojima, whom Green called “the first Gen Z Oscar-winner” for his work on One.
Nojima began doing visual effects as a hobby while he was still a teenager before joining animation house Shirogumi as a compositor. After Yamazaki noticed a crude animation of waves that Nojima was working on, the director tasked the budding animator with developing the idea. Nojima turned around a fully rendered shot of ocean water over rocks that looked indistinguishable from reality. After that, Nojima recalled, Yamazaki said, “OK, I think you’re ready to animate and do VFX for Godzilla now.”
During the panel, Nojima broke down how he created a shot from the trailer showing Godzilla bursting out of the ocean while chasing a seaplane. “I simulated 200 million particles to get the whitewater effect correct in Godzilla Minus One,” he said. “With this shot in Godzilla Minus Zero, the scale is absolutely different with the new Imax aspect ratio, plus there was no live-action plate, so we're dealing with a lot of CG on screen. We required 2 billion particles.”
Godzilla Minus Zero is set to hit US theaters on November 6 and Japanese theaters on November 3, which has become known as Godzilla’s birthday since it marks the date in 1954 that Ishirō Honda’s original film was released in Japan.
