A video of late actor Nana Patekar is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) amid the Cockroach Janata Party’s protest at Jantar Mantar. In the video, Patekar apologises to a man named Abhijeet before speaking in Marathi. The video is being shared with claims that Patekar was apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending an event and was supposed to accompany him to the protest at Jantar Mantar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending the protest at Jantar Mantar.
Fact: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to Marathi film producer Abhijeet Gholap for missing the NAFA Marathi Film Festival. Gholap, who produced the 2011 Marathi film Deool, shared the video on his Instagram account on 8 October 2026, stating that Patekar was unable to attend the festival. The video is unrelated to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke or the protest at Jantar Mantar. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
After reviewing the video with Google’s NotebookLM tool, we found that Nana Patekar speaks in Marathi, apologises to Abhijeet, and regrets not attending an event. Addressing Abhijeet, he says, “It was great working with you in the film Deool.”
Deool is a 2011 Marathi film in which Nana Patekar acted, and Abhijeet Gholap produced it. This suggests that Patekar was referring to Abhijeet Gholap in the video, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. Patekar also praises Sonali Kulkarni, who acted in the film.
Further search revealed that Abhijeet Gholap had posted the video of Nana Patekar on his Instagram account (archived) on 08 October 2026. In the caption, he wrote, “Nana was unable to attend the NAFA Marathi Film Festival, and he promised he would definitely come this year. We will miss you very much.” In a Facebook post, he wrote, “Nana, you missed your visit. Now we will just keep waiting.”
Abhijeet Gholap is the founder of the North American Film Association (NAFA), which was established to promote Marathi films in North America. According to the organisation’s website, Gholap founded NAFA to bring together actors, directors, choreographers, singers, cinematographers and editors to create Marathi films, web series and documentaries based on local stories and subjects in North America.
To sum up, this viral video shows Nana Patekar apologising to film producer Abhijeet Gholap, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke.

China 'dumped' aluminium windows, doors in Australia, preliminary trade report shows
In short
The preliminary report from the Australian Trade Remedies Commission found that Chinese aluminium windows and doors were sold here at unfair prices.
From October 15, importers must provide financial guarantees of up to 73.3 per cent of the product value when their goods enter the country.
What's next
The commission is due to make its final recommendation to the minister by December 16.
Australia's international trade monitor has found Chinese aluminium windows and doors were "dumped" here, heavily undercutting local prices and damaging the Australian industry.
Starting today, companies importing these goods will also have to put down a financial guarantee when their products enter the country, prompting a warning about higher construction costs and potential retaliation by China.
In a preliminary report, the Australian Trade Remedies Commission, formerly the Anti-Dumping Commission, found all Chinese exporters except one had dumped the goods between July 1, 2024 and June 30 last year.
The commission found the goods were sold with dumping margins ranging from 5.3 per cent to 70.4 per cent of their normal price, depending on the exporter.
Some exporters were also found to have received modest subsidies from various levels of government in China.
The commission found the Chinese imports had "caused material injury" to the Australian industry.
It estimated the local aluminium windows and doors market was worth about $2.8 billion during the investigation period.
Chinese imports accounted for 19 per cent of total sales, Australia accounted for about 79 per cent, and the remaining 2 per cent came from other countries.
According to the report, local manufacturers' sales volumes fell by about 19 per cent from July 2021 to June 2025.
Meanwhile, the value of their sales dropped about 14 per cent from a peak in the 2023 financial year, according to the report.
The commission found that half of the tenders and quotes they examined were about 30 per cent lower than the expected prices, while more than a quarter were undercut by 40 per cent or more.
It estimated the Australian industry had lost about $350 million due to undercutting by "dumped and/or subsidised imports from China".
The commission has proposed recommending Industry and Innovation Minister Tim Ayres publish a dumping duty notice for Chinese goods, which would lead to duties imposed on those imports.
Chinese-made aluminium windows and doors currently face no tariffs under the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement.
A spokesperson for Mr Ayres said the Albanese government supported free and fair trade.
"The Australian Trade Remedies Commission initiates its rigorous, evidence-based investigations based on applications from industry," they said.
"Any trade remedies imposed are fully consistent with Australia's obligations under its trade agreements."
Securities could 'effectively lead to price increase'
While the investigation continues, the commissioner said financial securities were needed to "prevent material injury" to the Australian industry.
From today, importers will have to provide financial securities worth between 5.3 per cent and 73.3 per cent of the value of their products. The percentage will depend on the exporting company.
These securities are financial guarantees against duties that may become payable later. The industry minister will make the final decision on whether any duties are imposed.
UNSW international economic law professor Zhou Weihuan said duties were likely to be imposed, because it was "hard to change" the findings in the commission's preliminary report.
He said securities could "effectively lead to price increases" because importers would account for them in their pricing.
"The price impact would involve an increase in imported aluminium windows and doors, which in turn would push up construction costs for commercial and residential premises," Professor Zhou said.
'Protect competition from unfair trading'
The investigation began on November 25 after an application by Ventora Group and the Australian Glass and Window Association (AGWA).
The application alleged the local industry had "suffered material injury" through lost sales and price suppression.
"We're not asking government to protect Australian businesses from competition," Clinton Skeoch, AGWA's CEO, told the ABC.
"We're asking government to protect competition from unfair trading."
AGWA welcomed the securities and said they were "an important and positive development" for an industry that had faced significant pressure from dumped imports.
The ABC has approached China's Ministry of Commerce and the Chinese embassy for comment.
Professor Zhou said Chinese retaliation was unlikely, because China had historically taken far fewer anti-dumping and countervailing actions against Australia than Australia had against China.
"But it's not impossible, and if China decides to take action, then agricultural exports might be the target," he said.
Ventora commissioned testing on imported Chinese windows and AGWA made the results public.
The commission said it did not consider the testing results or other allegations about product quality or compliance in its preliminary findings.
Builders raise cost concerns
Melissa Byrne, Acting CEO of Master Builders Australia, said the group would "carefully review the commission's findings".
"At the same time, any measure that increases the cost of construction comes at a time when housing affordability and project feasibility remain under significant pressure,"
she said.
She said Australia "must not restrict the flow of high-quality, compliant building products and materials".
The final recommendations are due no later than December 16. The minister's decision is expected within 30 days of receiving them.
The final report will be published after the minister's decision.

Sally Rooney's books to be withdrawn from sale in UK over Palestine Action support
Bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because she has expressed support for direct action group Palestine Action, which the British government banned as a terrorist organisation last year.
Rooney said after Palestine Action was banned that she would use proceeds from her book sales to support it, which would constitute a terrorism offence under UK law.
The novelist said on Wednesday: "I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.
“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence."
Rooney added: "After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK.

"I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."
Rooney cancelled a trip to England last September to collect a literary award over the fear of being arrested.
Her books Normal People, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World were bestsellers in the UK.
'To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher'
– Faber, Rooney's publisher
Both Normal People and Conversations With Friends were made into television shows by the BBC.
Rooney's publisher, Faber, said: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.
"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories."
'Disgraceful attack on freedom of expression'
Keir Starmer's Labour government proscribed Palestine Action in July 2025, meaning that expressing support for or membership of the direct action group – which aimed to cause property damage to companies manufacturing weapons that would be sold to Israel – is a criminal offence that could lead to a prison sentence of up to 14 years.
The ban has been widely denounced as draconian by human rights organisations. Thousands of people have been arrested since it came into effect for holding up placards expressing support for the group.
Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action, is appealing a Court of Appeal decision earlier this year which upheld the proscription as lawful.
The case is due to be heard at the Supreme Court later this year.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said last month that Andy Burnham's government is “looking at” whether the ban on Palestine Action was politically sensible, arguing that the government had not intended for mass arrests to take place by implementing the proscription.
He argued: "I don’t think anyone’s intent was to have those people criminalised, but obviously the Supreme Court has got to look at this issue, and obviously it’s something we keep looking at as government."
Kerry Moscogiuri, the chief executive of Amnesty International UK, told the Guardian: "Whatever one’s views on Palestine Action, we should all be concerned when laws intended to combat terrorism end up silencing artistic freedom and the ability to engage in peaceful political dissent.
"Writers should not find their books disappearing from shelves because of their political beliefs. Nor should people have to choose between expressing their conscience and pursuing their livelihoods.
"Sally Rooney’s willingness to accept the personal consequences of her convictions deserves recognition.
"There is a real danger that others, seeing the price she has paid, will decide they cannot afford to speak out."
Labour MP Ian Byrne posted on X that when he voted against the proscription of Palestine Action, he and many others "warned of the draconian consequences it would bring".
He said that since then, thousands have been arrested and criminalised "simply for holding a sign".
Byrne added: "Now this injustice against one of the finest writers of her generation.
"An utterly disgraceful attack on freedom of expression. This ban must be overturned."

) Limiting global warming to around 1.8 degrees Celsius, instead of allowing it to reach 4.4 degrees Celsius, could prevent the loss of 1.89 billion years of healthy life to causes such as extreme heat and air pollution, according to a new LancetCommission.
Researchers said that the true burden could be even greater and that without sharp cuts to emissions, health losses would continue to compound beyond 2100, increasingly intensify other threats, such as migration, in ways not yet reflected in these numbers.
The authors of The Lancet Commission on "21st Century Global Threats to Health", launched at the World Health Summit 2026 in Berlin, Germany, examined hundreds of possible threats.
They identified 17 threats posing the greatest danger to human health and survival between 2025 and 2100. These are also the threats that can be averted through policy changes, funding decisions and innovation, they said.
The 17 interlinked "catastrophic" threats spanning diseases, social and economic conditions, environmental change, technology and conflict will shape the health of the next generation, the team added.
If current trends continue, the 17 catastrophic threats collectively could account for tens of billions of years of lost health, the analysis found.
Every country faces significant risks, even as the scale varied by threat and region. Within each country, people with limited resources and marginalised communities bear the greatest burden, compounded by existing inequalities, it said.
Nuclear conflict and the malicious use of artificial intelligence (AI) were identified as the two threats with a potential for extinction, even as their likelihood of occurring were deemed 'low'.
Accounting for both their potential impact and probability, the commission's assessment found that action to prevent nuclear conflict could avert an estimated 133 million deaths and 9.35 billion years of healthy life lost by 2100, while action to reduce the risk of malicious AI could avert an estimated 10.4 billion years of healthy life lost.
"The estimates highlight how much health loss could be avoided in each area. Some are already imposing substantial health burdens today, while others carry a real danger if they materialise. Crucially, all 17 threats are interconnected, which is why they must be addressed together, not in isolation," commission co-chair Christopher JL Murray, director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington, said.
"The striking finding is not only the scale of these threats, but that humanity still has the agency to act. Across all 17 catastrophic threats, the decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation. But delaying action will only serve to shift and increase the costs into the future," Murray added.
The other catastrophic threats to health are air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition, conventional conflict, a declining development assistance for health, high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics, obesity, poor mental health, smoking and unhealthy ageing, the authors said.
The commission also puts forth a framework to inform action before harm becomes embedded -- create and fund threat-ready health systems, increase investment in innovation and reassess threats regularly and independently, they said.

The Delhi Police crackdown on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest on October 10 has drawn international scrutiny, with human rights bodies and press-freedom organisations flagging police excesses, and international media outlets reporting on the severity of force used against young protesters.
Police detained over 2,000 protesters and used force to suppress the mobilisation in the national capital. In arguably the most brutal assault on press freedom in India since the Emergency, journalists from both independent and mainstream media outlets were stopped from doing their work and detained in a display of police excess that bordered on madness. Some were dragged by their clothes, pushed and manhandled, some had their phones snatched, and pressured to delete footage of police action.
‘Restrictions Violate India’s Obligations under Int’l Law’
The global human rights non-profit Amnesty International on Friday put out a statement urging Delhi police to ensure that the fundamental right to peacefully protest is guaranteed to Indian citizens. In the statement, titled, ‘Delhi police must facilitate right to peaceful protest amid lockdown-like restrictions in capital’, Amnesty highlighted that “approximately 22,000 armed personnel from across the country have reportedly been brought to Delhi, in addition to more than 10,000 Delhi police officers expected to be deployed.”
Aakar Patel, chair of board, stated: “From denying permission for a peaceful demonstration, halting all Delhi-bound trains, and sealing the city’s borders, to issuing an internet suspension order near the protest site, and pre-emptively arresting activists – India’s authorities are leaving no stone unturned in their bid to prevent this march from happening. The right to protest is protected in India’s constitution. The authorities must immediately lift all these arbitrary restrictions, which violate India’s obligations under international law.”
After reports of rapid mass detentions began to surface on Saturday, the United Nations Human Rights Commission published a press release: ‘Concerns over mass detentions before and during protests’. Spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan called for the unconditional and immediate release of all those arbitrarily detained. “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled. Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality. The Indian authorities should also ensure law enforcement forces exercise utmost restraint in response to peaceful protesters, consistent with the country’s democratic traditions and human rights obligations,” read the statement.
Similarly, the global media watchdog Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) urged Delhi police to “immediately release all detained journalists and media workers, return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests…and the police response without interference.”
CPJ highlighted the detentions of Newslaundry reporters Ashwine Kumar Singh, Astha Savyasachi, and Anmol Pritam, and Scroll reporter Ayush Tiwari. “Newslaundry has also reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports indicate that journalists were physically manhandled,” the statement read.

Trump says military execution will not be livestreamed
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday (Oct 15) the execution of the Fort Hood gunman would not be livestreamed but that immediate families of the victims would be able to view it in person.
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed. That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!"
Some of Trump's fellow Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, as well as religious leaders and international observers, had expressed doubts about the Pentagon's plan to livestream the Dec 3 execution of Nidal Hasan. Recent polls have also shown a majority of Americans opposed livestreaming it.
Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, was found guilty in a military trial of fatally shooting 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

The rise and fall of a MAGA princess
How Kimberly Guilfoyle lost her ambassadorship.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, is out of a job after serious corruption allegations.
What happened? Guilfoyle resigned on Tuesday after being shown the door earlier in the day by Trump’s brand-new White House press secretary, who announced at a briefing that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign.
Her departure comes just six days after a bombshell Wall Street Journal story, which described Guilfoyle’s efforts to solicit money from a Trump donor, including $100,000 to pay down a credit card bill, in exchange for access to Trump officials and conservative media figures.
Guilfoyle also attempted to conceal those efforts: In one text to the donor, Eric Deters, she wrote, “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing.”
Who is Guilfoyle? Fallen MAGA royalty. Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality, is also the ex-fiancée of Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. (and, more distantly, the ex-wife of current California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat).
There appears to be little love lost between Guilfoyle and Trump, however. On Tuesday, he told reporters that Guilfoyle “wasn’t a member of my family. She I guess dated my son a long time ago.” (The Don Jr.-Guilfoyle relationship is thought to have ended in 2024.)
Why was she forced out? Corruption allegations are not, generally speaking, dealbreakers in Trumpworld; the president and his children are all innovators when it comes to profiting off the presidency, and there’s plenty of self-dealing going on around them.
That being said, Guilfoyle may have crossed the line in two specific ways: one, her alleged corruption benefited her and not the Trump family. And two, the allegations are embarrassingly unsubtle even by the standards of the second Trump administration. The combination appears to have been too much.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

We know junk food isn't healthy, but scientists are trying to determine if it's also bad for our brains
New research suggests brain health could be affected by consuming too much low-nutrient processed food
Most people have food in their fridges and cupboards that they know aren't the healthiest choice.
A box of chocolate chip cookies you grab for a bedtime snack. Instant noodles for when you can't be bothered to make dinner. Or that bag of ketchup chips you grabbed on a late night stroll home from the bar.
But it's not just guilty pleasures. Nearly half of the calories Canadians consume — 45.7 per cent on average, according to Statistics Canada — comes in the form of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and includes everything from breakfast cereals to frozen meals.
Over the years, research has shown that UPFs can negatively impact everything from our weight to our cardiovascular health, and could even be linked to some types of cancer.
But a new study co-authored by two professors at Hamilton's McMaster University, published Thursday by JAMA Network Open, signals that our brains could also suffer as a result of consuming too many foods produced to be cheap and ready-to-eat.
The authors say that the people with the highest intake of UPFs in their diets may face an increased likelihood of experiencing changes to the brain that could serve as precursors for stroke, dementia and cognitive decline.
People wouldn't necessarily be aware of these potential harms, says study co-author Russell de Souza, an associate professor at McMaster's Mary Heersink School of Global Health and Social Medicine.
But he says the findings could encourage people to shift their eating habits now, before experiencing serious consequences later in life.
Feeding the furnace
De Souza and co-author Dr. Sonia Anand, a vascular medicine specialist, examined the diets and brain MRI scans of more than 8,700 Canadian adults, with a median age of about 58, and broke them down into four groups, from those with the lowest intake of UPFs to those with the highest.
The latter cohort was made up of people who consumed nearly 45 per cent of their calories from UPFs, or the equivalent of 16 servings a day, which they self-reported in a survey listing 150 to 170 food items consumed in the past year.
By comparison, the group with the lowest consumption got 15 per cent of their daily calories from UPFs, equal to three servings.
Anand, a professor of medicine and epidemiology at McMaster, says they analyzed the scans of higher-risk participants and found that their UPF-heavy diets were associated with increased body fat and visceral fat — the kind stored deeper in the body and around organs.
"Fat tissue in the wrong places can be almost like a furnace spewing out a whole bunch of inflammatory proteins that then affect our brains," she said.
Ultra-processed foods like instant noodles are mostly or entirely made from substances derived from plant and animal sources and combined with additives, preservatives, stabilizers, dyes and artificial flavours, rather than minimally-processed ingredients. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
Anand says the MRIs of the higher-risk group showed changes to the brain similar to silent strokes, a type of stroke that doesn't present any noticeable symptoms but damages the tissue.
These injuries add up over time and make it more likely that people could develop neurological problems, such as vascular dementia, says Dr. Michael Hill, a neurologist and professor at the University of Calgary who is not affiliated with the study.
"The more injuries you accumulate, the more likely you are to have neurological problems later in life, most commonly vascular dementia," he said.
- THE DOSE Reducing ultra-processed food intake requires rethinking our 'food environment,' experts say
- McMaster University study links ultra-processed food to range of health risks
While the damage a UPF-heavy diet may do can't be reversed, Hill says dietary changes can reduce further progression.
"Feed your brain," he said. "It's not just about your gut, right? It's about your whole body."
He says the findings are consistent with a growing body of evidence about the health impacts of UPFs.
'Eat foods that rot, not rotten foods'
De Souza notes that not all processed foods are ultra-processed and, in fact, many processed products in grocery stores have a lot of nutritional value.
"Some degree of processing is absolutely necessary in the food supply," he said. "It helps keep food safe and shelf stable."
But a can of beans, a bag of frozen vegetables or a container of yogurt are all different from a fast-food meal or a box of sugar-coated cereal.
Foods are classified using what's known as the NOVA system, where foods are determined to be ultra-processed if they are mostly or entirely made from substances derived from plant and animal sources and combined with additives like salt, sugar, fats and oils, as well as preservatives, stabilizers, dyes and artificial flavours.
They also tend to be lower in fibre, vitamins and minerals that benefit overall health, de Souza says.
Hill says that while "one Snickers bar isn't going to hurt you," ultimately, ultra-processed food isn't going to benefit your health — especially if you're eating it regularly.
And even when people want a sugary or salty treat, he says it's going to be better if they make it at home from whole or minimally-processed foods.
"Eat foods that will rot, but not rotten food," he said.
Anand and de Souza note that their study doesn't provide the full picture of the potential toll UPFs can have on brain health and say more long-term research is needed to determine if dietary changes later in life can make a difference.
The next phase of their research will see 2,000 people who took part in the first round of scans receive a second round to determine if reducing the amount of UPFs in their diets results in changes or improvements to brain health.
Improving health literacy
Anand notes that not everyone has the time or money to prepare high-quality food, which she says is a systemic issue that would require government intervention to reduce the amount of UPFs available and make healthy food more affordable.
It's also a matter of improving health literacy, which she says would increase awareness about the repercussions of consuming too many UPFs.
Canada, she says, could follow the lead of other countries that have successfully minimized the consumption of UPFs. One such country, Chile, implemented mandatory front-of-package labels for UPFs that are high in sugar in an effort to curb childhood obesity.
She says there are things individuals and governments can do "and we need both to happen to make Canadians healthier."

New Delhi, October 15, 2026: India’s edible oil imports fell 7% in September to 15.44 lakh tonnes, mainly due to a sharp decline in shipments of crude sunflower oil, according to industry body the Solvent Extractors’ Association of India (SEA).
Imports stood at 16.58 lakh tonnes in the same month last year.
According to data released by the SEA on Thursday, imports of crude sunflower oil in September plunged to nearly 1.05 lakh tonnes from 2.72 lakh tonnes in the year-ago period.
However, total edible oil imports rose 3% to 151.64 lakh tonnes in the first 11 months of the 2025-26 oil year (November-October), compared with 146.83 lakh tonnes in the corresponding period of the previous oil year.
Total vegetable oil imports, including edible and non-edible oils, stood at 154.64 lakh tonnes from November 2025 to September 2026, compared with 150.31 lakh tonnes in the year-ago period.
Refined Oil Imports Decline Sharply
During November 2025 to September 2026, refined oil imports declined sharply to 7,40,441 tonnes from 16,89,228 tonnes in the corresponding period of the previous year, the SEA said.
As a result, the share of refined oil in total edible oil imports fell to 5% from 12%. This was mainly due to negligible imports of refined palmolein from Indonesia and Malaysia.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

On 12 October, Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site in the national capital. Instead, three new venues – Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground, and CBD Ground – were designated for the purpose. For over three decades, Jantar Mantar stood as the beating heart of protests in the national capital. It was known as a place where the angry, the aggrieved and the unheard gathered to make their voices count. But the move by authorities in Delhi put the iconic stage of dissent away from the capital’s political heart and corridors of power. Two of the new sites — CBD ground and Burari are several miles away from Central Delhi where Parliament stands. The other one Ramlila is near New Delhi railway station and comes with a cost to stage protests. The decision to denotify Jantar Mantar came at a time when Opposition parties, civil society groups such as the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), and student organisations, including the All India Students’ Association (AISA) and the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), held protests and marches around Jantar Mantar demanding resignation of Chief Election Commisisoner (CEC), Gyanesh Kumar over irregularties in Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls. The move was criticised for world over protests are usually held in spaces close to the corridors of power. Protest across the worlds are organised at the doorstep of power. Lafayette square in Washington is right across White House in the US, Parliament square and whitehall in London and Place De La Republique in Paris, France are classic examples. The recent spate of protests began on 6 June, when the CJP launched a stir against Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, seeking his resignation over irregularities in conducting the NEET medical competitive exam. The minister eventually resigned after about a month-long protest at Jantar Mantar, the erstwhile designated site for demonstrations in New Delhi, the national capital The CJP protesters have again come together with opposition parties, this time demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over irregularities in the Election Commission's functioning during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. India saw 18,629 demonstrations in 2026 till 2 October, according to Reuters. Of these, 17,691 were majority peaceful protests, and 687 were categorised as violent demonstrations, according to ACLED or the ‘Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project,’ an independent, non-profit global conflict monitor. At least 1,200 protests were met with police intervention, the Reuters report said. While Delhi remains the hub for CJP’s major demonstrations this year, the total number of protests there fell to 364 from 543 in 2016. Protests were held in Mumbai too. Demonstrations in India have risen significantly, growing from 10,642 in 2016 to over 18,629 by 2 October 2026, after peaking at 22,130 in 2024, according to ACLED. More than 2,500 demonstrations - including peaceful protests, protests with police intervention and violent demonstrations took place across India in August 2026. This surge has brought increased police intervention, with over 200 demonstrations met with force in August 2026, a decade high for any single month. the Reuters report said. Protest is a fundamental right in democracy, enabling citizens to register dissent, demand accountability and effect change in public policy. The struggle for independence is embedded in India’s protest culture. From the Chipko movement for environmental conservation to the Mandal Commission protests against caste-based reservations, the right to protest has been India’s democratic lifeline. Protests have ranged from the historic march to Dandi in the Salt Satyagraha led by Mahatma Gandhi to Anna Hazare’s 2011 movement. The famous farmers' protest of 2020-21 led the government to withdraw the controversial agrarian laws. Although Indian law constitutionally protects the right to assembly, a report authored by human rights lawyer Vrinda Grover for International Center for Not-for-Profit Law (ICNL), and highlighted in the Reuters report, finds this protection often fails in practice. Ultimately, the decision to intervene rests with executive magistrates or police. Once an intervention is decided, Indian policing rules require a phased approach: persuasion and warnings before force. If necessary, only minimum force should be used and stopped once order is restored. Those refusing to disperse may be legally detained. Reuters was unable to verify with police how closely these guidelines are followed. When can law enforcement authorities stop a peaceful protest? Do the organisers need permission before holding the protests? A peaceful, unarmed protest is protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b), according to Bhargav KS, Managing Partner at KS & BKS Law Associates, Bengaluru. “It is not inherently a law-and-order problem. Dissent, criticism of the government or inconvenience does not, by itself, establish a threat to public order,” Bhargav KS told LiveMint. Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of Constitution guarantee freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. But Articles 19(2) and 19(3) allow authroities to impose reasonable restrictions, including in the interests of public order. “Authorities may address specific unlawful acts and protect public access, but restrictions must have a lawful basis and be necessary and proportionate. The distinction is between regulating unlawful conduct and suppressing constitutional expression,” he said. Apart from whether the protest is peaceful or not, there is also another aspect that drives police crackdown. In case the organisers move out of designated place, even if peacefully, it also amounts to breach of permission, as per experts. Where a valid law requires prior permission, the state may enforce that requirement even against a peaceful gathering, Bhargav KS said. "However, the permission process cannot become an arbitrary veto over constitutional rights. Refusal must rest on legally sustainable grounds, and restrictions must satisfy Articles 19(2) and 19(3). The mere absence of permission does not, by itself, establish a threat to public order or justify disproportionate police action, he said. Recently, CJP leades were held by police calling it prevent arrest. The decision on preventive action is taken by the authority empowered by law. Under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate or specially empowered Executive Magistrate may issue preventive orders, recording material facts warranting immediate intervention. “Under Section 170, police may arrest to prevent a cognisable offence only where they know of a design to commit it and it cannot otherwise be prevented. Both powers remain subject to judicial review,” he said. On 9 October, the Supreme Court, during a hearing on restrictions ahead of the CJP protest, questioned the proposed transport restrictions and invoked the principle of proportionality while cautioning against using a “hammer to kill a fly”. The Court said measures could regulate transport where necessary but should not indiscriminately shut it down. In Himat Lal K Shah vs Commissioner of Police (1973), for example, the Supreme Court, held that the State can regulate assemblies on public streets since streets have competing public uses. But regulation cannot become an arbitrary power to prohibit assemblies altogether, the courts have held in past instances. In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan vs Union of India (2018), the case about protests at Jantar Mantar, the Court rejected a blanket prohibition and required authorities to devise a regulatory mechanism balancing protesters’ rights against those of residents and commuters. Even if police considers that a certain venue is not appropriate because of its capacity or security concerns, an alternative should ideally be provided, according to a former Delhi police official who did not want to be named. Thus a permission before a protest is key. In case of CJP protest held at Jantar Mantar against Dharmendra Pradhan, permission was sought for one day. But CJP extended the protest beyond one day and continued for about a month till Pradhan quit. On 13 October, Union Home Minister Amit Shah taunted Rahul Gandhi saying that the Congress party had lost election after election under his leadership. Shah said merely assembling a crowd of 8,000 people within an area of one-and-a-half km would not make Rahul Gandhi the voice of the nation. Shah said Rahul Gandhi needed to engage in some self-reflection, noting that the Congress had repeatedly been rejected by voters across northern and northeastern India. Shah's remarks came after Rahul Gandhi on 12 October led a massive protest of INDIA bloc on the streets of central Delhi against election commission and CEC Gyanesh Kumar. On October 10, BJP MP Ravi Shankar Prasad said based on the events of today and the preceding three days, two things have become clear. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by Parliament, not by the streets," the former Law Minister said. “We are not opposed to protests, but you have weaponized street protests because of your electoral defeats,” Prasad said indirectly blaming the Congress and other political parties for the street protests. Anarchy is a state of society without government, laws, or a central authority, or a political philosophy that opposes state rule in favor of voluntary cooperation. The word comes from the Greek anarkhia ("without a ruler"). In a literal sense, it means a complete lack of government, police, or enforced legal systems. A protest does not automatically become anarchy, as most protests are expressions of political grievance or demands directed at the government rather than attempts to destroy the state itself. However, a protest transitions into a state resembling anarchy or severe civil disorder under specific conditions: A demonstration shifts into practical anarchy when established legal authorities, police, or governing institutions completely lose the ability or power to maintain order, enforce laws, or arbitrate disputes in that area. Or when demonstrators abandon peaceful assembly or structured demands and instead engage in widespread lawlessness, unpunished crime, destruction of property, and the complete breakdown of public safety. Politically, a protest evolves into a revolutionary anarchy only when it actively seeks to dismantle or overthrow a government and replace state hierarchy with a leaderless or decentralised community structure. Cardiac rehabilitation, a multidisciplinary approach to recovery and risk-reduction, is an important addition to medications, interventional and surgical procedures in heart patients. A cardiac rehab programme usually includes medical assessments, supervised exercise, nutritional guidance, psychosocial counselling and health education tailored to the clinical, cultural and behavioural needs of the patient.
Cardiac rehab has been incorporated into the routine care of patients in developed countries, while it is just now gaining inroads in low- and middle- income countries like India. The primary benefits of attending a cardiac rehab programme are faster recovery from cardiac procedures, reduced risk of future complications, improvement in blood sugar, blood pressure and lipid levels, increased cardiorespiratory fitness, adherence to a heart healthy diet, better weight management, abstinence from tobacco and excessive alcohol consumption, better emotional health and health-related quality of life, and decreased mortality.
The scenario in India
There is now a growing prevalence of heart diseases in the young Indian population, both in urban and rural parts of the country. According to the Global Burden of Disease, 2021, heart disease is the most common cause of death in India, accounting for 28.6 lakh deaths. Estimates indicate that nearly 27% of all deaths in India are due to heart disease, while 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease in the country are premature, between the ages of 40 and 69 years. Among those who survive, the effects can linger for years, affecting productivity and quality of life. This has brought to the fore, the urgent need for more widespread and accessible cardiac rehab facilities. There is a wide gap in the number of heart patients requiring cardiac rehab and the actual numbers being referred for these services.
Barriers to rehab
Even among those who access and enrol in cardiac rehab programmes, not everyone completes the programme. The main barriers to completing the cardiac rehab program after enrolling include patients’ work commitments, family responsibilities, financial constraints, and medical complications. Programmes that can offer personalised solutions including flexible scheduling, return-to-work counselling, sliding scale payment options and close collaborations with the referring cardiologist to identify and treat complications early, could help decrease drop-outs. Programme facilitators must also be able to proactively identify cues for potential non-adherence and work with patients and their families to circumvent challenges and complete the programme.
What works
A ‘TRACK and CARE’ policy could help in improving patient engagement in cardiac rehab programmes. TRACK denotes establishing Trust, involving the patient’s Relatives, helping them set clear Aims for the programme, Checking on the progress made on a daily, weekly and monthly basis and finally remembering to say Kudos to every single positive behaviour change made by the patient. The CARE refers to multidisciplinary care, comorbidity care and holistic care, where various specialists work together to address the different medical and psychological needs of the patient.
Young people are increasingly contracting heart disease. Getting them back to be productive, healthy and happy members of society is vital. While prevention remains the most important goal, cardiac rehabilitation must become an important part of treatment, not just an add-on that is optional. And to do that, we have to proactively address the potential barriers to access, adherence and programme completion.
(Dr. Priya Chockalingam is the clinical director, Cardiac Wellness Institute, Chennai. drpriya@cardiacwellnessinstitute.com)

North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
- Published
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours.
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them.
Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty.
The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.
It is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".
Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.
A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC.
"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds.
"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."
Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.
But the alliance is not without tension.
Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan.
China's attitude has shifted more recently.
"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC.
Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war.
At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops.
Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day.
So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties.
Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

India's 'cockroach' leaders jailed after holding protest
- Published
Two top leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.
Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka appeared before a magistrate on Wednesday after being detained at Jantar Mantar, a longstanding venue for demonstrations that police recently removed from the city's list of authorised protest sites.
The two were among a group who climbed a locked gate and crossed barricades to enter the site on Tuesday.
The GenZ-led movement has been protesting for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud - charges the poll panel denies.
Police accused Das, Ranka and their fellow activist Ajinkya Shinde of trespassing, breaching a peace bond, violating prohibitory orders and obstructing public officials - charges they deny.
Delhi's Special Executive Magistrate Court remanded Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody, while Shinde was released on a personal bond. The two leaders can seek bail from a higher court.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who has been holding separate protests against the Election Commission, condemned the arrests, describing them as "an act of cowardice", and expressed support for peaceful demonstrations at Jantar Mantar.
"Students. Youth. Journalists. The [opposition's] INDIA bloc. Different banners, one cause. All protests are one: citizens demanding their constitutional rights," he wrote on X.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was travelling to Delhi after the arrests, accused the government of cracking down on dissent and challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to "declare the Emergency officially", according to news agency PTI.
His comments drew parallels with India's 1970s Emergency, a period when civil liberties were curtailed under then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
The CJP, which is a pressure group and not an official political party, has been demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
Wednesday's actions follow a weekend of protests during which Das, Ranka, Shinde, and Dipke were taken into preventive custody ahead of planned demonstrations at Jantar Mantar. They were later released by a magistrate.
Police imposed extensive security restrictions across Delhi, closing several metro stations and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site. Thousands of people, including journalists, were detained and later released, while videos showed police forcibly dragging some protesters into buses.
Following the weekend protests, Delhi police removed Jantar Mantar from its list of authorised protest sites, instead designating three other venues - Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground.
The CJP criticised the decision, saying it would make demonstrations less visible and harder for protesters to make their voices heard.
On Tuesday, the activists returned to Jantar Mantar despite the restrictions. Videos shared by Dipke and other CJP leaders showed Das and Ranka climbing over police barricades, carrying Indian flags and chanting slogans.
"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.
Ratna Singh, head of the CJP's legal team, alleged that the activists were denied access to lawyers for several hours before being taken to Parliament Street Police Station in a private vehicle at about 03:00 local time (21:30 GMT on Tuesday).
She also rejected a police allegation that CJP leaders had called on others to join the protest at Jantar Mantar.
"Absolutely false! No public call was ever made," she wrote on X.
The CJP emerged from student-led demonstrations earlier this year over alleged exam irregularities and demands for education reforms.
Weeks of protests led by the movement culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group began as an online satire movement after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May.
He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people demanding change.
Following the summer protests, the CJP developed into a wider pressure group, tapping into discontent over unemployment, examinations and government accountability.
The CJP launched its latest nationwide protests in Mumbai on 2 October, following an Indian Express report alleging that Chief Election Commissioner Kumar had ignored objections from his two fellow commissioners over changes to voter registration.
The newspaper reported that commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised concerns at least 14 times over 10 months about decisions taken without their knowledge, including changes affecting voter databases and electoral rolls. The Election Commission has denied the allegations, saying its decisions were unanimous.
The controversy has intensified scrutiny of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, a voter verification exercise that opposition parties allege has benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the government denies this.
Although the CJP and opposition parties have not held joint protests, their demonstrations have coincided in recent days. Gandhi is among politicians, lawyers and journalists detained during protests across several cities.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) announced a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission for the demonstration and detained thousands of people, including CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were detained after arriving at Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International AIRPORT. With Jantar Mantar barricaded, some demonstrators protested at other locations. The three leaders were released on 11 October 2026 while the Supreme Court directed authorities to uphold the rights of peaceful protesters. On 12 October 2026, opposition leaders led a march towards the Supreme Court against the SIR exercise, but police stopped them before they reached the court amid heightened security and temporary metro station closures (here, here, here, and here).
In this context, a video showing people breaking through barricades and advancing is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows visuals from the protests in Delhi on 11 October 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows people breaking through barricades and advancing during the protests in Delhi on 11 October 2026.
Fact: The video predates the October 2026 protests in Delhi and shows a farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, in July 2026. The farmers were demanding 100% government procurement of moong crops at the Minimum Support Price (MSP), a legal guarantee for MSP and the cancellation of the e-token system, among other demands. The protest was later called off following talks with the government and assurances regarding their demands. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple social media posts (here, here, and here) from July 2026 featuring the same visuals from a different angle. This confirms that the viral video predates the October 2026 protests in Delhi and is unrelated to them. According to these posts, the video shows a farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, over demands including a legal guarantee for the Minimum Support Price (MSP), 100% government procurement of moong crops and the cancellation of the e-token system. The posts also state that protesters were stopped about seven kilometres from the Chief Minister’s residence and were sitting on the road with food and water.
We then conducted a Google search using relevant keywords and found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) stating that the farmers were protesting to demand 100% procurement of their moong (green gram) crop at the Minimum Support Price (MSP), among other demands. The farmers had marched from Narmadapuram to Bhopal, seeking the abolition of the e-token system for crop procurement and fertiliser distribution.
A report published by Dainik Bhaskar in July 2026 carried visuals from the same location and reported that a large crowd had gathered during a farmers’ protest against the moong procurement and fertiliser token system, with people breaking through police barricades and advancing. Other media reports stated that the farmers later called off their protest following talks with the government and assurances regarding their demands.
To sum up, a July 2026 video of a farmers’ protest in Bhopal is shared as showing the CJP protests in Delhi on 11 October 2026.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

In a case of alleged medical negligence involving a 14-month-old boy who suffered brain damage following routine ear surgery, the Bengaluru Urban District Health Officer (DHO) and the Karnataka Private Medical Establishments (KPME) Grievance Redressal Authority have officially referred the matter to the Karnataka Medical Council (KMC) for an inquiry and report.
The decision follows a complaint lodged by Sampath Kumar K.P., whose son was taken to Cloudnine Hospital, Nagarabhavi, on July 26, 2026, for emergency surgical repair of a full-thickness ear laceration. During the procedure, the toddler suffered a cardiac arrest in the operation theatre and subsequently sustained severe brain injury due to lack of oxygen.
Lapses in anesthesia administration
A detailed inquiry conducted by an expert medical panel — comprising Raghunatha M. (anaesthesiologist) and Nagaraju (paediatrician) from the State-run Sir C.V. Raman General Hospital — said there were critical lapses during the administration of anesthesia.
According to the technical committee’s report submitted by doctors to the KMC, the operating room was satisfactorily equipped, but the attending anesthesiologist was “not well trained to administer anaesthesia for small children”.
Describing how the lapse led to oxygen levels plummetting, the report states that the doctor attempted to intubate the child with an uncuffed tube, leading to hypoxia, bradycardia, and eventual cardiac arrest.
While hospital logs claimed cardiac arrest was reversed within seven minutes, the expert committee stated in the report that brain hypoxia persisted for 15 to 20 minutes, causing severe, irreversible brain damage. An MRI scan performed three days later confirmed partial prolonged hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury.
Current condition and referral
Following initial resuscitation, the toddler was transferred to the Paediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) at Cloudnine Hospital, Jayanagar, for advanced critical care.
The clinical evaluation conducted by Dr. Nagaraju noted that while the child has been weaned off mechanical ventilation and is currently hemodynamically stable, he suffers from profound neurological sequelae. The toddler remains unresponsive to verbal commands, has lost his sight, exhibits decerebrate posturing, and is dependent on Ryle’s tube feeding. He requires ongoing multidisciplinary care.
During the hearing held on October 8, the DHO and KPME Authority reviewed the expert panel’s findings and the parents’ submission. Noting that the medical panel’s findings explicitly indicate prima facie medical negligence, the Bengaluru Urban DHO, formally transferred the case files to the KMC president on October 12, for disciplinary proceedings and further action.
