CBI names Nanded resident in new NEET leak charge sheet
The agency has added Nanded resident Sheshrav Bajrang Suryawanshi as an accused and included forensic findings in its final investigation report.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on Wednesday filed a supplementary charge sheet containing an additional name in the list of accused as well as forensic findings in the investigation into the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test-Undergraduate (NEET-UG) 2026 paper leak case, people familiar with the development said.
The submission of the supplementary charge sheet before a special court in Delhi concludes the agency’s investigation in the case, these people said.
CBI had named 13 people, including three subject experts hired by the National Testing Agency (NTA), middlemen and coaching centre representatives, in the first charge sheet on July 28. Both charge sheets do not name any government official.
HT had first reported last week that CBI didn’t find any evidence against any government official in the case.
Also read: No govt, NTA official named as CBI files supplementary chargesheet over NEET paper leak
Nanded man named as additional accused
The additional accused, Nanded resident Sheshrav Bajrang Suryawanshi alias Raj Suryawanshi, was arrested on September 2. He is allegedly a close associate of co-accused Shubham Khairnar, who played a key role in distributing exam papers to various candidates and was arrested on May 13.
An officer said that Suryawanshi had called exam candidates to a location in Nanded and provided them with the question paper. “He kept their original documents like educational certificates and identity cards to ensure that they made the payment after the examination,” the officer added.
A second officer said that the supplementary charge sheet also includes forensic experts’ findings. On May 12, NTA announced the cancellation of the 2026 NEET test after at least 120 questions in a guess paper – a compilation made by subject experts and teachers of suggested questions, based on previous trends and patterns – were found to be the same as those in the NEET exam paper on May 3.
The leak was only detected a week after the exam was conducted, triggering massive protests spearheaded by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) that eventually leading to the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Outstanding sound quality. Premium build materials. Highly customizable EQ. Most comfortable Nothing headphones. Great ANC and transparency.
TIRED
Love-it or hate-it case. ANC is great, but not the best.
Nothing headphones have always stood out from the competition, and the Headphone (1) Pro is no different. It’s the brand’s most premium option yet, putting it up against the best from Sony, Bose, and Apple. After nearly a month of testing, I’d say these headphones belong among those top-tier choices, while bringing a few unique ideas to the table.
Exquisite Materials
Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Specs
Wireless connectivity
Bluetooth 6.1 with Multipoint, Auracast
Wired connectivity
USB-C (supports lossless up to 24 bit/192 kHz), 3.5-mm aux (supports lossless up to 24 bit/96 kHz)
Battery life
Up to 30 hours (ANC on), up to 68 hours (ANC off)
Weight
327 grams
Codec
LDAC, LC3, SBC, AAC
Water/dust resistance
IP52
Design is the first standout in the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro. On the outside, it follows the same formula as the Nothing Headphone (1) and Headphone (a), with a distinct square shape and two-tone, transparent outer shell.
The Headphone (1) Pro pushes this design to 11, largely by using premium materials instead of plastic. The square cans are made from a solid aluminum block. The arms are made of titanium. The transparent outer window is made of glass. There’s very little (if any) plastic to be found, yet they actually weigh 2 grams less than the Nothing Headphone (1).
The case is … interesting. It’s basically a hard-shell version of the purse-like case for the Apple AirPods Max 2—a near universally loathed case, I might add. The Headphone (1) Pro case offers better ear cup protection, but the headband remains exposed. It’s something you use once, then promptly forget.
All that being said, these are Nothing’s most comfortable headphones yet. The softer, thicker padding, wider headband, and reduced clamping force make these noticeably more comfortable than the Headphone (1).
Mixing It Up
Noise canceling and transparency are also great, thanks to extra microphones and impressive sound isolation. It’s not quite as bulletproof as Sony and Bose, but it was more than enough for any New York City situation I threw at it.
Inside, things get even more interesting. The headphone uses a triple-driver design—a bass dynamic driver, a precision dynamic driver, and a treble xMEMS driver. The idea is that each driver handles a different frequency range, delivering clearer, fuller, less distorted sound. When every other major ANC headphone brand uses a single dynamic driver for the full frequency range, this triple-driver design is a big risk. Fortunately, sound quality is outstanding.
I’m not going to pretend I’m an audio engineer (I’m not). But songs I’ve listened to for years came back to life with the Headphone (1) Pro, with added emphasis, clarity, and energy in the midrange and treble I didn't expect.
I don’t usually make the stank-face to “Staring at the Sun,” by TV on the Radio, but I did pretty consistently with these headphones. Stevie Wonder’s “Another Star,” with its dense mix of vocals, hi-hat, trumpet, and guitar, sounded more spacious on the Nothing headphones than on the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen). Bass is clear, but not as punchy as headphones like the Sony XM6. I didn’t mind, but it was a little less fun with artists like Bad Bunny and Kendrick Lamar, or anything in the EDM genre. A simple EQ adjustment changed this (more on that later).
This focus on engaging mids and highs meant that music on the Nothing headphones commanded my attention more often. I actually had a harder time achieving deep focus at work with these headphones than with more bass-forward mixes on the Sony XM6 and Bose QC Ultra 2nd Gen.
That was a lot of sound talk, and everyone has different ears, different hearing, and different taste. Luckily, you don’t have to settle for one sound profile with these headphones.
The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro has some of the most customizable EQ settings I’ve ever seen in consumer ANC headphones.
First, there’s a physical “FLAT” switch tucked away on the left ear cup. When you turn it on, it changes to a neutral EQ designed for “reviewing music, producing, or mixing,” according to the brand. As someone who does none of those things, I still had a lot of fun using this mode. I even started to prefer Flat with certain songs and certain genres. One quirk: It increases the volume—I consistently had to lower the volume by two steps.
Second, the Nothing X app offers ample EQ settings. There are two EQ modes: simple, with a familiar three-band EQ (bass, mid, and treble), and advanced, where things get a little crazy. In advanced, you can dial in a +6 dB to -6 dB change for individual frequency bands on both the main driver and precision driver. This level of control is rare in consumer over-ear ANC headphones and will frankly overwhelm some people. That’s why I think more people will enjoy the Explore tab, where Nothing has curated five EQ presets to try out.
Add spatial audio modes on top of that, and you’ve got plenty of options to find your ideal EQ. Though I suspect many people will be happy with the sound out of the box.
Playing in the Big Leagues
The $400 price tag puts these headphones squarely in competition with the established, well-regarded $450 Sony WH-1000XM6, $450 Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen), and $550 (but always on sale for $450) Apple AirPods Pro Max 2. Those are three of the best ANC headphones you can buy.
I think the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro fit in that mix nicely. No, they don’t win in ANC or transparency performance (though both are solid). But it stands out with a unique design, tactile on-ear controls, an excellent sound profile, and in-depth EQ customization. It’s a toss-up whether I’ll use these or the Sony XM6 as my daily driver, and that’s high praise for Nothing's first take on premium over-ear headphones.

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

- Snopes reviewed lawyer directories from the bar association and supreme courts of all 50 U.S. states and Washington, D.C., and found no evidence she had passed the bar examination in any of them.
- A review of Chinese rules suggested she could not have passed China's equivalent of the bar exam as a U.S. national, or practiced as a lawyer, even by the current requirements, which are looser than they used to be.
- A spokesperson for Pepperdine University confirmed in an email to Snopes that Zacharia graduated with a Juris Doctor degree in 2011.
- John Ohnesorge, an expert in Chinese law from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told Snopes in an email "There's no possibility that she passed the Chinese bar exam, ever."
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the White House for more details and are waiting for a response.
In October, social media posts questioned new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia's claim that she passed the bar examination in China.
The posts emerged after several reports asked whether Zacharia had the credentials to practice law anywhere in the U.S., though she has repeatedly identified herself as a lawyer in the past, including in an archived version of her X profile and during a television interview.
When asked Oct. 13 where she passed the bar (the examination that allows people to practice law), Zacharia responded, "When I moved to China." She did not say she passed the bar in any U.S. state.
People on Facebook and Reddit expressed doubts, while Rep. Ted Lieu, a Democrat from California, wrote on X, "Are Katie Zacharia and trump lying when they say she is an attorney?" (archived):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers emailed and searched the website, asking us to examine whether Zacharia could have possibly passed the bar in China.
An extensive search turned up no evidence Zacharia was a member of any state bar in the U.S., nor in Washington, D.C. In addition, current Chinese law made it unlikely that she was ever in a position to pass China's examination to practice law, as she is not a Chinese national. There was no evidence that she could do when she lived there between 2011 and 2013, though China only formalized rules about foreign lawyers in 2017.
For this reason, we have left the claim unrated.
"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Katie Zacharia told Snopes in an emailed statement. Neither she nor the White House press office answered follow-up questions, nor did they share any documentation showing she could practice law as an attorney in good standing in any jurisdiction.
"Katie graduated with a JD [Juris Doctor, a law degree] from Caruso School of Law in 2011, and with a bachelor of arts in political science from Seaver College in 2007," a spokesperson for Pepperdine University wrote in an email to Snopes.
Asked whether Zacharia could have taken and passed China's law examination before 2017, John Ohnesorge, a law professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who researched Chinese regulations of lawyers, said in an email to Snopes, "There's no possibility that she passed the Chinese bar exam, ever." 
"What she did in China was to work in an elite Chinese law firm on international business matters, and doing that kind of work does not really require being a member of a bar anywhere," he added.
We also searched lawyer directories across the U.S. and found no record of Katie Zacharia — also searching by her maiden name, Black — in any of them.
Zacharia's resumé and Chinese rules
Zacharia's LinkedIn profile indicates she worked in China between 2011 and 2013, at Zhong Lun Law Firm.
In 2020, the Chinese Justice Observer — a consulting platform and analysis outlet about the Chinese legal system — said foreigners cannot practice law in China. In 2019, China established a pilot program to allow foreign lawyers to act as legal consultants in China, not lawyers, though one condition is that the person should have practiced as a lawyer in their home country for at least two years.
Even under this program, Zacharia could not have practiced as a legal consultant as she had not practiced law in the U.S. long enough after she graduated.
Zacharia's LinkedIn indicates she later worked as "general counsel" for Fix California, a conservative organization that aims at ensuring "election integrity." It is unclear how she could hold this position without having passed the state's bar examination. We reached out to Fix California asking for more details.
A sheet of advice for French lawyers seeking to work in China from 2017 confirms that only Chinese nationals can practice law in China. In other words, any foreign lawyer practicing in China can do so only with credentials from the countries where they obtained their degrees.
However, China's current rules were implemented in 2017. Ohnesorge, who wrote a research paper in 2023 about the history of the regulation of lawyers in China, said this measure was most likely protectionistic. 
"It's true that the 2017 regulation started requiring two years of practice in a home jurisdiction in order to qualify as a foreign legal consultant, but that's best understood as a protectionist measure used to keep Chinese firms from hiring too many foreign lawyers, not a requirement that actually makes any sense," Ohnesorge said via email. "People doing the work she did aren't really practicing the law of their home jurisdiction anyway, so why require that at all?"
For further reading, Snopes covered several rumors about Zacharia's predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, including the claim that she said the war in Iran would be over if President Donald Trump had "better intelligence."

Menopause may not be a gradual process taking years as is commonly thought -- instead, the female body could be traversing a "physiological cliff" around the time of the last menstrual period, a new study has found.
Analysing more than 300 million laboratory test results from over one million women in the US and Israel, researchers at Weizmann Institute of Science identified abrupt changes in dozens of measures of bodily health and function, far beyond the familiar shifts in sex hormone levels and the loss of fertility.
Findings published in the Nature Medicine journal showed that the changes appeared in 52 of the 90 types of laboratory tests examined, covering nearly all body systems, including tests of bone health, liver and kidney function, and cholesterol levels.
The changes were found to be less pronounced among women receiving menopausal hormone therapy.
Further, the sudden shifts were preceded by accelerating changes in sex hormone levels that began more than a decade before menopause -- several years earlier than previously thought.
None of the abrupt changes were observed in men of similar ages, the study found.
It "revealed a step-like physiological cliff at the FMP (final menstrual period) including endocrine, skeletal, hepatic, renal and lipid systems," the authors wrote.
Because most of the abrupt changes identified in the study are associated with increased disease risk, the findings could help women take preventive steps, such as exercising and improving their diet, years before menopause, the researchers said.
"Our study extends the window for potential preventive care to almost a decade before menopause. More broadly, the method we developed may help study other major changes in life, such as puberty, pregnancy or the onset of disease," author Uri Alon, from Weizmann Institute of Science, said.
Two sets of data were analysed -- results from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, conducted over more than two decades, and medical records collected over around 20 years by Israel's health insurer Clalit.
The researchers said that such large datasets are rarely used in menopause research because they generally lack information about the age at which women had their last period.
To overcome the limitation, the team developed a computational method which they said is inspired by astronomy.
Just as astronomers can sharpen an image by mathematically correcting distortions caused by a telescope, the new method removed the 'blur' in medical data caused by differences in the age at which women reach menopause, the researchers said.

Trump is taking his midterms anger out on Ukraine
The Ukraine-Trump-SpaceX debacle, briefly explained.
Welcome to The Logoff: Is Trump turning on Ukraine?
What’s happening? Ukraine says its access to Starlink, the satellite internet system run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company, and Starshield, the military version of the same technology, is being throttled as President Donald Trump’s animosity toward the country mounts.
Why is Trump angry with Ukraine? Trump has been hot and cold on Ukraine since he returned to office, but his current anger is driven by oil prices and successful Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries — particularly ahead of the US midterm elections.
Last week, Trump announced a US-Russia diesel deal, which has elicited bipartisan anger and probably won’t do much, if anything, for diesel prices in the US. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticized the deal, leading Trump to lash out and call for Zelenskyy’s replacement.
Over the weekend, Trump also announced an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” between Ukraine and Russia that doesn’t really seem to exist. “Both parties have agreed,” he wrote. “Do not break it!” (Russia appears to have broken it the same day, while Ukraine is complying for now.)
Is Ukraine actually to blame for high oil prices? Partially, but not primarily; as the BBC explains, while Ukrainian refinery strikes play a role, ongoing disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf oil industry from Trump’s war with Iran have had a greater impact (though Trump has tried to shift the blame to Ukraine).
Why is Starlink so important? Starlink and Starshield provide vital communications infrastructure in Ukraine, especially on the battlefield. The technology is also used to control offensive and defensive Ukrainian drones, which have emerged as a key part of Ukraine’s military efforts against Russia.
What’s next? Despite the fact that neither Russia nor Ukraine seemingly signed on to Trump’s “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” and Russia is still attacking Ukrainian energy facilities, Trump is trying to bind Ukraine to it: The US has reportedly threatened to suspend US intelligence sharing, which has helped give Ukraine early warning of Russian missile attacks, if Ukraine strikes more Russian refineries.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

SC to issue orders on preventive steps taken by Centre to curb online child sexual abuse content
SC agreed to issue orders on preventive steps to be taken by the Centre and other stakeholders against child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM) online
The Supreme Court on Thursday agreed to issue orders on preventive steps to be taken by the Centre and other stakeholders against child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM) online, citing the seriousness of the matter.
The order was passed after the ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) submitted a draft Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) to the court. “As part of the future preventive action required to be taken with respect to dissemination of CSEAM content, MeitY has drafted an SOP for the intermediaries for prevention, direction, removal and reporting of CSEAM content to a government portal (Sahyog),” the ministry said.
The SOP has been prepared in consultation with the ministry of women and child development (MoWCD) and other stakeholders, besides the ministry of home affairs (MHA) and department of telecommunications (DoT), the affidavit said.
Solicitor general Tushar Mehta appearing for Centre said, “We are serious about this matter. There were discussions that took place based on which we have given our suggestions on how to tackle this problem. We require some more time to finalise the SOP.”
The bench said, “This is a very serious matter. We want the Union government to take it seriously. We will pass an order. You study our order. We will suggest you some things that will be helpful for you.”
The court posted the matter after a month to allow the Centre come up with further developments on preventing CSEAM online.
The Centre’s affidavit gave examples of how in an instance, MeitY issued notice in July 2026 to the Meta’s compliance officer regarding dissemination of paid advertisements promoting CSEAM. The proceedings are still underway. Meity said it has been regularly communicating and coordinating with various stakeholders, including the intermediaries, regarding the need for enhanced monitoring, reporting and removal of CSEAM content.
As part of these efforts, Centre pointed out that in February this year, the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 were amended to incorporate specific due diligence obligations for preventing and reporting CSEAM content on their platforms.
The Centre was responding to an order passed by the court last month in a petition filed by Just Rights for Children Alliance (JRCA). The petitioner sought compliance of a 2024 judgment and a uniform SOP to be framed to ensure timely reporting by intermediaries.
The judgment passed on September 23, 2024 held that social media intermediaries have a duty to report cases of child abuse and exploitation to the local authorities under Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (Pocso) Act.
The verdict held, “In view of the salutary object and the mandatory character of the provisions of Sections 19 and 20 of the Pocso read with Rule 11 of the Pocso Rules, we are of the considered view, that an intermediary cannot claim exemption from the liability under Section 79 of the IT Act for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, unless due diligence is conducted by it and compliance is made of these provisions of the Pocso.”
It further stated that the compliance required includes not just removal of child pornographic content but an immediate report of such content to the concerned police.
The JRCA application said that Instagram carried paid advertisements promoting CSEAM, raising concerns over compliance of the top court’s judgment. The petitioner sought a comprehensive mechanism to ensure effective implementation of obligations of social media platforms and prevent the online circulation and exploitation of children. It sought a uniform SOP for intermediaries covering detection and mandatory reporting of CSEAM, preservation of evidence and inter-agency coordination among relevant agencies.
It further demanded prompt uploading of offenders’ particulars to the National Database of Sexual Offenders (NDSO), timely action by law-enforcement agencies on every report received from an intermediary, and initiation of criminal proceedings against intermediaries that fail to comply with mandatory reporting obligations, in accordance with law.
The petitioner even sought the establishment of a centralised online reporting portal to facilitate reporting of CSEAM by intermediaries.

BookMyBai co-founder Anupam Sinhal has revealed the disturbing incident that prompted his company to stop providing domestic workers to Bollywood celebrities nearly a decade ago. In an interview with Hindustan Times, Sinhal recalled how a worker arrived at the company’s office with burn marks on her body after an incident involving an iron. “The Bollywood celebrity decision was taken the day a worker stepped into her office and she had burn marks on her body through the clothes iron because she accidentally burnt the clothes of that particular celebrity while she was ironing her clothes,” Sinhal said. The incident, he explained, became a turning point for the company. “That is when we thought enough is enough and now we are not doing this anymore,” he added. The account highlights the vulnerability of domestic workers, whose employment often takes place inside private homes, away from public scrutiny. Sinhal’s remarks also raise questions about the safeguards available to workers when they face mistreatment at work. Asked whether the restriction remained in force almost 10 years later, Sinhal offered a qualified answer, “Yes and no.” He said BookMyBai continues to refuse requests from celebrities who approach the platform directly. However, exceptions can be made when a trusted contact personally vouches for a prospective employer. “If a celebrity contacts us directly that she needs a domestic helper, we flat outrightly refuse that we will not be able to provide you with the service because we have a blanket ban on this,” he said. Sinhal cited Soni Razdan, actor Alia Bhatt’s mother, as an example of someone whose recommendation could lead the company to accept a request. He clarified that Razdan, rather than Bhatt herself, contacts the company in such cases. The distinction, according to Sinhal, is between an unsolicited request and one supported by a trusted reference. Despite the restrictions, Sinhal said some celebrities treat their domestic staff with consideration and generosity. He named Alia Bhatt and Dia Mirza among those who, according to him, have shown respect towards their workers. He also mentioned filmmaker Farah Khan, casting director Shanoo Sharma, cricketer Rohit Sharma, Sherlyn Chopra and actor Tina Datta. Sinhal recalled that Bhatt had given ₹50 lakh to a cook placed through the company, asking him to use the money to buy a house. He said the worker subsequently purchased a home in Virar. “There are very, very good employers who are there in the celebrities also, but they are a handful,” he said. Sinhal also described less severe but concerning situations involving wealthy employers, including domestic workers being expected to remain awake until 4 am during parties, even when they did not wish to do so. Sinhal said employer behaviour had improved considerably since the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent lockdowns. When part-time workers could not travel to employers’ homes, families had to manage household responsibilities themselves. That experience, he suggested, helped employers recognise how much they relied on domestic workers. He also pointed to a change in language, saying workers were increasingly described as “domestic workers” rather than “servants”. For Sinhal, the shift reflected a broader change in how their role was perceived. While he said major incidents had become less frequent among the households served by his company, his account underlines the importance of treating domestic work as employment that demands dignity, clear safeguards and accountability. Telecom giant Jio Platforms has set a price band of ₹1,065-₹1,119 per share for its IPO, which is set to open for public subscription next week. India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.
A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Police authorities didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.
The CJP said that among those detained was a group of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being taken away in a bus to an unknown location.
The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.
The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.
The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.
The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.
The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.
“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture student who attended the Bengaluru protest.
There were also protests over police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.
On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of using “brute force” to briefly detain party leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, and other lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.
Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.
BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.
Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

In a bankruptcy proceeding that kicked off yesterday, Disney has offered to buy some of the technology that powers the controversy-plagued chatbot Character.AI.
Disney is willing to pay $20 million for “a non-exclusive perpetual license” of certain Character Technologies intellectual property, the chatbot maker said in a press release that did not go into much further detail on which assets Disney wanted.
The move may be surprising. In September 2025, Disney joined others in publicly criticizing Character.AI for stealing content and harming kids. Specifically, Disney sent a strongly worded cease-and-desist letter that accused Character Technologies of weaponizing Disney characters “in a way that could damage its brand long term,” Axios reported.
“Character.AI’s infringing chatbots are known, in some cases, to be sexually exploitive and otherwise harmful and dangerous to children, offending Disney’s consumers and extraordinarily damaging Disney’s reputation and goodwill,” Disney wrote at the time.
That scandal ended with Character Technologies wiping all Disney-owned characters from its platform, but since then, Disney has hired former Character.AI chief Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer, Deadline reported.
Disney did not respond to Ars’ request for comment on whether the company plans to use Character.AI technology in products for kids.
It’s possible that Disney will be outbid and not acquire any Character.AI intellectual property. But ever since Disney’s potentially lucrative partnership with OpenAI fell through after Sora’s abrupt shutdown, the entertainment giant has been looking for more ways to “get in the AI game and profit from its boom,” Deadline reported. (Meanwhile, OpenAI apparently plans to revive Sora without Disney, insiders told The Information.) So, Disney may be moving early in the hopes of acquiring chatbot technology proven to resonate with its fanbase. It may possibly even take over the platform in a transition that preliminarily would be managed by Character.AI employees, the press release said.

Sony is taking on DJI with its new ECM-W5 wireless microphone kit
The kit includes two transmitters and a receiver, and it supports 32-bit float recording.
Sony has announced the ECM-W5, a $400 wireless microphone kit that's clearly designed to be as easy to use as DJI's affordable wireless mics, provided creators are willing to pay a comparatively premium price to use it. The ECM-W5 combines wireless transmitters and a receiver that can directly record to a Sony camera (or other devices over USB-C), capturing 96kHz audio from up to 500 meters away in line-of-sight conditions.
The ECM-W5 is easiest to use with Sony's Alpha series cameras, where it can connect over the Multi Interface Shoe (Sony's modern answer to the hotshoe) to receive power and transfer data. A kit only comes with one rectangular receiver and two microphone transmitters, but if you're willing to purchase multiple $120 transmitters separately, you can record up to four tracks at once. Each transmitter includes 64GB of internal memory, which should work great as a backup. The internal memory also enables 32-bit float recording, which means the ECM-W5 can capture both quiet and loud sounds without forcing you to make gain adjustments.
Each transmitter can be attached to a separate microphone, and the transmitters themselves have 11 hours of battery life and come with magnetic backplates so you can pin them to a shirt. If you don't have a Sony camera, the receiver also includes a USB-C adapter that lets it connect to a smartphone or a PC for other recording scenarios. And while you're making adjustments on the receiver's touchscreen, you can listen to playback wirelessly using Bluetooth LE and a pair of Sony headphones.
In comparison to the $259 DJI Mic 3 or the $99 DJI Mic Mini, it's hard to imagine the ECM-W5 would be a compelling alternative unless you're specifically interested in using the new microphone kit with Sony's cameras. If you can stomach paying $400, though, 32-bit float recording could simplify your post-production workflow significantly.
The ECM-W5 is available to pre-order today for $400 and ships in November. You can also pre-order a standalone $190 ECM-W5R receiver or $120 ECM-W5T transmitter if you plan on expanding your kit.

Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief
- Published
Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility as it prepares to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, according to Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), .
Banka was speaking at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi where he held talks with President William Ruto, government and sports officials, the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (Adak), athletes and representatives of law enforcement.
Wada said the visit was intended to build on recent progress in Kenya's anti-doping programme at a critical time following Nairobi's selection to host the 2029 World Championships.
"Kenya calls itself probably 'home of champions', but every home has to have a good host and has to be clean to be credible," Banka told the BBC.
"We absolutely need to instill the culture of clean sport."
Kenya was awarded the 2029 championships in September, making it the first African country selected to host the event.
The decision has increased scrutiny of its efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem.
More than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017.
The Polish former sports minister said he had received a clear commitment from Ruto's government to a policy of zero tolerance towards doping, but warned promises would have to be matched by results.
"Wada will monitor this situation and observe the dynamic. Action speaks louder than words," he said.
Banka said his discussions with Ruto also focused on strengthening an independent Adak, and ensuring it has sufficient government support.

2029 will be the real test
Nairobi 2029 could provide a global test of Kenya's ability to protect its sporting legacy.
For a country whose distance runners have helped define global athletics for generations, the stakes extend beyond staging a successful championship.
"The problem with anti-doping is not with rules and standards," Banka said. "The problem is with implementation."
Another challenge is testing infrastructure.
Africa currently has no Wada-accredited doping control laboratory following the loss of accreditation of the facility in Bloemfontein, South Africa.
Wada initially suspended the laboratory in March 2024 because of multiple failures to comply with its International Standard for Laboratories.
Its accreditation was formally revoked in May 2025 after those problems were not satisfactorily resolved.
Banka said Kenya has shown political interest in establishing its own facility, but cautioned against expecting a laboratory to be accredited in time for the 2029 championships.
The process, he said, takes years because the consequences of laboratory error can be enormous for an athlete.
That leaves Kenya facing a more immediate priority: strengthening the system around testing rather than relying on a new laboratory as a solution.
'Doping has no colours and flags'
Banka also rejected the idea that doping should be viewed as an exclusively Kenyan, or African, problem.
"Doping has no colours and flags," he said, pointing to cases across established sporting nations including the United States, Germany and his native Poland.
"The problem would be to ignore this issue, not to tackle, or to pretend that there is no doping here."
Wada, he added, can investigate sport but cannot dismantle the criminal networks supplying prohibited substances.
"We are not a superpower. We are not law enforcement," he said.
"They have tools to really go after those who are destroying the credibility of the sport and the country."
He said intelligence indicated performance-enhancing drugs were being produced in Kenya and described Africa as a significant market.
According to him, athletes are often the "weakest points in the ecosystem", arguing that anti-doping authorities need to pursue not only competitors who break the rules but also the coaches, doctors, managers and suppliers who enable doping.
Some athletes, he suggested, are being exploited by people "who have money, who have power" and see them as a route to profit.

The CEO of Compass Pathways said Wednesday that the company, which is preparing to complete the submission of its psychedelic therapy for regulatory review this quarter, will “go slow before we go fast,” warning that negative patient or provider experiences early in the launch could damage the broader sector.
As the psychedelics field races toward its first potential approval by the Food and Drug Administration, the executive, Kabir Nath, underscored that a cautious rollout would be essential. But he also said the mental health field was on the brink of a major change.
“I think this is a really big deal for patients, for providers, and incidentally for Compass Pathways as well,” Nath said, speaking in Boston at the STAT Summit.
Compass is preparing to complete a rolling FDA submission this quarter for COMP360, its synthetic psilocybin treatment for treatment-resistant depression, with aims to launch early next year.
Nath said the company expects its treatment, if approved, to be subject to an FDA risk evaluation and mitigation strategy, or REMS, and is investing in training for providers who would administer the drug.
Unlike conventional antidepressants, which can take weeks to work and require daily dosing, psilocybin has shown the potential to produce rapid and lasting improvements after just a handful of administrations, Nath said.
In Compass’s Phase 3 trials, roughly a quarter of patients experienced a clinically meaningful response after a single administration of COMP360, which involves a roughly six-hour supervised session. That figure rose to about 40% after a second dose three weeks later. Nath said the company’s longer-term data suggest that patients who respond to treatment can experience benefits lasting as long as a year after two or three administrations.
But Steven Hyman, a Harvard University professor and former director of the National Institute of Mental Health, cautioned that significant scientific questions remain about psychedelic treatments, including how to establish their efficacy in clinical trials.
One challenge is that patients who receive a psychedelic drug often know they have received it because of its distinctive effects, potentially compromising the blinding of trials. This was one concern when an MDMA-based therapy from Lykos Therapeutics was rejected by the FDA in 2024.
“The unblinding remains a challenging problem,” Hyman said.
He raised another fundamental question: whether the psychedelic experience itself is necessary for the drugs to work.
Some companies are developing compounds designed to produce antidepressant effects without hallucinations or other intense subjective experiences. If successful, such treatments could potentially be prescribed for patients to take at home, eliminating the need for lengthy supervised sessions.
“It would be nontrivial if you could separate these, because then somebody could write a prescription and send somebody home,” Hyman said. “But we don’t know.”
That question also has implications for psychotherapy, which has traditionally been considered an important component of psychedelic treatment.
Nath said Compass deliberately separated psychotherapy from its clinical trials, arguing that the company’s responsibility is to develop a drug rather than dictate how physicians provide psychological care. He noted that an analysis of recorded treatment sessions found that roughly 80% of the time was spent in silence.
Hyman said psychotherapy following a psychedelic experience could nevertheless help patients process powerful emotions, memories, and other psychological effects. But he emphasized that researchers have yet to determine how much of the clinical benefit comes from the drug’s pharmacological effects and how much from the experience itself.
The discussion also touched on the risks of moving too quickly to bring psychedelic treatments to market – particularly since officials in the Trump administration have expressed support for accelerating their development.
Hyman said the field’s credibility would depend on rigorous research, responsible marketing, and long-term safety monitoring.
“I don’t mean this as a pun,” Hyman said. “But being really sober about the way this research is presented — the only way to gain credibility is to be absolutely rigorous.”
He drew a comparison to cannabis, where early perceptions of safety did not anticipate all the risks associated with increasingly potent products.
Even if COMP360 wins approval, another major challenge will be ensuring that patients can afford and access the treatment.
Asked about potential pricing relative to Johnson & Johnson’s Spravato, an esketamine treatment for depression, Nath said Spravato provides a reference point but declined to commit to a specific pricing benchmark.
The treatment’s costs would extend beyond the drug itself, given the need for several hours of monitoring in a clinical setting. Nath said Compass has spent years working on reimbursement mechanisms for that monitoring and is engaging with commercial insurers and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to secure coverage.
For Hyman, the promise of psychedelics is clear, particularly given the limitations of existing depression treatments. But their emergence also underscores how much psychiatry still needs to learn about the biological underpinnings of depression and why patients respond differently to treatment.
“We’re awash in subjectivity still,” he said, pointing to the lack of objective biomarkers that could help researchers identify which patients are most likely to benefit from a given drug.

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993
- Published
Rwanda has signed a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali and next to the city's new international airport. It will be the first F1 race in Africa since 1993.
A statement from F1 said the project came as a result of "years of collaboration to ensure the right foundations, with the best partner, are in place to deliver a successful, sustainable and world-class grand prix for generations to come".
The circuit, designed by the former F1 driver Alex Wurz, has been "designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans," the statement added.
F1 hopes the race will provide an opportunity for the sport to expand its profile in Africa, a relatively unexplored market compared to Europe, Asia and the Americas.
It has not yet been established where the race may best fit into the schedule during the year.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published7 hours ago
The sport is likely to want to avoid holding the race in the main rain season of March to May. There is a shorter, less disruptive rain season from October to November.
F1 is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: "For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.
"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.
"The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."
F1 president Stefano Domenicali said the new contract was "a landmark moment for F1", which would mean the sport was racing "on every inhabited continent".
Domenicali added: "Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."
Sportswashing controversy
The race is likely to lead to opposition from human rights groups accusing Rwanda of sportswashing, as has been the case with its sponsorship of Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa.
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
A spokesperson for F1 said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."
The track's build process will be overseen by three companies, with long-time F1 track architect Tilke and DAR working alongside WurzDesign as the creator of the circuit.
It is designed to be fast and flowing, with significant elevation change, using the natural contours of Rwanda's hilly landscape.
The first grand prix in Africa was the final round of the World Championship in Morocco in 1958.
South Africa hosted a race during the apartheid era - from 1960-66 in East London, now known as KuGompo City, before the race moved to Kyalami near Johannesburg from 1976-85.
Kyalami returned for two races in 1992 and 1993 as apartheid was coming to an end.
The country has held talks with F1 in recent years about a return at various venues, including Kyalami and Cape Town, but a deal has not proved possible.

Infantino apologises to Fifa Council - but told he's still not fit to lead
- Published
President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he releases all of the documents and answers key questions.
The Fifa Council met in Zurich on Thursday for the first time since Infantino's secret Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal emerged.
Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been given to a private investment firm.
In a three-and-a-half-hour meeting, Infantino also faced questions about US striker Folarin Balogun's suspended red-card ban, the Fifa Peace Prize and funding for national associations.
Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that many questions remained unanswered.
"One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested - for example getting the papers from FFE," Hewitt said.
"I asked the question 'why not?' - and we were asked to submit those questions in writing.
"I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president - and that was what was shared in the meeting."
Hewitt acknowledged there had been "some contrition" in Infantino's apology.
"Then there were no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what had happened," she added.
"What he really apologised for was not bringing it to the council. If you regret it that deeply, share it with us."
Uefa - European football's governing body - has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down.
It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released.
Asked if there was any change in stance from Uefa about Infantino, Hewitt added: "From my position, nothing has shifted. I've no new information that makes me feel any differently, other than we do have a president who is apologetic."

There were days when Dr. Koyyala Ruth John Paul struggled to find food. Estranged from her family after coming out as a transgender woman, she spent years trying to make ends meet, searching for jobs while refusing to give up on her dream of becoming a doctor. When the path to postgraduate medical education was blocked by the absence of clear admission procedures for transgender candidates, she turned to the courts.
On Saturday (October 10, 2026) her perseverance culminated in a milestone. Dr. Ruth John Paul cleared all subjects in the recently announced MD/MS examination results, completing her postgraduate degree in Emergency Medicine at the ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar, Hyderabad, where she studied during the 2023-26 academic session. She has become the first transgender person in India to complete a postgraduate medical course. “I am feeling very happy. It is a matter of pride for me and my community. It is a great achievement in my life,” she said.
A childhood marked by loss
The youngest of three siblings, Dr. Ruth John Paul hails from Khammam district and grew up in a family with limited financial means. She lost her father when she was eight years old and was raised by her mother. She completed her schooling and intermediate education in her native district before clearing the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) and pursuing undergraduate medical education. She came out as a transgender woman during her undergraduate years. This led to her family rejecting her, leaving her separated from them for nearly six years.
The period that followed was marked by financial insecurity and the struggle to survive independently. “There were times when I did not even have food. I struggled to survive and looked for jobs,” she said.
In 2021, she found part-time work at Mitr Clinic (now Sabrang Clinic), which is India’s first transgender clinic. She worked there for around two years while continuing to prepare for postgraduate medical entrance examinations.
A legal battle to pursue her dream
Clearing the entrance examination was not the end of her struggle. Dr. Ruth John Paul said she encountered difficulties during postgraduate medical counselling because there were no clear protocols for accommodating transgender candidates.
With the assistance of transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli, she approached the Telangana High Court seeking relief. The legal proceedings continued for nearly two years. An interim order from the High Court eventually enabled her to proceed with admission. In 2023, she secured a seat in Emergency Medicine at ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar.
Her admission marked a turning point, but the challenges did not end there. She said she continued to encounter stigma and apprehension from people who were unfamiliar with transgender individuals.
From apprehension to acceptance
Working in a clinical environment brought its own challenges. As an emergency medicine trainee, she had to interact with patients during some of their most vulnerable moments, while also navigating the prejudices that transgender people can face. She recalled how some people were initially hesitant or uncomfortable around her. “Initially, some people were scared and did not know how to respond. But when I interacted with patients and treated them with care, they began to appreciate me. People who were initially apprehensive have now become comfortable with me,” she said.
A doctor with a larger purpose
Now that she has completed her postgraduate course, Dr. Ruth John Paul wants to use her medical training to help people in need, particularly transgender individuals who require emergency and critical care. “I want to serve everyone, especially transgender people who face critical medical emergencies. I want to provide care without discrimination based on gender identity or sexuality,” she said.

Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
- Published
On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.
Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"
Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.
The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).
"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.
In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".
Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.
It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.
They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.
"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.
"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."
Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception."
When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers.
A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual.
Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m.
The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!"
The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them.
This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson.
The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.
The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.
She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.
But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises.
One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy.
For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.
Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days.
Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here.
"I really like it here."

October has rolled around, and that means only one thing: Spooky season is here! And what better way to celebrate Halloween than with some of the finest fright fests of the last 50 years?
We’re bringing you a more retro-tinged selection of the best films on streaming this month, but the mix of crowd-pleasers and cult classics offers something for horror fans of all tastes. For instance, David Cronenberg’s grotesque revamp of The Fly, buzzing onto Hulu, and Ken Russell’s Altered States materializing on The Criterion Channel, both bring uniquely visceral takes on body horror to your screens, while sleeper hit Under the Skin on Netflix offers slow-burn sci-fi scares, and Midsommar on Prime Video takes to the hills for a sun-drenched approach to folk horror.
If you fancy something a bit newer, fear not. Well, fear lots actually—Zach Cregger’s shockingly original horror debut Barbarian smashes its way onto Hulu, while Netflix brings the final chapter in the sumptuously scary Mononoke trilogy, an anime extravaganza that looks like nothing else. Plus, there’s even one post-credits stinger of an entry that’s too scary to mention here …
Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.
Barbarian
When Tess (Georgina Campbell) finds her Airbnb in a sketchy neighborhood double booked with Keith (Bill Skarsgård), you’ll probably think you know where Barbarian is headed. You don't—and you should brace yourself for everything that follows. Written and directed by Zach Cregger (in a seismic departure from his early comedy background), Barbarian constantly flips the script, regularly subverting viewer expectations of horror movie clichés at every turn.
Smartly written, brilliantly shot, and psychologically disturbing on multiple levels, Barbarian is a genuinely terrifying entry in the modern horror canon. If you’ve discovered Cregger’s work from the Academy Award–winning Weapons or his recent horror-comedy reboot of Resident Evil, this is where he first made his mark on the silver screen.
Under the Skin
Under the Skin almost defies explanation. Scarlett Johansson plays an alien in human form, roaming Glasgow and the Scottish Highlands, luring isolated and lonely men to their doom, drowning them in an inexplicable oily abyss that seems to exist in a null space. All the while, she’s observed by a motorcyclist, trailing her from victim to victim.
No names are given, no purpose explained (not even to the cast; director Jonathan Glazer shot many of the alien’s initial encounters with humans using hidden cameras, only explaining and asking for their involvement afterward), but it’s far better to watch this blind and make your own mind up. Be warned, though—Johansson’s performance is truly unearthly, and in conjunction with Glazer’s bizarre imagery and a soundscape that maddeningly claws at your nerves, this is a deeply unsettling slice of sci-fi.
Midsommar
This acclaimed indie horror movie stars Florence Pugh as Dani, an American student struggling to deal with a family tragedy, who joins her boyfriend Christian (Jack Reynor) and his friends on a trip to Sweden. The vacation sounds like the perfect escape—nine days of communing with nature at a festival held only once every 90 years; a true once-in-a-lifetime experience. The problem? The festival is a front for a pagan cult, and things get rapidly, wildly out of hand.
Midsommar is a deeply effective and distressing folk horror film, with none other than Jordan Peele, director of the smash hit Get Out, declaring it has "the most atrociously disturbing imagery I've ever seen on film." Perfect date night material for Halloween season, then.
Train to Busan
South Korean cinema seems to love combining the end of the world and trains. Bong Joon Ho’s Snowpiercer got things on track in 2013, but director Yeon Sang-ho really left the station with this 2016 zombie horror masterpiece.
Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) starts his journey on the express train from Seoul to Busan just wanting to drop daughter Su-an off with her mother. Unfortunately, the last passenger to board might be a teensy bit infected with the zombie plague that’s kicking off outside, turning the ride into the express train to hell. The tight confines allow for some incredibly inventive action choreography, while genre fans are treated to a revolting twist on the undead themselves, a misshapen, juddering, ravenous horde that moves like a liquid mass of corpses.
Like all the best zombie films, though, it’s the social commentary that really elevates Train to Busan, with its exploration of class and status standing alongside Romero’s work at his peak. A decade on from release, this is still one of the freshest takes on zombies you’re likely to find—look up animated prequel Seoul Station and stand-alone sequel Peninsula if it leaves you wanting another bite.
Altered States
A bit of a deep cut, but director Ken Russell’s 1980 outing will really mess with your head. No, really—this tale of psychological horror and transformational terror is loosely based on real-world tests of the effects of psychoactive drugs and sensory deprivation on the human brain. The film sees researcher Eddie Jessup (William Hurt) subjecting himself to highly questionable experiments with hallucinogenics and isolation in an effort to tap into other states of being. Unfortunately, he’s wildly successful, not only opening his mind to genetic memories and shared consciousnesses, but seeing his physical body horrifyingly warp and devolve beyond recognition with each trip.
And what a trip—Russell masterfully creates a sense of psychedelic overload with a pioneering use of bizarre imagery and sound, the film shifting with each of Jessup’s transformations until you feel you’ve taken mind-altering substances yourself. An uncomfortably weird experience, Altered States will stay on your mind long after the credits roll.
Colossal
Anne Hathaway is literally a monster—at least she is in this darkly comedic crossover between kaiju flick and character study. After her life in New York falls apart, Gloria (Hathaway) moves back home to New Hampshire. At the same time, a giant monster starts rampaging across Seoul, destroying buildings and causing mass panic. Yet these two incompatible events aren't unrelated, as Gloria starts to realize that she can somehow control the beast from half a world away—but her heavy drinking and constant bad decisions may get in the way of saving the world. Director Nacho Vigalondo lovingly pastiches the likes of Godzilla, Gamera, and King Kong in this quirky film festival favorite.
Mononoke The Movie III: The Curse of the Serpent
A nameless Medicine Seller (Hiroshi Kamiya in Japanese, Crispin Freeman in English) traveling Edo period Japan may seem a humble figure, but his strange tinctures and concoctions make him one of the few capable of tackling mononoke—powerful spirits corrupting places and people alike. This trilogy-capping third movie takes the enigmatic traveler back to the cursed Imperial Palace visited in predecessors Phantom in the Rain and Ashes of Rage, seeking to uncover once and for all why it seems to attract so many dangerous monsters.
A master class in tension and otherworldly horror, Mononoke maintains its stunning visual approach of kaleidoscopic watercolors swirling on parchment, making for one of the most sumptuous and visually striking pieces of animation you’ll ever see. It’s worth noting that there is some real-world controversy over a returning voice actor embroiled in a scandal in Japan, so this might be a rare case where the English dub is the better option.
The Fly
Despite being a remake, David Cronenberg’s quintessential slice of 1980s body horror has almost completely supplanted the 1958 original in the public consciousness (although the original stars Vincent Price and is definitely still worth checking out on Prime Video).
This wholesale reimagining twists expectations away from mad science clichés—it almost feels like a superhero origin movie to start, with scientist Seth Brundle (Jeff Goldblum) accidentally splicing his genes with a fly during a teleportation experiment, and emerging with enhanced physical prowess in every respect. But with great power comes great personality shifts, wiry black hairs growing along his back, and the need to vomit acid onto his food before eating. And, as animal instincts take over, the self-proclaimed “Brundlefly” starts looking at science reporter Ronnie Quaife (Geena Davis) very differently.
The groundbreaking effects work that marked Brundle’s slow metamorphosis into a repulsive hybrid monster won the film the Oscar for Best Makeup, but its ability to pack in some genuine emotion alongside the scares make it easy to see why this is the de facto iteration of The Fly.
The Social Network
Oh, you think this isn’t horror? Ask yourself: What could possibly be scarier than the deleterious impact social media has had on the human condition? Director David Fincher and writer Aaron Sorkin’s biopic telling of the rise, and rise, and rise of Facebook, is the kind of film you watch through your fingers, too.
There’s an almost predatory hunger in Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg, as he goes from a Harvard student whose hotness-ranking website was popular enough to crash the college’s whole network to a Silicon Valley darling attracting unheard-of sums of investment and power. Like most “based on a true story” horror films, it’s not entirely historically accurate and, true to genre norms, there’s a not-as-good sequel, with Sorkin returning to write and direct the newly released The Social Reckoning, but if you’ve been paying attention to reality the past few decades, this will definitely chill you to the bone.
