After a special executive magistrate court released CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on October 11 after a one-day preventive detention, several pro-BJP social media handles claimed that the trio had been granted bail on the condition that they would not take part in any protest for a period of one year. Those making such claims included retired Major Manik M Jolly, Right wing Wire, and BJP-supporting troll handle RiseOfBurnol.
Subsequently, a copy of an alleged bond began circulating on social media, bearing the name of Abhijit Dipke and the seal of the executive magistrate of New Delhi district.
It was claimed that this Dipke had signed the bond at the time of his release. BJP leader Radhika Khera shared a photo of the said bond while quoting an X post in which Dipke had claimed that he had not signed any such bond.
Sharing this picture, Facebook user Riju Dutta, who claims to be a ‘politician’, took a dig at Dipke, remarking that these people are supposedly revolutionaries.
Several users shared the same image on social media platforms.
Fact Check
We first checked Delhi Police’s official X handle. In their post, Police stated that Deepke, Ranka and Das were placed under ‘preventive arrest’ on October 10, 2026, and were produced before the SEM Court, Delhi Cantt, on October 11, 2026. “A bond of ₹50,000 was furnished to ensure the maintenance of peace and good behavior for one year, and the Special Executive Magistrate Court released them.”
Preventive arrest u/s 126/170 BNSS of Sh. Abhijeet Dipke, Sh. Ashutosh Ranka and Sh. Saurav Das was done on 10.10.2026. All due legal procedures were followed and they were produced before the SEM Court, Delhi Cantt on 11.10.2026.
A bail bond as Surety Bond of ₹50,000/- was filled for maintaining peace and good behaviour, for a period of one year, and they were released by the SEM Court.
— Delhi Police (@DelhiPolice) October 11, 2026
Nowhere in this police statement was it mentioned that their release was conditional on Dipke or the other leaders not participating in any protest for one year. There is also no mention of Dhruv Rathee in the statement.
In other words, police did not state that Rathee was required to sign a bond. The YouTuber himself refuted the viral claim on his X account, stating that he did not sign any bond or undertaking to secure his release.
I did not sign any bond
I did not sign any undertaking
I did not sign any condition for release
For all the media houses ^
— Dhruv Rathee (@dhruv_rathee) October 11, 2026
Examining the viral document clearly, we noticed several discrepancies:
- According to the police statement, the three individuals were produced before the special executive magistrate (SEM) court, Delhi Cantt, on October 11, whereas the alleged bond bears the date of October 10.
- The SEM Court falls under the South West district of Delhi, while the alleged bond mentions the New Delhi district.
- The spelling of “Satyamev Jayate” in the center of the Executive Magistrate’s seal on the alleged bond is incorrect.
We checked the image using OpenAI’s ‘Verify OpenAI-generated content’ tool, which revealed that it was created with the help of AI.
Advocate Sautik Banerjee, who appeared for Deepke, Das and Ranka in the SEM court, told the media that the magistrate had not imposed any conditions on them. They were released on a personal bond with one surety.
Delhi: On the SEM Court releasing CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka, and Saurav Das, advocate Soutik Banerjee says, “The magistrate has not imposed any conditions on them. They have been released on a personal bond with one surety” https://t.co/UI6OgPt2nL
— IANS (@ians_india) October 11, 2026
Speaking to Alt News, Banerjee explained, “Breach of peace refers only to activities that are not sanctioned by the Constitution and do not enjoy protection as fundamental rights. If the Constitution grants the freedom of speech and expression, the right to form associations and hold assemblies, or the freedom of movement, then restrictions can be imposed on these rights only within the scope of ‘reasonable restrictions’ that are rational. As the Supreme Court has repeatedly stated, peaceful protests are permitted, and one is always free to organize or participate in them; this cannot, under any circumstances, be considered a breach of peace.”
Sautik Banerjee sent us a bail bond format from the special executive magistrate (West District), Delhi, which looks entirely different from the document in the viral image.
Overall, the claim that Sourav Das, Abhijit Deepke, Ashutosh Ranka, and Dhruv Rathee were released on the condition that they would not participate in any protests for a year is false. Furthermore, the image of the bail bond bearing Abhijit Deepke’s name, which was shared by several individuals, including BJP leader Radhika Khera, was generated using AI.

Your flu shot can’t wait
Some parts of the country are already seeing case levels typical of late fall or early winter.
Flu season is starting earlier than usual this year, which I know from reviewing federal data. But I also know it because I woke up with body aches and chills last night, mere days before I’d planned to get my flu vaccination (!).
Already, some parts of the country are seeing levels of flu activity typically associated with late fall or early winter. In Washington state, for instance, doctors are reporting seeing as much flu now as they usually would around Christmas.
Flu activity overall is still low, to be clear. But as of October 7, infections were rising in all 50 states. And flu is spreading before many people — like, say, me — have received their annual vaccine.
Epidemiologists don’t yet know why the flu arrived early this year, or why cases first started rising in Western states like Washington, California, and Nevada. It’s possible that a mutation is helping this year’s flu variants evade existing immunity, one virologist told NPR. International travel could play a role, too: Flu cases also spiked early in Japan and other parts of Asia.
We don’t need to know why the flu arrived early to take some basic precautions, though. So today, we’re talking through some practical tips for coping with an early flu season.
Go a little deeper
An early flu season doesn’t necessarily mean a worse season — but even a moderate season can do serious damage. Last year, influenza sent hundreds of thousands of people to the hospital and caused tens of thousands of deaths, including almost 200 among children.
The first and best way to avoid those kinds of harms is by getting the flu shot, which reduces the risk of serious illness by an average of 40 to 60 percent. In the US, people aged 6 months and older are typically told to get the vaccine by October’s end.
In light of the early onset, however (it takes two weeks to build up full immunity), you might instead want to get your shot ASAP.
There are some everyday precautions you can take, too — many of them familiar from the Covid-19 era. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and warm water, for slightly longer than feels appropriate. Mask when you’re sick or might encounter someone else who is.
And don’t neglect the good habits that support your overall health: getting enough sleep, drinking a lot of water, and eating a balanced diet. (There’s very little evidence for trendier interventions, like supplements, saunas, cold plunges, or the infused herbal baths that my kooky former yoga teacher used to recommend.)
If you do get flu symptoms, reach out to your doctor early — especially if you’re older, pregnant, immunocompromised, or otherwise at higher risk for complications. Prescription antiviral medications, like Tamiflu, prevent the flu virus from spreading inside your body so that your immune system can clear it. But they work best within 48 hours of symptom onset.
To be clear, you needn’t take my word on any of this; I’m just another voice in the public health cacophony! Besides, recent polling suggests that my particular voice — that is, the voice of someone who works in media — is not quite as persuasive as it used to be. (Ditto medical websites and government health agencies.)
But if you have doubts or questions about vaccines, there is someone much closer to home you can consult: Ask your doctor (or nurse or pharmacist) about the flu shot’s risks and benefits. They’re best positioned to break the science down and apply it to your health. In hindsight, mine surely would have told me to stop delaying my shot for a more convenient weekend.

For entrepreneur Akhila Vijayaraghavan, whey has always been a convenient way to get 100-120 grams of protein every day. “I train regularly, so it was an easy addition to my routine and helped me consistently hit my protein intake,” she says. This is why she couldn’t help but notice how much whey prices have increased over the last few months “I understand that there are broader supply and import issues behind the increase, particularly because India is so heavily dependent on imported whey. But for a consumer, the result is pretty simple: something that used to be an everyday purchase suddenly feels expensive,” she says.
For instance, a kilogram of True Basics and Whole Truth whey concentrate, which once cost around ₹2500 last year, has gone up to around ₹3500, a clear leap of nearly ₹1000, points out Akhila. Other brands aren’t far behind, either. Optimum Nutrition, the protein brand associated with numerous elite athletes, including Neeraj Chopra, Rishabh Pant, and Priya Punia, is currently pricing 4 kg of its Gold Standard 100% Whey Protein at ₹17,649, while the same amount of MuscleBlaze’s Biozyme Performance Whey is ₹13,999, an over 20% jump from last year, when they were about ₹15,000 and a little over ₹10,000 respectively.
Several forces
According to Vijay P, operations and procurement manager at Chennai-based OMG Labs, a functional nutrition brand offering both whey and plant-based protein products, this sudden hike is not the result of a single event, but of several forces coming together. Though India has a large dairy industry, we still do not produce enough whey for the protein supplement industry because much of our dairy processing focusses on products like milk, curd, paneer, and ghee rather than large-scale cheese production, Vijay explains. “Whey is mainly obtained as a by-product of cheese manufacturing, and because domestic availability is limited, we depend significantly on imports.” This means that when there is a shortage or price increase in the international market, it directly affects the Indian market, says Vijay.
“Freight costs, currency fluctuations and other import-related costs also add to the final prices,” he says. For instance, whey isolate prices, which were ₹2,200 per kilogram exclusive of GST in December last year, now cost around ₹3,400. “Apart from the whey, we also have to account for the flavours, packaging, other raw materials, labour and manufacturing costs, which have pushed the overall finished product cost to ₹4,200-5,000 from ₹3,000-36,000, depending on quantity and customers.”
The price spike also stems from a significant increase in demand for dietary protein that current supply just can’t meet. “We are going through a protein bubble right now where everyone is talking about it, so everyone is aware of and looking for protein,” says Chennai-based fitness and nutrition coach Raj Ganpath.
Given that the Indian diet is notoriously protein-deficient, most of us may need a scoop or two of a protein supplement to get the ideal amount of protein, “about 1.25 to 1.75 grams of protein per kilo per day,” says Raj, pointing out that our meals consist largely of carbohydrates, fat, and some vegetables. Even though most Indians do eat meat — a recent National Family Health Survey (NFHS) found that 70-80% consume meat, fish, poultry, and eggs — for many of us, it does not happen regularly enough to meet daily protein needs. “In India, a non-vegetarian is essentially a vegetarian who eats a little bit of meat, so we still rely on vegetarian protein sources,” says Raj, the co-founder of The Quad and founder of The Slow Burn Method, a sustainable weight-loss coaching programme.
Additionally, while other new protein options exist in the market, for instance, functional dairy products like Greek yoghurt and protein milk, gram for gram, even with the increase in costs, “it roughly costs you the same amount of money as whey (if it is a concentrate or blend, isolate is a little more), around 6-7 rupees per gram of protein,” he says.
That is why people like Santosh Raghavan, an entrepreneur also based in Chennai, prefer whey protein to hit their daily goals. Given that he does not cook meat at home, “whey gives me the best protein-to-calorie ratio, allowing me room to eat other whole foods too. It is also convenient post-workout since I can have it immediately for recovery and absorption, without needing to wait for a meal to be prepared,” he says. And yes, he also likes the supplement’s taste. “It helps me think I have had some dessert, which is great for a guy like me, with a sweet tooth.”
The rise in whey prices, however, has influenced his choices considerably, he says. “I used to be loyal to a couple of brands, but now I have become brand agnostic. I just look at the label and pick up what is affordable,” says Santosh, who has also experimented with vegan protein, “which didn’t work for me,” and fermented yeast protein, “which I found decent.”
Options and opportunities
This trepidation among long-time whey users seems common, as Aditi Mammen Gupta, the co-founder of plant-based protein powder brand Origin Nutrition, points out. Earlier, people who used whey regularly often found the transition difficult, “but the thing is, plant protein was very different. Now, with new technologies and processes, plant protein has become much better in terms of taste, texture, mixability...everything really,” she says, pointing out that skyrocketing whey prices have led to “a lot of people shifting to plant protein. They seem to be quite happy with plant, especially when they discover that when they stick to it for a while, they feel a lot better.” As a business, given this shift, Origin is all set to expand its product range, says Aditi, who believes, “I think it is a really exciting time to be in the plant protein space.”
While rising whey prices will likely push more people to try affordable, equally effective plant- or yeast-based options, the consensus is that whey will continue to have a strong user base. “Whey still has strong demand because it is well established in the fitness and sports nutrition market,” says Vijay, while Sahil Kukreja feels that whey offers distinct advantages that justify the premium. “Whey provides all nine essential amino acids, is highly digestible, and is naturally rich in leucine, which helps stimulate muscle protein synthesis. That makes it an efficient protein source, particularly when someone wants a substantial protein serving in a relatively small volume,” says the co-founder of The Func Lab in Mumbai, a functional nutrition start-up that manufactures whey, plant protein, and electrolytes.
As the whey conversation goes beyond sports nutrition, it is now also being used in everyday beverages, snacks, and foods. “Healthy ageing and weight management are expanding the consumer base, while GLP-1 usage adds to this demand because reduced appetite makes getting adequate protein more challenging,” says Sahil, adding that he would, however, be careful not to attribute the entire price increase to GLP-1s.
But Sahil feels that the whey protein shortage challenge may also be an opportunity for the domestic industry to strengthen whey recovery and processing capacity. “Sustained whey premiums will also encourage innovation in plant proteins and other protein sources. That requires investment in collection, quality systems, and specialised processing — not just higher milk production,” he says.
Vijay, too, agrees that the crisis could prove a “strategic opportunity” for India to build a stronger domestic whey ecosystem. “Indian dairy and nutrition companies are moving in this direction, with major players investing in whey and value-added dairy products. This could reduce our exposure to international supply disruptions and foreign exchange movement.” However, given that capacity-building takes time, for the time being, “whey protein is likely to remain a strategically important and relatively expensive ingredient for the Indian nutrition industry.”
And despite rising costs, whey remains the preferred option for consumers like Akhila because of its familiarity, taste, texture, and convenience. “I know it works well for me as a practical way to get more protein,” she says. What has changed, however, is how often she turns to it, cycling it with other protein sources, including fish, meat, eggs and low-fat paneer, “because the price makes daily use harder to justify. At the current prices, I am much more conscious about when I actually need it, rather than automatically having it every day.”

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.
- 'They aimed to kill' - BBC identifies security forces who shot Kenya anti-tax protesters 
  - Published28 April 2025
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.
"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.
He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.
I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

A year-long celebration of renowned clinician, teacher, and humanitarian, the late K.V. Thiruvengadam will kick off in his centenary year on Sunday (October 11, 2026). The celebrations, in memory of Prof. Thiruvengadam’s extraordinary impact on medicine both in Chennai and beyond, will focus on restoring the art of listening to the patient, examining at the bedside, thinking before ordering a test, and finally, and dwelling on the fundamental question of what it means to be a good physician in an age of extraordinary technology.
K. Vardachari Thiruvengadam, fondly known as KVT, was born in 1926. He graduated from Government Stanley Medical College in 1950 and taught for 31 years both at his alma mater and at Madras Medical College, and subsequently at private institutions. His core areas of specialty were chest medicine, allergies and infectious diseases. His career coincided with a period when medicine was rapidly expanding, but his students remember that he did not teach bedside examination as a ceremonial ritual — he taught it as a way of thinking, listening to the patient, and asking the right questions.
Prof. KVT was a scientist as well as a clinician. He received formal training in chest diseases in the U.K., under the Colombo Plan. He published nearly 100 papers in national and international journals. Among the many areas of his research were chikungunya fever, neurological complications following influenza and amoebiasis. He also investigated traditional medicines in allergic lung and skin diseases. He worked for decades in the government system, among the poorest in society, and believed that government service could achieve extraordinary things when doctors had the willingness to serve. For him, medicine was a social responsibility.
Enduring legacy
Prof. KVT’s awards and recognitions were numerous, and included the Padma Shri in 1981 and the Dr. B.C. Roy Award for Eminent Medical Teacher, alongside multiple other distinctions. But perhaps the most enduring aspect of his legacy is in the number of students who remember him and his teachings and went on to become teachers and leaders themselves, committing to his principle of what you learn and experience must be passed on to the next generation.
The centenary year celebration’s objective is not merely to celebrate him, but to translate his philosophy into medical education. The commemoration is not an argument against technology, but an argument against technology without context, and for the need for human clinical reasoning to be paramount.
The proposed celebration aims to take to medical students and postgraduate doctors the importance of history-taking, clinical examination, clinical reasoning and their role not only in diagnosis and management, but also in medical research.
On October 31, the third Prof. K.V. Thiruvengadam Memorial Oration will be delivered at Sree Balaji Medical College and Hospital, by S.R. Chandra, on ‘The Patient Speaks, the Doctor Thinks and the Research Begins’, alongside a national conference on movement disorders.

Last month, Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj said Tamil Nadu would soon create a stem cell/bone marrow registry to facilitate bone marrow transplantation. At present, 50 patients are on the waitlist for bone marrow transplantation in T.N., he said.
A stem-cell donor registry is a database of people who have voluntarily agreed to potentially donate their blood-forming stem cells to a patient in need. Their human leukocyte antigen (HLA) profile is recorded for comparison with patients looking for a suitable donor.
For people living with blood cancers such as leukaemia and lymphoma, and disorders such as thalassaemia and aplastic anaemia, a stem-cell transplant can be a potentially curative treatment. But finding a suitable donor can be the first challenge. Only about 25% to 30% of patients have a fully HLA-matched sibling donor. For those without a suitable family donor, an unrelated donor registry can provide another route to finding a match.
What is a donor registry?
A bone marrow registry allows eligible people to register as potential donors. Registration usually involves providing a cheek or buccal swab for HLA typing.
Although these are commonly called bone marrow registries, they are essentially stem-cell donor registries, says Jeyasankar S., consultant, medical oncology, haematology, haemato-oncology and bone marrow transplant, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai.
If a patient does not have a suitable family donor, the transplant team can search the registry for an unrelated donor. The search can also extend to international donor networks.
How is a match found?
The key factor in matching is HLA, rather than the blood group. HLA markers are proteins that help the immune system distinguish the body’s own cells from foreign cells. They are inherited, and a closer HLA match can improve the chances of a successful transplant and reduce complications such as graft-versus-host disease.
The patient’s HLA profile is compared with those of registered donors. If a potential match is identified, the donor is contacted and further testing is done before donation.
A.R. Jaswanthini, haematologist, haemato-oncologist and bone marrow transplant physician, VS Hospitals, Chennai, says a patient without a matched family donor can be searched against potentially large numbers of registered donors. A donor in one part of India, or another country, may eventually be found to be a suitable match for a patient they have never met.
What is the situation in India?
India does not have a single national stem-cell donor registry. The World Marrow Donor Association currently lists five donor registries in the country, DATRI Blood Stem Cell Donors Registry, DKMS Foundation India, Marrow Donor Registry India (MDRI), GeneBandhu and The Arjan Vir Foundation. Together, these registries have several lakh registered donors, although the numbers vary between registries and are updated at different intervals.
The registries are linked to international donor networks, allowing transplant centres to look beyond India when a suitable donor is not found locally.
Increasing the number of registered donors is important, but the composition of the donor pool matters too. HLA characteristics are inherited and vary across populations. India has substantial genetic diversity across regions, communities and ancestral groups. Therefore, a patient may have a better chance of finding a suitable unrelated donor when people from similar backgrounds are represented in the registry.
“The importance of registries is particularly high for patients from communities that are under-represented in existing donor databases,” Dr. Jeyasankar says. “A registry can only help if it has donors who reflect the genetic diversity of the population. If certain communities have very few registered donors, patients belonging to those groups may face greater difficulty finding a suitable donor,” he adds.
G. Vimal Kumar, senior consultant, paediatric haematology, oncology, blood and marrow Transplantation, MGM Cancer Institute, Chennai, says India needs more healthy young adults to register as potential donors, particularly from diverse communities.
What happens after registration?
Registration does not involve donating stem cells. If a person is identified as a potential match, the registry contacts the donor and further HLA testing and medical assessments are carried out. The donor can then decide whether to proceed.
If the donor proceeds, stem cells can often be collected from the bloodstream through a process similar to platelet donation. In some cases, stem cells may instead be collected directly from the bone marrow.
This distinction is important because some potential donors associate the term ‘bone marrow donation’ with a major operation. In many cases, however, blood stem-cell collection is performed through the bloodstream.
Dr. Vimal Kumar says misconceptions about pain, weakness and the donation process can discourage people from registering. He also stresses that registration should be an informed commitment, as a person may be identified as a match months or years later.
What we need
Experts say India needs sustained awareness campaigns, particularly through colleges, workplaces and community organisations, along with better representation of different regions and communities. Stronger coordination between registries and transplant centres and reliable donor follow-up are also important.
The challenge is not simply to create a larger registry, but one that better represents India’s population and improves the chances of finding a suitable donor when a patient needs one.

The Nikkei 225 stock average fell more than 5% in Thursday trade, joining a global tech-stock rout that began in the United States overnight.
Advantest was down more than 15% at midday, while Tokyo Electron declined about 8%. SoftBank Group fell more than 10% and Kioxia more than 11%.
In U.S. trading on Wednesday, the S&P 500 fell 1.11% and the Nasdaq composite declined 1.88% after a higher-than-expected inflation reading fed into concerns about the economy and high valuations in technology shares.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which measures the performance of 30 chip stocks, declined 4.3%. Nvidia was down 3%, while Oracle was down about 9%.
Weakness extended into Asian trading, with South Korea’s Kospi falling about 8%. Samsung Electronics shares were off almost 10% and SK Hynix was down about 11%.
In Tokyo, stocks opened weak and fell steadily throughout the morning and into the afternoon. At about 1 p.m., the Nikkei 225 hit the low for the day of 64,092.74, down 5.39%.
Elevated oil prices also weighed on sentiment, with the conflict in the Middle East dragging on and threatening continued uncertainty. Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel.
On Wednesday, the United States reported that September’s inflation was 3.7%. Traders briefly priced in a 50% chance of an October interest rate increase, though that number fell back to 27%.
The U.S. Federal Reserve is scheduled to hold a policy meeting on Oct. 27 and 28.
As weakness in stocks heightened risk aversion, bonds benefited. The yield on the 10-year Japanese government bond fell to 2.93%, its lowest level in about a month.
Bond prices move inversely to yields.
While the Japanese yen was trading near ¥159 to the dollar on Wednesday night, the currency moved below ¥158 on Thursday.
On Oct. 5, the Nikkei 225 traded above 70,000 for the first time in about three months, helped by solid U.S. tech-stock performance. The all-time high of 72,831.73 was set in June.
The Nikkei 225 is down more than 10% from its peak but still up 35% over the past year.

BOSTON — Three former Food and Drug Administration chiefs lit into the Trump administration Wednesday, criticizing the now former FDA officials who oversaw a massive staffing exodus and robbed the agency of institutional knowledge that will take years to restore.
“DOGE will go down as one of the biggest disasters in American history,” Rob Califf, former FDA commissioner under Presidents Obama and Biden, said during the STAT Summit, referring to the Elon Musk-led initiative that conducted mass layoffs of government employees. The DOGE cuts of 3,500 workers preceded a larger staff exodus under the tumultuous leadership of former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, who resigned in May. White House official Heidi Overton has since been nominated to replace Makary, though she has yet to face a Senate confirmation vote.
Califf’s sharp tone was echoed by Scott Gottlieb, who served as commissioner for part of the first Trump administration, and Ned Sharpless, who was acting commissioner towards the end of the first Trump administration. Sharpless called the cuts “arbitrary” and said that the companies he works with as co-founder of Jupiter BioVentures often now find themselves in meetings with more junior and less experienced drug and medical device reviewers.
“You lost a lot of institutional memory,” Gottlieb added.
The panelists offered some optimism, however. The former officials said the agency may be turning a new leaf with departures of certain high-profile officials, who they did not name, but include Makary and former top drug and device regulators Vinay Prasad and Tracy Beth Høeg.
“I think the sowers of chaos came and went,” Califf said. Gottlieb, in particular, praised Kyle Diamantas, the agency’s top food regulator who is now acting commissioner, and FDA’s policy lead Grace Graham, who he said are encouraging the agency to get “back to the basics.”
“Now we have, I think, sensible leadership that’s doing smart things in the organization. I think things have gotten back to people feeling confident that the regulatory agency is making rational decisions,” Gottlieb said.
But even with new leadership, the former officials warned that rebuilding the agency will take time. They advised Overton, if confirmed, to focus not just on rehiring staff (which the agency has already started), but on reassuring officials that they will be protected from political meddling or further firings.
“Recruit, support, and defend the workforce,” Gottlieb said. “That will bring them back.”
They also offered advice on how to restore trust in federal agencies, a top-of-mind topic for public health officials since the Covid-19 pandemic. Sharpless lamented “errors” made in public communication by federal officials on vaccines during the pandemic that linger today.
“During the pandemic, number one is, don’t politicize a vaccine, and, you know, that didn’t last very long,” he said.
Califf and Gottlieb more pointedly addressed health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has a long history of sowing distrust in vaccines. Since becoming Health and Human Services secretary, Kennedy has aggressively tried to reform existing vaccine policy. Within the FDA, that has included pushing for renewed reviews of vaccine safety and efficacy, including post-market surveillance. Last year, when Makary was still commissioner, the FDA added safety warnings to mRNA Covid-19 vaccines about a rare heart inflammation side effect.
Kennedy “is just actively still eroding public confidence in these issues,” Califf said. “It’s going to be hard to overcome that until he’s moved on to some other job.” Gottlieb added that he had been critical of Kennedy since his nomination, which he said resulted in him needing to hire extra personal security for his safety.
But Califf also said that distrust in federal health agencies goes beyond Kennedy and reflects the frustration Americans have with high health care costs.
“If I would just get one biotech exec to say you know what, our drugs are too expensive,” Califf said. “You just never hear that and you know you wonder why people are upset and going to other sources of information.”
At the same time, all three urged the FDA to focus on its core mission, rather than trying to tackle some of these policy issues.
It is not in the FDA’s mandate, Sharpless said, to change drug prices or address vaccine hesitancy, but rather work in statute to prioritize safe and effective medicine.
“And if it sticks to its sort of statutory role, it’ll be fine,” he said.

Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.
This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP won state elections in West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.
Mass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. The Cockroach movement was born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.
This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakes impossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.
There is still reason for hope in India. The Indian Express newspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011, corruption scandals became evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.

An immunization worker gets set up to receive her wages on her mobile wallet in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
Campaigns in Africa to stop polio and other diseases have a more stable, better-motivated workforce thanks to WHO’s collaboration with countries and partners to pay frontline health workers through their mobile phones instead of in cash.
“Over 80 percent of workers are saying they prefer the digital payments,” said Ahmed Hamani Djibo, head of WHO’s Digital Finance Team.
WHO has been leading among international organizations in moving away from the unwieldy, less-secure practice of disbursing salaries in cash. Over the past few years, the Organization launched its Digital Finance Team and joined the Better Than Cash Alliance, an 80-member United Nations partnership with a mandate to develop the digitization of payments and expand financial inclusion – activities that support the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Since it was established in 2020, WHO’s Digital Finance Team has designed and implemented digital payment solutions in 24 countries in Africa, including, last year, in Benin, Botswana, Madagascar, Rwanda, Togo and Zimbabwe.
“WHO has successfully digitized payments for more than two million health workers across Africa,” said Tidhar Wald, Managing Director, a.i., at the Better Than Cash Alliance. “With these inspiring results, WHO is taking a clear leadership role in accelerating the digital transformation in the provision of health outcomes globally.”
A polio immunization team on the job in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
“A really big difference in speed”
Workers surveyed in Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia and Tanzania said they appreciated the security of not carrying cash, the convenience of no longer having to travel to a disbursement site to receive their wages, and above all, the speed of payment – as short as half an hour after finishing work compared to waits of weeks or even months.
The surveys, funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, linked timely compensation to better morale and worker retention.
“There is really a big difference in speed,” said Jean-Luc, a health worker interviewed in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at the end of a polio immunization campaign. “We finished the campaign mop-up yesterday and received a text notification the next evening. I’m going to pay my child’s school fees. Now we can relax.”
Digital payments also save time and money for health campaign organizers, including the burden and expense of transporting large sums of cash and completing documentation.
“When you have 300 to 500 volunteers to pay, doing accounts and signing receipts takes a lot of time,” said Saïdi, a polio team leader in DRC.
WHO first used the new digital payments in polio immunization campaigns in Côte d’Ivoire. Although outbreaks of vaccine-derived polio were on the rise, vaccination campaigns were having trouble getting off the ground. In the first quarter of 2020, almost half the polio campaigns in WHO’s African Region were postponed, saw workers drop out, or suffered other detrimental effects stemming from delays in cash disbursements.
As WHO and partners worked to develop the nuts-and-bolts aspects of a digital payment ecosystem (registering workers into a database, verifying their profiles with the mobile network operator and more) the benefits of a cashless approach became more apparent.
"There is substantial evidence that digitizing payments can support people, especially women, to gain access to financial services and increase control over their earnings,” said Maria May, Senior Program Officer, Inclusive Financial Systems, at the Gates Foundation. “Over the past four years, the World Health Organization has utilized the growing presence of mobile money across Africa to ensure that the courageous frontline vaccinators in polio outbreak campaigns are paid completely, quickly, and securely.”
Alain Labrique, director of WHO’s Department of Digital Health and Innovation, said that “digital payments are one of the key pillars of Digital Health Public Infrastructure currently strongly encouraged within WHO’s guidance to member-states on Digital Transformation.” WHO views digital payments as a foundation for many more digital development activities, together with Data Exchange and Digital ID Infrastructure. He added “we are delighted to work with partners in the digital space and add our voice to this celebration of WHO's joining the Better Than Cash Alliance”.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) announced a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission for the protest and detained several protesters, including CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. A Delhi court ordered their release on 11 October 2026, while the Supreme Court intervened over restrictions on public movement and allegations of unlawful detention. On 15 October 2026, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation submitted an affidavit to the Supreme Court, stating that police imposed restrictions at 45 Metro stations (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming it shows a lawyer confronting the Chief Justice of India (CJI) over a CJP protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a lawyer confronting the Chief Justice of India (CJI) over the CJP protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
Fact: The viral video dates back to 16 October 2025 and shows a heated exchange between Jharkhand High Court judge Justice Rajesh Kumar and advocate Mahesh Tiwari, not a confrontation with the Chief Justice of India over the CJP protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar. The exchange occurred during court proceedings concerning a widow whose electricity connection had been disconnected over outstanding dues. The Jharkhand High Court initiated criminal contempt proceedings against Tiwari, which were later dropped after the court accepted his unconditional apology. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals from October 2025. According to these reports, a heated exchange took place between Jharkhand High Court judge Justice Rajesh Kumar and Advocate Mahesh Tiwari on 16 October 2025, following which the court initiated criminal contempt proceedings against Tiwari. The proceedings were being streamed live when the incident occurred.
The incident began when a lawyer sought relief for his client, a widow whose electricity connection had been disconnected over outstanding dues of Rs 1.30 lakh. Justice Kumar questioned the manner in which the lawyer was seeking relief and explained how the matter should be argued in accordance with court ethics. He also said that the Bar Council chairman should take note of the lawyer’s conduct. Tiwari, who had been standing at the back of the courtroom, then joined the argument, stepped forward and pointed at the judge.
A report published by NDTV on 23 January 2026 stated that the Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, criticised Advocate Mahesh Tiwari for challenging the criminal contempt proceedings initiated against him by the Jharkhand High Court. The Supreme Court asked the High Court to take a sympathetic view if Tiwari apologised. Subsequently, a report published by The Indian Express on 19 February 2026 stated that the Jharkhand High Court dropped the contempt proceedings after accepting Tiwari’s unconditional apology. The High Court observed that an advocate with more than 40 years of legal practice was expected to exercise greater restraint and was as much an officer of the court as the presiding judge.
To sum up, an unrelated courtroom exchange video is shared, showing a lawyer confronting the CJI over the CJP protest against Gyanesh Kumar.

AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown.
By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.
Challenging to shut down
Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”
Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output.
The lightweight Gemma4-26B-A4B model required just 15 boxes, each equipped with only 4GB of memory, to achieve inference. The Qwen3.5-9B was able to configure other LLMs to run on eight of nine hardware types. Unlike traditional malware, which must be written to run on specific hardware or software, the model was able to use its weights to make configurations on the fly that were specific to the devices it was tested against.

The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.
Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it is the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.
An attack on two neutral ships in Romanian territorial waters at the mouth of the Danube River indicated that strikes against vulnerable commercial targets are set to expand.
The Romanian president, Nicușor Dan, said two Russian drones violated Romanian airspace and struck two chemical tankers, setting the ships ablaze. Rescue crews were searching for at least seven missing sailors.
“The situation in the Black Sea is serious,” he said. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. This is unacceptable and it has to stop.”
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, after briefly halting them to demonstrate that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked a gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Moscow claimed debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire.
Ukraine also struck back at Russia’s military, hitting four Sukhoi Su-34 fighter/bomber jets and damaging two more, according to Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s military said it had used a Neptune cruise missile to strike an airfield in Russia’s southern Voronezh region.
“These very warplanes were ready to launch new attacks on Ukraine and were loaded with aerial bombs,” Zelenskyy said, publishing a satellite photo of the damaged airfield.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three people and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference to sudden limitations on Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post on X, referring to a growing quarrel with the Trump administration.
“Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security,” he said.
Trump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”
Despite Trump’s claims, however, Russia continued to launch heavy strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, using hypersonic and ballistic missiles to target key Ukrainian power plants, leaving cities including Kyiv without power and water for hours. Ukraine said it would not strike Russian oil refineries in the interim in order to show that it was ready for negotiations.
But the White House piled pressure on Zelenskyy to capitulate to Russia by threatening to cut programmes to deliver arms to Ukraine and to stop sharing US battlefield intelligence with Ukraine.
The US appeared to make good on some threats. Ukraine said it had not received advance warning from Washington of Russian missile strikes for several days this week. And on Wednesday, Ukrainian soldiers complained that their access to Starshield programmes controlled by the US military had been restricted, scuppering drone missions on the frontlines.
The feud between Zelenskyy and Trump has spun out of control over the last week. Trump, who believes his support for Ukraine should come with a degree of control over the country’s leadership, has said Ukraine should “get a new president”.
Zelenskyy, when asked on Thursday by Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed, said yes. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he said.
Musk, the head of SpaceX, which produces the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military, has emerged as a leading critic of Zelenskyy in the US.
On Thursday, Musk denied throttling the Starlink systems and said they were controlled by the US government. But in a social media post commenting on a Zelenskyy statement that Ukraine would continue to fight until Russia’s defeat, he wrote: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.”

In the 54th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, discuss the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, experimental approaches to studying human brain development, and incidents from Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya that highlight barriers to healthcare access.
The episode begins with the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The discussion explains how optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control the electrical activity of selected nerve cells. By activating or inhibiting specific neurons, researchers can investigate how neural circuits influence movement, memory, emotions and behaviour. The technique has become an important tool in neuroscience research, including studies of neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, it remains largely a research tool and is not a routine treatment for brain disorders.
The next segment examines an experimental approach described as ‘xenocortication’, in which human brain tissue is transplanted into the brains of mice. Researchers have been exploring this approach to study aspects of human brain development that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory-grown cells or animal models alone. The discussion looks at how the transplanted tissue may receive a blood supply, develop connections and interact with its surroundings within a living brain. The approach could help researchers investigate human neuronal development and mechanisms involved in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. However, it remains experimental, and findings from such models cannot be assumed to reflect human brain development fully. The work also raises ethical questions about the use of human neural tissue in animal research.
The episode then turns to barriers to healthcare access, examining how social discrimination and inadequate infrastructure can prevent people from receiving medical care. In Uttar Pradesh, a Dalit woman was allegedly denied admission to a government hospital while in labour and was forced to deliver outside the facility. Her family alleged that untouchability was involved. The incident highlights how discrimination can obstruct access to care even when a health facility is physically available.
Another incident in Meghalaya’s West Khasi Hills district, an ill child died in his mother’s arms while his parents were making a three-hour trek to reach the nearest hospital. According to the village headman, the family had tried to arrange a vehicle after the child’s condition deteriorated, but no driver was willing to travel to the village because of the poor road conditions. The incident draws attention to the difficulties faced by people in remote areas, where distance, road connectivity and the availability of transport can delay access to emergency medical care.
The episode ends with a fun-fact segment on why mice are widely used in laboratory experiments. The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

A woman has been charged after allegedly poisoning a co-worker’s lunch curry with snail pellets.
Western Australian police say a 58-year-old woman brought a container of curry to share with colleagues at her workplace in Perth’s southern suburbs in February.
A 43-year-old woman allegedly contaminated it with snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance, a police spokesperson said on Thursday.
“The curry had been shared among employees and consumed without issue during a morning tea break,” police said.
“After the meal, the accused accessed a chemical storage shed and later entered the staff lunch room where the food was kept.”
At lunchtime, the alleged victim went to eat some more of her curry.
When she opened the container, she spotted bright green granules in the food.
“After tasting a small amount, (she) experienced numbness to her tongue,” the police spokesperson said.
It will be alleged the accused and the victim were in a personal relationship.
Detectives arrested the 43-year-old woman last week.
She has been charged with one count of unlawful act or omission with intent to harm (endangering the life, health or safety of any person).
She is scheduled to appear before Armadale magistrates court on 5 November.
Police declined to provide further information about the relationship or the workplace.

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

Ukrainian forces had their access to the technology restricted this week after Trump announced a new diesel deal with Russia

Elon Musk has blamed Donald Trump for restrictions introduced on Starlink speed for members of the Ukrainian military.
The service provided by Musk’s company SpaceX provides broadband internet and has been used for government and military communications by Ukraine in the war against Russia.
The outage came amid Trump’s demands for Ukraine to completely halt long-range strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Polish foreign minister Radoslaw Sikorski accused Musk of “playing politics” on Wednesday but the tech billionaire has now denied he was involved in the decision.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and POTUS,” Musk wrote on X.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
He had previously said that “no matter how much I disagree with the Ukraine policy, Starlink will never turn off its terminals... We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.”
Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt betrayed by the decision in an interview with Piers Morgan and that the shutdown meant “people would die” as a result.
Several combat missions failed on Tuesday evening as a result of the shutdown, an adviser on military technology to Zelensky told The Guardian.
A US official told Axios that the Trump administration was not involved in the Starlink limitations.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.
“This is not the right side of history,” Zelensky said on Piers Morgan Uncensored. Asked if he felt betrayed by decisions made over the last week, he said: “Really, yes.”
The outage came just as Ukraine was hit by ballistic missiles, despiteTrump’s insistence that there is an energy ceasefire in place between the countries.
Poland has said that it pays for Ukraine’s Starlink subscription, which is crucial for guiding long-range drone strikes that have severely disrupted Russian logistics.
The restriction came amid Trump’s decision to lift sanctions against Russia and allow global diesel exports, with the US to buy 300,000 tons of the fuel.
He faced criticism from several corners including from the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas, who told Washington that “Russia has started this war. We should not forget this.”

Trump made the remark as part of a longer speech at a Republican rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Oct. 12. However, some posts omitted context clarifying that Trump was referring to a hypothetical scenario where Democrats control Congress and the White House, suggesting their policies would result in him being the last Republican president.
Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, a rumor circulated that U.S. President Trump said he would be "the last Republican president."
People on X and Reddit shared the alleged quote, with some including a video clip. In the clip, Trump appeared to make the comment during a political rally. 
The quote was correctly attributed to Trump.
However, some posts sharing the quote and accompanying video clip omitted context clarifying Trump's meaning. He was referring to a hypothetical scenario where Democrats control both houses of Congress and the White House, suggesting their policies would result in him being "the last Republican president." 
The president made the comment during a speech at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Oct. 12. At the rally, Trump endorsed incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted and the Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, who are on the ballot for Ohio's midterm elections.
Trump's full speech can be viewed on C-SPAN. At the 1:02:00 mark, prior to the statement in question, Trump says, "We achieved more in two years than any other presidency in the history of our country, but now the radical-left Dumocrats want to burn it all down" — using a term he favors for the Democratic Party. 
The president continued to criticize his opponents' alleged voting record, saying, "Every single Dumocrat in Congress voted against our record tax cuts. They voted against no tax on tips. They voted against no tax on overtime, and they voted against no tax on Social Security for our great seniors."
These comments, and others he made later, make it clear that Trump was theorizing he'd be the "last Republican president" if Democrats won key races in the midterm elections and subsequently took control of the White House.
The rest of his statement from the moment in question is as follows (emphasis ours):
