Defence tech startup Tonbo Imaging’s IPO was fully subscribed within hours of opening for bidding, with demand led by non-institutional investors (NIIs). The public issue received bids for 1.26 Cr shares against 85.26 Lakh shares on offer, translating into an overall subscription of 1.47X as of 13:06 IST. The NII portion was subscribed 2.73X, receiving bids for 49.82 Lakh shares against an allocation of 18.24 Lakh shares. Within this category, the portion for applications above ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 1.92X, while that for applications above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was booked 4.36X. Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) bid for just 7,707 shares against the 24.32 Lakh shares reserved for them. Meanwhile, retail investors bid for 75.07 Lakh shares against their allocation of 42.56 Lakh shares, subscribing to their portion 1.76X. The employee portion was booked 3.93X, attracting bids for 55,083 shares against 14,000 shares on offer. The opening-day demand follows Tonbo’s ₹255.4 Cr anchor allocation ahead of the public issue. The startup allotted 36.5 Lakh shares to 43 anchor investors at ₹700 apiece. Domestic mutual funds accounted for 57.7% of the anchor allocation, with 12 funds participating through 25 schemes. Other anchor investors included Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, WhiteOak Capital, Aranda Investments, and Allianz. Tonbo has set a price band of ₹665–₹700 per share for its ₹852.1 Cr IPO, which will close on October 19. The issue comprises an OFS of up to 1.2 Cr shares, meaning the startup will receive no proceeds. Selling shareholders include cofounders Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza, alongside CEAQ Technologies and Artiman Partners. Inside Tonbo’s Defence Tech Business Tonbo develops imaging and sensor systems for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting, and other military applications. Its products include thermal weapon sights, driver-vision systems, fire-control systems, and missile seekers. The startup outsources manufacturing to partners such as Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology, while handling prototype development, system integration, and qualification testing in-house. The IPO comes after a decline in Tonbo’s annual revenue and profit. Operating revenue fell 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹469.1 Cr in FY25, while net profit dropped 30.2% to ₹50.8 Cr from ₹72.8 Cr. In Q1 FY27, Tonbo reported an operating revenue of ₹36 Cr and a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr.

Nasdaq slides to near one-month low as AI rout deepens
NEW YORK: The Nasdaq fell to near one-month lows on Thursday (Oct 15), weighed by a worsening selloff in AI-linked stocks on fears rising interest rates could impact artificial-intelligence investments, and fresh data pointing to building US price pressures.
The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq marked their biggest one-day fall since July on Wednesday after hotter-than-expected consumer inflation data fuelled expectations of further interest-rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve, dragging on tech stocks.
Semiconductor maker TSMC's cautious note for 2027, citing macroeconomic uncertainties, also dented sentiment.
Reports that AI lab Anthropic's third-quarter revenue surged 45 per cent compared to the previous quarter failed to lift investor spirits.
Heavily indebted data-centre operator CoreWeave sitting in the eye of the recent tech storm, lost 8.5 per cent following a 15 per cent drop on Wednesday, while cloud computing giant Oracle was down marginally after a nearly 9 per cent fall in the previous session. The companies' bonds also fell, pushing their yields to record highs.
Chipmakers lost ground, with Nvidia down 3.3 per cent, and Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices losing 5 per cent and 6.4 per cent, respectively.
The broader chips index will have shed US$2 trillion in a more-than-14 per cent slide in seven sessions, if losses hold. It would mark its longest losing streak since May 2025.
The S&P 500 information technology sector was the biggest drag, down 2 per cent. The slump pushed investors to government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield at a three-week low of 5.0725 per cent.
"Investors are increasingly questioning how much future growth is already priced into valuations, how expansion is being financed and when these investments will generate sufficient returns," Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said in a note.
"The repricing of CoreWeave's debt suggests that investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost."
At 9:50am ET (11:50pm, Singapore time), the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 163.58 points, or 0.32 per cent, to 51,785.06, the S&P 500 shed 32.20 points, or 0.42 per cent, to 7,686.74, and the Nasdaq Composite .IXIC lost 283.07 points, or 1.06 per cent, to 26,409.80.
The CBOE Volatility Index, known as Wall Street's fear gauge, hit a two-week high and was last up 0.83 points at 17.74.
Investors continued to segue into traditionally defensive sectors, with healthcare .SPXHC and consumer staples .SPLRCS rising more than 2 per cent each. Gains in these stocks propped up the Dow.
The Nasdaq has dropped more than 4 per cent from record highs touched last week, with concerns about higher borrowing costs and AI spending threatening to eclipse the third-quarter earnings season, when S&P 500 profits are expected to grow 30.6 per cent, according to LSEG data.
Data showed US producer prices increased by the most in 4-1/2 years in September amid rising goods and services costs, the latest indication of inflation broadening out beyond energy products.
Markets will now scrutinize Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's speech before the International Monetary Fund Annual Meeting.
Shares of Rocket Lab dropped 15 per cent after the space company said the inaugural launch of its new, larger Neutron rocket was delayed until next year.
FMC slid over 38 per cent after the agrichemicals company sharply cut its third-quarter outlook, which includes a US$625 million-US$675 million hit from commercial actions.
Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.78-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.05-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq.
The S&P 500 posted 20 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 29 new highs and 261 new lows.

How high inflation is hurting Trump's Republicans in U.S. midterm campaign
With less than 3 weeks until election day, gas and diesel prices show no signs of falling
For nearly a year, U.S. President Donald Trump has been trying to persuade voters not to get riled up over rising prices.
Trump has brushed off concerns about affordability as a "con job by Democrats," insisted consumer prices had fallen during his term when they'd actually risen, and repeatedly claimed the costs of gas and diesel — up sharply after he launched the war against Iran — would start falling soon.
Numerous polls suggest voters aren't buying Trump's sales pitch, with respondents giving him low marks on the cost of living.
On average, more than 70 per cent of American respondents in recent polls disapprove of Trump's handling of inflation, according to Silver Bulletin, which aggregates public polling.

The latest inflation data won't make things any better for Trump and his Republican Party as they try to maintain control of U.S. Congress in the midterm elections on Nov. 3, less than three weeks from now.
The consumer price index was up 3.7 per cent in September compared with the previous year, driven largely by increases in the prices of fuel and clothing, the U.S. Department of Labour reported on Wednesday.
Polling indicates that the economy is the top issue for voters across the U.S. heading into the midterms, says Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling Center in Boston.
Drill down further into the data, and he says it's the cost of living — rather than jobs or taxes — underlying those concerns about the economy.
'Everyday expenses'
"It looks like it's just everyday expenses that are beginning to pile up and people are concerned about being able to afford," Kimball told CBC News.
"It's hard to imagine in the next three weeks there'll be a solution to the gas price or the other costs of living associated with that," he said.
Trump flew to Wasilla, Alaska, Tuesday to hold a campaign rally at a hockey rink. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)
The political impact can be mapped out through Trump's recent travels across the U.S. as he tries to boost Republicans' chances of winning U.S. Senate seats.
In the past two weeks, Trump has flown to a series of previously reliably red states, including Alaska, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, all of which he won by double digits in the 2024 presidential election.

Tim Malloy, polling analyst with the Quinnipiac University Poll in Hamden, Conn., describes Trump's travels as "a last mad dash" to try to shore up Republican candidates who should not have been in jeopardy during the midterms but are now at risk of losing largely because of cost of living issues.
"What Hail Mary pass or home run can you hit at this point if you're the Republicans? I don't know. It's really, really late in the day," Malloy told CBC News.
He says gas prices are the predominant concern showing up in polling and voters are pinning the blame on Trump.
"All of that is tied into the fact that the president said the war would be over very quickly," Malloy said. "The president has not lived up to the promise he made to Americans, and they're kind of fed up and the midterms are coming."
Outside a supermarket in Martinsburg, W.Va., Juliana Kaiser said she's started baking her own bread, making soup stocks and limiting her driving to save costs. She says rising prices will be a factor she keeps in mind when voting in the upcoming U.S. midterms. (Jonathan Austin/CBC)
In the staunchly Republican community of Martinsburg, W.Va., on Wednesday, people told CBC News that they're feeling the price pinch.
"It's hard to even do grocery shopping anymore. I've had to really survive off of food pantries," said Christalyn Levy, a cashier in a local thrift store. "Literally I pay my rent, and I have nothing left."

As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.
Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.
“This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman, was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.
“We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.”
Since January, almost 900,000 hectares have been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s “godzilla” El-Nino and as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists.
For months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including a class action lawsuit filed last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze.
Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness.
The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents.
In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two.
On Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility.
The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported.
But experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief.
“It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group.
“Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way.”
In the Indonesian province of central Kalimantan on Wednesday, the ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200 – or four times the “hazardous” level of 300 – environment ministry data showed.
Local news footage showed thick haze blanketing the provincial city of Palangka Raya, cutting visibility for motorists to a minimum.
Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto has ordered firefighting efforts to be stepped up, and called for a crackdown on those suspected of starting fires.
But the government has struggled to combat the fires, the worst of occur in peatland areas, which can burn for weeks underground and are difficult to extinguish.
“As time goes by and climate change kicks in, I think it could become a global problem, not just the fix that one country needs to find,” said McRae, of the widening regional issue. “There’s a lot of interconnectedness on a global scale.”

The 'leap second' could disappear. How a minor time adjustment became a major problem
International time-keeping body may vote to ditch the decades-long tradition Thursday
For more than 50 years, humanity has used "leap seconds" to keep our clocks aligned with the rotation of the Earth.
On Thursday, an international timekeeping body in France is expected to do away with leap seconds and let the clocks slip until they're out of alignment by a full hour, which could take centuries or even millennia.
The precise atomic time we use to track our days — developed in the 1950s and measured by tracking the natural vibrations of atoms — is slightly out of sync with solar time, which is based on the position of the sun in the sky relative to a specific location on Earth, because the planet's rotation has been gradually slowing.
The leap second was introduced in 1972 as a way to correct the discrepancy. Ten seconds were added immediately, says Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre.
Since then, the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, which tracks the difference between the solar day and atomic time, has monitored the discrepancy to determine when an extra second is needed.
When that threshold is reached, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures adds a second at either the end of December or the end of June. Leap seconds have been added 27 times, most recently in 2016.
Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre, says leap seconds are becoming increasingly difficult to manage as more systems rely on precise timekeeping. (National Research Council Canada)
If we didn't make those tiny adjustments, nothing would perceptibly change in our lifetimes. But eventually, Beattie says, "you might get the brightest part of the day at midnight and the darkest part of day at noon."
The concept is similar to leap years, whereby a day is added to the end of February every four years to keep the Gregorian calendar aligned with the seasons because the Earth's orbit around the sun takes about 365¼ days.
Without leap years, our hottest months would eventually fall during what is now winter, and the colder months during summer, Beattie says.
What's the problem?
But the time has come when leap seconds seem to be causing more trouble than they're worth.
"The basic global agreement is that we want to do away with these abrupt leap seconds," Beattie said.
That's because the small adjustment can be a headache for tech and telecommunications companies and infrastructure that relies on precise timekeeping.
Companies also have different ways of implementing leap seconds, such as changing their clock rates to stretch the extra second over several hours or an entire day.
Beattie says that variation among networks creates a risk of system failures.
The leap second was blamed for Reddit and LinkedIn crashes in 2012, for example, and brief outages at Cloudflare in 2016.
"The problem is that the needs for timing and network synchronicity are just going up and up, they're ever increasing," Beattie said. "And so the risks are just increasing along with them, because all you need is for some system to not implement it properly and then you could have a cascade effect that could cause quite significant problems."
Negative seconds?
There's another complicating twist.
Over the last six years or so, the Earth's rotation has actually sped up, raising the possibility that a "negative leap second" — in which a second would be taken away — could be needed in the future.
Tech giant Meta said in 2022 that a negative leap second could have a "devastating effect" on software, adding, "In any case, every leap second is a major source of pain for people who manage hardware infrastructures."

The proposed fix, which would take effect in May 2027, is instead to let those extra seconds add up to 3,600 — a full hour — before adjusting the clocks, pushing the issue many generations down the road.
Not everyone is impressed by this approach.
Paul Delaney, a York University physics and astronomy professor emeritus, says he was "surprised" to hear the proposal.
"It is a problem for an increasingly computerized, AI-oriented economy, and that's obviously what we have," he said. "But that said, gosh, don't we still hire computer programmers to sort these sorts of things out? Some part of me says that we're throwing in the towel and saying, 'Oh, it's too difficult to do, and what the heck, it is just a second.'"
'Not a perfect system'
Samantha Lawler, an associate professor of astronomy at the University of Regina, says many factors affect the Earth's rotation speed, but it has tended to slow over time, in part because of the moon's effect on Earth's tides.
But complex variables, including climate change and glacial melting, can cause changes in that trend.

She says there is no perfect system for our clocks to account for these shifts and "we'll be fine" without leap seconds.
"This is a real human problem that we've been struggling with forever, as long as we've been watching the stars move across the sky and tracking when the sun rises and sets, and trying to get the patterns right," Lawler said.
"It's always going to be a little bit wrong, and I think we just have to accept that."

Food, from the moment it’s in the mouth until it’s excreted as poop, goes through digestion—and this process is a wild journey. Food containing carbohydrates, proteins, or lipids is chewed into a mush in the mouth, where some degree of starch and lipid digestion occurs before it is swallowed. In the stomach, the swallowed ‘ball’ of chewed food is continuously ground and churned until the food particles are small enough to enter the small intestine. Simultaneously, hydrochloric acid (HCl) and pepsin (an enzyme) in the stomach break down complex proteins in the food.
The food, now in a semi-liquid form, reaches the digestive enzyme-rich small intestine, where its fate is sealed for major chemical digestion before being converted into absorbable nutrients. Enzymes in the small intestine break down the partially digested macronutrients—carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids—into smaller molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream, along with vitamins and minerals.
What remains is indigestible food, along with leftover digestive fluids and cellular waste, which enters the colon (large intestine), where digestive enzymes are lacking. However, the gut microbiota—the body’s dynamic ‘organ’—in the colon compensates for this dearth by fermenting indigestible food, including dietary fibres and indigestible proteins. Enzymes produced by the gut microbiota break this indigestible food into useful metabolites and gases before the remainder is expelled as poop.
What are intestinal gases?
In humans, intestinal gases include nitrogen (N2), oxygen (O2), carbon dioxide (CO2), hydrogen (H2), methane (CH4), and trace amounts of hydrogen sulphide (H2S)—the gas with the rotten egg smell. While N2 and O2 mostly reflect swallowed air, H2 and CH4 are odourless gases produced by gut microbiota. It is H2S that is primarily responsible for the smell of gas.
The colon—which hosts the highest microbial densities—harbours microbes that prefer indigestible carbohydrates as food, or as an energy source. These indigestible-carbohydrate-loving microbes (carbohydrate-fermenting) flourish in the colon region close to the small intestine (proximal colon), where their energy source availability is higher. Microbes including Bacteroides scavenge (ferment) human-indigestible carbohydrates such as dietary fibres and resistant starch, producing substantial quantities of hydrogenas a major by-product.
Also thriving in this oxygen-poor, hydrogen-rich ecosystem are microbes that compete for, and convert hydrogento methane, like methanogenic archaea. Likewise, sulphate-reducing bacteria (SRB) in these regions of the colon convert hydrogeninto hydrogen sulphide in small amounts. As the food passes through the colon, the availability of indigestible carbohydrates decreases over time. Microbes like SRB in regions of the colon close to the rectum (distal colon) also ferment human-indigestible proteins for energy, producing hydrogen sulphide in the process.
Studies so far suggest that host cells (through distinct mechanisms) and microbial cells utilise intestinal gases. Excess gases are eliminated as exhaled gas (from the lungs) and flatulence.
What do intestinal gases do?
Recent studies suggest intestinal gases are more than just gas. They can, in fact, serve as markers of gastrointestinal (GI) health, and can regulate gut motility and transit time. Gut motility refers to the muscle contractions in the digestive tract that move the food, and gut transit time is the time it takes for food to move through the gastrointestinal tract before being excreted.
Advancing research reveals that hydrogencan influence gut motility and, in experimental models, shorten transit time. Methane, by contrast, has been shown to slow gut motility and increase transit time. However, findings on the effect of hydrogen sulphide on gut motility and transit time have been mixed.
Microbiota research has also pointed to links between imbalances in gut microbiota and intestinal gas levels and gastrointestinal(GI) diseases/symptoms.
A real-world study measured hydrogen, methane, and hydrogen sulphide levels using breath testing in 3,004 participants with GI symptoms, especially excessive bloating and flatulence, from the United States. The study found associations between intestinal gas levels and GI symptoms: higher hydrogen levels (≥20 ppm above baseline) with diarrhoea; higher methane levels (≥10 ppm) with constipation; and higher hydrogen sulphide levels (≥2 ppm) with severe diarrhoea and abdominal pain. The study also suggested dysregulated hydrogen sulphide production was associated with greater diarrhoea, urgency, bloating, and symptom severity.
Animal models and clinical studies have reported similar associations between intestinal gases and GI symptoms. However, these studies lack identical methodologies and comparison with healthy participants as controls.
Monitoring gases for diagnosis
The most commonly adopted method for measuring intestinal gases is breath testing—measuring gases in exhaled breath. Microbial fermentation activity and gut motility are also assessed indirectly with this method.
However, new techniques are being devised for non-invasive, real-time continuous monitoring of intestinal gases. To capture eliminated intestinal gases (exhaled gas and flatus), researchers have designed respiration/fermentation chambers (airtight rooms with gas sensors and continuous air supply) to explore microbial fermentation activity, track intestinal gases, and monitor the effects of therapeutic interventions.
Alternatively, as flatus has relatively higher concentrations of intestinal gases, researchers at the University of Maryland have developed a device that can be attached to underwear. The device, designed to objectively measure hydrogenin flatus, monitors real-time gas profiles and gas-release patterns, providing insights into gut microbial activity and digestive health.
Why this is important
Measuring and monitoring real-time gas profiles could enable researchers to expand gut microbiota research: define ‘normal’ and ‘abnormal’ levels in intestinal gases, establish mechanisms behind gas effects, and study diverse populations, involving both healthy people and people with GI diseases, over long periods. Doctors could also potentially tailor a treatment plan—diet or gas-targeted medication—to rebalance the gut microbial ecosystem and modulate gas production and track GI health progress.
Therefore, the next time someone lets one rip, remember that intestinal gases have uses beyond popular humour or emptying out a room. These gases are part of a dynamic system that shapes the gut microbiota and influences digestive health, including how one poops, and can serve as markers of GI health.
(Smruthi Prabhu is an independent science writer from Mangalore. smruthigp@gmail.com)

For patients with advanced cancer and other life-limiting illnesses, palliative care often needs to extend beyond hospital wards to their homes, where families grapple with pain, emotional distress, and the demands of long-term caregiving.
At the State-run Kidwai Memorial Institute of Oncology (KMIO), the Department of Palliative Medicine has made home-based care a key part of its services, reporting more than 750 home-care visits, over 12,000 km travelled and more than 3,000 beneficiaries, including patients and caregivers.
These services were highlighted while observing World Hospice and Palliative Care Day on October 10, which this year carried the theme ‘Pain management: An essential part of palliative care’.
“With the help of volunteers and NGOs, we also extend financial support for children’s education. We provide waterbed and airbed, ration kits, and nebuliser machines for use at home. It is not just about treating the patient,” M.K. Yadhuraj Gowda, Head of the Department of Palliative Medicine at KMIO, told The Hindu.
The home-care service is intended for patients who find it difficult to travel to the hospital because of advanced illness, reduced mobility, or other challenges. Multidisciplinary teams provide medical assessment, symptom management, nursing care, and support in familiar surroundings, helping reduce the burden of repeated hospital visits.
The department’s approach also recognises that serious illness affects entire families. Caregivers may need help managing the practical demands of looking after a patient, as well as support in coping with emotional and financial pressures, Dr. Gowda said.
Beyond death
Palliative care also includes bereavement support for families after the death of a loved one. KMIO’s department provides guidance to help family members cope with grief, manage emotional distress and access support during the grieving process.
The service reflects the broader role of palliative care, which addresses not only physical pain and other symptoms but also the psychological, emotional, social and spiritual needs of patients and their families. Volunteer services add another layer of support for families navigating serious illness and loss.
Pain relief and care for children
Institute director R. Krishnappa said the department provides inpatient palliative care for patients who require specialised management of pain and other distressing symptoms, with capacity for more than 30 patients. Its services include medication and interventional procedures such as nerve blocks and neurolysis for selected patients with severe cancer-related pain that remains inadequately controlled with conventional treatment.
It also provides paediatric palliative care, with age-appropriate pain and symptom management, emotional support and guidance for families caring for children with cancer and other serious illnesses, he said.
Music and sound therapy sessions are conducted for inpatients on Wednesdays, while yoga therapy sessions are held on Thursdays to promote relaxation and emotional well-being alongside medical treatment.
Teleconsultations extend specialist support
The department has relaunched its ‘Call for Care - Neravina Kare’ service to connect patients living outside Bengaluru and in distant locations with specialist palliative care. Through telephone and video consultations, a team comprising a palliative care physician, nurse and clinical psycho-oncologist offers guidance on symptom management and emotional support. Patients and caregivers can contact the service on 9008441708.

Bhima Jewellers has appointed actor Janhvi Kapoor as its brand ambassador as the jewellery retailer looks to strengthen its presence across markets and connect with consumers across different regions. The association is part of the brand’s efforts to expand its audience while continuing to focus on craftsmanship, trust and cultural relevance.
Janhvi Kapoor appointed brand ambassador of Bhima Jewellers as brand eyes wider reach
With a legacy spanning 100 years, Bhima Jewellers has built its presence in the jewellery retail sector by catering to customers across generations. The appointment of Janhvi Kapoor aligns with the brand’s plans to reach a wider consumer base while maintaining its established relationships with existing customers.
Janhvi’s visibility across India is expected to support the brand’s efforts to connect with consumers across regions and demographics. The collaboration also reflects Bhima Jewellers’ approach to engaging with a new generation of buyers whose preferences combine cultural traditions with contemporary relevance. Through the association, the brand aims to strengthen its consumer engagement while adapting to changing purchasing patterns.
The partnership also draws a connection between Janhvi’s association with South India and Bhima Jewellers’ regional roots. The brand intends to use this alignment to introduce its South Indian heritage to a wider national audience while continuing to build on its existing market presence.
Sharing her thoughts on the association, Janhvi Kapoor said, “Some of my fondest memories are of seeing jewellery become a part of our family’s celebrations and milestones. It holds stories that are passed down through generations. That’s what makes my association with Bhima Jewellers so special. With a legacy spanning 100 years, Bhima Jewellers beautifully reflects trust, tradition, and timeless craftsmanship, and I’m delighted to join its legacy.”
Commenting on the appointment, a Bhima Jewellers spokesperson stated, “At Bhima Jewellers, we have always believed that jewellery is much more than an ornament. It is a part of life’s most treasured moments, carrying memories, emotions, and traditions across generations. Janhvi Kapoor’s warmth, elegance, and deep appreciation for her roots make her a natural fit for our brand. There is an authenticity about her that resonates with the values we hold close, and we are delighted to welcome her to the Bhima Jewellers family. We look forward to celebrating timeless stories, meaningful connections, and special milestones together.”
Founded in 1925 by Shri K. Lakshminarayana Bhattar, Bhima has established itself as a jewellery brand associated with craftsmanship in South India. The company currently operates 21 stores across Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, alongside an e-commerce platform.
With Janhvi joining as its brand ambassador, Bhima Jewellers aims to build on its regional foundation and expand its reach across India. The collaboration forms part of the brand’s broader strategy to increase visibility, engage with a wider consumer base and support its long-term growth across markets.

Jammu, Oct 15: BJP general secretary Satish Poonia on Thursday dismissed the Jammu and Kashmir government's argument that the dual power arrangement had hindered the fulfilment of its promises, saying its performance should be judged by results, not such explanations.
Poonia, the BJP in-charge of J&K here for a high-level party meeting, also dismissed allegations that the BJP was responsible for the failure to hold panchayat and local body elections in Jammu and Kashmir.
"It is for the government to decide how it wants to explain this, because it received the mandate, came to power and made the commitments. How many promises it fulfilled and how many it failed to deliver cannot be explained away. What matters is the outcome and the results," he told reporters before the party meeting.
"The people of Jammu and Kashmir are well aware of the results of these two years,” Poonia said, replying to a question about the government''s claims that the dual-power arrangement -- the elected National Conference-led government and the Lt Governor administration -- prevented it from fulfilling the promises it had made during the past two years.
Poonia said the government had received the people's mandate, assumed power and made commitments, adding that its performance should be judged by the results rather than explanations.
With the government blaming the BJP for failure to hold panchayat elections, he said “How are we (BJP)responsible? The tradition of holding elections under the Panchayati Raj system in Jammu and Kashmir was initiated by the Bharatiya Janata Party and the party also followed it very effectively."
He said that the District Development Council (DDC) elections were held for the first time during the BJP's regime. "Therefore, such allegations are baseless."
On the BJP's organisational meetings, including meetings of its various cells, Poonia said the party had received a good mandate in Jammu and Kashmir after a long time.
He said the BJP was committed to working for the prosperity and development of Jammu and Kashmir, citing the governance model of the Narendra Modi government.
“The construction of the Chenab Rail Bridge, the operation of Vande Bharat trains and the benefits of schemes such as Ujjwala and Ayushman Bharat reaching the people of Jammu and Kashmir are examples of this governance model. This demonstrates our commitment to working for the prosperity of Kashmir,” he said.

In late September, Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna of California introduced the Free Child Care for America Act, an $80 billion-a-year proposal to make childcare free for nearly every family with kids under six. The bill would let families choose between sending their child to a daycare center, having a relative, friend, or neighbor paid a living wage to care for them, or taking a $1,000 monthly stipend to keep the child home for the first three years. It comes from a lawmaker who openly says he’s considering a run for president. “I want 2028 to be a big-ideas primary,” Khanna told ABC. “A contest on who’s going to have ideas of the future that meet the moment.”
Universal childcare is set to be a 2028 presidential test
Democrats are already rolling out big plans.
If you buy something from a Vox link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Khanna’s is not the only big Democratic childcare proposal released in the last few months. In July, Project 2029 — a group of liberal policy experts developing an agenda for the next Democratic administration — proposed something similar to Khanna’s plan: giving families a choice between free daycare and $1,000 a month to provide care at home or pay a trusted caregiver. The group estimates that would cost about $200 billion annually. Third Way, a centrist Democratic think tank, unveiled its own universal childcare pitch, guaranteeing every family at least three affordable options within a 15-minute drive of home or work by expanding home-based, infant, and after-hours care, and leveraging employers as partners.
Key takeaways
- Childcare is emerging as a major 2028 issue, with big new proposals from Rep. Ro Khanna, Project 2029, and Third Way.
- “Universal childcare” means different things to different people — free for all, affordable for most, or simply enough slots to go around.
- Polls show broad, bipartisan appetite for government action on childcare, with debate over how much families should chip in.
Early childhood policy is quickly becoming a defining issue for 2028 hopefuls. On the right, Vice President JD Vance has staked out an early and controversial position, to pay married stay-at-home parents roughly $9,000 per child annually using existing federal childcare funds. On the left, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is spearheading a new House working group to develop a federal childcare plan. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has been pushing free pre-K for all 4-year-olds, something California Gov. Gavin Newsom has already enacted in his state. And New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who can’t run for president but is widely seen as an influential voice in the party’s future, has made universal childcare one of the top goals of his administration.
Michelle Lujan Grisham, the Democratic governor of New Mexico, recently told Semafor that any politician seeking to run for president in 2028 “absolutely should” run on universal childcare proposals. Last year New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to families regardless of income. Her advice echoed David Plouffe, a Democratic strategist who managed Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign, who said that universal childcare should be in the Democrats’ 2028 party platform.
This new wave of enthusiasm marks a pivot for an idea that has long been seen as a distant pipe dream in American politics. It wasn’t always that way: When women filled factories during World War II, the federal government funded thousands of daycare centers to watch their kids. In 1971, Congress actually passed a bipartisan childcare bill, though President Richard Nixon vetoed it, saying it would weaken the family. In the 50 years since, Washington lawmakers have focused their energies on other big battles, offering little on childcare beyond subsidies for some low-income families. Over that time, the US has fallen out of step with nearly all its peer nations around the world, which help parents pay for childcare, on top of offering paid parental leave after birth.
It’s not hard to understand why the idea is finally getting a serious look in the US. With voters citing affordability as a top concern, politicians are looking for ways they can bring down costs facing families. After paying rent or a mortgage, childcare often stands as many parents’ biggest monthly expense. Businesses have started to care too, as access to reliable care affects both people’s ability to hold down jobs and businesses’ ability to attract and retain workers. It’s why organizations like the Chamber of Commerce have taken up the issue and why red, blue, and purple states alike have been elevating childcare in recent years.
In Congress and in the Democratic campaign world, there’s a strong sense that childcare, long overshadowed by climate, infrastructure, voting rights, and health care, is now at the front of the line should Democrats regain power. Insiders credit both donor influence and a feeling that childcare advocates have duly waited their turn.
But as Democrats begin jockeying for 2028 and universal childcare becomes a rallying cry, it’s also become clear that there’s a big unanswered question at the heart of the politicking: No one yet agrees on what “universal childcare” actually means. Does it refer to care that’s totally free, or just affordable? Is it for everyone, like public school, or targeted at families below an income line? Does it start at birth, and include parents who stay home? Are employers involved, or neighbors and grandparents?
The answers will determine who benefits, how much it costs, and whether the party’s next big promise to families is one it can actually keep.
What is universal childcare?
When I asked Rep. Khanna how he defines universal childcare, he said that it means “childcare should be free” and that families should have flexibility and choice of how to get that care. Workers, he added, should also be paid a living wage in a universal childcare system.
Later, he described the vision for universal childcare as a public good, akin to public school. “From the time a child is born to the time they’re finished college,” he argued, America has the wealth to provide for kids’ education and development.
Others, however, are defining the idea differently. Linda Smith, who leads Child Care Trust, a national policy think tank, helped design the military’s well-regarded childcare system and oversaw federal early childhood programs under Obama. Earlier this summer, she released a framework for universal childcare that emphasized it does not inherently mean free care.
Smith says she wrote it after realizing that even the legislative staffers drafting childcare bills didn’t mean the same thing by the term. “After some candid conversations with congressional staff this summer working on child care policy, it became clear that there are many interpretations of ‘universal child care,’” she wrote on LinkedIn. “If we can’t agree on what the term means, we can’t build durable policy around it.”
She argues the “universal childcare” slogan tends to blur three separate goals: universal access, universal affordability, and universal free care. To Smith, the urgent priority is access. Her vision for universal childcare policy would be a system where all families have access to “affordable, high-quality options” that reflect their needs. Her organization estimates that about 4.2 million children under six with all available parents in the workforce lack a childcare slot within a reasonable distance of home, and she warns that cutting costs without adding new supply could worsen shortages and leave families without available options.
Her answer is a mix of building more supply and sharing the cost. She recommends families paying what they can and employers and government covering the rest. Spreading the cost across several payers, she argues, is likelier to sustain the full mix of care families actually use — including home-based care — than leaning on government or parents alone.
Chris Herbst, a childcare policy expert and professor at Arizona State University, told me he agrees with Smith that there’s no consensus regarding what universal childcare means today. Even in New Mexico, he pointed out, which is regularly touted as an example of universal childcare, a light work requirement exists for families to be eligible. “These are fluid definitions, and as such they are a bit up for grabs at the moment,” Herbst said.
His own view is that a universal childcare system should make the subsidy easy to get and be guaranteed by law, so eligible families get it automatically instead of landing on waitlists when funding runs short.
Another childcare expert, Elliot Haspel, has embraced a definition closer to Khanna and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, arguing that universal childcare means all families can easily secure the type of care they want, and pay no fees to do so. He acknowledged, though, that many things can be called “universal” and be technically correct. “The ambiguity of the term is both what lends it rhetorical power and what can present a major weakness,” he writes.
Some states are adding benefits — but avoiding “universal”
With federal childcare legislation stalled, many states have spent the past few years trying to patch the system themselves. Some states are investing in making care cheaper for families, others in paying childcare workers more, and most in trying to get more providers to open their doors.
The National Conference of State Legislatures has also aimed to get involved. Over the course of a year and a half, state lawmakers across 13 states worked together to hash out a bipartisan policy framework for strengthening childcare systems, a rare cross-party effort on the issue. The NCSL report, released this past summer, steers clear of the term “universal childcare,” but does describe state systems under strain and concludes that incremental fixes alone are unlikely to solve it. The lawmakers stressed there is no one-size-fits-all solution and offered a menu of options organized around seven priorities, from expanding access to investing in the childcare workforce.
In interviews with the working group’s two co-chairs, I asked why their cohort stayed away from the “universal” language. Jim Burgin, a Republican state senator from North Carolina, told me he doesn’t find it to be a helpful term because it could conjure up the image of public schools, which are mandatory and government-run. “I don’t like the term,” he said. “I think we ought to have safe, affordable childcare available to everybody and I don’t want everybody to immediately think we’re setting up government indoctrinated childcare…a lot of people would just push back from that.”
The Democratic co-chair, Washington state Sen. Claire Wilson, said her hesitation was more about precision. “When you say ‘universal’, I think that alone is a question about what do we mean by universal?” she said. In Washington, she explained, it means care open to all families regardless of income, employment status, or immigration status, “but for other states, universal may mean something different.”
Where the public stands
Polling suggests Americans do want to see lawmakers take action on childcare, even if it’s not voters’ top priority when asked to rank among different issue areas. An AP-NORC poll from last year found about three-quarters of Americans say childcare is a “major problem,” and majorities across both parties backed federally funded “free or low-cost” daycare. More recently, YouGov and the 19th News found 52 percent of Americans think the federal government should increase its spending on childcare.
The evidence that most Americans want childcare to be free rather than affordable is less clear. The recent YouGov/19th News found about 40 percent of Americans think parents and government should share in the cost of daycare, compared to 21 percent who thought the government should pay the full cost, and 26 percent who thought parents should cover it all.
A recent New America survey found similar results. When asked if K–12 public education should be a free, taxpayer-funded right, 60 percent of respondents agreed. But only 38 percent said the same of childcare. And among those who “somewhat” or “strongly agree” that childcare should be offered to families for free, paid by taxes, and considered a right, only 31 percent of independents agreed, and just 23 percent of Republicans.
Lena Bilik, a childcare researcher at the Roosevelt Institute, a progressive think tank, told me she thinks public opinion will shift more in favor of free universal childcare when public programs can demonstrate a track record of success, as the country saw with Social Security and more recently the Affordable Care Act. “If we build high-quality public goods that work, I think that with time that problem solves itself,” she said. “But they have to be well-resourced.”
The politics ahead
While states like New Mexico, Vermont, and Connecticut have taken major steps in recent years to expand access to affordable childcare, Bilik of the Roosevelt Institute said even those places vary in how explicitly they pursue the goal of universal childcare, or define it.
The last time Democrats went big on childcare, via the Build Back Better Act, they failed. The bill packaged much of the Democratic agenda into one piece of legislation — climate, healthcare, housing — with childcare bundled alongside paid family leave, elder care, universal preschool, and an expanded child tax credit. It collapsed in late 2021 after talks with West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin fell apart.
When I interviewed lawmakers, advocates, funders, congressional aides, and policy experts in 2024 about what lessons they drew from that experience, I found the field divided over strategy. Childcare never got a vote of its own, and the argument ever since has been whether it should have been pulled out and pursued separately. Some argued activists should have narrowed their focus to one or two care priorities. Others saw that critique as premature capitulation, a sign of a limiting “scarcity mentality.” Many of those advocates emphasized that they had come very close to passing everything, losing in the Senate by a single vote, and pointed to the climate movement, which took decades of sustained organizing and spending to win major federal legislation. Care advocates, they said, just needed to keep pushing.
Two years later, the consensus view among Congressional Democrats and national childcare advocates has shifted, with far more now saying what’s needed first and foremost are “big and bold” solutions that the party can run on — even bigger than the ideas laid out in the Build Back Better Act.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren argued this year that childcare failed in Build Back Better because not enough Democrats were “willing to fight for it” and because the $400 billion proposed spending package for childcare and universal pre-K wasn’t nearly big enough. It was “an exercise in how weak and ineffective we could make the childcare program and still call it childcare,” she said.
Bilik has watched the same change from the research side. The coalition she works with, she told me, has moved away from programs that help only families below a certain income. “What I’m excited about is that we’ve gotten more ambitious with our proposals across the board since Build Back Better,” she said. “We’re finally having conversations about whether implementing something halfway will cause more problems than solutions, so I think the field has moved really far towards being open to a true public program.”
These sentiments are reflected in the recently released Khanna bill, the Project 2029 proposal, and comments over the summer from Democratic Rep. Sara Jacobs, who said free childcare for all should be at the top of the House’s legislative agenda if Democrats take control after the midterms.
How that vision translates into legislation remains an open question. Some advocates I talked to for this story, who spoke off the record to describe private coalition conversations candidly, said they worried their allies were going to make the same mistake of over-promising and then failing to prioritize goals when faced with tough budget realities. Should Democrats take power, leaders will also face pressure to restore Medicaid and SNAP funding, expand ACA subsidies, and address housing costs, all while large federal deficits make new spending harder to finance.
Khanna told me his proposals could be funded by shifting priorities away from increased military spending, particularly the $200 billion increase in the Pentagon budget and the war with Iran. The Project 2029 proposal suggests financing through raising the corporate tax rate, repealing the pass-through business tax deduction, and reforming estate taxes and the “stepped-up basis” tax break on inherited assets. Third Way would also fund its plan partly through a corporate tax increase. But those same dollars could be claimed by other Democratic priorities, which means childcare advocates may end up competing for them.
“Everyone is excited to put out the biggest idea, but there’s no real conversation about how to get there, and I feel like that’s the frustration, where ‘how to get there’ just means electing Democrats and demonizing any incremental progress,” one advocate told me. “That is not a strategy.”
For now, think tanks, presidential hopefuls, and congressional working groups are testing the waters, floating ideas that meet families where they are and, in some cases, go further than what voters say they want. The practical details are unlikely to get settled once the 2028 race is fully underway. If a Democrat wins, the window will narrow further, with unresolved details colliding with other priorities in the first months of a new administration.
“Universal childcare” may remain an amorphous term, meaning free care to one politician, shared costs to another, and a menu of state options to lawmakers who avoid the word altogether. But all of us voters should expect to hear much more of it.

Srinagar, Oct 14: Police, in coordination with the Army, railway police and CRPF, conducted an anti-Fidayeen attack drill on Wednesday at a railway station in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam district, officials said.
"Kulgam Police, in coordination with the Army, GRP, RPF and CRPF, conducted an anti-fidayeen mock drill at Harnag Railway Station to assess operational preparedness and inter-agency coordination," a police spokesperson said.
During the exercise, road cut-offs were established at designated locations, and participating agencies carried out coordinated response measures to neutralise the simulated threat and ensure the safe evacuation of passengers and civilians, he said.
The exercise aimed to enhance operational readiness, improve response time and strengthen coordination among security agencies to ensure an effective response to any eventuality, he added.
Handwara SSP Sajad Khaliq Bhat reviewed the security and operational preparedness in the North Kashmir police district.
Bhat, who assumed charge on Monday, undertook a detailed review of critical security and policing aspects, including investigation of cases under the NDPS and the UAPA Acts, identification of security hotspots, vulnerability mapping, deployment arrangements, law-and-order preparedness and preventive security measures.
He directed officers to strengthen the security grid, intensify patrolling and naka checking, maintain heightened vigilance at sensitive locations and ensure timely preventive action against elements likely to disturb peace and public order.
Bhat also stressed the importance of effective surveillance outside prisons, in accordance with established legal procedures, to identify and prevent potential security threats.
Emphasising the importance of social media surveillance, the SSP directed officers to closely monitor online platforms for provocative, misleading and unlawful content that could affect public peace and security, and to initiate appropriate action in accordance with law.

My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed.
Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD.
While there he became involved with Operation Omega, a group that smuggled humanitarian aid across the border from India to Bangladesh during its war with Pakistan in 1971. This led him to cut short his studies so that he could begin work as a consultant economist and project planner. Over the years he worked on many projects, including for the University of New South Wales from 1984 to 1986 in the Solomon Islands on a smallholder project and a post-cyclone survey.
In 1989 his work took him back to Bangladesh, where he was employed by the World Bank to develop a flood action plan. Fourteen years of his life, from 1992 to 2006, were then spent with the Department for International Development, working on ways to help tackle the social and economic problems related to rural poverty in India.
He was also particularly proud of a cyclone recovery and reconstruction project he worked on in 2007 for the World Bank, which led to the building of cyclone shelters in Bangladesh.
In 2006 he became a trustee and then chair of trustees of the Humanitarian Centre in Cambridge, which later became the Centre for Global Equality. Two years later he had to leave work after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, but eventually he was lucky enough to receive a lung transplant that prolonged his life considerably.
That allowed him to focus on being a trustee, chair and patient president of the charity Action for Pulmonary Fibrosis, giving over the last decade of his life to fighting on behalf of people with the disease so that they can be provided with better diagnosis, care and treatment. He was also president of the European Pulmonary Fibrosis Federation.
In 1976 he met Hilary Gretton, a nurse, and they married five years later. She survives him, along with their children, Rosie, David and Euan, and seven grandchildren.

“Bacchon, police ki maar ka bura nahi maante. Yeh aapko samjhane ke liye kari gayi hai” (Translation: Children, don’t take offence at being beaten by the police. This was done to teach you a lesson.)
This is what a Delhi Police official had to say after protesters were allegedly subjected to a vicious assault inside a prison van fitted with ‘cages’, while being taken to a detention centre at Pandwalan Khurd, a village in the Kapashera tehsil of Najafgarh in South West Delhi, on October 11.
One detainee was called in. Then came the screams. Another followed, and the screams came again. Inside the pitch-dark van, protesters were allegedly punched, kicked and beaten by police personnel before being shoved into cramped, grille-enclosed compartments. They could hear the violence unfold but could barely see who was inflicting it.
Two detainees who were in the same van spoke to Alt News, recounting what they described as a nightmare that would haunt them for the rest of their lives. Each detainee, they said, was made to board the vehicle one at a time, assaulted and then forced into one of the cages inside.
Their offence: Joining a protest on the streets of Delhi against alleged electoral malpractices and supporting the call for the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
An Evening of Unspeakable Horror
Twenty-three-year-old Tarang Balani, who works at an e-commerce startup, saw a video posted by Neha Bora urging people to reach R K Ashram at 2:30 pm. “I saw that post at 2. So I reached Connaught Place (CP) directly because I thought if they’re marching from R K Ashram towards Jantar Mantar, and if I’m reaching late, I should definitely find the march somewhere around CP. I reached around 3:30 pm,” he said.
With several routes blocked in the area, Balani had to take multiple detours. He eventually came across a group marching towards Jantar Mantar and joined them. “We were told to form a human chain in case the police came to detain us,” he said.
The group was marching past Chilli’s restaurant and about to turn left when the police moved in to detain them. “As soon as police came, half the crowd had dispersed around, trying not to get detained, and 10-15 people sat down and locked hands with each other to form a human chain. I saw male police officers pulling the women protesters. Then women police officers arrived and did the same thing.”
After a tussle with the police, the protesters were forcibly made to board a Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) bus.
In the video below posted by BBC, as Hemansh speaks, a policeman inside the bus can be seen slapping or punching a young man in the face.
View this post on Instagram
“Soon after, they stopped outside the Pind Balluchi restaurant in CP and some police officers started asking us to deboard,” Balani said. The protesters refused to get off the bus since the area was teeming with security personnel and there were no media persons around. “We felt that the media should be able to document what was happening.”
“But if three people are trying to get hold of one person, there’s not much you can do,” he said. According to Balani, police officers began pulling a female protester by her wrists, breaking her bangles and leaving her wrists bleeding. She then clung to the window grille as the officers pulled at her trousers and shoes, leaving her almost suspended in the air. Two women police officers approached her from outside the window and pulled her hair, forcing her to let go. “I saw it happen in front of me,” he recounted.
Outside Pind Balluchi, the protesters were separated by gender. The women were made to sit in a van and taken away, while the men were made to sit on the street for at least half an hour before the next ordeal began.
“If anyone took out their phones, it was immediately snatched, even if they were not recording. They were asking them to open their gallery and delete all media files from the day, even from the recently deleted files. We were told that if we just co-operated, nothing was going to happen to us. So most of us were just sitting quietly,” Balani said.
A Journey that Turned into a Nightmare
Half an hour later, another police van arrived, and the men were asked to board it. Twenty-seven-year-old IIT graduate Hemansh Kashyap recounted how the police allegedly assaulted detainees one by one as they entered the vehicle.
“Some of the policemen started playing good cop, saying that nothing would happen to us if we boarded it. People were taken in one at a time. An official was collecting our phones at the entrance. The first person went in, and then came blood-curdling screams. Then the second person went in, and the same thing happened. We realised that they were being assaulted.”
“We said we wouldn’t board, but the cops said: ‘Aur nahi marenge’ (We won’t hit anymore). But it obviously wasn’t true, and there wasn’t a lot we could do. When I went in, I was immediately slapped very hard, repeatedly, so hard that my glasses flew off. I was shoved into my compartment, and the cops gave me my glasses back,” he said.
Balani said the van had four compartments separated by grille partitions, with a narrow aisle that could accommodate only one person at a time. The vehicle was completely dark, making it impossible for him to see clearly.
“I was beaten up right there in the narrow passage by three policemen. Initially, two of them started beating me up; they punched me and kicked me. And then somebody said, ‘Iska chashma utaar’ (Take off his glasses), and so they took out my specs and started beating me again. I couldn’t even see their faces in the dark; I just saw policemen without name tags,” he recounted.
“I really thought they had confused me with someone else because I was quiet from the start. I was protesting peacefully. As I tried to save myself from the blows, they kept beating me, and beating me, and I just kept pleading with them (to stop). Once they realised that the regular punches and kicks were not working, they started using their elbows. One of them kicked my knee, and I fell in the aisle, and then they hit me more.
“Once I started screaming, that is when they opened the compartment where they pushed me in and just threw my specs. They closed the door behind me and locked it. As soon as I sat down, another person came; he was not wearing glasses, so they literally just took his face and smashed it into a pole in that aisle. I saw it because I was sitting right next to the division between the aisle and my compartment. There was one guy who refused to surrender his phone, and he was beaten by the police as if they had a personal grudge against him,” Balani recounted.
Both Balani and Hemansh Kashyap told Alt News that each of the blocks or cages inside the police van could accommodate six people at most. Each had two benches facing each other, with space for three people on either side. However, 10–12 detainees were crammed into each block, forcing some to sit on the floor and others to sit on fellow detainees’ laps.
The van was completely dark, making it difficult for detainees to even check the time on their watches.
What emerged from both testimonies was the methodical nature of the violence — perhaps its cruellest aspect. One detainee was taken in, beaten and shoved into a cage; then the next was called. The screams were followed by more screams. There was no frenzy, no confusion, but a grim, repeated sequence, with each person left to await their turn, knowing what awaited them in the darkness of the van.
Families Lose Contact as Detainees’ Phones Go Dead
Both detainees had shared their live locations with family members. Kashyap had shared his with his partner, Barshana, who is currently in the United States.
“At 3:45 am Pacific Daylight Time (4.15pm IST) on October 11, Hemansh called me and said he had been detained. He had been detained the day before as well and was held at a farmhouse in Chhattarpur for about six hours before being released. There wasn’t much explicit violence then, so I wasn’t too worried.
“We texted for a while as he told me he was on a bus, and he even sent me a few videos from it. But soon there was complete silence from his side. After two hours of no contact, my calm gave way to worry. I kept checking his location, but it stayed parked at CP for a long time.
“Soon, I received a message request on Instagram from an unknown account. It was Hemansh sending a message from someone else’s phone informing me that he was in a police van and had been assaulted. He told me that his phone was possibly with the cops, and also asked me to track his location. I noticed that the van was moving very fast, heading towards the Haryana border. At around 7 am PDT, the location stopped updating. I had checked, and his battery was at 40%, so it couldn’t have died. I guess the phone was switched off. His friend, who was with him in the van, was also not getting his WhatsApp messages delivered, so both phones seemed to have met the same fate.”
“I kept texting the Instagram account, which, I later found out, belonged to a detainee who had managed to sneak in a phone, but I couldn’t bombard it with messages, as the same phone was being used by thirty others. At around 7:27 am PDT, he called me for a minute, told me they had been brought to a detention centre in the middle of nowhere, and shared the location with me. That is when I mobilised my lawyer and activist friends, who reached the spot to get him out.
“The entire ordeal, from the time he was detained to the time he returned home, lasted about eight hours. It was extremely worrying for me,” Barshana recounted.
Tarang Balani, too, said his brother, with whom he had shared his live location, lost track of him when the police van reached Raota in Delhi. “I’m guessing it was because someone switched it off. An app installed in my phone still shows 70% battery in brother’s phone. The location update was stopped between 6:36 pm and 6:40 pm,” he said.
Kashyap also recounted the assault of a young man, around 19–20 years old, inside the police van. The man allegedly screamed that the police had assaulted him on his private parts and manhandled him. “(He) fell on the ground while being assaulted, and the police started hitting him in between his legs. He told his cellmates after the van started moving. He was probably the first or second detainee to be taken into the van, and he was beaten up brutally. We told him, ‘Don’t get too agitated; they’ll beat you up even more.’ It was very scary,” Kashyap said.
Neither Kashyap nor Balani has got back his phone yet.
Both of them told Alt News that four minors were inside the police van and that all four were assaulted.
Locals Come to Detainee’s Aid at Pandwalan Khurd
The van dropped them at the detention centre around 7:30 pm. The detainees expected their phones back but were told by CRPF personnel that Delhi police had not handed over the phones.
One detainee with a fractured arm received medical attention only at 9:15 pm. “There was just one canister of water, and it ran out pretty quickly. There was no food or medical help. An AIIMS doctor finally came after someone contacted them through their connections,” Hemansh said.
Initially, lawyers were not allowed to enter the detention centre. Meanwhile, a crowd began gathering outside, with some villagers, including children, reportedly protesting the detention.
“They were recording us from outside the gate. We told them to go away or they would get beaten up, but they seemed quite aware of their rights and started asking questions like, ‘How can they beat us up?’ They went away for a bit and came back with their parents, I think. These were ordinary people from the neighbourhood. They came back with water and fruits. Later, when we were released, a man was going around giving everybody 100-rupee notes if they needed to get home,” Kashyap said.
At around 9:30 pm, another van arrived, and some detainees, including 51-year-old journalist Raj Shekhar, were offered the chance to leave. The detainees unanimously refused to go without their phones. The police allegedly told them they could collect their phones from Connaught Place, offering no accountability for their confiscation. Lawyers who had reached the detention centre advised the detainees to call the emergency helpline 112 and submit written applications and complaints.
Between 10:30 pm and 11 pm, buses were arranged to take the protesters to Dwarka More metro station. Unsure whether the buses would actually drop them at Dwarka More, Balani chose not to board one. Instead, he left in a car provided by volunteers, who had been sent sent by journalist Meghnad S to help detainees return home. Kashyap, too, left with lawyers who were present at the scene.
Balani also noted that most Delhi Police personnel involved wore no name tags; only officers with two or three stars had them. He identified one officer as Ashutosh Bishnoi, who, while the detainees waited outside Pind Balluchi, had repeatedly assured them that nothing would happen to them.
