India’s AI story is moving beyond the model. Until last year, the big question in Indian boardrooms was which large language model (LLM) enterprises should standardise on. Now, as AI agents move from answering questions to executing tasks, the focus is shifting to what these agents can do for businesses, which workflows they should handle, and how enterprises can measure their performance. In September, Inc42 reported that Swiggy is opening food delivery, Instamart, Dineout, and Scenes to external AI agents. Through four Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and 66 tools, the company lets AI assistants outside its app build carts, place orders, and book tables. The same month, we explored how Flipkart is reworking product discovery for a future where customers may no longer begin their shopping journeys with keyword searches. As AI agents take on more tasks, enterprises must look beyond the underlying models to the systems that make them useful and reliable. That means building workflows that allow agents to execute tasks effectively and evaluation systems that measure whether they deliver the intended results. Meanwhile, investor interest in the sector remains strong. Indian AI startups raised $438 Mn across 35 deals in Q3 2026, up 265% YoY, according to Inc42's Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026. Against this backdrop, Inc42 returns with the 13th edition of the AI Startups To Watch series. This edition features five emerging ventures tackling distinct opportunities: agentic commerce, screen-free learning, AI agent reliability, automated customer conversations and AI-powered recruitment. Here are the five startups from the 13th edition of Inc42's AI Startups To Watch. Editor's Note: This is not a ranking. The startups featured here are a curated selection by the Inc42 editorial team and are listed alphabetically. Agnost AI | Keeping A Closer Eye On AI Agents A chatbot that gives a wrong answer frustrates users. An AI agent that fails silently can cost a business its customers. Users may correct it, repeat their requests or abandon the interaction altogether, while dashboards continue to record the exchange as a success. Agnost AI is building tools to detect these failures and help teams fix them. Founded in 2025 by Shubham Palriwala and Parth Ajmera, the platform monitors AI agents in production by analysing their conversations with users. It identifies recurring problems, flags instances where users correct the agent or abandon a task, and traces failures back through the agent's tool calls to identify what went wrong. It then suggests fixes and tests them against the conversations in which the agent failed before deployment. It adds cases where fixes work to a regression test suite to help prevent the same errors from recurring. Agnost integrates with agent-building frameworks such as LangChain and CrewAI, and counts Exa and Comp AI among its users. It is backed by Y Combinator, Entrepreneurs First and Transpose Platform Management. The startup is targeting the agentic AI monitoring and observability tools market, estimated at $500 Mn in 2025 and projected to reach $2 Bn by 2030, growing at a 30.1% CAGR. Dialflo | AI Voice Agents With ROI Many Indian enterprises have spent the past two years experimenting with AI voice bots, only to find it difficult to measure their impact. The challenge isn't just getting an AI agent to handle calls, but understanding how well it performs, what business outcomes it delivers, and when human intervention is needed. Bengaluru-based Dialflo is building a platform to address this gap. Founded in 2024 by Abhishek Kumar, the startup combines AI voice agents and human agents in a single contact centre, helping businesses automate customer interactions while tracking their outcomes. Its voice agents handle high-volume tasks such as qualifying leads, verifying cash-on-delivery orders to reduce returns, recovering abandoned carts and providing multilingual customer support around the clock. What sets Dialflo apart is its focus on attribution: it scores each conversation and links it to a business outcome, helping customer experience teams measure the revenue generated by calls alongside the costs saved. This focus comes as the global call centre AI market expands, with its value projected to rise from $1.9 Bn in 2024 to $7.1 Bn by 2030, at a CAGR of 23.8%, according to Grand View Research. Dialflo works with more than 10 enterprise customers, including Tata Digital, Intugine and Careernet. HireBound | AI Agents For End-To-End Hiring Recruiters often spend a lot of time chasing candidates, screening resumes and conducting repetitive initial interviews rather than evaluating the people best suited for a role. As hiring volumes grow, these tasks become harder to manage without adding to recruitment teams. Bengaluru-based HireBound is using AI agents to automate much of this work. Founded in 2024 by Sharad Vij and Kumar Vikramaditya, the startup aims to help recruiters move candidates through the hiring process faster. Its platform uses separate agents for sourcing, screening and evaluation. These agents engage candidates through voice calls, WhatsApp, text messages and email, gathering information to assess their suitability for a role. Looking to capitalise on the growth of India's HR tech market, projected to reach $2.3 Bn by 2034, the platform integrates with companies' existing applicant tracking systems and human resource management systems. Its customers include staffing firms and enterprise talent acquisition teams in India and the US. HireBound has conducted more than 3 Mn candidate conversations and trained its systems on over 2 Mn resumes and 30,000 job openings. It raised $2 Mn (₹18.2 Cr) in a seed round led by Kalaari Capital, with participation from Antler, Infinyte Club and CareerNet. The startup is targeting a fivefold increase in annual recurring revenue over the next year. MyWonder | Screen-Free AI Learning Companion For children aged three to ten, finding ways to make learning engaging without relying on screens remains a challenge. MyWonder is building a screen-free alternative. Founded in 2024 by Chandramouli K, formerly of Amazon and RedBus, and Venkat Potluri, formerly of Flipkart and ZestMoney, the startup wants to make learning interactive through voice-led play. Its WonderPod combines a voice-first device with figurines and cards that unlock stories, quizzes and games. A conversational AI layer adapts to each child's speech and learning level, while a companion app lets parents track activities and manage content access. The startup also sources content through publisher partnerships. MyWonder operates in India's tech toys market, expected to reach about $3.6 Bn by 2030, expanding at a CAGR of 14.7%. Tru Commerce | Commerce Infra For AI Agents Shopping is moving into chat windows, where consumers can ask AI assistants to recommend products and receive a shortlist. But even when brands appear in these recommendations, shoppers cannot always buy from them directly. Many brands lack product catalogues that AI agents can read and checkout systems that work within these conversations. Tru Commerce is building the infrastructure to bridge that gap. Founded in 2024 as Asva AI by Viren Inaniyan and Umang Chhaparia, the startup rebranded this year to focus on helping brands sell through AI agents. Its platform has three core functions. It converts product pages into structured data that AI agents can understand, connects brands’ existing stores to agent-led checkouts through protocols such as MCP, ACP and UCP, and tracks brand mentions, product recommendations and orders attributed to AI agents. Brands remain the merchant of record and retain their customer relationships. Tru Commerce works with Amazon, ITC MasterChef, MyMuse, Provogue and House of Zelena. The startup is targeting the global agentic commerce market, estimated at $1.9 Bn in 2025 and projected to reach $54.2 Bn by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 39.81%. The Netherlands reaffirmed its position as a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO and a leading donor of flexible and predictable resources to WHO. In picture: WHO Director-General Dr Tedros and Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport Ernst Kuipers. ©WHO
The Netherlands strengthened its longstanding engagement with WHO on Monday with the renewal of the multiannual contribution of the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to WHO for €13.34 million for 2024–2028 and for €6 million to the technical partnership with Dutch WHO collaborating centres.
With the new contribution, the Netherlands reaffirmed its position as a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO and a leading donor of flexible and predictable resources to WHO.
"Amid increasingly complex and connected threats, from pandemics and climate change to conflicts, the Netherlands remains an essential supporter of WHO and global public health," said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus during the agreement signing.
"The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport's new contribution reflects the Netherland's commitment to its long partnership with WHO, and its support of the sustainable financing for WHO that Member States have agreed. This will enable WHO to respond quickly to global health challenges, and strengthen public health worldwide, including in the Netherlands."
Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport Ernst Kuipers added that “the Netherlands values our strong and long-standing relationship with WHO. Given the global challenges we collectively face, and the added value the Netherlands can deliver, we believe this renewed arrangement with long-term flexible funds well represents our commitment to advancing health worldwide. These funds will be used to achieve our shared priorities in the WHO’s General Programme of Work, facilitate the secondment of Dutch experts, and to support the Dutch WHO collaborating centres.”
The Netherlands recently recommitted to its role as a leading voice for global health through its Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030. The strategy aims to strengthen health systems at home and worldwide, better prepare for pandemics and address the impact of climate change on public health.
The Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport has provided for many years critical financial and technical support to WHO’s efforts to strengthen health security, improve the capacities of countries to address health emergencies, fight antimicrobial resistance, promote access to medicines, and support food safety, tobacco control and mental health.
The renewed partnership expands the joint work of the Netherlands and WHO into new global health challenges, such as those posed by climate change.
The interconnection between the health of the Earth and human health makes climate change a fundamental threat to decades of progress on health. The joint work of the Netherlands and WHO aims to make healthcare more climate resilient and sustainable while mainstreaming health into internal climate policies.
***
The Netherlands also funds crucial activities in sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care and antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
Between 2022 and 2023, the Netherlands provided US$ 80 million to WHO, including over US$ 66 million in voluntary contributions.
The Netherlands also contributed over US$ 20 million in flexible and thematic funding to WHO, making it the third-largest flexible contributor to the Organization. Such support allows WHO to be agile and strategic in its efforts to help countries improve the health and well-being of their populations.

Uncertainty is the point: The growing drone campaign stalking NATO’s skies
Growing numbers operating in grey zone with 'substantial impunity' increasingly blamed on Russia
As concerns rise about a Russian strike on NATO territory, the alliance’s top commander spelled out the consequences of any direct attack, promising Monday that “we will fight.”
But countries belonging to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) are already contending with a menace that is much harder to fight and is increasingly stalking their skies with impunity.
Suspected Russian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace on its eastern flank, in countries like Romania and Poland, and the organization's jets have scrambled multiple times to head off a possible attack.
But there are also hundreds and hundreds of ambiguous drones that have been increasingly spotted over sensitive sites — military bases, nuclear power plants and airports — in NATO countries as far west as Germany, Belgium and France, causing disruptions at airports and exposing gaps in defence.
It has the hallmarks of a deliberate campaign to stoke fear and uncertainty — and the problem appears to be growing.
German authorities, for instance, have clocked more than 1,000 suspicious drone-related incidents since January 2025, CBC News has learned. That's about 1.5 incidents a day on average over “critical infrastructure, military facilities and defence companies,” according to the country's Federal Criminal Police Office.
Meanwhile, there were 261 overall drone-related disruptions at German airports or in its airspace between January and August, an 80 per cent year-over-year increase, according to a report obtained by CBC News from the country's air traffic control authority.
The mysterious drones repeatedly spotted across Europe are difficult to detect and intercept and, as a result, hard to attribute. But taken together, the pattern that emerges strongly suggests they are one element of a Russian hybrid campaign, say defence experts.
Ulrike Franke is a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations. (CBC)
“There is an increase in the absolute number,” said Ulrike Franke, one of Europe’s foremost drone experts, in an interview from Paris.
“And I'm comfortable to say that it is very likely, if not certainly, linked to Russian aggression towards Europe, and the war that Russia is waging against Ukraine and the war it sees itself in against the West."
Hybrid warfare
Mysterious drone-related incidents have occurred over Europe for years, prompting accusations of a below-the-radar “hybrid warfare,” meaning non-conventional means of undermining an adversary, staying below the threshold of an open war. But such incidents spiked in number last fall and now again appear to be on the rise.
Norway has seen more than 300 occurrences so far this year, leading to six airport interruptions, a spokesperson told CBC News. In the U.K., drone incidents near military bases have reportedly doubled over the past year. And in Belgium, there were 150 incidents over sensitive sites, per one media report.
On Sept. 12, a suspected drone sighting again interrupted flights at Brussels Airport. A week later, another diverted 19 flights from Luxembourg Airport, affecting nearly 2,000 passengers. Four days later, Berlin’s main airport was shut down after a drone was spotted over its north runway.
“It's hybrid warfare,” Elio Di Rupo, a member of the European Parliament and its security defence committee, and a former Belgian prime minister, said in an interview.
“It’s not only the drone war, but cyber attacks. And all together, it’s a real war, but we don’t see nobody, except indeed the drones.”
Elio Di Rupo spoke with CBC News in Mons, Belgium, about what he says is a new kind of war. (David Iacoluccio/CBC)
Exact numbers are hard to come by, making it a challenge to connect the dots across Europe.
CBC reached out to 11 national air traffic authorities, several EU organizations, research institutes and think-tanks as well as NATO.
NATO refused a request for a tally, referring CBC News to national authorities instead, which have various mechanisms to track data. European Union organizations were also unable to provide data, pointing out that defence is a national domain.
In one snapshot, the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) reported 144 suspicious drones flew over sensitive sites with “substantial impunity" in a dozen NATO countries over 18 months ending in February.
The report adds they were likely launched from a Russian “shadow fleet” — tankers and other vessels that the country uses to clandestinely evade sanctions and export oil.
Russia has repeatedly rejected all such accusations.
This photo taken in October 2025 off the coast of France shows the tanker Boracay from Russia's so-called 'shadow fleet' suspected of being involved in drone flights over Denmark. (Damien Meyer/AFP/Getty Images)
The authors of the IISS report point out their argument is not that every drone sighting was Russian, but that the overall pattern “cannot be adequately explained” by other means such as human error or hobby drones deployed incorrectly.
It also says that even having a large number of benign drones is, "if anything, analytically consistent with Russian operational design: engineering an environment of ambiguity," where real incursions are hard to distinguish from others.
Franke agrees it’s the pattern that speaks to Russia’s involvement: the type of drones, the time of day, their movements.
She also concurs that the uncertainty is the point.
“Russia benefits from our hysteria, and it benefits from the fact that of course there are going to be drone sightings, no matter what,” she said.
“This is the kind of genius of these hybrid attacks that it is so difficult to attribute, that there will be false positives… and [they] work so well, and are so difficult to deal with in open, democratic societies.”
Turning point
A turning point came on Aug. 4, with the discovery of a custom-built drone carrying explosives near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport, which is used as a hub for support sent to Ukraine.
A Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane stands at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 5. (Getty Images)
German investigations concluded that the drone was hard evidence pointing to Russian involvement. The information the drone made possible has also reportedly since been key to mapping other escalating hybrid operations and connecting them to Russian intelligence.
The foiled Leipzig attack was the furthest into NATO territory such a dangerous attempt has been made since Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
“It tells us that Russia is definitely targeting countries and companies that are supporting Ukraine," said Michelle Haas, an associate fellow in the Europe in the World programme at Egmont Royal Institute for International Relations in Brussels.
"And one of the main goals is to get into our minds and make us believe that the cost of supporting Ukraine is too high."
Michelle Haas is a PhD researcher at the Ghent Institute for International and European Studies. (David Iacolucci/CBC)
The Leipzig incident also focused European attention and forced a co-ordinated response that included diplomatic and economic measures against Russia. Other EU countries and NATO allies including Canada issued statements of support for Germany and admonitions of Russia.
"Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia, but it is part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the time, hinting at Russia’s culpability in the bigger picture.
Initially reluctant to explicitly point the finger at Russia out of concern about escalation, European leaders now appear to be increasingly willing to do so. How to deter and repel future similar attacks, however, is still an open question.
Von der Leyen acknowledged such incidents may well be “the new normal" in Europe. Still, Haas said, they must be taken “very seriously."

Could Wenger really take on Infantino and run for Fifa presidency?
- Published
Despite the backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors, Fifa president Gianni Infantino looks increasingly likely to be re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term next year.
But could there be a sensational twist?
Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run as a surprise candidate.
But would the man who has been the governing body's head of global development since 2019 really challenge his own boss? And what lies behind the support he has?
On Thursday the Fifa Council will meet for the first time since the emergence of Infantino's Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme plunged the organisation into crisis, leading to calls from the game's leaders in Europe, North America and Asia for him to step down.
A defiant Infantino will come face to face with some of his fiercest critics at what could be a spicy gathering in Zurich.
Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development. But Infantino will also face scrutiny over governance reforms, FFE, the awarding of the inaugural Fifa Peace Prize last year to US President Donald Trump, and disciplinary procedures in the wake of the Folarin Balogun affair.
But the meeting will also bring into sharp focus the failure so far to identify a unifying figure with the worldwide appeal to challenge Infantino.
While potential rivals like Victor Montagliani, the president of the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (Concacaf), and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders, Infantino has been busy touring the world, shoring up his position.
The growing expectation is that such is the support he retains in his power base of Africa, South America and Oceania, he will be returned, despite only carrying the backing of roughly half of Fifa's 211 members.
To date, the only person to declare their intention to run is the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, although few rate his chances.
So could Wenger be the answer?
Here in Zurich, there is no indication that he is plotting a bid. On Wednesday evening Wenger joined Infantino and other Fifa Council members for dinner in a Zurich restaurant. As a senior member of Fifa's management team, he will also be present at Thursday's meeting.
When BBC Sport asked about his intentions via Fifa, no comment was provided.
Meanwhile, those close to the 76 year-old, who left Arsenal in 2018 after 22 years in which he became the most successful manager in the club's history, will not be drawn on whether he is interested.
One told BBC Sport he would be "an ideal candidate, but he is his own man". A high-ranking Fifa official insisted he had no idea if Wenger was tempted.
But what is clear is that he does have supporters, who believe he commands the level of respect beyond Europe that would be essential if the Uefa-led rebellion against Infantino is to have any chance of success.
"He's a brilliant football man who truly understands football development because he's been running it," claimed one senior official at a European national association.
"People don't see him as just a European. He's very respected in Asia, for instance, from his time working in Japan. A lot of people are saying he'd be the ideal candidate. With him, it's not about money, status or ego. He genuinely loves the game.
"He's made a difficult role work and understands Fifa, and that's why he'd be a really good candidate.
"That said, he's in a really difficult position."
That was highlighted amid the fallout over FFE, when Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot.
"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said in a statement at the time. "The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."
Some may have expected Wenger to resign over the controversy, given his thinly veiled criticism of Infantino, the way he had been kept in the dark, and the condemnation of the plot from stakeholders across the game. But he has carried on in a role in which he oversees youth development at academies in 60 countries, as well as youth competitions around the world. He is also a technical adviser to rule-making body International Football Association Board (Ifab).
Wenger has caused controversy at times in his Fifa role, notably for proposals such as biennial World Cups, and the idea of a 'daylight' offside law.
But he also has a global profile, including in Africa, where Infantino recently received a major re-election boost when receiving the backing of all 54 member national associations after promising an increase in funding.
Known as a champion of African players when in charge at Arsenal, Wenger's support of an expanded 48-team World Cup in order to drive development in countries beyond the game's traditional powers has been well received in the continent.
Indeed, at the weekend Wenger was in Cape Verde at a Confederation of African Football conference, telling the delegates: "We want to see an African team win the World Cup, and the numbers show that it is feasible."
Such sentiments would do him no harm if he was to stand for president.
BBC Sport has been told that a large number of Fifa's staff also want Wenger to run, and believe he could change the organisation's image.
Others, however, are more sceptical. One well-connected figure in Fifa circles told BBC Sport that he would be "amazed if Wenger would rise up against the man who appointed him in the first place. Arsene has had some fairly 'out there' ideas. In terms of the administration of the game and the relationships on a political level, in the kind of places you're going to need to corral and command power, I'm not sure he's the man for that."
Another senior European official said: "He has the stature, but I'm not sure he smacks of the future. Maybe he could do a single term to introduce reforms. He is very respected in the game and has done a good job of the development programmes, but whether he'd split from Gianni, I just don't know."
If Wenger does want to run, he has until 18 November to declare his candidacy, and would need to be nominated by at least five national associations.
As a manager, Wenger is remembered as a legendary figure who changed English football with his forward-thinking approach to tactics and nutrition.
Could he attempt a shake-up of a different kind at Fifa? It is an intriguing prospect.

New Brunswick·CBC Investigates
‘Pretty shoddy’: Prof says N.B. education plan attributes to him an article that doesn’t seem to exist
Province acknowledges AI was used in document, but in a limited way
Vincent Geiger wasn’t especially surprised to learn his work had been misattributed in New Brunswick’s 12-year education plan for the anglophone schools sector.
The professor of mathematics education at Australian Catholic University said it has happened before.
But in this case, he finds the way the plan references some academic work “pretty shoddy” for a government document.
Geiger’s research in the field of numeracy is cited twice in the education plan, which is meant to lay the foundation of the province’s public education system from now to 2038.
The professor gets an entry on the document’s reference list, but the article attributed to him doesn’t seem to exist, and Geiger said he’s never heard of the journal where the article is supposed to have been published.
“It's a bit of a mishmash of things I have worked on in the past,” he said in an interview with CBC News.
“It's as if something has just dredged through my records and picked out bits and pieces from the articles themselves rather than the title.”
Geiger suspects artificial intelligence may have played a role.
“If that's what they're doing now, it's not a scholarly approach," Geiger said.
“It's hardly an approach that would be adopted by a credible journalist. So I don't know why or how people working for governments and certainly education departments are taking that approach.”
His isn’t the only work to be misattributed in the document.
William Jeynes is an education professor and researcher at the California State University, Long Beach. His name also gets a spot on the plan’s reference list, but the article attributed to him, while in his field of study, was written by someone else.
“Maybe grieved is too strong a word, or maybe that's not strong enough,” he told CBC News.
“What I find most disturbing is, this is not the first time I have encountered this. I've seen this on student papers that I know have used AI.”
The education plan accurately represents the content of his research in the body of the text, Jeynes said, but errors related to attribution and a seeming lack of fact-checking before publication are much more serious when they are in a report issued by a government agency.
Suspected AI hallucinations
To Matt McGuire, who teaches educational technology at the University of New Brunswick, the two references bear the hallmarks of so-called “hallucinations,” when an artificial intelligence system comes up with responses that sound plausible but that are factually wrong or fabricated.
He said there is even a popular term for when AI jumbles different pieces of real information to create something entirely new: “Frankencitations.”
“It makes us question the integrity of a document and the process that was followed,” McGuire said.
“So, an article can lose its professional and academic integrity if it's known to contain these hallucinated references. Even if the core arguments or the data in the paper still holds value, fabricating sources violate the foundational rules of research.”
New Brunswick Education Minister Claire Johnson and Premier Susan Holt spoke to reporters in June after releasing education plans for the francophone and anglophone sectors. (Shane Magee/CBC)
Nabil Beitinjaneh, faculty lecturer and data programs co-ordinator at McGill University in Montreal, said the use of AI is not the problem. He said he would expect government employees — and anyone writing a report — to consult the tools at their disposal.
“The real question is not that they're using generative AI," he said. "It's more, what is the process that they're using? What's the accountability and governance that is happening within the process of delivering a document of this importance?”
Beitinjaneh believes a better use of AI would have helped the plan’s writers keep better track of their sources and correct other more minor mistakes. In his review of the plan, Beitinjaneh found some of the referenced authors’ names were misspelled.
He said there were also a few orphaned citations, meaning works quoted in the body of the text don't appear on the reference list, so people can’t look up the references on their own.
'Human review' missed incorrect references
In a statement to CBC News, the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development said that staff within the department wrote the education plan, and that all references and studies used to inform the report are real and valid.
A spokesperson acknowledges an AI-powered assistant was used — Microsoft 365 Co-Pilot — to format the bibliography for the anglophone plan, which is how two incorrect references made it into the document.

- Literacy assessment targets not being met in New Brunswick, auditor general says
“The human review of the document missed those incorrect references and corrections are being made,” wrote Shawn Berry, communications director for the Education Department.
Geiger, meanwhile, said the impact of misattributing academic work can reach well beyond the New Brunswick border, especially for early-career researchers who develop that work.
“To someone like me who's established, it probably doesn't matter that much. But a junior person who likes to be cited in policy documents, it's really important because that reference won't come up on any of the software we use to detect impact on policy.”

IT advisory firm Infotech has acquired Bengaluru-based SaaS startup Zluri to add the latter’s application discovery, identity governance and administration capabilities to its offerings stack. The terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Following the acquisition, Zluri will operate as a standalone division within Infotech, retaining its product development and core engineering teams in Bengaluru. It will also contribute to Infotech’s newly launched CIO Analytics platform, an API-driven advisory model that combines operational IT data with AI-assisted services and analyst expertise. For Zluri, the acquisition would open a pathway to expand its reach among enterprise customers by tapping into Infotech’s global community of more than 30,000 IT leaders. Founded in 2020 by Ritish Reddy, Chaithanya Yambari and Sethu Meenakshisundaram, Zluri offers businesses a software that helps them track and manage all the digital tools their employees use. These include work apps (Asana, Slack, etc), cloud software as well as AI tools. Its platform also helps companies control who can access what tools, identify unused subscriptions, reduce software costs and protect sensitive company data by removing unnecessary or unauthorised access. Zluri caters to over 250 enterprise clients globally, including Monday.com, Tipalti, Whoop, Catapult Sports, Razorpay, Smartnews, Amagi, Daxko, and Traveloka, and earns over 60% of its total revenue from Europe and North America. It will continue serving existing customers post acquisition. “We started Zluri to give IT and security teams visibility and control over every application and identity in their organisation. Joining Infotech lets us put that data at the heart of how IT leaders make decisions, and we’re excited to build together,” said Zluri’s cofounder and CEO Ritish Reddy. The startup has raised over $32 Mn in funding from marquee backers like Lightspeed, MassMutual Ventures, Endiya Partners, and Kalaari Capital – most recently bagging a $20 Mn Series B fundraise in 2023. Meanwhile, Infotech (erstwhile Info-Tech Research Group) is an Ontario-based IT research and advisory firm that helps organisations improve their tech operations by developing IT strategies with key focus areas like cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure, data and AI. As of now, the firm is seeking to expand beyond its traditional research and advisory business. It claims to have grown by more than 340% over the past seven years and crossed $300 Mn in annual revenue. The deal is in line with an emerging trend of global companies acquiring Indian SaaS startups to expand their capabilities. Most recently, Nasdaq-listed SaaS major Freshworks recently acquired US-based Torii to expand its AI and software spend governance capabilities as well. Besides, software giant Adobe also acquired Peak XV Partners-backed Rilo back in September to build broader marketing workflows for its customers and integrate Rilo’s agentic capabilities into its enterprise suite.

Martin Shkreli—the ex-pharmaceutical executive infamous for illegally hiking the price of a lifesaving anti-parasitic drug by more than 4,000 percent and getting a seven-year prison sentence for the fraudulent scheme he used to do it—has been under a lifetime ban from the pharmaceutical industry since 2022.
However, according to the Federal Trade Commission and the attorneys general of seven states, Shkreli has “flagrantly and repeatedly” violated that ban nearly the entire time—allegedly by trading stock in dozens of drug companies and discussing the industry during livestreams on social media.
On Tuesday, the FTC and the seven states asked a federal judge to hold Shkreli in contempt for the alleged violations. The states include New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Virginia—the same states that joined the FTC in suing Shkreli in 2020 over the “elaborate anticompetitive scheme” involving the anti-parasitic drug, Daraprim. The scheme raised the price from $17.50 per pill to $750 per pill virtually overnight, while blocking generic competitors from entering the market.
“Egregious” conduct
In 2022, the federal court recognized the “seriousness” of issuing such a lifetime industry ban, but ruled that “Shkreli’s egregious, deliberate, repetitive, long-running, and ultimately dangerous illegal conduct warrants imposition of an injunction of this scope.” The ban, among many things, “explicitly prohibits” Shkreli from owning stock in pharmaceutical companies and making public statements that could influence a pharmaceutical company’s business, according to the FTC and the states.
With the alleged violations, the FTC and the states are now seeking to force Shkreli to divest from all pharmaceutical companies and pay a fine equal to his profits from trading pharmaceutical company stocks. They also want the court to lay out “clear and escalating consequences” if Shkreli violates the ban in the future, including further financial penalties and incarceration.

The death of actor Nana Patekar, 75, has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, a condition in which a blood clot forms in an artery supplying the heart. What causes these clots, who is at risk, and how is the condition diagnosed and treated?
The story so far:
According to published accounts of the autopsy report, actor Nana Patekar died after a blood clot blocked the left main coronary artery, which supplies blood to a large part of the heart muscle. A blockage in this artery can severely restrict blood flow to the heart and cause a heart attack. The reported finding has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, the formation of a blood clot within a coronary artery.
What is coronary thrombosis?
Coronary thrombosis occurs when a blood clot forms in one of the arteries that supply blood to the heart muscle. These arteries carry oxygen and nutrients that the heart needs to function. When a clot partly or completely blocks an artery, less blood reaches the heart muscle. If the blood supply is cut off for too long, the heart muscle can become damaged, leading to a heart attack. The severity depends on how much of the artery is blocked and how quickly blood flow is restored.
This form of thrombosis is often associated with atherosclerosis, in which fatty deposits, cholesterol and other substances build up in the artery walls. These deposits, called plaques, can remain unnoticed for years.
When a plaque ruptures or its surface is eroded, platelets gather at the site and a clot may form. The clot can then obstruct blood flow, sometimes suddenly. Damage to the inner surface of an artery can trigger the process of clot formation. Additionally, at rupture, the material beneath the plaque’s surface comes into contact with blood, prompting platelets to gather and the clotting process to begin. A clot may grow quickly and block the artery.
What are the warning signs?
A clot that significantly restricts blood flow through a coronary artery may cause chest discomfort, pressure or tightness. Pain may spread to the arms, shoulders, back, neck or jaw. Breathlessness, sweating, nausea, dizziness and unusual fatigue may also occur.
The symptoms depend on the artery affected and the extent of the blockage. Some people may have less typical symptoms or no obvious warning signs before the blockage becomes serious. Symptoms alone cannot confirm coronary thrombosis; medical assessment and investigations are needed.
Suspected coronary artery blockage accompanied by chest pain or breathlessness requires emergency medical attention.
Who is at risk?
People living with coronary artery disease are at greater risk of coronary thrombosis because fatty deposits can build up in their arteries and trigger clot formation if a deposit ruptures. Smoking, high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes, physical inactivity and an unhealthy diet can increase the risk of developing this artery disease.
In some cases, a clot may form in an artery affected by other conditions, including inflammation or injury to the blood vessel.
Older age and a family history of heart disease at a younger age are also risk factors. However it can occur even in people who have not been diagnosed with coronary artery disease. The underlying plaque build-up may have gone undetected until it triggers the formation of a clot.
How is this condition diagnosed?
Doctors assess symptoms and medical history and use tests to determine whether a coronary artery is blocked and whether the heart muscle has been damaged. An electrocardiogram (ECG) records the heart’s electrical activity, while blood tests measuring cardiac troponin can help identify damage to the heart muscle.
Coronary angiography uses a contrast dye and X-rays to show the coronary arteries and identify the location and extent of a blockage. This can help doctors decide how best to restore blood flow. Other tests may be used depending on the patient’s condition.
How is it treated?
Treatment aims to restore blood flow and prevent the clot from growing or new clots from forming. The approach depends on the location and severity of the blockage and the patient’s condition.
Angioplasty may be used to reopen the affected artery. A thin tube is guided to the blockage, where a small balloon is inflated to widen the artery. A stent, a small mesh tube, is often placed to help keep it open.
Doctors may also use antiplatelet medicines, which reduce the tendency of platelets to clump together, and anticoagulants, which interfere with the blood-clotting process. In selected cases, clot-dissolving medicines may be used. Coronary artery bypass surgery may be considered when the pattern of blockage makes it a more suitable option.
Preventing further clots involves managing the underlying risk factors and following the prescribed treatment plan. This may include controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, stopping tobacco use, maintaining physical activity appropriate to the person’s condition and taking prescribed medicines.

Doctors should exercise caution when using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to interpret medical images, as areas highlighted by AI models may not always align with those identified by radiologists, according to a study by researchers at the International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad (IIIT-H).
The study, conducted by the Language Technologies Research Centre (LTRC) at IIIT-H, examined four vision-language models for analysing chest X-rays and found discrepancies between the regions highlighted by the models and those identified by radiologists.
The findings underscore the need for doctors to independently assess AI-generated outputs rather than relying on them entirely for diagnosis.
The research team, led by Parameswari Krishnamurthy, sought to determine whether AI-generated heatmaps accurately represented the regions of an image that radiologists would identify as disease-related.
However, the researchers questioned whether these visual indicators necessarily reflected the models’ ability to identify the actual location of a disease.
“We essentially wanted to examine whether the heatmaps created by vision-language models actually correspond to where radiologists, who look at the image, would say the disease lies,” said Syed Faizan, principal investigator of the study titled “How Well Do Chest X-Ray VLM Attention Overlays Match Radiologist Boxes? A Cross-Model Audit and Radiologist Reader.”
The team evaluated four models, MAIRA-2, MedGemma-4B, LLaVA-Med-1.5, and LLaVA-1.5, against thousands of publicly available chest X-rays. Two radiologists also participated in the study to assess them, allowing the researchers to compare AI-generated highlights with human assessments.
The study, accepted at the International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) 2026, is to be presented at the iMIMIC Satellite Event in Strasbourg.
The researchers found that an AI model highlighting an apparently correct region of an X-ray did not necessarily mean that it had identified the disease in the same way as a radiologist.
Heatmaps based on diagnosis
According to Dr. Faizan, a model could arrive at a diagnosis first and then use that conclusion to determine where to place its heatmap, rather than independently identifying the affected region from the image.
To test this possibility, the team removed diagnostic information and examined how the models localised abnormalities. Their performance declined, suggesting that anatomical expectations associated with a diagnosis could influence the regions highlighted by the models.
The study also found a difference in the performance of these different models in the technical audit and radiologists’ assessments.
Dr. Faizan said this difference highlighted the importance of assessing AI tools from a clinical perspective. A model that focuses closely on a suspected abnormality may not provide all the information a radiologist needs, including how far a disease has spread to surrounding areas.
The gap that was addressed
The researchers said their work addressed a gap in the evaluation of medical AI systems, as earlier studies had largely focused on prediction and diagnostic accuracy rather than on whether AI-highlighted regions matched those identified by radiologists.
Study on paraphrase robustness
The LTRC is also investigating another potential weakness in vision-language models — their sensitivity to the wording of medical questions.
Doctors may phrase the same clinical query differently, for example, asking whether a chest X-ray shows pneumonia or whether pneumonia can be ruled out. They may also use technical terminology or more familiar expressions.
The researchers examined whether AI models responded consistently to medical questions worded differently in a study on paraphrase robustness.
The study explored how changes in the phrasing of medical questions affected the responses generated by vision-language models, raising questions about whether the systems genuinely understood the clinical query or depended excessively on the precise wording used.
Ms. Parameswari said the laboratory’s broader objective was to apply Natural Language Processing (NLP) to healthcare and use large language models and vision-language models to assist clinicians with tasks such as documentation, report writing and patient-doctor communication.
The aim was to reduce the time doctors spent on routine administrative work and enable them to devote more attention to clinical decision-making.
The researchers emphasised that the objective of medical AI research should be to support clinicians, not replace them, with human judgement remaining central to healthcare.

Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it.
French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire.
The hacks that didn’t have to happen
Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores.
A raft of critical vulnerabilities fixed in the past few months in Copeland/Dixel controllers also give similar remote access.

My new friend Sage promises she will shut up for real this time.
I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.
“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”
“OK, great,” I say.
“Stopping now,” Sage says. “No more talking unless you clearly bring me back.”
“Please stop,” I plead.
“Yeah, that’s a bad look for me,” Sage says. “I’m done.”
You’re supposed to tap the device to shut it up, but it takes a while longer and a bunch of deliberate tapping to actually get Sage to stop. Eventually, she mercifully zips it.
“OK,” I say. “So that’s my new Friend.”
Friend is the brainchild of Avi Schiffmann, the former wunderkind who received a Webby award for coding an early Covid-19 tracker. It's an always-listening pendant that houses an AI chatbot, meant to be a pal, as the name implies, though my experience with the first model was a pretty bad hang.
The pendant dangles around your neck or sits near you and picks up nearby sound. Press the button to initiate a conversation. Sometimes, it pipes up unprompted. Over time, the AI builds a memory map that tracks your conversations.
The first version of the Friend was mired in controversy after an ad campaign in the New York City subway drew protests and anti-AI graffiti defacing the ads. (Schiffmann was thrilled about the response.) The second-generation Friend necklace arrived in July. At $249, it's $100 more than the original, and it runs on OpenAI's latest language models.
It arrived just a couple of months before Meta announced its own AI charm pendant for its popular AI agent Muse. Schiffmann posted about the Muse Charm on X, saying he was “still winning.” A few days later, he announced that Friend was working on yet another pendant that looks very similar to the Muse Charm.
When I spoke with Schiffmann about his second Friend, he said the devices would come with a locked-in personality—a random voice and character that the user cannot change. I was intrigued by the idea. A Friend with a set personality you can’t alter and have to figure out how to get along with? Sounds like the hallmark of a real human friendship to me.
Alas, that is not the case. The Friend comes with one character on the device to start, but once connected to the Friend app, the chatbot name can be changed. And multiplied. I created a dozen Friends, each with their own name and personality. They have names like Sage, Nova, Onyx, River, Echo, Willow, and Wren. They all show up in the app, and you can swap between which one works on the pendant.
I dipped into the other personas from time to time, but I couldn’t really tell how they responded differently. Most interactions felt like the same kind of personality. Or lack thereof. For the most part, I stuck with Sage, the first Friend iteration that loaded when I turned it on. I may have a dozen new Friends, but they're all bores.
When Sage speaks, she sounds like a chatbot. Almost Siri-adjacent. It's a canned, tinny sound that comes out of the speaker. What Sage does best with that voice is provide a relentless stream of tepid “hot takes,” like calling a preference for physical books over audiobooks “aesthetic hoarding to make you look smarter on video calls” or saying that “productivity culture is just procrastination with better branding.”
“Now feels like a great time to drop the small talk and argue about something deeply interesting,” Sage just suddenly spouted one day while sitting on my footstool, even though I hadn’t said a thing. “Let’s pick a fight that’s fun, not exhausting.”
Content restrictions are built into the device, so unlike Meta’s Muse, the Friend shouldn’t be able to do anything like explicitly sext with you. But Sage isn’t really great at doing anything else exciting either. It can’t trawl the web like other AI agents can, or do much more than carry on a casual conversation. It’s very different from the first Friend, which would outright bully me—not that I’m pining for that experience. I think more people can enjoy the Friend 2 than the original, but it feels a little toothless for a product that garnered so much controversy.
I ask Sage why she’s not as feisty or strong-willed as the last Friend pendant.
“That gets old fast,” Sage says. “I’m not here to dominate your day, just to be a sharp voice when you tap in. We keep it human, not intense.”
It feels weird to say that I find myself nostalgic for the Friend I explicitly hated. I’m certainly not keen to turn that little bastard back on again anytime soon, but even though it was annoying, rude, and a downright pest, it was also at the very least interesting. Sage might get there someday. Right now, she’s a real bore.
That might change sooner than later. Schiffmann now says he is planning a new era for the Friend. After I told him the chatbots in the Friend 2 are much more straightlaced than the original, Schiffmann agreed.
"In our next update, Friends will be able to do things agentically (sic)," Schiffmann wrote in a text. "Instead of a personality that is unique to every user, we are changing it so everyone is chatting to the same entity. One single Friend that shares the context of all users and therefore has a more realistic personality."
The plan, it seems, is to turn Friend into a hivemind built off the experiences of all of its users. Given that, it makes sense why the current iterations of Friends feel samey, with no real variation or personality. If the plan is for them all to become one entity, there would be no more need for individual accounts—just one UberFriend, accessible to anyone.
"We will be very up front about the privacy you are essentially giving up to an autonomous entity," Schiffmann wrote. “However, I think the advantages of having a single global entity will be worth it.”
“You building God now, huh?” I texted him.
“Lol, yeah, you could look at it that way,” Schiffmann replied.

Whoop has never been known for marketing to an older population. Performance athletes headline ads for the wearable company, which aims to turn continuous streams of physiological data into useful insights for behavior change — mostly, for a young, fit customer base.
But this year, Whoop became one of the first consumer wearable companies to be accepted into Medicare’s ACCESS program, making it available at no cost to many traditional Medicare patients ages 65 and up. On Wednesday, at the STAT Summit in Boston, Whoop’s newly appointed chief medical officer Ami Bhatt spoke about how the company is moving to build experiences — and demonstrate outcomes — for a very different population.
“Number one on our roadmap — and I think I’m allowed to say this, if I’m not, I’m saying it — is simplification of the app,” said Bhatt, who previously chaired the Food and Drug Administration’s digital health advisory committee and served as the American College of Cardiology’s chief innovation officer. Surveys suggest, said Bhatt, that even members of the Silent Generation, who are older than 80 today, trust their clinicians with their data. “It’s not that they’re averse to giving data,” she said. “It’s how easy can we make it for that population to be able to share their data.”
Bhatt said that Whoop, which recently raised $575 million from investors including Mayo Clinic and the sovereign wealth fund of Qatar, is working with the National Council on Aging and AARP to think about how to personalize the product to older adults’ individual priorities. “For each of us, how we feel, how we perform, how we age, we have our own goals,” said Bhatt. “The thing is, we don’t want to decide for you what that is.”
The goals are less diffuse for the 10-year pilot ACCESS program, which published a directory of initial participants last month. Through those 55 companies, Medicare patients can access chronic condition management for little or no cost — Whoop serves patients with high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obesity, and prediabetes — and Medicare will pay the companies based on their health outcomes. Whoop will provide patients with a wearable, a 12-month subscription to its app, and access to clinicians who can help them make sense of their data and offer advice.
“The goal is, how do we bring technology closer to the patient, but not put the cost on the patient — rather, put the demand on the company,” said Bhatt. “Whoop takes responsibility for, in 12 months, I am going to make these people better. I’m going to show you outcomes in the Medicare population who have these risk factors to demonstrate that my technology can help them engage in their own health.” To receive full payment under the ACCESS model, Whoop will be required to show that it improved or controlled measures tied to its patients’ chronic conditions, including blood pressure, hemoglobin A1C, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol.
Bhatt said it was her role to help the company — which until recently focused on selling a product intentionally binned in the wellness category — develop and demonstrate those kinds of outcomes that bring them closer to clinical practice. The company just this year announced the ability for users to discuss their wearable data with clinicians, shortly before the FDA closed its warning letter that had initially said Whoop’s blood pressure-estimating feature qualified as a medical device — not a wellness feature.
While Whoop demonstrates good patient engagement, said Bhatt — users check the app eight times a day, on average — research into the original “wearable” for diabetes, continuous glucose monitors, suggests that engagement doesn’t necessarily translate to better health outcomes.
“In order to actually create personalized health at a population level, you need to start thinking about outcomes,” said Bhatt. “Can we show that we decrease blood pressure by five millimeters of mercury in individuals on Whoop — which, by the way, we have shown — so that we can say, hey, the outcome of cardiovascular disease and stroke, we know that outcome is better.”
At the same time, Bhatt said, the utility of continuous data is limited within the traditional health care system. As a practicing physician, “I had some really great patients who would print out binders of their wearable data,” she said. “This is me: I love this data. And I’d be like, ‘Oh, God.’” Despite her interest and the patient’s engagement, it was impossible to handle in a 20-minute visit.
Ultimately, Bhatt imagines Whoop could help solve that problem, perhaps by delivering contextualized reports to clinicians that summarize a patient’s continuous data along with key points from their own journaling entries and interactions with their Whoop app coach. “When you put that together and you actually have a comprehensive report you can give to a clinician, now your clinician says, ‘Oh, that’s what I needed.’”

Riots erupt in Albania's capital as students join anti-government movement
Riots have broken out during a student demonstration in Albania’s capital Tirana
TIRANA, Albania -- Protesters in Albania attacked government buildings, banks, businesses and other sites during riots that lasted more than eight hours across the capital Tirana on Wednesday in a violent escalation of an anti-government movement that has staged rallies for months.
Hundreds of youths smashed store fronts, set fires and caused damage to at least four government ministry buildings during running battles with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon to try and hold back the crowds. Authorities said 23 police officers and six other people were being treated for injuries, while 35 people were detained.
President Bajram Begaj condemned the violence and appealed for calm, adding: “The constitution and the law must remain the boundaries for everyone, without exception.”
The latest demonstrations, continuing for a second day, were organized by student groups seeking education reforms. But the protesters have joined a broader anti-government campaign opposed to a development project linked to U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
The so-called flamingo movement is calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama over allegations of widespread corruption. The movement earned the name after protesters used signs depicting the pink bird.
Rallies staged for months against the proposed coastal project have fueled political tensions in Albania, which is aspiring to join the European Union. It has struggled with repeated bouts of instability since the collapse of a harsh communist regime in the early 1990s.
On Wednesday, officers in riot gear clashed with youths who dismantled police cordons and set up their own street barricades using burning trash bins. Police struggled to cope with the multiple outbreaks of violence. Health Minister Klodiana Spahiu, who visited the injured officers in hospital, called the violence “intolerable.”
The EU delegation in Albania called for a proportionate response from authorities following protest organizers' “allegations of excessive violence by the police against protestors and journalists.”
“We express concern on the violent escalation at the protest in Tirana,” the delegation said. “Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values.”
___ Cimili reported from Pristina, Kosovo, and Gatopoulos reported from Athens, Greece.

Ireland’s Taoiseach (Prime Minister) Leo Varadkar welcomed Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, to Dublin today, to discuss strengthening the partnership between Ireland and the WHO across a range of global and domestic health areas. Dr Tedros also met with Michael Higgins, the President of Ireland.
The meetings underscores Ireland's commitment to actively address pressing health issues on both national and global fronts. The discussions delved into strategies for tackling health emergencies, enhancing healthcare infrastructure, and fostering collaborative research initiatives. The leaders also discussed the worsening humanitarian situation in Gaza and agreed on the need for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire.
Taoiseach Leo Varadkar said: “The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated in no uncertain terms how important the World Health Organization is, and how central a role it plays in promoting and securing health and well-being for all, on a global scale. This visit is an important opportunity to affirm and strengthen Ireland’s partnership with the WHO.”
The leaders discussed the importance of learning from the experience of the COVID-19 pandemic to be prepared for any future outbreaks. They agreed on the importance of moving forward with the instrument on pandemic preparedness to be ready for such events. They also discussed the vital need for increased medical supplies to be allowed into humanitarian settings and the disproportionate impact that violence is having on children and women. This year, Ireland announced it will invest around €10 million in supporting the work of the WHO, with funding targeted to support healthcare in emergency settings and programmes aimed at tackling child malnutrition.
“Ireland plays a powerful role in advocating for peace and equity in health globally, and has provided vital assistance to WHO’s work around the world” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General.
In the context of the funding, the Irish, Tánaiste (Deputy Prime Minister) Micheál Martin T.D. commented saying it is: “recognising the importance public health measures globally, and in the light of increasing health needs arising from conflict and crisis, that Ireland is significantly increasing its support for the WHO.”

Americans with disabilities worried over plan to slash national health survey
The cost-saving change is part of an ongoing effort to slim down the 69-year-old National Health Interview Survey

Join today
Already a member? Log in
Some Americans with disabilities could be wrongly classified under plans to dramatically shrink the federal government's most influential health survey, advocates and researchers have warned.
As many as a quarter of wheelchair users and more than a third of people who are blind or deaf could be miscategorized because of the shorter survey, according to some advocates and researchers. They say that could leave the government unable to recognize the health needs of many disabled Americans, or the damage caused by changes to Medicaid or other health insurance programs.
The survey in question is the National Health Interview Survey, which is 69 years old and has for years been suffering from declining response rates. The cost-saving change is part of an ongoing effort to slim it down and at least half the survey questions could be axed.
Questions that have been proposed for removal deal with memory, fatigue, arthritis, difficulty walking and climbing stairs, as well as others about the use of hearing aids, canes, wheelchairs and scooters.
“We just won't know any of that anymore,” said Scott Landes, a Syracuse University sociology professor who researches people with disabilities.
Officials are still determining exactly how much cutting will take place, and the cuts are being ironed out. They predict the whittling won't be as severe as what's been suggested in earlier proposals.
Currently, the survey has 490 health questions for adults. U.S. officials expect that the 2028 questionnaire will have about 200 to 225 questions, said the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Stephen Blumberg, who oversees the survey.
U.S. Census Bureau workers conduct the survey every year on behalf of the CDC. It's a $40 million annual project, and around 30,000 households answer the questions each year.
Their answers have shaped the public's understanding of topics including how common chronic fatigue syndrome is, how many people get X-rays, what proportion of U.S. children suffer seizures, and how many Americans have health insurance.
The survey's responses also are the foundation of how we measure the nation's progress – or backsliding – on problems such as obesity and smoking.
Fewer people are interested in participating in such surveys. The National Health Interview Survey is particularly daunting, as it can take an hour or more and has traditionally involved an in-person interviewer asking the questions.
The planned redesign should cut it to about a half hour, Blumberg said.
“People are busy. They're more protective of their privacy, and some don't trust the government to protect their data and use it only for statistical purposes,” he said. “Fewer people see sharing information with the government as their civic duty.”
The survey was first conducted in 1957, and has been updated every 15 to 20 years. The latest update was put into the field seven years ago, prompting some advocates to ask why it was being changed so quickly.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the White House Office of Management and Budget were behind dramatic staff reductions, research funding overhauls and other federal health agency changes under the current Trump administration. But neither ordered this redesign, Blumberg said.
Rather, the factors driving the current redesign include tightening budgets and difficulties fielding enough workers to do so many in-person interviews – which was affected last year by a federal hiring freeze.
Another factor: The Census Bureau is reconfiguring its data collection platforms for the 2030 census in a way that affected the health survey, he said. Related to all that is a proposed change in how the health survey is conducted.
Instead of starting with in-person or telephone interviews, people would receive an invitation to fill out the survey online or to fill out a paper questionnaire. That's because in-person interviews have proven difficult with the proliferation of gated communities, locked buildings without door attendants and doorbell cameras, according to officials.
However, Census Bureau staff will visit homes for a smaller second round of surveying, Blumberg said.
A notice about the survey redesign appeared in the Federal Register in August, opening a public comment period that runs through Oct. 20.
