Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands.
With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation.
A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated.
It is understood that the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands.
An oil project known as Sea Lion in the north Falklands basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors.
In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood.
Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.”
She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”
It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character.
Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.
The intensity of the Argentinian menace relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.
Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation.
Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project.
A draft national sovereignty introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers.
The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.
Workers in the oil and fisheries sectors on the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – are understood to be concerned that they could be targeted should they travel, particularly to South America where there is support for Buenos Aires’s sovereignty claim.
In a tandem move to kill off Sea Lion, Argentina is expected within 24 hours to escalate further its dispute with the UK by requesting arbitration under annexe VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (Unclos) over the oil project.
On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline to stop the project or face such a legal action. The deadline passed on Monday and Argentinian newspapers said an application for arbitration would follow.
Under it, Buenos Aires will claim that the UK is in breach of a UN resolution inviting the parties to negotiate over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from “unilateral modifications” to the situation. It will be seeking a binding ruling that the UK must stop the drilling. However, UK government sources are confident that Unclos will not wade into a sovereignty dispute.
At a public meeting on Monday evening, one of the Falkland Islands’ assembly members, Dean Dent, told constituents that the UK government was working hard on a tough response to the Argentinian Unclos threat.
“The UK government has assembled quite an in-depth team of legal advisers, KCs – that is the first step,” he said. “There have been four recent similar cases where a case of sovereignty has been taken to Unclos and all four were disregarded by the tribunal as all four cases were a sovereignty issue, not a maritime issue.”
The UK government is expected to be increasingly muscular in its approach to Argentina in the coming days. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Monday that he had raised the issue and “the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British” with the US president, Donald Trump.

These workers help train robots who could one day steal their jobs
KARUR, India — Three men stride across a cavernous textile factory floor of Texworth in the southern Indian city of Karur, handing GoPros and smart glasses to workers, including 40-year-old Shoba Kirubakaran. She's packing yellow aprons decorated with chickens into plastic wrapping for the brand Designs By Danica. It's the third time Kirubakaran says she's been told to don a GoPro.
It's recording her every hand gesture, to train AI robots to take over this job — a fact that she says the company did not share with her. NPR informed her when they interviewed her on a recent day. "Nobody told me anything about it," she says.
Kirubakaran has worked in the factory for 10 years, six days a week, from around 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. She makes $90 a month. With that money, she's helped her husband, a rickshaw driver, raise their two sons. And she adds, "I only know how to do this job."
Scenes like these shook the Indian public in April after a video went viral showing rows of textile factory workers wearing these headsets. "This is not a scene from a science fiction film," warned one news anchor from outlet News9Live. "That is happening right now on factory floors across India." Another outlet, AsiaNet News warned: "Indian workers are training AI robots to take their jobs."
Seeking "egocentric data"
India is emerging as one key place to record this kind of footage because of its large population, relatively low wages and relative openness to new tech. And developers need millions of hours of this footage, what the industry calls egocentric data — data gathered from the perspective of a human with a camera to train AI robots.
"That can be obtained only by emulating or collecting data from real human beings that does the job," says Prathosh A.P., a professor at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. Like many other Indians, he uses initials to refer to his family name. "Think of today's AIs as brains without a body," he says. "Now you have to give them all motor skills ... to do all kinds of intricate motions that we do using a physical body."
Some workers are signing up because they're paid by the hour for the data. But it appears many others, like Kirubakaran, are simply made to record herself working without any explanation. "Call it what it is, which is exploitation of labor," says Astha Kapoor, co-founder of the Aapti Institute, which studies the impact of technology on people.
What will the impact be for India's workforce — the world's second largest, with 600 million people working or seeking work? "Training workers, retraining workers, absorbing them into new occupations," says Amit Basole, economics professor at Azim Premji University. "Do we have the policy agility to do that? I doubt it."
The power question
But that vision of a future full of factory and domestic robots isn't exactly around the corner, say some experts. AI robots are unlikely to be deployed at scale in India — in the near future at least — because they cost a lot of money and consume a lot of power, which is both unreliable and costly across parts of India. "We may be able to make the robots, but they're bloody expensive to run, right?" says Kapoor of the Aapti Institute. "Humans are cheaper to run than robots."
That power crisis is evident even in Karur, where an Indian tech company, Objectways, gathers egocentric data to sell onto AI developers. Massive generators loudly rumble to ensure seamless electricity in the buildings it powers. The company appears to be one of the town's biggest white-collar employers, occupying at least four building blocks in the town.
The CEO, Ravi Shankar, is a Karur native who migrated to Arizona decades ago. He's in perhaps unlikely agreement with Kapoor about the deployment of AI robots in India. "I think it will be more expensive," he says of AI robots, in comparison to human labor. "I don't think it's going to be cheaper."
He says his Indian clients want help designing AI robots for jobs that they can't find people to do, like tapping rubber from rubber trees; jobs that are geographically isolated, like dusting off solar panels in rural areas, and jobs that are physically grueling, like destemming chiles for processing.
Inside Objectways, employee Rajeshkumar Ramaswamy shows us how they are training other robots to do repetitive industrial jobs for foreign clients, through what he calls collecting exocentric data — that's data collected from the point of view of a robot. Instead of filming hands of actual workers, young men with GoPro cameras strapped to their heads record themselves doing jobs while holding and manipulating what look like grippy robot claws. One man records himself using the claws to screw bottle lids off and on.
There are dozens of bottles — big, small, plastic, metallic. Ramaswamy says it's to teach robots how to identify all the different shapes and sizes of this thing called a water bottle. The "robot needs to learn what is [a] water bottle," he says.
Ramaswamy says they'll repeat this process of screwing bottle tops about 100 times and feed that data into an AI robot, so it can see for itself how to use its own grippy hands to do the job.
"The robot is like a child," Ramaswamy says. "We are the humans. We are teaching the robots what needs to be done."
The company also trains robots to do household tasks — like folding towels, putting away books and unpacking bags. It sells that data to AI companies hoping to create domestic robots — there's already a few on the market, including one prominent model that looks like a faceless servant and retails for $20,000.
Working in a fake kitchen
Up a few flights of stairs, Ramaswamy shows us where they have humans recording themselves doing domestic jobs, on a floor kitted out to look like an Ikea-style three-bedroom house. In a fake kitchen, a woman, Rani N., records herself chopping onions.
Most clients who want first-person recordings of domestic chores are in the U.S., so Ramaswamy says they also pay Americans to record themselves doing housework — so their clients can train AI robots on American-specific data.
For instance, in India, many folks use stainless steel plates to eat. A robot trained to pick up a stainless steel plate could use a lot of pressure to grip it, and could drop it — no harm done. But if the same robot tried to pick up a ceramic plate, which is what many Americans use, the same pressure would cause it to "be separated into minute particles," Ramaswamy says — that is, smashed to bits.
And to amass recordings of humans doing work with their hands for clients who request ecocentric data, Ramaswamy says, they pay hundreds of people across India to undertake domestic jobs, like Sneha Jegadish, a 24-year-old who lives on the edge of town.
Jegadish clipped her smart phone to a headset and began chopping a carrot, her phone recording her every hand movement.
She records herself doing housework for a few hours a day, for about $2.60 an hour, and makes around $120 a month. Jegadish folds clothes, wipes the floor, does the dishes — jobs she was never expected to do growing up, because her mother wanted her to focus on her studies. So when she got this gig a few months ago, "my mother had to show me how to do those jobs," she smiles.
Money or not, it's still drudgery, says Jegadish. One day, she hopes, she'll have a robot to do her housework. "The work we are doing now is going to be done by robots in the future," she says.
That's the same conclusion that 42-year-old textile worker Kannagi Periyasaamy has come to.
At the textile factory, Periyasaamy was folding and packing aprons with a GoPro fastened to her head.
She's one of the few workers who is paid about $2.60 an hour to record herself, and she's been told why. She explains: "We are training them [the robots] on how to package the aprons, how to do a quality check, how to fold the aprons."
Periyasaamy says she's been doing this for the past three months, enough for her to be convinced that someday, a robot will take over her job. When that day comes, she says, "I'm thinking about taking up farming" — the family owns a scrap of land where she could raise cattle. Meanwhile, Periyasaamy thinks of AI robots as her students and says, "I'm proud I can teach it to do a good job."

STAT Summit, Day 1
The first day of the STAT Summit did not disappoint. We had biotech’s biggest stars, the perils and promise of AI, and moving anecdotes from patients. Here are a few snippets of the day’s action.
- FDA heads sound off: In this extremely juicy panel, former Food and Drug Administration commissioners offered sharp criticisms of the current health regime and candid reflections about their own time at the helm. No agency was spared. As Rob Califf opined, “DOGE will go down as one of the biggest disasters in American history.” Read more from STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo.
- Whoop! (There it is): Whoop built its reputation as a wearable company mainly used by young, fit consumers. That may soon change. Whoop’s newly appointed Chief Medical Officer Ami Bhatt spoke about the company’s recent acceptance into Medicare’s ACCESS program, which would make their wearables available at no cost to many traditional Medicare patients ages 65 and up. What else did Bhatt say about AI and wearables? Read more from STAT’s Katie Palmer.
Ovaries don’t go gentle into that postmenopausal night
Ovaries stop having a clear function relatively early on in life. For decades, women carry around an obsolescing organ — but is nothing truly all ovaries do after menopause? New research from Northwestern University suggests the answer is no. In a study of healthy ovaries from 28 women aged 50 to close to 80, published on Wednesday in Aging Cell, researchers found that there were hundreds of proteins in the ovaries evolving in the decades after menopause.
“It wasn’t that there was just a cluster of proteins that are being turned on and they’re staying constant; we actually saw quite dynamic changes that were happening across this period of time,” said Francesca Duncan, a professor in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the study’s corresponding author. As they age, the ovaries’ tissue changes, showing increased inflammation as well as higher concentration of proteins associated with ovarian cancer. This doesn’t mean all aging ovaries will develop ovarian cancer, though it does raise the potential question “of whether or not at a certain point it actually could be beneficial to take your ovaries out,” said Duncan.
40%
Forty percent of high school students in the United States reported binge eating in the last month, according to a new government survey.
It’s the first time the biennial survey, conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, has asked about binge eating, and the first data on disordered eating collected by the Youth Risk Behavior Survey in a decade. The high rates were striking, especially among young people of color.
Digging into the crosstabs, the survey found that binge eating was more prevalent among female than male students (19% versus 16%). It was also more common among Black (19%), Hispanic (20%), and multiracial (20%) students compared to white (15%) and Middle Eastern or North African students (10%).
Read more from STAT’s Sarah Todd about this striking survey.
The maddening journey to not to share patient data with Epic
Alex Rosenblat had a goal: stop her Ohio hospital from sharing her health data with Epic’s gigantic health network.
But when she logged into her MyChart account, there was no button to easily opt out. The simple-seeming request turned into an arduous task that would require scores of emails, multiple phone calls with Epic employees, a flight to Las Vegas, and a software update.
That was just one of three months-long journeys Rosenblat embarked on last year to keep her hospital from sharing her personal health data with outside vendors. Read on to find out why the researcher and reporter had to call a notary.
Kenya reports second Ebola case
Another person has fallen ill with Ebola in Kenya. The 39-year-old man is a relative of the country’s first case and had already been in quarantine when symptoms appeared, according to Kenya’s Ministry of Health.
A World Health Organization official said Wednesday that despite the two cases, there was no evidence of an Ebola outbreak in Kenya. The initial patient — a Kenyan citizen — caught the deadly virus while living in Congo and died earlier this month. The Kenyan Ministry of Health identified 128 people who had been in contact with this patient; 108 are in quarantine, 5 have left Kenya, and 15 have not been tracked down. Tracing the second patient’s contacts has now begun.
The situation in Congo is still quite dire. Authorities have confirmed more than 4,000 deaths and 9,000 cases as officials have struggled to contain one the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record.

Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
- Published
Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary.
The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988.
Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election.
Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.
Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it.
The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one.
Flávio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote.
Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers want to see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it."
The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters.
Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment.
Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers.
"It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media.
Critics of the measure have warned that it will raise production costs, which will eventually be passed on to the consumer, resulting in higher prices.
But its supporters argue that having two days off a week will allow workers to be better rested and therefore more productive in the hours that they do work.
The change is due to be phased in, with the working week first being shortened to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and then again to 40 hours at a later stage.
The changes will take more than a year to entirely take effect but many of its backers are already celebrating.
Luciana de Almeida, 36, who works six days a week as a cashier in a supermarket, said it would "make a lot of difference" to her life.
The single mother, who lives in Rio de Janeiro, said she has been missing out on time with her three children as the only day off she had was usually spent doing domestic chores.
"My body, and my mind in particular, are very tired," she told BBC Brasil.
"I need time with my daughters, have some leisure time, or even just some time resting at home."

For almost two years, the Liberal National party’s strategy for government in Queensland has been to stay well clear of issues that risk burning through political capital.
On Wednesday, one of the most tentative conservative governments in recent history announced plans for sweeping and controversial changes to workplace laws.
In doing so, the LNP risks placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire.
The proposals would give the increasingly influential deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, the power to break strikes by public sector workers in certain circumstances, including if it is deemed “in the public interest”.
The government will also make it more difficult for public servants, including emergency services workers, to claim compensation for psychological injuries. Under the proposed laws, workers with such claims will only be entitled to support if they can show their workplace was the primary cause.
Law firm Slater and Gordon said the changes would make it harder for Queenslanders to access support for psychological injuries. The United Workers Union, which represents paramedics and some healthcare workers, said the changes were “an underhanded attack on Queensland ambulance officers and other hospital staff”.
Several business groups welcomed the changes.
The opposition leader, Steven Miles, said on Thursday morning the proposals were a “Newman-era attack on workers”, and the only thing surprising about that statement was that it took so long (roughly 14 hours) for the spectre of Campbell Newman’s government to, once again, loom over Queensland politics.
The collapse of the Newman government explains almost everything about the current one. The premier, David Crisafulli, and Bleijie had front-row seats for the “crash through” tactics that quickly turned voters off Newman, including proposals to sack public sector workers, and led to mass protests.
The lessons since have been that most suburban voters are uncomfortable with the LNP putting ideology on show. And so it went to the 2024 election – and won comfortably – talking mainly about crime and keeping all those vote-losing positions on things like abortion and budget cuts off the table.
Approaching the midway point of the term, the LNP has finally decided to show its teeth.
There are readers who will, understandably, take issue with the idea that the Crisafulli government has been “tentative” or has been, up to this point, unthreatening.
It has been unapologetic in attacking Indigenous representation within government, trans healthcare, and suppressing pro-Palestine protests.
These moves have been underpinned by a simple calculation: that the issues are marginal for most suburban and regional voters, whose concerns are mostly the cost of living and crime.
Those who care about evidence-based policy, human rights and civil liberties have every right to be furious. The polls suggest that fury hasn’t gone mainstream, and that suburban voters are OK with the government punching down, so long as it doesn’t affect them.
Workplace reforms affect them. If nothing else, those survivors of the Newman government who still sit in the cabinet room will have learned a lesson that in Queensland, the public sector (which employs more than 320,000 people) is a powerful political bloc in its own right.
The morning after announcing the changes, Bleijie seemed only too aware of the scale of the coming fight.
“You’re going to see a mammoth campaign by the Labor party,” he told reporters at a press conference at Newstead.
“It’s going to be a lot of mistruths and misinformation, and I think everything they will be able to say … we will be able to debunk with facts.”
The Crisafulli government remains comfortably ahead in the relatively few public polls, a recent snapshot in Brisbane Times seemed to show Labor in Queensland had taken the biggest hit from the rise in support for One Nation.
But the bright orange cloud is still looming. And a simple look around the country reveals that in modern times, whether policy is decided by ideology or focus group, there’s no guarantee political capital will last.
Better use that capital while you can. Even if it means, as it will for the Queensland LNP, picking a fight with many of the suburban middle-class voters who put the party into office.
- Ben Smee is Queensland state correspondent

- The claim that Ukrainian strikes on Russian bot farms caused right-wing or MAGA social media activity to decrease is unproven.
- On Oct. 12, after the Russian technology giant Yandex reported that drone strikes damaged its servers in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had seen "less hate, less division, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots" online after the strikes.
- However, Snopes found no credible evidence that Ukrainian strikes on Yandex servers starting on Oct. 8 took Russian propaganda bots offline. Social media posts that attributed changes in online activity on certain topics such as MAGA, the far-right German political party Alternative für Deutschland or various health-related topics failed to directly connect those changes to Russian bots.
- Zelenskyy's office reportedly told the BBC on Oct. 13 that he was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity when he made the remarks about the effect of Ukrainian strikes.
- Darren Linvill, an expert on the effects of foreign information manipulation and interference, told Snopes that Ukraine's strikes had likely mainly affected legitimate, automated Yandex traffic rather than propaganda operations, which Russia often runs from overseas.
In early October, a claim (archived) circulated that Ukrainian strikes on Russian bot farms caused right-wing or MAGA social media activity to decrease.
Yandex, a Russian technology giant that provides search engine, email and cloud services and facilitates payments, ride hailing and food deliveries, confirmed on Telegram and to local media that drone strikes damaged its servers in Sasovo, Kaluga (archived) and Vladimir from Oct. 7 to 11. Work to restore services affected by the strikes continued on Oct. 13.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Oct. 12 that Ukraine had struck "Yandex data centers" and that "a lot of people" had seen fewer Russian bots on social media platforms as a result.
The Facebook page Occupy Democrats, which spread the claim about the consequences of Ukrainian strikes against Russian bots, wrote:
Zelenskyy might just have saved our democracy. The genius is brilliantly bombing Russian data centers linked to FAKE NEWS pro-MAGA bot farms in Moscow. Without them, Putin's midterm influence will accidentally fall from a 30th floor window.
MAGA, an acronym for Make America Great Again, is a political movement supportive of U.S. President Donald Trump. The U.S. has previously accused Russia of using "bot farms" to create false social media accounts that spread disinformation in the U.S.
On Oct. 11, Tomáš Zdechovský, a member of the European Parliament, shared data (archived) he claimed showed a drastic decrease in online activity around Germany's far-right Alternative für Deutschland political party in the days following the strikes. Other social media users claimed searches for various health-related topics (archived) and the number of social media accounts advocating for Alberta to seek independence from Canada (archived) also fell after Ukraine's strikes.
Whether Ukrainian strikes on Yandex servers had indeed taken Russian bots that spread propaganda or misinformation offline was unproven at the time of this writing. As we will lay out below, social media users claiming a direct connection between Ukraine's strikes and falling web traffic generated by Russian propaganda bots tended to identify correlation rather than causation.
Darren Linvill, who studies the tactics, strategies, and impacts of foreign information manipulations and interference at Clemson University, told Snopes via email on Oct. 13 that the Russian propaganda campaigns he studies do not use physical infrastructure within Russia for their efforts, meaning they would be unaffected by Ukraine's strikes. Linvill, along with U.S. and international media, also said that a lot of the traffic that was affected by the strikes was likely legitimate, automated traffic, such as web crawlers that index Yandex's search engine.
Data from the global internet infrastructure company Cloudflare shared by some accounts (archived, archived) as proof of Russian "bot traffic" decreasing after Ukraine's strikes showed graphs accounting for all automated traffic, not propaganda bot accounts specifically. Linvill described measuring a drop only in Russian propaganda bot accounts as "exceedingly difficult."
Lacking credible proof that Ukrainian strikes on Yandex servers starting on Oct. 8 took Russian propaganda bots offline, we leave this claim unrated.
On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy's office appeared to redefine his statement from the previous day that there was "less hate, less division, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots" online after Ukraine's strikes. The office reportedly told the BBC that Zelenskyy was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity.
Snopes has contacted Zelenskyy's office to verify this statement to the BBC.
Parsing the 'evidence' of falling Russian bot activity
Some social media users shared data from the global internet infrastructure company Cloudflare that they suggested showed that Russian bot traffic "dropped to nearly zero" after Ukraine's strikes.
The data in question, called "Bot vs. Human Traffic," tracked HTTP requests, which are messages that a client (this could be a browser or a mobile app) sends to a server. Cloudflare assesses HTTP requests a given client sends and scores them according to whether it thinks a human or a bot sent the request.
Cloudflare's data showed that HTTP requests from Yandex bots dropped on Oct. 8 and again on Oct. 10, dipping to 0.3% of maximum levels. Bot requests had been at 88.2% of maximum levels the week before. Cloudflare's data also showed that almost all (99.6%) of the HTTP requests sent by Yandex clients were automated, which Cloudflare described as being from bots.
It is important to note that "bot" in Cloudflare's terminology is not just propaganda bots but any requests that the company classifies as automated. The technology publication Mashable and Euronews reported that Yandex's automated traffic likely included web crawlers, which are tools that search engines use to keep their database of websites up to date. Mashable reported that damage to a Yandex's data centers or servers would bring traffic such as web crawlers to a halt.
Linvill also credited the fall in "bot" traffic from Yandex to legitimate, automated traffic such as web crawlers not operating from damaged servers. He wrote that Cloudflare's data did not suggest there was "a particular reason to believe the strikes would have a significant impact on social bot activity from Russia."
Other claims about a decrease in Russian bot traffic failed to directly connect Russian bots to any perceived changes in online activity. For example, Zdechovský's post presented a graph with no source that did not specify what it measured. Another post that claimed a decrease in Google searches for various health-related topics compared data across only two weekends, which was unlikely to be enough to establish and analyze a trend.
An account that claimed accounts calling for Alberta to seek independence from Canada "fell off the face of the earth" after Ukraine's strikes provided no supporting evidence for the claim that linked it to Russian propaganda bots.
We contacted Zdechovský to ask for the source of his graph and await a reply.
Russian propaganda campaigns hard to track
According to Linvill, actually documenting a fall in Russian propaganda bot activity would not be straightforward. He wrote:
It would be exceedingly difficult to measure. You would first have to figure out what it was, exactly, you were measuring? There is no one path to influence and no one way malign propaganda is conducted. These efforts are run on global systems across a multitude of platforms and emanating from multiple actors even within the same country. They make it hard on purpose.
Linvill added that the Russian campaigns he followed did not use bots they ran themselves, instead paying for services run from outside Russia. He wrote: "It has clearly become important for Russia to outsource these services than to run them in house. It's likely cheaper and easier, but also more secure and decentralized."
In sum, readers should be cautious of blanket claims that Ukraine's strikes on Yandex's servers heavily affected Russia's propaganda operation. While that may be the case, there was no credible evidence at the time of this writing directly linking strikes on servers to a fall in Russian propaganda activity online. Linvall suggested that Russian propaganda campaigns could come from overseas, meaning domestic strikes would not be effective against them, a point that Mashable's reporting also made.
For further reading, Snopes previously published a guide to spotting bots on social media.

10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర సవరణ (SIR)లో జరిగిన అవకతవకల కారణంగా, ఇష్టానుసారంగా ఓటర్లను తొలగించారని ఆరోపిస్తూ, ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ కాక్రోచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద నిరసనను నిర్వహించింది. ఈ ప్రదర్శనలకు ప్రతిస్పందనగా, అధికారులు రాజధాని అంతటా భద్రతా చర్యలు చేపట్టారు. డజన్ల కొద్దీ మెట్రో స్టేషన్లను మూసివేశారు, రైళ్లను రద్దు చేసి నిషేధాజ్ఞలను అమలు చేశారు. పోలీసులు అరవింద్ కేజ్రీవాల్, పినరయి విజయన్, మమతా బెనర్జీ వంటి రాజకీయ ప్రముఖులతో పాటు, CJP వ్యవస్థాపకుడు అభిజీత్ దీప్కేతో సహా వేలాది మందిని అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు, అయితే వారిని తరువాత విడుదల చేశారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, పోలీసు నిర్బంధాల మధ్య ఢిల్లీకి పెద్ద ఎత్తున నిరసనకారులు చేరుకున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో బాగా ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద కాక్రోచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) చేపట్టిన నిరసనను చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియో అస్సాంలోని తిన్సుకియా నగరంలో జరిగిన మహాలయ సంబరాలకు సంబంధించినది. దీనితో 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనలకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, అవే దృశ్యాలతో ఉన్న మరిన్ని వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) లభించాయి. వాటి ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియో అస్సాంలోని టిన్సుకియా నగరంలో 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న జరిగిన మహాలయ ఉత్సవాలకు సంబంధించినదని తెలిసింది. వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపించే దృశ్యాలను, ఈ ఉత్సవానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియోలతో పోల్చి చూడగా, ఇది టిన్సుకియాలో జరిగిన మహాలయ ఉత్సవానిదేనని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
అలాగే, గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ ద్వారా పరిశీలించగా, ఈ వీడియోను అస్సాంలోని టిన్సుకియా నగరంలో ఉన్న ఠాణా చరియాలి ప్రాంతంలో చిత్రీకరించినట్లు నిర్ధారించవచ్చు. దీన్ని బట్టి, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోకు ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనలతో ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదని చెప్పవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, అక్టోబర్ 10న జరిగిన CJP నిరసన దృశ్యాలంటూ అస్సాంకి చెందిన వీడియోను తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

On paper, Alejandro González Iñárritu's new movie had all the trappings of a hit.
The Oscar-winning director had assembled a star-studded cast led by the inimitable Tom Cruise. He had a twisty and surprising script that uses satire to tackle ambitious topics, and a talented team that built set pieces impressive enough to match.
But he was still nervous about the execution.
"The acting tone was the most scary part for me," Iñárritu told Business Insider shortly before the movie's opening weekend. "Tone, you cannot write — you have to feel it and hear it."
Four days later, the verdict at the box office came in: "Digger" was a bomb. The climate-change satire starring Cruise, John Goodman, Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg, Jesse Plemons, and Emma D'Arcy made $8 million in its opening weekend on a reported $180 million budget, making it the lowest opening weekend for Cruise in 19 years. The movie is projected to bring in only $50 million worldwide by the end of its theatrical run.
To add insult to injury, film critics, who helped make his previous work like "The Revenant" and "Birdman" Oscar darlings, lambasted Iñárritu for even attempting something as grandiose and ambitious as "Digger."
The Hollywood Reporter called it "so meta that you watch in excruciating weariness as it disappears up its own ass." IndieWire described it as "so detached from human truth that its most believable character is a one-eyed animatronic cat."
The movie currently holds a 53% critic rating on Rotten Tomatoes, the lowest for Iñárritu and lowest for Cruise in close to a decade.
Not everyone disliked the movie. Anne Hathaway, Mandy Patinkin, Jane Fonda, and Iñárritu's close friend Guillermo del Toro all shared positive reactions on social media after the movie opened. "Love the arts FUCK the charts," del Toro wrote on X.
The movie has proved divisive in part thanks to its plot twists, the basics of which we'll reveal here. (Stop reading now if you don't want spoilers!)
"Digger" follows oil tycoon Digger Rockwell (Cruise), who learns one of his wells in the Arctic has exploded and a chunk of a glacier is racing towards Europe to wreak havoc. But about a half hour into the movie, it's revealed that the saga of Digger Rockwell is actually a stage play. Rockwell is being played by an actor named Curtis Markson in a satirical stage production titled "Fossil Fools."
At the movie's end, there's another twist: "Fossil Fools" is based on actual events that happened years prior. There really was a Digger Rockwell, and one of his wells did explode, causing an environmental catastrophe that changed mankind. Markson is performing the play in of an audience living decades after those events occurred, and the world is still paying the price.
See more in this series
It's an ambitious attempt by Iñárritu to deliver commentary on climate change while stretching the audience's capacity for nonlinear storytelling. Whether it was successful or not depends on whom you ask. But if Iñárritu has learned anything from making "Digger," he said it's that "satire is a motherfucker."
For the latest interview in Business Insider's Director's Chair series, Iñárritu spoke about traveling to the Arctic, choosing the movie's ending, and the unique way he worked with Tom Cruise to develop the script.
On reading the script to Tom Cruise 'like an 8-year-old' and what 'Digger' is really about
Business Insider: You have said the idea for this movie came to you ten years ago. What was that idea, and how did it evolve?
Alejandro González Iñárritu: I can tell you it started when we ended the shooting of "The Revenant." We struggled with a lot of weather — dramatic changes at the locations where we were shooting in parts of Canada. Things were happening, weather-wise, that had never happened before.
A one-degree difference in the climate, people don't understand what that means. You say, "Well, the planet is 1.5 degrees hotter," and people go, "Who cares?" That's the difference between water and ice, and we experienced that dramatically. It was surprising. We were shooting ice in the summer.
So Sabina Berman, my writing partner, and I, started thinking. The Arctic was melting. The powerful people were excited because, with the ice receding, there were suddenly more channels to transport more materials. The absurdity in that was the beginning of this, the narrative madness.
I would think the next step is: How am I going to tell this story using my own brand of creativity?
I think as a storyteller it's our duty to try to say or express a story in the most original way possible. The original title on the script was "Blah, Blah, Blah," and that's what this story is about. It's about the most scary weapon that all human beings have: the tongue. That's the weapon. We didn't want to tell a story about climate change, or about politics. I hope this story transcends politics. We wanted to talk about the human nature of the blah, blah, blah.
The result of the blah, blah is no one is listening to each other. The movie's brutal final few minutes show the result: a dystopian world.
Language is a tool. It's a bridge to bring a common reality. But it's also a weapon to destroy. Once an idea comes — an ideology, a religion, whatever — suddenly the reality that is experienced by the body, not our abstract thought, becomes almost a reality. I think it's one of the traps that we are now in as a society.
Then you need someone as big and as brash as the Digger Rockwell character to take us on that journey, right? Did you need to cast someone at Tom Cruise's level to accomplish this movie?
Let's start even before that. Before the casting, I realized that nobody cares about an abstract thought or reflection. Perception has become reality, and for the last nine years, the reality seems to be secondary to the stories people are telling us. They want us to believe things for a reason. But nobody cares what I think.
So I realized the only way to explore this phenomenon is we need a character. It can't be a political commentary or a "Saturday Night Live" sketch. We need a strong character to navigate the story truthfully.
Once I had that, I knew I needed an incredible actor who can sustain this weight on his shoulders and deliver it with candor, not preaching, and someone who's very American, because we are all Digger, in my opinion. The conclusion was that there are not many who can play this, but Tom was it. But will he accept? He was very brave and was never scared.
You didn't send him the script; you read it to him. In that unique experience, could you tell while reading that you had him hooked?
He asked me to do that, read it to him.
Had an actor ever asked you before to read the script to them?
Never. But I have to say, I thank him because it was useful for him. He said he needed that, to hear it. He didn't want to come in with his own perceptions; he wanted my years of knowledge that I put into the material. That surprised me.
But he was like a kid; he'd react with worry and excitement throughout the telling, like, "What's going to happen!" [Laughs.] I felt like I was reading the story to an 8-year-old. It was fantastic, the curiosity.
Did you read it with a Digger Rockwell voice? Or act bombastic when the president spoke?
You are exactly right. I'm a terrible actor, but I knew where we were going. So I would play a little bit with the pauses, the power. I was trying to point him to where I was thinking. And between lines, I would explain to him how I thought I would shoot a sequence and why, for him to have some images.
On struggling to figure out the movie's tone and doing rewrites
Are you a filmmaker who thinks of the visual before the dialogue?
It's both ways. Like a song, sometimes you have the lyrics first, and sometimes it's the melody that's first. In this case, when I read it to Tom, by that time, I had so many images. The universe of "Digger" was already built in my head. We were building sets in Canada in 2019.
Doing that reading to Tom helped me so much because it was the first time, after years of writing, hearing those words out loud. And things changed. It helped me with things that worked and things that didn't work.
You gave us breadcrumbs to follow before the big reveal of what the movie really is, right? The cat's head almost coming off its body at the start of the movie, Riz Ahmed's character, Dr. Ganesh, coming in from a door that seems to lead nowhere.
Yes. You are on the money. The corridor we discussed because I said, "No, theater is like that." That was one of the most difficult aspects, because I had to be thinking in two channels: One, a director of theater, Hannah (Sophie Wilde), and one as the film director.
The decisions as Hannah were sometimes challenging as a film director because I had to shoot in three walls, with all the limitations, trying to take advantage of the gags and the theater play. But the most difficult thing was the tone of the theater play.
The theater play is a satire; she wants black satire. The projection of the voice, you have to talk very strongly; in cinema you can whisper. So every lens for the theater scenes was wide — I wanted to see the feet, hands, which normally in film and TV shows you have close-ups. I wanted to show the whole concept.
And then the scenes that are off set, that's when you go in tight with the lens.
Exactly. I changed the language. The sound design, the palette, everything changes. There are two realities.
With the visuals I did in advance, everything was pre-staged; I knew the camera angles. It was very prepared for the VistaVision because it was expensive. But when the actors arrived, we were rehearsing and rehearsing. Sometimes the scenes were super funny and I was cracking up. But then I'd watch the dailies the next day and I said, "This is crap."
So we would return to the rehearsals. We would do it, I'd watch the dailies and realize, "This is too naturalistic, this is not a comedy." So to find the speed and the tone of the first 30 minutes was the most challenging thing for you to believe that it's a film, but that there's something off. But then when the reveal happens, it isn't a trick; it plays like a theatrical production. I wanted to be honest. That was the scariest.
It seems your actors felt that uncertainty as well. Michael Stuhlbarg told me that the whole cast discovered what they were actually making through the rehearsal.
The tone. And then I had to rewrite scenes to do the right tone. I was lucky to be editing at the same time, because we had a hiatus.
In the hiatus, I rewrote the whole long table scene completely. Because it was not working, it was too much. It didn't have the dramatic tension that it needed, despite it being a satire.
It was a luxury to be able to be moving the pieces, to change things around, but you need an amazing cast to do all that. John Goodman, Jesse Plemons, Riz Ahmed, Michael Stuhlbarg, all of them, I felt like I had a great jazz band. I was obsessed with the rhythm. We found the tone together. It was a joy but it was scary. We couldn't find it for a while.
On finding the movie's ending and feeling like he was writing a documentary
Speaking of rhythm, was it a challenge in the edit to find the right moment where you have the tree fall and the giant hand coming in to fix it, basically revealing what we'd been watching was an illusion?
Every shot in the film was pre-designed, pre-lit. We built huge walls of fabric in Pinewood Studios, and with a little camera I staged every single scene with stand-ins, reading the words, measuring the timing of the words, measuring every height of the windows, the light direction; I storyboarded. There's nothing in any frame that is incidental. It was all preconceived.
I wanted to give the audience a lot of context. To have all the reasons why these guys were the way they were, because of the world they inhabit. I wanted people to feel lost in the frames, in the windows. That was decided. But again, the challenge was the tone to match it all.
What I found fascinating, going back to the star power, is how you end with Tom Cruise in "Digger." In "Birdman," Michael Keaton has his big closing moment at the end of the movie. Leonardo DiCaprio is alone in the wilderness in the final frame of "The Revenant." Cruise is very much part of the ensemble at the end of this movie. He's among his cast mates celebrating the end of the show, and then you take us to what's happening outside of the theater. There's no big final shot for Tom. Was that always the intention?
It always was like that. Always.
When you do a film like this, reality and fiction do not stay still, and the last nine years have moved so fast.
So if you made this movie a few years earlier, it would have a completely different ending?
It would have been another movie. It was the same story: Greed, power, the stories we tell ourselves; we have never spoken so much and heard so little. But the approach was all the disasters were going to be shot in real locations in water tanks, but we changed all that and put it on TV screens and iPads — framed reality. To show that we are so certain in our opinions that we are lost in our stories.
At a moment, honestly, I felt lost. How can I tell this story? It's so complex. I felt like I was writing a documentary. What the fuck is this?
So the pandemic happened, I made "Bardo," and as time passed, "Digger" collapsed two times. It was very traumatic. I lost three years of my life, lost pre-production. I traveled to the Arctic twice. I interviewed every single scientist available. Everything Ganesh says is exactly what could happen. This is science-based, this movie.
So reality wasn't enough for me in the film. It's the crossroads of reality and imagination. But there was a time that the more we stretched our imagination, it would become reality! [Laughs.] When we started this movie, no ice shelf had been detached; we thought that was a huge stretch of reality. That was crazy to imagine. Now, Greenland is in the conversation.
That's where the people coming together to see a play comes from. I was on this walking holiday with my family, and suddenly I saw these glaciers melting. That's when I realized that only by separating from the representation of reality is it more real. We see reality through a representation; we get together, and we can separate ourselves from what we see. That's the key.
Are you concerned because of the political climate that we're in, and your own concerns about getting the story right, that this film will get sucked into a vortex of noisy commentary?
Absolutely. Because nobody cares about it because we hear about it all the time. The news is satire. Everything is performative, Jason. The commentary will end up matching what's in the movie.
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
"Digger" is in theaters now.

Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta, both of which declined to back new legislation.
The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants.
“The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework. The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.”
OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon was more cautious but still supportive, backing a statutory framework and an international convention. Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. “We don’t think basing everything on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is a good long-term plan,” he said.
However, their rivals would not follow. Asked directly whether he supported a statutory framework, Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta’s Rob Sherman pointed to Britain’s existing regulators, telling MPs they were “not writing on a blank page.”
The hearing exposed an existing divide on the subject of regulation, putting the conflicting approaches of AI leaders on the British parliamentary record. Exposing this divide in a second jurisdiction was the point, according to select committee chair Liam Byrne. The committee set out “to light up the wide differences in opinions between some of the wealthiest firms on Earth,” he told WIRED after the hearing, and to show “that you couldn’t rely on voluntary self-regulation.”
While the four executives gave evidence to the committee on AI safety, only a few hundred meters away, Britain’s security service director issued a warning about the dangers of AI.
MI5 director Ken McCallum used his annual threat update to warn of bioweapon misuse as a significant threat from AI. “Not yet realized, but the misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight, is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” McCallum said.
Responding to this comment, Byrne told WIRED: “The fact that the head of MI5 is warning about incredibly dangerous capability uplifts for bioterrorists in one part of Whitehall, and then in another part of Whitehall the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office is basically admitting that our regulatory regime for AI is voluntary, tells you everything you need to know.”
In the final part of the evidence session, civil servants conceded to the committee how little the current system compels. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) tests frontier models before release, but only when companies choose to hand them over.
Henry de Zoete, director of AISI, acknowledged that the institute was entirely reliant on the cooperation of the companies and foreign governments in order to gain access. Cat Little, the top civil servant at the Cabinet Office, which houses AISI, was pressed on whether the whole regime was voluntary. “At the moment, yes, it is,” she said.
When asked what would happen if AISI judged a model to be too dangerous, but it was released by a company anyway, de Zoete acknowledged AISI had no ability to prevent them from doing so.
“What we’re not doing is kite marking,” de Zoete said, using the British term for a safety certification. “We’re not saying yes or no to any sort of model.” He added: “These companies are either American or Chinese who are building at the frontier … There’s only so much we, as the UK, can do in that kind of context.”
The frontier executives also made plain that British access runs through Washington. “We provide our models predeployment to CAISI,” OpenAI’s Duff Gordon said, referring to AISI’s US counterpart. “We will continue to provide our models pre-deployment to AISI in the UK … and as long as we’re able to do that under the US government, we will continue to do it.”
The tension of the existing arrangement was made clear to British officials by Anthropic’s Booth-Smith. “We unfortunately were not able to provide full unrestricted access to [Mythos 5.1] to UK AISI at that time ... That’s a question for the US government,” he said before adding that AISI now had access.
The session also heard from four former lab researchers, among them ex-OpenAI staffer Daniel Kokotajlo. “I don’t think the companies can be trusted to self-regulate,” he told MPs. Steven Adler, who left OpenAI in late 2024, said he was “not confident in the safety culture across the industry.” Geoffrey Irving said the labs believe they are locked in a race that governments will not interrupt and that they cannot leave. “Both of those are false,” he said. “They could just stop.”
Following the hearing Byrne told WIRED that his committee would now dedicate a lot of time examining the UK’s path forward as a middle power on AI. He wants ministers to use Britain’s coming G20 presidency, alongside South Korea, which follows it in the chair, to broker an international convention that does not depend on the current White House. “The G20 presidency will outlive the US presidency of Trump,” he said.
“The risks,” he added, “are multiplying faster than our safety regime can control.”

Some key voters say deep frustration and disappointment with President Trump are motivating their election plans just weeks before Election Day.
NPR observed two online focus groups Tuesday night with 12 Georgians who voted for President Biden in 2020 and then supported Trump in 2024.
Almost every voter — 11 out of 12 — said they were disappointed with the overall job Trump has been doing. And 10 said they regret voting for him.
"I've been disappointed," said Charles P., 43, who identified as a Democrat. (The voters participated under the condition their last names would not be used.)
"I just don't feel like there's any positive to this administration at all," he continued. "Inflation has only gotten worse, there've been more wars. The tariffs haven't done anything. It seems like we have more enemies now than ever. I just don't see anything positive with his tenure."
Richard A., a 56-year-old Republican, said he's been out of work for 10 months and there is a long list of problems he sees with the direction of the country under Trump.
"Food crisis, starting the war with Iran, inflation," he said. "ICE immigration has just torn families apart, has caused deaths. ... It just seems like everything has gone downhill."
The comments align with Trump's faltering approval rating and a darkening midterm outlook for Republicans. Trump has picked up his campaign travel in recent days, touting his record and arguing for the GOP to retain control in Washington.
These focus groups with swing voters are conducted every month in battleground states across the country. They are run by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting. NPR partners with them each month as part of the Swing Voter Project.
Focus groups are not scientifically significant like polls, but they do provide insight into what voters are thinking. And in this case, they provide some insight into how voters are deciding who they are supporting this fall.
Swinging to Democrats
Rich Thau, president of Engagious, moderates these focus groups. He said for the first time this year, a majority of swing voters said Trump was going to influence their midterm decisions.
"In previous months, when we asked people whether President Trump would influence how they vote, they would say things like, 'Well, I'm looking mainly at the candidates themselves,' or 'I'm looking at the overall sort of environment in the country,'" Thau said.
"This month, seven out of 12 said that he would influence them to vote for Democrats. And that was new."
Karla S., a 49-year-old Democrat, was one of those seven.
"I did vote Republican for 2024," she said. "I made up my mind. I've been so disappointed that I'm just going to go straight and just do Democrat, Democrat, Democrat. Because I'm so disappointed with how this administration has been doing."
Cedric, a 41-year-old independent, said he won't be voting for any politicians that are closely aligned with Trump.
"I think we're not going in the right direction, so I don't want to vote for a candidate that's not going to stand up to him or they're going to go along with his policies," he said. "I'm looking for something different."
Ten out of the 12 participants said they plan on voting for Georgia incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Some voters said they wanted to keep him in office specifically because he wouldn't be aligned with Trump.
Restoring order
Thau said some voters felt that if Democrats take control of Congress, it could provide some needed stability to the country — and the economy, in particular.
"There was some sense that Democrats could restore some semblance of order, and that they'd be able to control a bit of what the president is trying to do or has been doing, to the point where that might restore some of their confidence in the economy," he said.
That's what Thomas M., a 65-year-old independent voter, said is his expectation of a Democratic-run Congress.
"I think there would be more controls placed on Trump with people who are not afraid to stand up to him," he said.
In contrast, if Republicans retain power, Thau said "some respondents told us they thought that the president would have even more control over what goes on because Republicans are afraid to stand up to him."
Jennifer W., a 43-year-old Republican, said she worries "Trump would have free rein."

A Republican super PAC, not the Republican National Committee, paid for the ad. A spokesperson for the super PAC, Defending Main Street Superpac, said media vendor Cross Screen Media had made the mistake. We await confirmation from the vendor and its parent company.
In October 2026, a rumor spread that Republicans had inadvertently paid for a campaign ad targeting Troy Jackson, Maine's Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate and incumbent Susan Collins' opponent, to air in Portland, Oregon, instead of Portland, Maine.
Posts multiplied on social media making the claim, including on Facebook and X. One X post by the betting platform Polymarket said "Anti-Troy Jackson ads intended for Maine voters are reportedly appearing in Oregon, sparking speculation that advertisers confused Portland, Maine, with Portland, Oregon" (archived):
The post included maps of the states of Oregon, on the West Coast, and Maine, on the East Coast.
The claim is true, although some social media users were imprecise about who paid for the ads, saying it was "the GOP" or "Republicans" as a whole. A review of Google's Ads Transparency Center revealed the anti-Jackson ad, paid for by Republican super PAC Defending Main Street Superpac Inc, aired not only in Portland, Oregon, but also Washington state, between Oct. 8 and Oct. 12.
A spokesperson for Defending Main Street Superpac acknowledged the mistake in an email to Snopes, saying it had originated with the super PAC's media vendor, Cross Screen Media, whose parent company is 1903 Group.
"During a recent independent expenditure, our media vendor mistakenly placed approximately $25,000 in digital advertising in the Portland, Oregon, media market instead of Portland, Maine," the email read. The spokesperson added Cross Screen Media was refunding the ad buy.
We reached out both to Cross Screen Media and to 1903 Group to confirm and we will update this report should we receive a response.
Ad buys and social media chatter
The ad in question attacked Jackson for seeking to raise taxes in Maine:
The super PAC is an independent political advocacy group that supports Collins, who is seeking her sixth term in the Senate (she was first elected in 1996). Collins' campaign had no say in the ad's content, nor where it aired. Polls revealed that Collins and Jackson were in a tight race.
Data from Google's Ads Transparency Center showed that the ad ran in Oregon for four days and was seen between 1 million and 1.25 million times there. The buyer spent between $15,000 ad $20,000. The ad also ran in the state of Washington during that time, and cost between $5,000 and $6,000, for 350,000 and 400,000 views.
"The error was identified, the ads were immediately stopped and corrected, and the vendor is refunding Defending Main Street the full amount of the misplaced spend. No donor funds will be lost as a result of the vendor's error," the super PAC's spokesperson told Snopes in the email.
Meanwhile, internet chatter indicated that people in Oregon had seen the anti-Jackson ad. On Oct. 11, an account on X named Lillian Belle, whose bio reads "Obsessed with Oregon Politics. Ask me about Oregon and the Judiciary," said (archived) "I've gotten 5 anti-Troy Jackson ads in the last 24 hours. I choose to believe they mixed up Portlands."
Someone responded to this post, saying (archived) "Ive gotten so many this week," to which Belle responded "Interesting that it's not just me."
Asked if the ads were "digital or cable," Belle said (archived) "Digital which isn't that precise but still a lol [laugh out loud]"
For further reading, Snopes has covered several rumors about the 2026 U.S. elections, including a false claim that voting ballots are disqualified with poll workers mark them.

The death of a laboratory worker in Siberia on October 2, 2026, and the subsequent quarantine of dozens of people have sparked concerns about a pneumonic plague epidemic, with Russia revealing little information publicly. The incident has revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations that the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab.
What happened at the Siberia lab?
The 28-year-old woman, Darya Shipilova, employed at a research institute in Siberia, fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people and dispatch the head of Russia’s health watchdog to the Irkutsk region.
The woman worked at the anti-plague research institute in the city of Irkutsk, where the plague occurs naturally in wild animals. She died at a hospital in nearby Shelekhov that the mayor said had been placed under quarantine. Following the incident, top Russian health officials have travelled to the region.
Russian authorities say the lab worker died of what initially presented as a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection.
Russia dismisses epidemic concerns
Meanwhile, Russia’s health regulator insists there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after the plague institute worker’s death.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on October 7 that it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic.
No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, it said, while adding that 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.
When asked about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution against using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
‘Causative agent behind death not known’
A top official with the World Health Organisation (WHO) said it doesn’t know how the lab worker in Siberia died. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the UN health agency doesn’t know what the “causative agent’ was behind the woman’s October 2 death.
She has urged Russia to provide more information about the incident that prompted global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague. The WHO initially said it estimated the risk of the Russia case to the public as low, but told a press conference on October 7 it could not make a fuller risk assessment due to insufficient information from the Russian authorities.
What is pneumonic plague, symptoms
Reports blamed the woman’s death on pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
Pneumonic plague causes a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time. The severe disease is less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages.
Pneumonic plague and bubonic plague are caused by the same bacteria. The former is spread by respiratory particles while the latter is spread through bites from fleas that have jumped from infected rodents.
Symptoms of pneumonic plague include shortness of breath and coughing-up blood, and they can occur in as little as 24 hours after exposure, according to the WHO. If untreated, the illness can be fatal.
Not linked to a biological weapon
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday (October 8) that the death of the Russian plague laboratory worker did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon.
Mr. Trump said Russia insisted it had the situation under control, but added that not much information was coming out. He, however, said that the United States will help Russia over the incident.
The European Union has also called on Russia to “share timely and transparent reporting” about the death of the plague laboratory technician.

Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'
Documentarian talks about going after the richest man in the world
Alex Gibney's nearly four-hour, fire-and-brimstone documentary Musk — about tech oligarch and the world's richest man Elon Musk — is not uplifting. Instead, it is one of the most depressing and terrifying pieces of public media since An Inconvenient Truth alerted a largely unaware public to its imminent annihilation by climate change.
Unlike An Inconvenient Truth, Gibney's Musk does not appear to offer a hopeful final message about how we might get out of this mess. Instead, we get an outline of how, in Gibney's view, Musk rose from upstart entrepreneur to political arriviste who orchestrated the dismantling of USAID, then attempted to create a baby farm and commune to survive a supposed civil war. That is all before, we are to believe, he supposedly upended all of Western democracy.
Sitting for an interview this September ahead of the film's showing at the Toronto International Film Festival, Gibney was not too surprised by the dour perception: he had spent the previous few days fielding defamation lawsuit threats from a similarly unhappy Musk, after all. That is along with Musk's descriptions of Gibney as "a shill for the far left," "horrible human" and, simply, a "douche."
Gibney also acknowledged the foreboding length: it was only after they finished their original two-hour feature that Musk allied himself with U.S. President Donald Trump. At that point, he said, HBO executives told Gibney they needed to expand the work, using it as a "building block for a much more epic drama … For this figure, who has so much influence on the future of the planet, it's deserving of that three hours and 45 minutes."
That relationship proved fraught on its own. The film hits North American theatres Oct. 16, but — at the time of the interview — Gibney was nervous. The international rights-holder, Universal, hadn't confirmed whether it would even distribute the film outside North America, given the potential of political pressure.
At the same time, he said Paramount's acquisition of HBO parent company Warner — with Paramount controlled by the Trump-friendly David Ellison — had him "concerned in the back of [his] mind" that the documentary's streaming release could be scuppered entirely.
Since that interview, Gibney has said international theatrical release plans are now being discussed; the documentary is slated for an early 2027 streaming release, though no specific date has been given. When, or if, audiences do see it, he hopes the reception isn't quite so bleak.
"It's not a funeral; it's a warning. But things are pretty dark. We're going to be lowered into the earth if we're not careful," the director said, even while recognizing the sheer inescapability of dread his film tends to elicit. "You know, and the film ends with the planet Earth exploding and Musk escaping on his spaceship. So that's about as pessimistic as it gets."
A question of objectivity
Though he started the project as an avowed Musk fan — a Tesla solar panel system-owner and all — by the time he began working on it in earnest, he says, any benefit of the doubt he had extended to his subject had evaporated. When he reached out to interview Musk himself, he said he was stonewalled.
Director Alex Gibney poses for portrait photographs for the film Musk during the 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival in Venice, Italy, in September 2026. (Scott A Garfitt/Invision/The Associated Press)
Outreach to those around Musk was similarly stymied: close business associates uniformly refused to speak without his permission. The workaround was to instead give Musk a voice of his own.
An AI-avatar, using Musk's own statements, narrates much of the documentary. Much of what it says, like the real Musk's statements about the "hit piece" Gibney came out with, is overtly critical of the documentary's framing.
The result is a somewhat bifurcated, but overwhelmingly negative picture of a man Gibney asserts is at the centre of modern politics' downfall.
There is the charting of Musk's early history as a self-described "founder" at Paypal and Tesla — including interviews ranging from journalists covering him at the time to his former wife, Justine Musk — that characterize his public persona as an engineer and genius as little more than a PR-crafted lie.
"There is a kind of generalised notion in modern societies that if you're rich, you must be very smart — you must be a genius," Gibney says, sharing the central thesis of the documentary. "But maybe you're just ruthless. And maybe you can be very rich and very powerful — and also, to some extent, unhinged."
And then there is Musk's time at the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and, in Gibney's telling, his role as an architect of the dismantling of the U.S. federal government.
