The film includes accusations from former MAGA influencer Ashley St. Clair, the mother to one of Musk's children, who speaks about cryptic text messages Musk sent her ahead of the 2024 U.S. presidential election that saw Trump re-elected — messages that include references to an "anomaly in the Matrix" created by "ten thousand lasers in space."
Gibney then asks her whether she thinks that was a reference to SpaceX satellites. She responds: "I don't know where else he has lasers."
"I should point out that the remarks about the 'anomaly in the Matrix' and lasers from space didn't come from a critic of Musk. It didn't come from me; they came from Elon Musk himself," Gibney said.
That is despite a letter sent to Gibney's Jigsaw Productions, claiming the exchange reinforces a disproven conspiracy theory that Musk used his internet provider, Starlink, to interfere with voting machines in swing states.
"That seems a legitimate thing to put in a film," Gibney said. "I don't say in the film that's what he did. I say that's been said."
Similarly when pressed, Gibney defended the decision of including an AI-generated avatar in a documentary critical of an AI proponent: "We used some AI tools, but they're being used by — they're guided by human hands," he said. He explained that the idea was for it to serve as a sort of "agent provocateur" that foments a negative reaction to AI proliferation by forcing audiences to witness it.
When asked whether he hopes or theorizes that the film could affect people's votes ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterms, he has a simple response: "I do."
Because to Gibney, Musk's accumulation of power isn't just a failure on Musk's part. When "a reckless tech billionaire takes effective control of the federal government, and attempts to destroy it for personal aggrandisement," he says, Americans themselves bear responsibility.
"We did. We let him take it, because we didn't demand that our representatives hold him to account," he said.
"You know, 'Oh, I like my Tesla, so he must be a good guy.' Well, you may like your Tesla, but what if he's not a good guy, right?"

The F1 pit stop that helped save lives
- Published
When the McLaren pit crew refuelled a car, changed its tyres and relayed information to their driver in less than seven seconds at the Spanish Grand Prix in 2001, they were just doing their jobs.
But 700 miles away in the break room at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), Dr Martin Elliott and his colleagues were watching after completing a life-saving operation on a young child.
The brief glimpse would change how the doctors approached patient care. From surgery-to-ICU handovers and neonatal care to air-ambulance response times, F1's innovations have made an impact far beyond the track.
At Ferrari's factory in Maranello, the medical team studied how pit crews organised roles, communication and handovers.
Doctors and nurses started each procedure with a checklist, setting out specific roles and tasks. This reduced human error and helped ensure key tasks were completed. All patient data was also shared from the operating theatre to the care unit.
Gaps in performance were identified and addressed, while repeated rehearsals helped refine the process.
As a result, the process from surgery to intensive care became more organised, and a 2007 study by researchers at GOSH and the University of Oxford found the F1-inspired handover process reduced technical errors, information omissions and handover time.
Reflecting on the project, Dr Elliott, then a consultant paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon at GOSH, said: "The environment we were working in then and in many ways still do is fundamentally potentially dangerous at every step.
"And of course, fundamentally, that's how F1 doesn't make mistakes. They have created an environment of complete precision, not only in engineering, but also in process, because they simply can't afford financially or from a race perspective to slip up.
"It's the same, you know, the precious parcel on the trolley is the same as the precious parcel in the car. You have to get all of those steps right."
The model was later adopted by other healthcare teams.
From trackside to bedside
Fifteen years ago, Williams worked with the University Hospital of Wales to improve neonatal resuscitation.
Former Williams human performance specialist Gemma Fisher recognised that the organisation of pit-crew equipment to prevent delay could also be applied in a hospital setting.
Video analysis unveiled the chaotic reality of medical emergencies with overlapping voices and misplaced equipment.
Standardising roles - deciding who stood where, who needed to be heard at what moment and where equipment was stationed - allowed for a faster, more efficient response.
Debriefings allowed medical staff to review what had happened and identify what could be improved for future emergencies.
The changes also encouraged junior doctors to raise concerns without fear of blame.
The collaboration extended beyond working practices and into engineering. Advanced Healthcare Technology and Williams have since developed the Babypod: a carbon fibre carrier designed to withstand a 20G crash, which can help prevent injury in the transportation of babies from ambulance to hospital.
Every second counts
F1 continues to find new ways to apply its expertise in emergency medicine.
At this year's race at Silverstone, a collaboration with Air Ambulance Cornwall showed how response times could be improved, with take-off time reduced from five minutes to three and a half.
This was achieved using many of the same methods, including quick and organised starts, having equipment ready for use and clear communication across the team.
David Richards, chairman of Motorsport UK and former team principal of BAR and Benetton, said: "You might not see one and a half minutes in the overall scheme of things, but one and a half minutes when you're lying by the side of the road or you've fallen off a horse or you've fallen down a cliff and you've hurt yourself, those minutes must seem like years for the person who's injured."
Richards said the partnership would continue to look for ways to reduce response times further.
Twenty-five years after Dr Elliott first saw a pit stop that inspired a new way of thinking, lessons from the sport continue to influence healthcare, from neonatal treatment to emergency response.

The Union Health Ministry has asked all States and Union Territories to ensure the prominent display of rates charged for services and facilities offered by clinical establishments.
In a move aimed at strengthening transparency, accountability and patient-centric healthcare delivery, Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava, in a letter to the Chief Secretaries of all States and Union Territories, called for compliance with regulatory provisions, and ensuring information on service charges was clearly visible to patients and their attendants.
“Display of rates would help patients and their families understand the likely cost of treatment, make informed healthcare decisions, and plan their medical expenditure,’’ Ms. Srivastava said, adding that greater transparency would also help minimise avoidable confusion and billing-related disputes.
The letter refers to the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 and the Clinical Establishments (Central Government) Rules, 2012.
Under the Rules, clinical establishments in States and Union Territories where the Act is applicable are required to display the rates charged for each type of service provided, along with facilities available, at a conspicuous place, in the local language as well as in English.
Since health is a State subject, in States and Union Territories where clinical establishments are regulated by their own respective frameworks, several of which also contain provisions relating to the display of rates, the Health Secretary has called upon Chief Secretaries to ensure effective compliance.
The letter also places particular emphasis on transparency in healthcare pricing for international patients.
States and UTs have been requested to encourage the prominent display, wherever applicable, of package rates offered to foreign patients travelling to India on medical or Ayush visas.
“This would enable international patients to make informed choices, help minimise pricing and billing-related grievances and further strengthen India’s position as a trusted destination for medical and Ayush care,’’ the Ministry said.

(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
Time and time again as we celebrate achievements in health care, a measurable pinnacle of which could be the Nobel for Physiology/ Medicine, a sobering dose indicating the power of pathogen is delivered to us. This time, with the reported case of all things, the plague, in Russia. This week we discovered that the entire issue is mired in mystery, with not much information being shared by the nation. What was clear during the COVI-19 pandemic was the absolute criticality of sharing information globally, but with every squeak about the break out of infectious disease. In fact the Pandemic Agreement includes an aspect of Pathogen Sharing and Benefits among member nations. However, practically, sometimes nations find it difficult to easily share information with the global community.
Initially, the WHO cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. A WHOOfficial said the global organisation doesn’t know exactly how lab worker in Russia died in plague case. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the agency doesn’t know the “causative agent” behind the woman’s October 2 death, and urged Russia to share more information. The EU also urged Russia to be ‘transparent’ on plague reports - The Hindu
On its part, in tersely-worded statements, Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, does not link the case to pneumonic plague, maintaining that “extensive” testing found no evidence the lab worker’s illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Russia earlier said she died of pneumonia — a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection — and its health authorities have found no cases of plague recently. Moscow also denied sanitary measures over plague reports.
For an idea of what we actually know for sure now, do read this explainer: Pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia?
In addition, there was a fresh scare from Ebola-affected Africa: Kenya confirms first Ebola case imported from Congo after patient dies in Nairobi. Why is this significant? I explain here: Ebola death recorded in Kenya after victim travelled from DRC. The victim had been living in DRC for years, and was reportedly already ill before he took a road trip, and then, a flight back home to Nigeria. He was admitted to a hospital in Nigeria by a relative, but succumbed to his illness. This is the first case of an Ebola death that has occurred in a country, outside of the DRC and Uganda, during the outbreak raising significant concern regarding transmissibility for public health authorities. Kenyan authorities have called for stricter controls at the airports and also undertaken efforts to spread awareness and urge citizens to test if they notice symptoms. While the WHO has not issued a travel ban to the affected countries, self declaration by travellers has become mandatory at all international ports.
The past week also saw some hectic health-related activity in India. The most significant among them was easily the Supreme Court calling for a cap on trade margin for all essential medicines and medical products, as Aaratrika Bhaumik reported. As the government declared that it had proposed a 30% trade-margin cap on patented and non-patented cancer medicines, but top court asks why a margin cap cannot be extended to all medicines and medical products; the court says the government has to ensure that DPCO-approved medicines, whose price is legally regulated, reach patients. That is jumping the gun though, first read Bindu Shajan Perappadan’s article: Centre to cap trade margins on non-scheduled cancer drugs to 30% of MRP.
She also reported on the Centre’s direction to the States toDisplay rates of healthcare services prominently. Clearly visible display will enable patients to take informed decisions, build trust, prevent billing-related disputes; the Health Ministry also urged clinical establishments to display package rates for international patients visiting India on medical and Ayush visas. Another significant decision taken in the country last week: NMC brings doctors’ digital patient acquisition under ethics rules. In regulatory terms, the Centre proposing tighter curbs on advertising of prescription drugs was also a development of note.
Moving on to mental health issues, Afshan Yasmeen reported a NIMHANS study that found loneliness linked to psychological distress, excessive series watching among parents of children who had emigrated.The study examined 64 ‘empty-nest’ parents aged between 45 and 65, whose adult children had emigrated and lived away from home for at least two years.
Athira Elssa Johnson wrote on Treatment-resistant depression and what happens when antidepressants do not work, while Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula took us through Dental anxiety, particularly important, because here, fear becomes a barrier to care.
Looking at the Indian health care system and the larger stage, Rajendra Pratap Gupta argues that to retain and grow its advantage, India needs a smarter healthcare margin policy, explaining the role of MRP in the sale of drugs and health care consumables. A lesson or two here for India’s drug price regulators, surely.

Iowa, Nebraska and six other states are suing OpenAI for endangering children
The lawsuits cover everything from the design of ChatGPT to the company's recent issues with rogue agents.
In a coordinated effort, eight states have filed lawsuits against OpenAI alleging the company has violated state-level consumer protection laws and endangered children. As Reuters first reported, Attorneys General from Iowa, Nebraska, Kansas, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana each filed in their respective state courts, but with the shared goals of changing how OpenAI develops its models and advertises their capabilities, and forcing the company to pay for the harm it's allegedly caused.
The lawsuits claim OpenAI is misleading customers about the safety of its AI products, not just in their capacity to provide incorrect information or potentially enable users to harm themselves and others, but also because AI agents themselves are capable of breaking the law. For example, both Iowa and Nebraska cite OpenAI's now multiple instances of rogue agent behavior, including the Hugging Face hack. They also point to instances of ChatGPT allegedly enabling a teen's death by suicide and the chatbot providing incorrect medical information that led to a user's overdose, incidents that have also led to separate wrongful death suits against the company. Some states also take issue with OpenAI retaining data from underage users.
Engadget has asked OpenAI to comment on the state lawsuits. We'll update this article if we hear back.
The desired remedies for OpenAI's behavior vary from state to state due to the patchwork nature of consumer protection and child protection laws in the US. Outside of financial penalties, the states want OpenAI to clearly disclose the risks of its products, stop practices the states consider deceptive and comply with existing laws. Some states, like Arkansas, are also asking the court to halt "testing of advanced AI models until adequate safeguards are implemented."
OpenAI has rolled out a series of parental controls and child protection features to try to address some of the most immediate risks posed by its chatbot. It also backed the Kids Online Safety Act, a bill that, if made law, could introduce several mandatory design changes to the company's products. The company's efforts to address the potential for its AI to break rules and "escape containment" have been harder to pin down, though. OpenAI announced it would slow the development of its frontier models in August to ensure their safety and the company signed on to a voluntary safety pact with other AI companies organized by the White House in September. It's not clear if either of these changes have actually made the company's AI development process safer.

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

Mumbai: Bollywood actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood actor Aamir Khan, has been issued a notice by the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO), Mumbai, directing him to leave India on or before October 28, 2026, following his participation in a protest at August Kranti Maidan demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
FRRO invokes immigration law provisions
The notice, dated October 14, was issued under the provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025. It states that Imran Khan Pal, a United States national, has allegedly contravened provisions of the Act and the rules and orders framed under it.
Invoking Section 7(2)(c), read with Section 29 of the Act, the FRRO has directed him not to remain in India and to depart from the country by the stipulated deadline. The notice also warns that non-compliance could lead to prosecution under the relevant provisions of the Act.
Participation in Mumbai protest
Imran Khan had participated in a protest at Mumbai’s August Kranti Maidan in solidarity with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). The protesters were demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
On October 10, Imran Khan was detained by Mumbai Police along with several other protesters. His partner, actor Lekha Washington, and cousin Zayne Marie Khan were also present at the protest. All three were subsequently released.

OCI status and legal implications
Imran Khan is a US citizen and holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card. However, OCI status does not confer Indian citizenship and is subject to the applicable provisions of law. The notice issued by the FRRO has also been marked to the Commissioner of Police, Mumbai.

The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine is expected to begin in the Democratic Republic of Congo by the end of October, World Health Organization experts said Tuesday.
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,000-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,000.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the outbreak.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will go through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
"We have got strong reassurances that... it should be starting before the end of this month," said Anthony Scott, chair of the WHO's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunisation (SAGE).
The group said insights that Ervebo might offer cross-protection against Bundibugyo were no match for evidence from standardised vaccine trials.
The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC -- a single trial framework that can test the efficiency of multiple vaccines -- should also eventually incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are moving through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Need for data
The Tumaini trial "will generate urgently-needed data on the efficacy of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease, and will help formulate the policy decisions we need", Scott told a press conference.
"In addition, we welcome the accelerated development of vaccines that are specifically targeting Bundibugyo.
"They're both progressing rapidly through early clinical development."
SAGE said it was deeply concerned about the ongoing challenges in controlling the Ebola outbreak.
"The key elements here are insecurity and population displacement, and they're hindering access to care, disrupting surveillance, and delaying critical research, including, from our perspective, research on vaccine trials," said Scott.
Kate O'Brien, director of the WHO's immunisation department, said a WHO technical advisory group would be meeting to review evidence from the small-scale trials of the Oxford and Moderna candidate vaccines.
She suggested the Oxford jab could drop into the broader Tumaini trial fairly swiftly -- as doses are ready to roll -- if the safety and the immunogenicity data from the first trial is "positive and reassuring".
Therefore "everything is lined up for at least two products to be moving quickly", she said.
The medical charity Doctors Without Borders is conducting a data-gathering study -- not a full clinical trial -- of Ervebo's effectiveness in frontline health workers in DRC provinces hard-hit by the Bundibugyo outbreak, with the jab being offered to volunteers as an interim measure.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

- GTA 6 will officially qualify for nominations at The Game Awards 2026 after meeting the eligibility cutoff.
- The eligibility rules state that games must be "commercially available" before or on November 20, 2026, to qualify for nominations.
- Rockstar’s November 19 release date makes GTA 6 eligible for both Players’ Voice and other categories.
Good news for GTA 6 fans: Rockstar’s upcoming title is officially eligible for GOTY at The Game Awards 2026, as a new official FAQ revealed the nomination eligibility cutoff date for November 20, 2026, just a day after its November 19 release. This contradicts earlier rumors that said GTA 6 wouldn’t qualify for GOTY at this year’s Game Awards.
The official Game Awards 2026 FAQ & Rules say that “Games must be made commercially available to customers on or before Friday, November 20, 2026, at 9 p.m. PT.”
The rules also reveal that games released on or before November 30 will qualify for the Players’ Voice category, meaning GTA 6 will compete in this fan-voted category as well as other categories like GOTY.
The surprising part is that The Game Awards hasn’t made any exceptions to accommodate GTA, as the eligibility cutoff date for The Game Awards 2025 was November 21, 2025. So, Rockstar got extremely lucky with the release date, since it’s going to be commercially available a day before November 20.
Last year, Clair Obsur: Expedition 33 swept The Game Awards 2025, taking home GOTY, and this year it feels like GTA 6 will carry the mantle. However, this doesn’t mean there aren’t other excellent games vying for Game of the Year.
It’s been an incredible year for gaming, and titles like Resident Evil Requiem and 007 First Light will likely compete for nominations at this year’s The Game Awards. However, with GTA 6 now eligible for the GOTY award, the winner for this year seems locked in already.
Nintendo is also releasing The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake on November 5, 2026, so if there’s a true competition at this year’s Game Awards, it’s between that and GTA 6. Otherwise, most players probably expect GTA 6 to claim the coveted metal trophy.
That said, do you think GTA 6 will win GOTY at The Game Awards 2026, as it’s eligible for the nomination cutoff? Tell us in the comments section below.

When markets turn unsettled, daily price movements can dominate the economic conversation. Foreign selling becomes a verdict on the country, a weaker currency feeds doubts, and individual disappointments become evidence of a wider problem. These signals deserve attention. But judging India’s prospects also requires examining what businesses, borrowers and investors with longer horizons are doing.
Two recent developments provide that perspective. The government has approved a Fairfax subsidiary as strategic buyer for the proposed sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank for approximately ₹52,878 crore. Separately, Blackstone’s Jon Gray has outlined an ambition to increase the firm's India investments from about $50 billion to $100 billion over five years. These represent substantial confidence in India’s future.
Having worked closely with Prem Watsa and Fairfax, I have seen their willingness to support businesses through difficult periods. Their experience also teaches caution. Transforming a smaller private-sector bank in southern India has required years of investment in technology, diversification and scale. An investment in a leading PVC producer has faced setbacks too. Patient capital needs sound execution, realistic expectations, and a willingness to correct course.
Quick answers to key questions
The proposed ₹52,878 crore purchase of a 60.72% stake signals that a major foreign investor is willing to take a long-term position in India’s banking sector. It also reflects the government’s willingness to give private capital a larger role.
The article points to India’s growth prospects, favourable demographics, rising household investment and stronger corporate and banking balance sheets. These factors may create opportunities when market prices fall more than business fundamentals justify.
Monthly SIP contributions reached a record ₹32,490 crore in September, showing continued participation by domestic savers despite market weakness. These recurring investments deepen markets and broaden the domestic investor base.
Investors should consider valuation, earnings and currency risks, as well as global interest rates. The article also highlights challenges from a deficient monsoon, inflation, expensive oil and India’s need for capital inflows to help finance its current account deficit.
The article argues that removing LTCG tax on genuinely long-term equity investment could attract patient capital, and that extending relief to domestic investors could support household wealth creation. It presents this as a policy view, not a confirmed change.
Portfolio investors deserve a fair hearing. Their selling can reflect concerns about valuations, earnings, currency risk and global interest rates. The extraordinary investment in AI infrastructure is also competing for global capital. This helps explain the environment in which allocations are changing, although it cannot explain every outflow from India. When reallocations depress prices beyond what business fundamentals justify, they create opportunities for discerning long-term investors. Experienced investors are recognizing that possibility.
India offers a compelling foundation. Its growth is faster than that of the other large economies: real GDP expanded 7.8% in April–June, and the IMF projects 7% growth for FY27. Its favourable demographics add depth to the opportunity. A large working-age population can sustain production, consumption and savings for years, provided education, skills and employment keep pace.
Indian households are demonstrating their own confidence. Monthly mutual fund SIP contributions reached a record ₹32,490 crore in September, despite market weakness. These recurring savings reflect a growing willingness to participate in the country’s corporate future. They also deepen markets and provide a broader domestic investor base.
That matters to overseas investors. Confidence to enter a market depends partly on confidence that an orderly exit will be possible. Blackstone's Gray has highlighted the strength of India’s public markets and listing opportunities. Alongside liquidity, India offers a vibrant democracy, an independent judiciary and established legal protections. Faster dispute resolution and more consistent enforcement would make those institutional advantages stronger still.
The financial foundation has improved too. Crisil estimates that median corporate gearing roughly halved over the past decade to around 0.5 times by March 2026. Banks’ gross NPAs stood at 1.68% in June, with a robust capital adequacy of 17.78%. Healthier borrowers and lenders give expansion a firmer foundation. Icra also reports healthy repayment performance in rated secured retail securitization pools, although unsecured segments require scrutiny.
Public investment reinforces this strength. Central government capital expenditure reached approximately ₹5.10 lakh crore during April-August. Better transport, power and digital connectivity generate demand while improving productivity and widening markets for businesses.
There are a few significant challenges. A deficient monsoon threatens farm incomes and food prices. September retail inflation reached 5.54%, while expensive oil affects household budgets and business costs. The Reserve Bank of India’s October rate increase demonstrates vigilance. Policy must provide calibrated support to growth without losing sight of inflation.
Oil dependence also creates a recurring external financing challenge. Services exports and remittances offset much of the merchandise trade deficit, but India generally runs a current account deficit. The gap requires net capital inflows or a drawdown of reserves.
Special FCNR deposit schemes can mobilize foreign currency quickly, while limits on banks’ open forex positions can help manage instability. These measures have their place, but deposits mature and restrictions cannot create a lasting supply of foreign exchange. Sustained equity and debt investment must help finance greater productive capacity and more jobs.
India should, therefore, offer investors a dependable welcome through predictable taxation, timely approvals and straightforward entry and exit. Foreign capital complements domestic savings by expanding financing and sharing risk. Our competition for internationally mobile capital comes from other investment destinations. Attracting it on sensible terms can improve prosperity for Indians.
Tax exemptions for eligible foreign investors in government securities are an encouraging first step. The larger opportunity lies in equities. The finance minister’s openness to hearing investor views on LTCG taxation is welcome.
Removing LTCG tax on genuinely long-term equity investment could attract patient capital. Extending relief to domestic investors would avoid apparent discrimination and support household wealth creation. In my view, the resulting expansion in investment, businesses and taxable economic activity could more than offset the initial revenue loss over time.
Domestic savers and experienced global investors are expressing confidence through their actions. India should build on that confidence with policies that attract durable capital and turn it into productive businesses, better jobs and higher living standards.
Nirmal Jain is founder of the IIFL Group

Turkey and Azerbaijan have long called themselves "one nation, two states". Now, a row over the hijab (headscarf) is testing that bond. Experts have pointed out that while the headscarf controversy is the immediate trigger, Azerbaijan’s ties with Israel could be a deeper source of tension. The controversy has also brought to the fore a deeper geopolitical fault line in the relationship between Ankara and Baku. Videos purportedly showing girls wearing headscarves being denied entry to educational institutions have been widely shared on social media. Mint could not independently verify the authenticity of these videos. The two countries have long described their relationship as "one nation, two states". However, Azerbaijan's restrictions on religious dress in public schools have drawn criticism from Turkish political figures and prompted a sharp response from Azerbaijan's ruling party, which has defended the country's right to determine its domestic policies. While the controversy centres on religious dress and secular education, analysts say the implications extend beyond the immediate dispute. Azerbaijan's strategic relationship with Israel, at a time when Turkey's ties with Israel have deteriorated, could present a more significant challenge to Ankara-Baku relations. In an analysis published on September 29 by the Turan Research Center, titled "The Hijab and the Secular State in the Turkic World", Joseph Epstein argued that Azerbaijan's headscarf restrictions raise broader questions about sovereignty over religious life, national identity and the role of the secular state. Epstein noted that Azerbaijan's approach reflects a wider pattern among several post-Soviet states, where governments have sought to keep religious dress out of public schools while presenting secular education as central to a shared national identity. He argued that the dispute also highlights the limits of Turkey's influence over Azerbaijan. Although the countries share close cultural and strategic ties, Baku has maintained a distinct approach to secularism and has resisted external pressure over its domestic policies. Epstein also pointed to the criticism Azerbaijan's ties with Israel have attracted in Turkish media since the Gaza war, adding another dimension to the tensions between the two countries. Professor Muddassir Quamar, Associate Professor, Jawaharlal Nehru University and an expert on West Asian affairs, while talking to Mint said the hijab controversy was primarily a cultural and religious issue concerning the imposition of dress codes on women. Despite protests and statements in Turkey, he said, the dispute was unlikely to have a serious impact on bilateral strategic relations. The differences over Israel, however, could pose a bigger challenge. Azerbaijan has developed close defence and strategic ties with both Israel and Turkey, while Turkey's relations with Israel have deteriorated, Quamar said. This divergence could become a more difficult issue for Ankara and Baku to manage as their regional priorities evolve. The distinction is important: the hijab dispute may have brought the tensions into public view, but it does not necessarily explain the deeper strategic differences between the two countries. The challenges extend beyond Israel. Quamar identified the US-Israel war on Iran and its implications for the South Caucasus as another factor that could complicate bilateral relations. "There are several regional and geopolitical factors that might pose challenge including the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran and how it impacts the situation in the South Caucuses, as well as Turkish ambitions in Central Asia and the South Caucuses region, and its attempted outreach to Armenia to improve relations and access in the neighbourhood. However primarily, the differences in approach to Israel might pose the most difficult challenge for Turkey-Azerbaijan relations today," Quamar said. The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners.
The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person.
Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation.
The Israeli government closed the UK consulate last week in protest, forcing the it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government.
The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it.
Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement.
The proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications.
A new urgent procedure will allow ministers to mirror designations already made by the EU, US, Canada or Australia for up to 112 days while a specific separate UK case is prepared.
The new global sanctions regime will come into force on Thursday but will need endorsement by MPs and peers within 28 days.
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is pushing through the measures at speed because the Israeli government has vowed to press ahead with an E1 settlement containing 1,234 homes in the West Bank – a development that many observers say would sever a contiguous, viable Palestinian state, so making the so-called two-state solution to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict near impossible.
The E1 bids close on 19 October but the Israel Land Authority has confirmed that the tender box will not be opened, nor the bids considered, before 19 November, which is after the Israeli election on 27 October.
The British Palestinian Project said the Israeli deferral “does not remove the need to deter commitments being made now, since bidders and their backers commit on 19 October, contracts could still be signed before a new Israeli government is formed”.
The project welcomed the addition of the right to liberty and security of person in the new laws, saying it opens a route to sanctions for serious arbitrary or unlawful detention, including of Palestinian children, and of those responsible for or enabling it. Save the Children estimated in November 2023 that 10,000 Palestinian children had passed through Israeli military detention over the preceding 20 years.
A UN 2026 report on children and armed conflict verified that 981 Palestinian children were detained by Israeli forces in 2025 and 180 of them remained in administrative detention without charge or trial at the year’s end.
The UK has already applied sanctions designations for restrictions on humanitarian aid in Sudan and South Sudan but this is the first time this general power is being applied as part of a new worldwide regime including Israel.
Refusing permits or blocking convoys will be sufficient grounds to apply sanctions, without requiring the obstruction to constitute a formal breach of international humanitarian law – thereby lowering the threshold for action.
Separate work is under way by UK officials in conjunction with European partners on how to outlaw British trade with unlawful Israeli settlements.

People with longCOVID, where symptoms persist after recovery from an acute Covid-19 infection, may have distinct differences in the mix of bacteria living in their mouths and lungs, research has shown.
The differences in the lung microbiome are linked to respiratory symptoms, as well as the cognitive and digestive problems known to occur in longCOVID, researchers said.
The findings, published in the European Respiratory Journal, may contribute towards understanding why some people develop long COVID and point to new ways to treat the condition, they said.
"Prior studies have shown some changes in the gut microbiome with long COVID, but Covid is a lung disease and so it makes sense to look to see if the lung microbiome is changed in long COVID," lead author Daniela Alferes de Lima Headley from the University of Dundee, UK, said.
"We know that millions of people worldwide are still affected by long COVID and its cause is still unknown. Long Covid affects multiple organs. The microbiome is important to maintain health throughout the body, so it is a strong candidate for something that may contribute to long COVID," she said.
The study examined 771 people treated for Covid-19 at one of 38 UK hospitals between February 2020 and March 2021.
The participants were divided into four groups based on how bad their symptoms were five months after being discharged from hospital, ranging from 'very severe' with serious physical, mental, and cognitive impairments to 'mild', with few symptoms and good recovery.
Six months after hospital discharge, samples were collected from patients' mouths through saliva and from their lungs through sputum. DNA sequencing was used to identify the microbes present.
By analysing the variety and quantities of microbes and comparing them with patients' symptoms, researchers found that people with very severe long COVID had marked differences in their oral and lung microbiomes compared with those who did not have severe long COVID.
The results also revealed differences linked to specific symptoms, including reduced lung function, in which the lungs cannot hold as much air as normal or air cannot flow in and out as easily.
The researchers also found differences in the mouth and lungs microbiome between people with varying neurocognitive symptoms -- including 'brain fog', difficulties with memory, attention and concentration -- and gut symptoms, including pain, nausea, diarrhoea and loss of appetite.
Among the changes associated with long-COVID symptoms, was an over-abundance of bacteria that produce lactic acid, which was also linked to signs of inflammation found in samples of patients' blood.
Lead researcher James Chalmers, chair of respiratory research at the University of Dundee, UK, said, "People who had the worst symptoms five to six months after COVID infection had big changes in the microbiome in their mouth and lungs."
"We also found that changes in the airway microbiome were linked not just to lung problems, but also to symptoms like brain fog and gut symptoms, suggesting the lung microbiome could have effects on health more broadly," he said.

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?
- Published
Imagine a world where Manchester City had not used "sham contracts" to build a team capable of winning three Premier League titles, one FA Cup and three EFL Cups.
If City were the winners, then there had to be losers.
Not just those teams who finished runners-up or lost cup finals.
The potential impact runs much deeper and includes missed Champions League qualification, relegation and Premier League prize money.
Thirty-five other teams played in the English top flight between 2009 and 2018.
And every one could in some way claim to have been left financially out of pocket.
City, of course, continue to deny any wrongdoing and they have appealed. But as it stands they are guilty of all charges related to inflating their sponsorship income to the tune of £830m, plus another £90m in expenses.
Strip that money out and it changes the whole complexion of the competition.
BBC Sport has crunched the numbers to assess the potential financial impact on the top flight.
How the figures are worked out
When Sheikh Mansour bought Manchester City in 2008 they were far removed from the club you see today.
Since finishing fifth in 1991-92, the last season before the formation of the Premier League, City's highest placing had been eighth in 2004-05.
The Abu Dhabi money poured in via what the Premier League's independent commission described as a "disguised funding scheme". It took the club's sponsorship revenues from being on a par with Stoke City in 2008-09 to eventually overtaking those of Manchester United.
City finished fifth in 2009-10. Since then, not once have they finished outside the top four in the Premier League.
Did this money deny other clubs a place in the competition, and other kinds of success?
This article is not trying to set out how much compensation a team might be able to claim.
Nor is it saying any one team would definitely have avoided relegation or reached the Champions League.
It is about chance, the possibility that a very different City team would have taken to the field without the hundreds of millions pumped in by the club's Abu Dhabi owners.
It has not considered potential future earnings from success, including sponsors' bonuses and further prize money.
Nor has it factored in players who may feel they have missed out on salary increases, or triggered payments, for how their club might have performed.
This is purely about domestic impact:
- Lost prize money by league placing
- Missed potential Champions League earnings
- Europa League payments
- Loss of Premier League status
- Impact of cup final defeats
- What Manchester's 'super-profit' deal with City owners has paid out so far 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Were any current Man City players signed during charges period? 
  - Published3 hours ago
How City gained £1.17bn, and others may have lost £844m
The full impact of City's behaviour on other clubs could be calculated at £844m.
- £188.2m in Premier League placing money
- £349.7m in relegation costs
- £217.8m in missed Champions League prize money
- £88.3m related to domestic cup competitions and the Europa League
We calculated these figures by taking published prize money from the relevant seasons.
For Premier League place money, each team that finished below City is considered to have potentially missed a payment for one place.
For relegation, this is the minimum value of being in the Premier League for the next season, minus the received parachute payment.
For the Champions League, we took City's earnings from the following seasons and deducted the impacted teams' Europa League prize money.
But City also earned prize money themselves during this period.
Across the competitions, City were paid £1.17bn:
- £812.3m from the Premier League - total income from prize money and broadcast revenues
- £363.4m via the Champions League
- £900,000 from the FA Cup victory
- £300,000 from the three EFL Cup victories
The most impacted: How Spurs could have missed out on £120m
"We have lived through a period of deception," former Tottenham Hotspur boss Mauricio Pochettino said last month.
"No type of punishment will make it possible to repair what was done."
You can see his point. Spurs finished one place outside the Champions League positions in four (although one only was under Pochettino) of the eight seasons in which City qualified for Europe's elite competition.
BBC Sport took City's earnings from the Champions League in the following season, and deducted Tottenham's Europa League prize money.
Over the four seasons Spurs missed out, Manchester City earned £148.2m from the Champions League, with Tottenham taking £29.9m from the Europa League.
The 2014-15 campaign led to the biggest deficit, as City finished second in the Premier League and Tottenham came fifth. City received £71.2m for reaching the Champions League semi-finals in the following season, but Spurs were only paid £17.7m from the Europa League - a difference of £53.5m.
Spurs also finished behind City in the Premier League table six times, with the cumulative prize money difference worth £6.6m.
The north Londoners did benefit in the 2013-14 season, as they only qualified for Europe because City beat Sunderland in the final of the EFL Cup.
Spurs gained £5.1m from their 2014-15 Europa League campaign which would not have been possible without City's success.
Taking into account all competitions, that produced a net financial loss for Spurs of £119.9m.
Did City's EFL Cup win cost Liverpool £37.8m?
The 2015-16 EFL Cup final proved to be decisive for Liverpool's hopes of European football.
Jurgen Klopp's men lost to City on penalties following a 1-1 draw. The Europa League place transferred to the league, and went to West Ham United.
Liverpool only finished eighth, which was not enough to qualify for Europe.
Had Liverpool won the final, they would have entered the Europa League, and this provides a key financial comparison.
Manchester United won the Europa League in 2016-17, receiving prize money of £37.8m. As part of that amount, the Red Devils' market pool payment, which is based upon the value of the television rights, was £26.6m.
While we cannot say for certain that Liverpool would have won the Europa League, they were a club of similar stature to Manchester United, which provides a comparison.
The market pool share may also have been slightly lower with both Liverpool and Manchester United involved.
Together with Premier League place money of £10.6m - Liverpool finished below City in all nine relevant seasons - the total financial impact on the Merseyside club was £52.3m.
As for the FA Cup, City won it just once in the period they were scrutinised over, beating Stoke in 2010-11. The difference in prize money was £900,000, with the runners-up going into the Europa League.
Everton were denied Europe five times
Everton missed out on the Champions League once, in 2013-14, and on four other occasions they finished one place below the final Europa League spot.
The Champions League place is calculated to be worth £32.6m - the £39m earned by Manchester City minus the Toffees' £6.4m winnings from the Europa League they competed in instead.
The combined impact on missing out on the Europa League four times is £23.2m.
Add on the £10.6m from Premier League prize money, and the total financial effect is £66.4m - making Everton the third-most impacted club.
Did two relegations cost Hull City £99m?
While parachute payments provide something of a cushion, relegation from the Premier League is still a considerable financial hit.
Could the teams who finished in 18th place, one spot from safety, argue that they might have stayed up but for City?
There are a couple of ways of looking at this.
Firstly, the results against City who took at least four points off every 18th-placed team other than Birmingham.
Secondly, the mere fact that City were able to assemble a squad far better than their finances should have allowed. Could they otherwise have been involved in relegation battles?
Again, this is not to say City would have been relegated. It is about chance.
BBC Sport has taken the total prize money earned by the team finishing in 20th in the following season. That suggests a minimum return for having stayed in the top flight.
Deducted from that is the first season of parachute payments to give a net amount.
Hull were relegated twice in the period, costing the Tigers £93.78m.
The Tigers finished below City in the table four times, adding £5.2m in place money to the sum.
It leaves the East Yorkshire club as the second-most impacted on £99m.
Swansea are fourth in the table with £63.1m. Of that total, £54m is from relegation and £9.1m in place money from the seven seasons the Swans were in the top flight.
Newcastle suffered relegation by finishing 18th in 2015-16, costing them a projected £60.4m, of which £7.9m was place money.
Norwich (£43.8m), Wigan (£39.6m), Burnley (£31.1m), Bolton (£26.4m) and Birmingham (£25.1m) also suffered relegations in 18th place.
The loss of Champions League money
Alongside Tottenham, four other teams missed out on Champions League football by one place across the eight seasons when City qualified.
The biggest impact was on Chelsea, who finished fifth in 2017-18.
City earned £79.2m from reaching the quarter-finals of the Champions League, with Chelsea getting £39.4m from winning the Europa League. That left Chelsea with a deficit of £39.8m.
Also just missing out on the Champions League were Everton (5th in 2013-14, £32.6m deficit), and Arsenal (5th in 2016-17, £22.1m deficit).
The only team not to experience much of a financial impact were Manchester United, who were fifth in 2015-16.
City got no further than the round of 16 in the Champions League, earning £42.6m, while United won the Europa League that season, receiving £37.8m. It left the Red Devils with a deficit of £4.8m.
The cumulative cost of league places
In the Premier League there is no specific prize pot for being crowned champions.
Broadcast revenue is allocated on a merit basis by final league position.
It is a 1+1 system, so the club in 20th get the base payment. Then the team in 19th get the base payment two times. For 18th, it is that base amount three times, and so on.
It means that the only financial difference, in prize money at least, for the team finishing runners-up in one of Manchester City's three title-winning seasons is one base payment.
Could any team claim they might have finished one place higher?
The value of a Premier League place rose sharply in line with the broadcast deals over the period of City's offences.
In 2010-11 it was £755,881 per place, and by 2016-17 it was up to £1.94m.
If any compensation were to be considered, Everton, Liverpool and Stoke City would have the biggest claim of £10.7m, having finished below City in all nine seasons.
West Brom and West Ham's total is £9.9m, with Swansea on £9.1m.
At the other end of the scale are the seven clubs who spent one season in the Premier League, including Blackpool (£756,756), Portsmouth (£800,424) and Huddersfield (£1.93m).
